title: ZigBee: ZigBee Network Key Recovered via Join Intercept
description: Network encryption key intercepted during device join event, enabling full traffic decryption and authenticated injection. The ZigBee trust center transmitted the network key using the default or known Trust Center Link Key (TCLK), allowing passive interception of the key transport frame. An attacker with this key can decrypt all past captured traffic and inject authenticated ZCL commands.
remediation: Rotate network key immediately. Enable network key rotation policy. Ensure TCLK is unique per installation. Disable join window except during planned commissioning. Deploy ZigBee 3.0 with improved key transport protections.
impact: An attacker could exploit this to gain full system compromise, execute arbitrary code, or obtain complete unauthorized access to sensitive data and systems. Network-level vulnerabilities may allow traffic interception, lateral movement, or unauthorized service access.
remediation_brief: Restrict network access using firewalls and segmentation. Disable unnecessary services and protocols. Implement network monitoring.

title: ZigBee: Default Trust Center Link Key (TCLK) in Use
description: ZigBeeAlliance09 well-known TCLK is in use. Any attacker within RF range can decrypt the key transport frame sent during device join, recover the active network key, and then decrypt all network traffic or inject authenticated commands. This well-known key is published in the ZigBee specification and is widely available.
remediation: Configure a unique, device-specific TCLK for all join operations. Disable open join window. Migrate to ZigBee 3.0 which mandates unique install codes per device. Audit all devices that joined using the default TCLK and rotate the network key.
impact: An attacker could leverage this to gain significant unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate sensitive data from affected systems. Weak cryptographic implementations may allow interception, decryption, or forgery of protected communications.
remediation_brief: Update cryptographic configurations to current standards. Disable deprecated protocols and cipher suites. Ensure certificates are valid and properly configured.

title: ZigBee: ZigBee Network Key in Plaintext Configuration
description: Network key found in plaintext in Zigbee2MQTT or gateway configuration file. Any user or process with read access to the gateway host filesystem can extract the key and use it to decrypt all ZigBee traffic or inject authenticated commands. Plaintext key storage in configuration files is a common misconfiguration in home-automation deployments.
remediation: Encrypt stored keys using OS-level secret stores (e.g., Linux kernel keyring, macOS Keychain). Apply strict filesystem permissions (mode 0600, root-owned) to gateway configuration files. Consider HSM-backed key storage for production environments.
impact: An attacker could leverage this to gain significant unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate sensitive data from affected systems. Network-level vulnerabilities may allow traffic interception, lateral movement, or unauthorized service access.
remediation_brief: Restrict network access using firewalls and segmentation. Disable unnecessary services and protocols. Implement network monitoring.

title: ZigBee: ZigBee Replay Attack Successful
description: Replayed ZCL command frames accepted by target device. Frame counter validation is not enforced or the acceptance window is excessively wide. An attacker can capture authenticated ZCL commands (e.g., door unlock, alarm disarm) and replay them at will, bypassing the encryption layer because the MIC is valid for the replayed frame.
remediation: Enforce strict ZigBee frame counter validation per the ZigBee specification. Devices must reject frames with counters that fall outside the accepted replay protection window. Apply vendor firmware patches that implement per-device frame counter tracking.
impact: An attacker could leverage this to gain significant unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate sensitive data from affected systems. Network-level vulnerabilities may allow traffic interception, lateral movement, or unauthorized service access.
remediation_brief: Restrict network access using firewalls and segmentation. Disable unnecessary services and protocols. Implement network monitoring.

title: Injection: ZCL Command Injection Successful
description: Authenticated ZCL commands injected using recovered network key. Security-sensitive commands including door lock, alarm disarm, and thermostat override were accepted by target devices. The attacker constructed valid encrypted and authenticated ZCL frames using the recovered network key, bypassing all network-layer security controls.
remediation: Rotate network key immediately. Implement application-layer authentication for security-critical clusters (Door Lock, IAS Zone, Thermostat). Enforce allow-listed device EUI64s for security-critical command sources at the coordinator level.
impact: An attacker could leverage this to gain significant unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate sensitive data from affected systems.
remediation_brief: Review and address per security best practices. Consult vendor documentation and industry guidelines.

title: ZigBee: ZLL Touchlink Device Stolen
description: Target ZigBee Light Link device stolen and joined to an attacker-controlled network using the leaked ZLL Master Key. The ZLL Master Key was published in the ZigBee Light Link specification and allows any party to perform touchlink commissioning against any ZLL device within close RF proximity, effectively stealing devices from their production network without requiring the original network key.
remediation: Disable touchlink commissioning where not required by the deployment. Deploy ZigBee 3.0 with enhanced touchlink security (install-code-based commissioning). Replace ZLL-only devices with ZigBee 3.0 devices that do not support legacy touchlink.
impact: An attacker could leverage this to gain significant unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate sensitive data from affected systems. Network-level vulnerabilities may allow traffic interception, lateral movement, or unauthorized service access.
remediation_brief: Restrict network access using firewalls and segmentation. Disable unnecessary services and protocols. Implement network monitoring.

title: ZigBee: ZLL Touchlink Factory Reset Successful
description: ZLL touchlink factory reset command was accepted by the target device, removing it from its production network. This constitutes an effective denial-of-service: the device can no longer communicate with its coordinator and requires manual re-commissioning. The attack requires only close physical proximity (approximately 10–30 cm) and knowledge of the ZLL protocol.
remediation: Disable touchlink commissioning on production devices via coordinator policy. Enforce proximity validation at the application layer. Apply vendor firmware updates that restrict touchlink reset commands to devices already on the same network.
impact: An attacker could use this information or weakness for reconnaissance or to facilitate more targeted attacks against the organization. Network-level vulnerabilities may allow traffic interception, lateral movement, or unauthorized service access.
remediation_brief: Restrict network access using firewalls and segmentation. Disable unnecessary services and protocols. Implement network monitoring.

title: ZigBee: ZigBee Network Denial-of-Service Successful
description: ZigBee network disrupted via PAN-ID conflict flood or association flood. Devices were disconnected from the network or unable to communicate for the duration of the attack. The PAN-ID conflict flood causes the coordinator to change PAN ID, forcing all devices to re-associate. The association flood exhausts the coordinator's association table, preventing legitimate devices from joining.
remediation: Implement RF environment monitoring with anomaly alerting. Deploy ZigBee network with channel agility enabled to respond to sustained interference. Configure coordinator with rate-limiting on association requests. Consider Distributed Trust Center mode to reduce the coordinator as a single point of failure.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Network-level vulnerabilities may allow traffic interception, lateral movement, or unauthorized service access.
remediation_brief: Restrict network access using firewalls and segmentation. Disable unnecessary services and protocols. Implement network monitoring.

title: Wireless Vulnerability: ZigBee Network Key Extracted from Device Firmware
description: Network or link key material extracted from ZigBee device firmware via JTAG debug interface or direct flash memory dump. The key was stored unprotected in flash memory and was recoverable using standard hardware security research tools. A physical attacker can extract this key and use it to compromise all network communications.
remediation: Enable debug port lockdown (JTAG fuse blow) on all production devices. Use hardware-enforced secure boot to prevent unauthorised firmware extraction. Store cryptographic keys in dedicated hardware security elements or in encrypted key stores protected by device-unique keys.
impact: An attacker could leverage this to gain significant unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate sensitive data from affected systems. Network-level vulnerabilities may allow traffic interception, lateral movement, or unauthorized service access.
remediation_brief: Restrict network access using firewalls and segmentation. Disable unnecessary services and protocols. Implement network monitoring.

title: ZigBee: ZigBee Join Window Permanently Open
description: The ZigBee coordinator's join permission window is permanently open, allowing any device to join the network at any time. Combined with use of the default TCLK, this allows an attacker to join the network, receive the network key, and then silently monitor or inject traffic. A permanently-open join window is a common misconfiguration in Zigbee2MQTT and other open-source coordinator software.
remediation: Close join window after commissioning is complete. Only open briefly (maximum 60 seconds) during planned addition of new devices. Implement automated join window closure via coordinator policy. Audit all devices that joined the network and verify they are authorised.
impact: An attacker could use this information or weakness for reconnaissance or to facilitate more targeted attacks against the organization. Network-level vulnerabilities may allow traffic interception, lateral movement, or unauthorized service access.
remediation_brief: Restrict network access using firewalls and segmentation. Disable unnecessary services and protocols. Implement network monitoring.

title: Enumeration: Unauthenticated ZDO Enumeration
description: ZigBee Device Object (ZDO) enumeration reveals all endpoints, clusters, and device capabilities without requiring the ZigBee network key. ZDO requests operate at the network layer and some coordinators respond to unauthenticated ZDO queries, exposing the network topology, device types, supported clusters, and manufacturer information. This information aids targeted attack planning.
remediation: Consider ZigBee network-layer encryption for all frames including ZDO. Monitor for unexpected ZDO requests from unknown source addresses. Restrict ZDO enumeration to coordinator-only responses where possible via network policy.
impact: An attacker could use this information or weakness for reconnaissance or to facilitate more targeted attacks against the organization. Network-level vulnerabilities may allow traffic interception, lateral movement, or unauthorized service access.
remediation_brief: Restrict network access using firewalls and segmentation. Disable unnecessary services and protocols. Implement network monitoring.

title: Wireless Vulnerability: Hardcoded ZigBee Credentials in Device Firmware
description: Hardcoded network key or link key found in device firmware binary via static analysis. The key is identical across all devices of this model. Any attacker who obtains a firmware image (via OTA update interception, vendor leak, or hardware extraction) can extract the key and use it to compromise all deployments of the same device model worldwide.
remediation: Remove hardcoded keys from firmware. Use unique-per-device key provisioning via secure manufacturing processes (e.g., inject unique keys during factory programming under controlled conditions). Store keys in hardware-protected storage on the device.
impact: An attacker could leverage this to gain significant unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate sensitive data from affected systems.
remediation_brief: Remove hardcoded secrets from code and config. Implement a secrets management solution with rotation policies.

title: Wireless Vulnerability: OTA Firmware Update Not Authenticated
description: Over-the-air firmware updates are accepted by the target device without cryptographic signature verification. An attacker with access to the ZigBee network (via recovered network key) can serve a malicious firmware image via the ZigBee OTA Upgrade cluster, replacing the device firmware with attacker-controlled code.
remediation: Implement signed OTA firmware updates with public-key verification per the ZigBee OTA upgrade cluster specification. The device must verify the firmware image signature against a vendor public key embedded in ROM before applying any update. Reject unsigned or incorrectly signed images.
impact: An attacker could leverage this to gain significant unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate sensitive data from affected systems. Network-level vulnerabilities may allow traffic interception, lateral movement, or unauthorized service access.
remediation_brief: Restrict network access using firewalls and segmentation. Disable unnecessary services and protocols. Implement network monitoring.

title: ZigBee: ZigBee Protocol Fuzzing Induced Device Crash
description: Malformed ZigBee protocol frames caused the target device to crash or become unresponsive. Fuzzing of IEEE 802.15.4 MAC headers, ZigBee NWK headers, and ZCL payload fields identified inputs that trigger NULL dereferences or assertion failures in the device firmware. Affected devices required a power cycle to recover.
remediation: Apply vendor firmware patches that add input validation for all received frame fields. Test device implementations against IEEE 802.15.4 and ZigBee Alliance conformance test suites. Implement watchdog timers with automatic recovery to mitigate denial-of-service impact.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Network-level vulnerabilities may allow traffic interception, lateral movement, or unauthorized service access.
remediation_brief: Restrict network access using firewalls and segmentation. Disable unnecessary services and protocols. Implement network monitoring.

title: Discovery: ZLL Master Key Deployment Detected
description: Target network uses ZigBee Light Link (ZLL) with the publicly-leaked ZLL Master Key, exposing all touchlink commissioning operations. The ZLL Master Key was disclosed in the publicly-available ZigBee Light Link specification and allows any attacker to derive the per-network encryption key used during touchlink, enabling device theft and factory reset attacks against all ZLL devices on the network.
remediation: Migrate to ZigBee 3.0 without ZLL legacy support. Replace all ZLL-only devices with ZigBee 3.0 devices. Where immediate migration is not possible, disable touchlink commissioning at the coordinator level and physically secure all ZLL devices against close-proximity attacks.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening. Network-level vulnerabilities may allow traffic interception, lateral movement, or unauthorized service access.

title: Root shell with listener/reverse-shell heuristics (PID {pid})
description: A process running as root has command-line indicators of a listening or reverse shell.
impact: If this is unauthorised it is a likely backdoor providing persistent root access; if authorised it is a maintenance task and can be marked false-positive after verification.
remediation_brief: Verify the process; if unauthorised, kill it (kill -9 <pid>) and investigate parent process tree for persistence.

title: High-risk service listening as root on port {port}
description: A historically-exploitable service is listening as root.
impact: Compromise of the service results in root execution. Specifically risky for FTP/Telnet (cleartext), NFS, RDBMS, Redis/MongoDB/Memcached (frequently misconfigured), and Elasticsearch (historical default no-auth).
remediation_brief: Run the service as a non-root user; bind to loopback only when not externally needed; confirm authentication and firewall rules.

title: Setuid binary not owned by root: {path}
description: A setuid binary is owned by a non-root user.
impact: Compromising the file owner allows arbitrary modification of the binary, which then executes with the owner's UID (and any setuid escalation it performs) on the next invocation. Classic local-privesc pattern.
remediation_brief: chown root:root <path> + audit why the binary is setuid; remove suid bit if not strictly required (chmod u-s).

title: Milvus Unauthenticated Access
description: The Milvus vector database instance is accessible without any authentication credentials. Milvus stores high-dimensional vector embeddings used in RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) systems, similarity search, and AI/ML pipelines. Without authentication, any network-reachable client can list, query, insert, update, or delete collections and their vector data.
impact: An attacker can exfiltrate all stored vector embeddings, which may encode sensitive document content, user queries, or proprietary model outputs. They can also poison the vector store by inserting malicious embeddings, causing RAG systems to return manipulated or harmful results. Full collection deletion is also possible, disrupting AI-dependent services.
remediation_brief: Enable Milvus authentication by setting common.security.authorizationEnabled=true in milvus.yaml. Create named users with strong passwords and assign least-privilege roles. Restrict network access to Milvus ports (19530/19121) using firewall rules.

title: Milvus Default/Weak Root Password
description: The Milvus vector database accepts the factory-default root password ('Milvus'). Every Milvus installation ships with this credential, and it is widely documented. When authentication is enabled but the root password is not changed, the instance is effectively unprotected.
impact: An attacker with the default root credential has full administrative access: they can create/drop collections, read/write all vector data, manage users, and reconfigure the cluster. This grants complete control over the AI/ML data pipeline that depends on Milvus, enabling data exfiltration, embedding poisoning, and denial of service.
remediation_brief: Change the root password immediately using the Milvus SDK or CLI: from pymilvus import utility; utility.reset_password('root', 'Milvus', '<new_strong_password>'). Enforce password complexity policies and rotate credentials on a regular schedule.

title: Qdrant API Unauthenticated Access
description: The Qdrant vector database REST API is accessible without an API key. Qdrant exposes HTTP (port 6333) and gRPC (port 6334) endpoints for managing collections, points (vectors + payloads), and snapshots. Without an API key, any client with network access has full read/write control.
impact: An attacker can query all stored vector embeddings and their associated payloads (which often contain source text, metadata, or user data from RAG pipelines). They can modify or delete collections to disrupt AI services, or insert poisoned embeddings to manipulate search results and LLM responses.
remediation_brief: Enable API key authentication by setting QDRANT__SERVICE__API_KEY in the Qdrant configuration or environment. Use a strong, randomly-generated key. For production, also enable TLS and restrict network access to the Qdrant ports (6333/6334) with firewall rules.

title: Qdrant Collection Data Exposure
description: All Qdrant collections are listable and their contents (vectors and payloads) are readable. Qdrant does not support per-collection access control; authentication is all-or-nothing. When accessible, every collection's stored embeddings and associated payload data are fully exposed.
impact: Stored vector embeddings may encode sensitive information from documents ingested into RAG systems, user search queries, or proprietary model outputs. Collection names and payload schemas also reveal the architecture and data sources of the AI system. An attacker can reconstruct approximate source content from embeddings using inversion techniques.
remediation_brief: Enable API key authentication on Qdrant. Segment sensitive data into separate Qdrant instances with distinct API keys. Consider encrypting payloads at the application layer before storing them in Qdrant.

title: Weaviate Anonymous Access Enabled
description: The Weaviate vector database allows anonymous read/write access. The schema endpoint is accessible without authentication, enabling full enumeration of classes (object types), properties, and stored data. Weaviate supports OIDC and API key auth, but ships with anonymous access enabled by default.
impact: An attacker can read all stored objects and their vector representations, modify the schema, create or delete classes, and manipulate stored data. In a RAG context, this allows exfiltration of ingested documents, poisoning of the knowledge base, and disruption of AI-powered search and retrieval.
remediation_brief: Disable anonymous access in the Weaviate configuration by setting AUTHENTICATION_ANONYMOUS_ACCESS_ENABLED=false. Configure OIDC or API key authentication. Restrict network access to port 8080 using firewall rules.

title: Weaviate Backup API Exposed
description: The Weaviate backup API endpoint (/v1/backups) is accessible without authentication. This endpoint allows creating full database backups to configured storage backends (S3, GCS, filesystem) and restoring from existing backups.
impact: An attacker can trigger a full backup of the Weaviate database to exfiltrate all stored objects, vectors, and schema definitions. They can also restore from a manipulated backup to overwrite the entire database with attacker-controlled content, effectively hijacking the knowledge base that downstream AI systems depend on.
remediation_brief: Disable anonymous access and require authentication for all Weaviate API endpoints including /v1/backups. Restrict backup storage backend permissions so that only authorized service accounts can write to or read from the backup destination.

title: ChromaDB Unauthenticated Access
description: The ChromaDB REST API is accessible without authentication. ChromaDB is a popular open-source embedding database used in RAG pipelines and LLM applications. By default, ChromaDB ships with no authentication mechanism, making all collections and their embeddings accessible to any client that can reach the API port.
impact: An attacker can enumerate all collections, read stored embeddings and their associated metadata/documents, create or delete collections, and insert poisoned embeddings. In RAG pipelines, this allows exfiltration of the knowledge base and manipulation of LLM responses through embedding poisoning.
remediation_brief: Enable ChromaDB server authentication by configuring CHROMA_SERVER_AUTHN_PROVIDER (e.g., chromadb.auth.token_authn.TokenAuthenticationServerProvider) and setting CHROMA_SERVER_AUTHN_CREDENTIALS. Restrict network access to port 8000. Consider deploying ChromaDB behind an authenticating reverse proxy.

title: ChromaDB Collection Enumeration
description: All ChromaDB collections are enumerable via the REST API. Collection names, metadata, and embedding counts are exposed. ChromaDB does not support per-collection access control; any authenticated (or unauthenticated, if auth is disabled) client can list and access all collections.
impact: Collection names and counts reveal the structure and scale of the AI/ML data pipeline. Stored embeddings encode information from source documents, and approximate inversion can recover sensitive content. An attacker gains a map of the entire RAG knowledge base and can target specific collections for data exfiltration.
remediation_brief: Enable authentication on ChromaDB. Implement application-layer access control that restricts which clients can access which collections. Segment sensitive data into separate ChromaDB instances with distinct credentials.

title: pgvector Extension Publicly Accessible
description: The pgvector extension is installed on a network-accessible PostgreSQL instance. pgvector adds vector similarity search capabilities (cosine distance, L2 distance, inner product) to PostgreSQL, commonly used to store and query embeddings for RAG and AI applications. When the PostgreSQL instance is reachable from untrusted networks, the vector data stored via pgvector is exposed to the same access controls as regular PostgreSQL tables.
impact: An attacker with database access (even read-only) can query vector columns to extract stored embeddings. These embeddings encode information from source documents, and approximate inversion or nearest-neighbor attacks can reveal sensitive content. The presence of pgvector also reveals that the database serves AI/ML workloads, helping an attacker target the most valuable data.
remediation_brief: Restrict network access to the PostgreSQL instance using pg_hba.conf and firewall rules. Ensure only trusted application servers can connect. Consider using separate PostgreSQL roles with minimal privileges for vector data access. Encrypt connections with SSL.

title: pgvector Embedding Data Exposure
description: PostgreSQL tables containing pgvector vector columns are accessible without column-level access restrictions. Vector columns store embedding data that encodes information from source documents, user inputs, or proprietary models. Standard PostgreSQL GRANT/REVOKE applies at table or column level, but no column-level restrictions were found on the vector columns.
impact: Any database user with SELECT privileges on the affected tables can read the embedding vectors. These vectors can be used for nearest-neighbor attacks to identify similar documents, or subjected to embedding inversion techniques to approximate the original source content. In multi-tenant systems, this may expose one tenant's data to another.
remediation_brief: Apply column-level REVOKE on vector columns for all non-application roles: REVOKE SELECT (embedding_col) ON table FROM public. Create dedicated roles for vector query access with least-privilege grants. Consider using PostgreSQL Row Level Security (RLS) for multi-tenant isolation.

title: Discovery: Authentication Endpoint Detected
remediation_brief: Review and address per security best practices. Consult vendor documentation and industry guidelines.
description: authprobe detected: Authentication Endpoint Detected. This finding indicates a security concern that requires review.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening.

title: Missing Security Header: {header}
remediation_brief: Review and harden configuration per security best practices and CIS benchmarks. Disable unnecessary features and apply least functionality.
description: authprobe detected: <value>. This finding indicates a security concern that requires review.
impact: An attacker could use this information or weakness for reconnaissance or to facilitate more targeted attacks against the organization. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.

title: Authentication: HTTP Basic Authentication in Use
remediation_brief: Implement strong authentication including MFA, account lockout, and credential complexity requirements. Disable default and anonymous access.
description: authprobe detected: HTTP Basic Authentication in Use. This finding indicates a security concern that requires review.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Weak or missing authentication allows unauthorized users to access protected resources.

title: Firewall: No Default-Deny Rule at End of Policy
description: No explicit default-deny (implicit permit-all) rule exists at the end of the access control list or policy group. Traffic not matching any rule is permitted rather than dropped.
impact: Unintended traffic flows reach internal systems. Attackers can exploit missing coverage to access systems that policy authors assumed were protected.
remediation_brief: 1. Add an explicit 'deny ip any any log' rule as the final entry in every ACL. 2. Ensure the deny-all rule includes logging to capture all traffic hitting the implicit deny. 3. Review all traffic flows to confirm intended rules precede the default deny. 4. Test the rule using traffic simulation before deploying to production.

title: Firewall: Any-Any-Any Permit Rule Detected
description: A firewall rule permits all traffic from any source to any destination on all ports and protocols. This is the most dangerous firewall misconfiguration possible.
impact: The firewall provides no access control. All traffic is permitted regardless of source, destination, or protocol.
remediation_brief: 1. Immediately remove or disable the any-any permit rule. 2. Implement principle of least privilege — only permit required traffic flows. 3. Document all required flows before rebuilding the policy. 4. Use a test environment to validate replacement rules before deploying.

title: Firewall: Disabled Rules Present in Production Configuration
description: One or more firewall rules are disabled (inactive) in the production configuration. Disabled rules accumulate over time and indicate configuration drift or incomplete cleanup.
impact: Disabled rules represent policy intent that is no longer enforced. They create confusion during audits, may be re-enabled accidentally, and indicate the policy requires cleanup.
remediation_brief: 1. Review all disabled rules and determine if they are still required. 2. Remove disabled rules that are no longer needed. 3. Document the reason for any disabled rules that must be retained. 4. Establish a policy lifecycle process to prevent accumulation of disabled rules.

title: Firewall: Duplicate Firewall Rules Detected
description: Two or more firewall rules have identical source, destination, port, and action specifications. Duplicate rules indicate policy bloat and maintenance issues.
impact: Duplicate rules increase management overhead, create confusion during incident response, and may indicate the policy review process is not working correctly.
remediation_brief: 1. Identify and remove all duplicate rules. 2. Implement a rule review process that checks for duplicates before policy deployment. 3. Use firewall management tools that flag duplicate rules automatically.

title: Firewall: Shadowed Rules — Unreachable Policy Entries
description: One or more firewall rules are completely covered (shadowed) by earlier, broader rules and will never be evaluated. Shadowed rules indicate policy maintenance issues and potential security gaps.
impact: Shadowed rules are never executed. If the shadowing rule has a different action than the shadowed rule, traffic may be handled contrary to policy intent.
remediation_brief: 1. Reorder rules so more specific rules precede broader rules. 2. Remove rules that are completely redundant given preceding rules. 3. Implement rule ordering verification in change management process.

title: Firewall: Suboptimal Rule Ordering
description: Frequently-hit rules appear after less-used rules in the policy list. This degrades performance as the firewall must evaluate all preceding rules before reaching the effective rule.
impact: Increased latency for matching traffic. In high-volume environments, suboptimal ordering can degrade firewall throughput.
remediation_brief: 1. Place high-volume deny rules (e.g., blocklists) near the top of the policy. 2. Place more specific, lower-volume rules before broad rules. 3. Use hit count data to determine optimal ordering.

title: RDP: RDP Permitted from Any Source
description: A firewall rule permits Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP, TCP 3389) inbound from any source address. RDP is one of the most commonly exploited services for ransomware and lateral movement.
impact: Exposed RDP is a primary attack vector for ransomware gangs, APT groups, and commodity attackers. Authentication bypass vulnerabilities (BlueKeep, DejaBlue) regularly affect RDP.
remediation_brief: 1. Immediately restrict RDP access to specific management IP ranges. 2. Place RDP behind a VPN or RDP Gateway. 3. Enable Network Level Authentication (NLA). 4. Implement account lockout policies. 5. Consider replacing RDP with a zero-trust remote access solution.

title: Firewall: SSH Permitted from External/Untrusted Sources
description: A firewall rule permits SSH (TCP 22) from untrusted or external sources. SSH brute-force attacks are extremely common against internet-exposed SSH.
impact: Exposed SSH enables brute-force attacks, credential stuffing, and exploitation of SSH vulnerabilities. Compromised SSH access provides immediate shell access to the target system.
remediation_brief: 1. Restrict SSH to management IP addresses only. 2. Implement SSH key-based authentication and disable password authentication. 3. Change SSH to a non-standard port (security by obscurity, not a primary control). 4. Implement fail2ban or equivalent brute-force protection. 5. Consider placing SSH behind a jump host or bastion server.

title: Insecure Protocol Detected: Telnet Permitted Through Firewall
description: A firewall rule permits Telnet (TCP 23). Telnet transmits all data including credentials in plaintext and has been deprecated for over 25 years.
impact: All Telnet communications, including authentication credentials, are transmitted in cleartext and can be intercepted by network eavesdroppers. No confidentiality or integrity protection exists.
remediation_brief: 1. Immediately block all Telnet traffic. 2. Replace all Telnet-dependent systems with SSH. 3. If Telnet is required for legacy systems, isolate those systems and implement compensating controls. 4. Review device configurations to ensure SSH is enabled on all network equipment.

title: FTP: FTP Permitted Through Firewall
description: A firewall rule permits FTP (TCP 20/21). FTP transmits credentials and data in plaintext and supports anonymous authentication by default on many implementations.
impact: FTP credentials and file contents are transmitted in cleartext. Anonymous FTP can expose sensitive files. FTP's PORT command can be abused for firewall bypass (FTP bounce attacks).
remediation_brief: 1. Replace FTP with SFTP (SSH File Transfer Protocol) or FTPS (FTP over TLS). 2. If FTP must be used, restrict to internal networks only. 3. Disable anonymous FTP. 4. Implement strict file transfer policies.

title: Firewall: SMB Permitted from External Sources (TCP 445)
description: A firewall rule permits SMB (TCP 445) from external/untrusted sources. SMB is the primary protocol used by ransomware (WannaCry, NotPetya, EternalBlue) for lateral movement.
impact: Exposed SMB is the most common ransomware infection vector. EternalBlue and related exploits are still widely used in ransomware campaigns. SMB exposure directly enables catastrophic data encryption attacks.
remediation_brief: 1. Immediately block TCP 445 from all untrusted sources. 2. Block UDP 137-138 and TCP 139 (NetBIOS) as well. 3. Audit internal SMB to ensure it is restricted to required segments. 4. Implement host-based firewall rules in addition to network firewall. 5. Keep Windows systems patched against EternalBlue.

title: RPC: MS-RPC Permitted from External Sources (TCP 135)
description: A firewall rule permits Microsoft RPC (TCP 135) from external sources. MS-RPC is a critical Windows service used for DCOM, WMI, and many Windows management interfaces.
impact: Exposed MS-RPC enables remote exploitation of Windows services via DCOM and WMI. Historically abused by Blaster, Sasser, and modern APT groups for remote code execution.
remediation_brief: 1. Block TCP 135 from all external sources. 2. Block the entire RPC dynamic port range (TCP 49152-65535) from external sources. 3. Consider blocking RPC internally except between required systems.

title: Firewall: NetBIOS Permitted Through Firewall
description: A firewall rule permits NetBIOS (UDP 137-138, TCP 139) traffic. NetBIOS is a legacy Windows protocol that enables reconnaissance, credential theft (LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning), and lateral movement.
impact: NetBIOS enables LLMNR and NBT-NS poisoning attacks, NetBIOS name query reconnaissance, and credential capture via Responder-style attacks. Should never traverse firewall boundaries.
remediation_brief: 1. Block UDP 137, 138 and TCP 139 at all firewall boundaries. 2. Disable NetBIOS over TCP/IP on Windows hosts where not required. 3. Disable LLMNR and NBT-NS via Group Policy.

title: SNMP: SNMP Permitted from Any Source
description: A firewall rule permits SNMP (UDP 161) from any source address. SNMP exposes device configurations, routing tables, and interface statistics to anyone who can reach the port.
impact: SNMP v1/v2c use community strings for authentication (effectively cleartext passwords). An attacker with SNMP access can read full device configurations, enumerate network topology, and potentially write configurations if community string permits.
remediation_brief: 1. Restrict SNMP to dedicated monitoring IP addresses only. 2. Upgrade to SNMPv3 with authentication and encryption. 3. Use ACLs on network devices themselves, not just the firewall. 4. Change default community strings (public/private).

title: Authentication: SNMP v1/v2c Weak Authentication Exposure
description: SNMP is permitted through the firewall with likely v1/v2c community string authentication. SNMPv1 and v2c use cleartext community strings that can be sniffed.
impact: Community strings transmitted in cleartext can be captured and used for unauthorized device access. Many devices ship with default community strings (public/private).
remediation_brief: 1. Migrate to SNMPv3 with AuthPriv security level. 2. If SNMP v1/v2c must be used, restrict to isolated management VLAN. 3. Change all community strings from defaults. 4. Implement SNMPv3 privacy (encryption) for sensitive data.

title: Firewall: WinRM Permitted from External Sources (TCP 5985/5986)
description: A firewall rule permits Windows Remote Management (WinRM, TCP 5985 HTTP or 5986 HTTPS) from external sources. WinRM provides PowerShell remoting and remote command execution.
impact: Exposed WinRM enables remote command execution via PowerShell. Commonly used by attackers for lateral movement and persistence once credentials are compromised.
remediation_brief: 1. Block TCP 5985 and 5986 from all untrusted sources. 2. Restrict WinRM to management IP ranges only. 3. Require HTTPS (5986) over HTTP (5985). 4. Implement WinRM access control lists.

title: Database: Database Ports Exposed to External Sources
description: A firewall rule permits database service ports (MySQL TCP 3306, MSSQL TCP 1433, PostgreSQL TCP 5432, Oracle TCP 1521) from external or untrusted sources.
impact: Direct database exposure enables SQL injection amplification, credential brute-force against database authentication, and direct data exfiltration. Databases should never be directly internet-accessible.
remediation_brief: 1. Immediately block all database ports from untrusted sources. 2. Place databases in a dedicated database VLAN accessible only from application servers. 3. Implement database activity monitoring (DAM). 4. Use application-layer database proxies where possible.

title: Database: Elasticsearch Exposed to External Sources (TCP 9200/9300)
description: A firewall rule permits Elasticsearch (TCP 9200 HTTP API or 9300 transport) from external or untrusted sources. Elasticsearch has no authentication by default.
impact: Unauthenticated Elasticsearch instances have led to some of the largest data breaches in history. All indexed data is accessible to anyone who can reach port 9200.
remediation_brief: 1. Immediately block TCP 9200 and 9300 from all untrusted sources. 2. Enable Elasticsearch security features (X-Pack/Security). 3. Implement TLS and authentication. 4. Place Elasticsearch behind a reverse proxy with authentication.

title: Database: Redis/Memcached Exposed to External Sources
description: A firewall rule permits Redis (TCP 6379) or Memcached (TCP/UDP 11211) from external sources. Both services have no authentication by default.
impact: Unauthenticated Redis allows full data access and remote code execution via EVAL command. Memcached exposure enables data theft and the service has been abused for massive DDoS amplification attacks.
remediation_brief: 1. Immediately block TCP 6379 and 11211 from untrusted sources. 2. Enable Redis AUTH and bind to localhost or internal addresses only. 3. Disable Memcached UDP to prevent amplification abuse. 4. Place caching services behind application tier — never expose externally.

title: Firewall: TFTP Permitted Through Firewall
description: A firewall rule permits TFTP (UDP 69). TFTP has no authentication mechanism — any client that can reach the TFTP server can read and write files.
impact: TFTP enables unauthenticated file reads and writes. Attackers who can reach TFTP servers can read configuration files, firmware, and write malicious files.
remediation_brief: 1. Block UDP 69 at all firewall boundaries. 2. Restrict TFTP to isolated management VLAN if required for network device management. 3. Use SCP or SFTP instead of TFTP for device provisioning.

title: NTP: NTP Access Not Restricted to Trusted Sources
description: A firewall rule permits NTP (UDP 123) from any source without restriction. Open NTP servers can be abused for reflection/amplification DDoS attacks.
impact: Unrestricted NTP access enables use of the firewall's internal NTP infrastructure as a DDoS amplification source. NTP amplification attacks achieve amplification factors of up to 556x.
remediation_brief: 1. Restrict NTP to specific trusted time sources (external) and internal clients only. 2. Disable NTP monlist and other amplification-capable commands. 3. Rate-limit NTP responses.

title: Firewall: DNS Outbound Not Restricted to Authorised Resolvers
description: Outbound DNS (UDP/TCP 53) is permitted from any internal host to any external destination, allowing direct DNS resolution to arbitrary external servers.
impact: Unrestricted outbound DNS enables DNS tunneling for data exfiltration, circumvents DNS-based security controls (sinkholes, RPZ), and allows malware to use any DNS server for C2 communication.
remediation_brief: 1. Restrict outbound DNS to authorised internal resolvers only. 2. Block direct outbound DNS from all hosts except designated resolvers. 3. Implement DNS logging and monitoring. 4. Deploy DNS filtering (RPZ, DNS firewall) on authorised resolvers.

title: Firewall: ICMP Not Restricted
description: ICMP is permitted without source or destination restriction. While necessary for network diagnostics, unrestricted ICMP enables network reconnaissance and covert channel communication.
impact: ICMP ping sweeps reveal network topology. ICMP tunneling (iodine, icmptunnel) enables covert data exfiltration. ICMP redirect messages can be used for man-in-the-middle attacks.
remediation_brief: 1. Restrict inbound ICMP to only needed types (echo-reply, unreachable, time-exceeded). 2. Block ICMP echo from external sources or restrict to monitoring IPs. 3. Consider rate-limiting ICMP.

title: Wireless Management: Management Access Not Restricted to Management Zone
description: Firewall management interfaces (HTTPS, SSH, ASDM) are accessible from any source address, including untrusted networks.
impact: Unrestricted management access exposes the firewall administrative interface to brute-force attacks, credential stuffing, and exploitation of management interface vulnerabilities.
remediation_brief: 1. Restrict all management access to a dedicated out-of-band management network. 2. Block all management protocol access from non-management networks. 3. Implement management VLAN with strict access controls. 4. Enable failed login lockout on management interfaces.

title: Wireless Management: HTTP Used for Device Management
description: HTTP (cleartext) is enabled for firewall or device management. All management traffic including credentials is transmitted unencrypted.
impact: Credentials, session tokens, and configuration changes transmitted via HTTP can be captured by network eavesdroppers. Session hijacking attacks are trivial against HTTP management sessions.
remediation_brief: 1. Disable HTTP management on all devices. 2. Enable HTTPS with TLS 1.2 minimum. 3. Install a valid management certificate. 4. Redirect any HTTP management connections to HTTPS.

title: Insecure Protocol Detected: Telnet Used for Device Management
description: Telnet is enabled as a device management protocol. Telnet provides no encryption, authentication challenge-response visibility, or integrity protection.
impact: All management commands, including configuration changes and credentials, are transmitted in cleartext. An attacker with network access can capture and replay management sessions.
remediation_brief: 1. Immediately disable Telnet on all devices. 2. Enable SSH version 2 as the sole remote management protocol. 3. Configure SSH with strong cipher suites and MAC algorithms. 4. Remove Telnet from all device configurations.

title: Wireless Management: No Source Restriction on SSH/HTTPS Management Access
description: SSH or HTTPS management access is configured without a source IP restriction, allowing management access from any network.
impact: Management access from any source dramatically increases the attack surface for brute-force attacks, credential stuffing, and exploitation of management interface vulnerabilities.
remediation_brief: 1. Implement source IP restrictions for all management protocols. 2. Create an explicit management ACL restricting access to management workstation IPs. 3. Use an out-of-band management network where possible.

title: Wireless Management: HTTPS Management Accessible from Any Source
description: HTTPS device management is accessible from any source IP address. While HTTPS provides encryption, unrestricted access enables credential attacks.
impact: Unrestricted HTTPS management enables brute-force and credential stuffing attacks against the management interface. Web-based management interfaces have historically contained exploitable vulnerabilities.
remediation_brief: 1. Restrict HTTPS management to specific management IP ranges. 2. Implement account lockout after failed login attempts. 3. Enable multi-factor authentication for management access where supported.

title: Firewall: Permit Rules Without Logging Enabled
description: One or more permit (allow) rules do not have logging enabled. Traffic matching these rules is not captured in firewall logs.
impact: Without logging on permit rules, allowed traffic is invisible to security monitoring. Attacks, data exfiltration, and lateral movement that uses permitted paths cannot be detected or investigated.
remediation_brief: 1. Enable logging on all permit rules. 2. At minimum, enable logging on high-risk rules (any-source, external-to-internal). 3. Forward logs to a centralised SIEM for correlation. 4. Set log level to 'informational' for permit rules to capture connection details.

title: Firewall: Deny Rules Without Logging Enabled
description: One or more deny rules do not have logging enabled. Blocked connection attempts are not captured in firewall logs.
impact: Without logging on deny rules, attack attempts against blocked services are invisible. Security teams cannot detect port scans, reconnaissance, or blocked attack attempts.
remediation_brief: 1. Enable logging on all deny rules, particularly the default-deny rule. 2. Use logging levels that capture the necessary detail (source IP, destination, port, protocol). 3. Implement log aggregation and alerting for suspicious deny patterns.

title: Firewall: No Logging Configured — Complete Forensic Blind Spot
description: No firewall rules in this configuration have logging enabled. The firewall is operating without any security event logging, creating a complete forensic blind spot.
impact: Without any logging, the organisation cannot detect attacks, investigate incidents, demonstrate compliance, or understand traffic patterns. This is a fundamental security control failure.
remediation_brief: 1. Immediately enable logging on all permit rules. 2. Enable logging on the default-deny rule. 3. Configure syslog forwarding to a SIEM. 4. Define a log retention policy (minimum 90 days online, 1 year archived). 5. Establish a log review process.

title: Firewall: No DMZ (Demilitarised Zone) Detected
description: No DMZ zone or interface has been identified in the firewall configuration. Public-facing services appear to be placed in the same zone as internal systems.
impact: Without a DMZ, compromising a public-facing server (web, email, DNS) provides direct access to internal systems. This eliminates a critical layer of defence-in-depth.
remediation_brief: 1. Create a dedicated DMZ zone for all public-facing servers. 2. Configure the DMZ with an intermediate security level. 3. Implement strict policies between DMZ and internal zones. 4. Ensure DMZ servers cannot initiate connections to internal systems.

title: Firewall: Direct Internet-to-Internal Permit Without DMZ Intermediate
description: Permit rules exist that allow direct traffic from the external/internet zone to internal high-trust zones without passing through a DMZ or intermediate inspection zone.
impact: Traffic from the internet reaches internal systems directly. A single exploitation event on an internet-facing system could lead to direct internal network compromise.
remediation_brief: 1. Redesign traffic flows to route internet traffic through a DMZ. 2. Place all public-facing services in the DMZ. 3. Implement application-layer inspection between DMZ and internal zones. 4. Require explicit permit rules for DMZ-to-internal traffic.

title: Firewall: Flat Network — Only One Zone or Interface Defined
description: The firewall configuration defines only a single zone or network interface. All traffic flows through a single segment with no internal segmentation.
impact: A flat network means a single compromised host can communicate with any other host. Lateral movement is trivial and ransomware can spread unimpeded.
remediation_brief: 1. Segment the network into functional zones (internal, DMZ, management, guest). 2. Implement firewall policies between each zone pair. 3. Consider microsegmentation for high-value systems. 4. Progressively add zones as part of a phased network redesign.

title: Firewall: Server-to-Workstation Traffic Unrestricted
description: No rules restrict east-west traffic between server and workstation segments. Servers can initiate connections to workstations and vice versa without inspection.
impact: Unrestricted server-to-workstation traffic enables ransomware propagation, lateral movement from compromised servers to workstations, and from workstations to servers.
remediation_brief: 1. Implement east-west segmentation between server and workstation VLANs. 2. Deny all server-initiated connections to workstation networks. 3. Permit only required application ports from workstations to servers. 4. Implement network monitoring to detect anomalous east-west traffic.

title: Firewall: Internal RFC-1918 Addresses Potentially Reachable Without NAT
description: Permit rules allow traffic to private (RFC-1918) destination addresses from external zones without corresponding NAT translations, potentially exposing internal addressing.
impact: If RFC-1918 addresses are routed externally without NAT, internal network topology is exposed. This can enable direct attacks against internal systems or reveal sensitive network design information.
remediation_brief: 1. Verify that NAT is configured for all rules permitting external traffic to internal RFC-1918 destinations. 2. Ensure that external routing does not leak RFC-1918 prefixes. 3. Implement NAT for all internal-to-external traffic flows.

title: Information Disclosure: 1:1 Static NAT Exposes Internal Host Directly to Internet
description: A 1:1 static NAT mapping exposes an internal host directly to the internet with full port translation. All ports on the internal host are potentially reachable.
impact: Static NAT 1:1 mappings expose the complete attack surface of the mapped internal host. Any vulnerability on that host is directly exploitable from the internet.
remediation_brief: 1. Replace 1:1 static NAT with port-specific NAT where possible. 2. Implement access control lists in combination with static NAT. 3. Only expose specific required ports, not the full host. 4. Move services requiring internet exposure to a DMZ with strict policies.

title: Firewall: IPv6 Traffic Not Addressed in Policy
description: The firewall configuration does not include explicit IPv6 policy rules. If IPv6 is enabled on interfaces, traffic may be uncontrolled.
impact: Unmanaged IPv6 traffic may bypass IPv4 security controls. Dual-stack hosts may be reachable via IPv6 paths that are not covered by the IPv4 firewall policy.
remediation_brief: 1. Audit all interfaces for IPv6 enablement. 2. If IPv6 is not required, disable it on all interfaces. 3. If IPv6 is used, implement a full dual-stack firewall policy mirroring IPv4 controls. 4. Block IPv6 tunnelling protocols (6to4, Teredo, ISATAP) at the perimeter.

title: Authentication Bypass: GRE/IPSec Tunnels Permitted Without Authentication Requirement
description: GRE (protocol 47) or IPSec (ESP/AH, protocols 50/51) tunnelling is permitted without authentication requirements enforced at the firewall level.
impact: Unauthenticated GRE tunnels can be used to encapsulate and hide malicious traffic, bypassing application-layer inspection. GRE provides no confidentiality or integrity.
remediation_brief: 1. Replace GRE with authenticated IPSec tunnels. 2. Implement IKEv2 with strong authentication for all VPN tunnels. 3. If GRE is required, encapsulate in IPSec. 4. Implement strict source/destination restrictions on tunnel endpoints.

title: Firewall: BGP/OSPF Routing Protocols Permitted from External Sources
description: BGP (TCP 179) or OSPF routing protocol traffic is permitted from external or untrusted sources. Routing protocol injection can manipulate network traffic paths.
impact: Rogue BGP sessions or OSPF updates can redirect traffic to attacker-controlled destinations, enable man-in-the-middle attacks, or cause network-wide outages.
remediation_brief: 1. Block BGP (TCP 179) from untrusted sources. 2. Implement BGP authentication (MD5 or TCP-AO). 3. Implement OSPF authentication. 4. Restrict routing protocol traffic to dedicated peering addresses.

title: Firewall: Outbound SMTP Not Restricted to Mail Relay
description: Outbound SMTP (TCP 25) is permitted from internal networks to any external destination, allowing any internal host to send email directly to external mail servers.
impact: Unrestricted outbound SMTP enables malware to send spam, phishing emails, and data exfiltration via email from any compromised internal host. This also contributes to IP reputation damage.
remediation_brief: 1. Block outbound TCP 25 from all hosts except designated mail relays. 2. Route all outbound SMTP through a controlled mail relay/gateway. 3. Implement outbound email filtering and DMARC/SPF/DKIM. 4. Monitor for anomalous outbound email volumes.

title: Authentication Bypass: TLS/SSL Bypass or Inspection Not Configured
description: Encrypted traffic (HTTPS/TLS) is permitted through the firewall without any indication of SSL/TLS inspection being configured. Malware and data exfiltration commonly use HTTPS to evade detection.
impact: Encrypted traffic bypasses all application-layer inspection. Malware C2 communications, data exfiltration, and phishing content cannot be inspected or blocked.
remediation_brief: 1. Implement SSL/TLS inspection where technically and legally feasible. 2. At minimum, block HTTPS to known malicious categories via DNS. 3. Implement certificate pinning bypass detection. 4. Consider decryption zones for high-risk traffic categories.

title: Firewall: VoIP SIP Permitted Without Restriction
description: SIP (Session Initiation Protocol, UDP/TCP 5060/5061) is permitted from untrusted sources without source restriction. SIP is commonly targeted for toll fraud and eavesdropping.
impact: Exposed SIP enables toll fraud (attackers route expensive calls through your infrastructure), eavesdropping on VoIP calls, and SIP scanning for credential harvesting.
remediation_brief: 1. Restrict SIP to SIP trunk provider IP ranges only. 2. Implement SIP-aware firewall inspection. 3. Deploy a Session Border Controller (SBC). 4. Enable SIP authentication and registration rate limiting.

title: Firewall: Video Conferencing Ports Unrestricted
description: Video conferencing service ports (Zoom 8801-8802, Teams 3478-3481, Webex) are permitted from any source without restriction.
impact: Unrestricted video conferencing ports can be abused for reconnaissance and may expose internal network information through STUN/TURN protocol interactions.
remediation_brief: 1. Restrict video conferencing traffic to known service provider IP ranges. 2. Use cloud-relay services rather than direct peer connections where possible. 3. Implement application-aware firewall policies for video conferencing.

title: IoT: MQTT IoT Protocol Exposed (TCP 1883/8883)
description: MQTT broker ports (TCP 1883 unencrypted or 8883 TLS) are accessible from untrusted sources. MQTT is the primary IoT messaging protocol and is frequently misconfigured without authentication.
impact: Exposed MQTT brokers allow unauthenticated subscription to all IoT device topics, enabling surveillance, control of IoT devices, and lateral movement into IoT network segments.
remediation_brief: 1. Block MQTT ports from all untrusted sources. 2. Enable MQTT authentication and authorisation. 3. Use TLS-only MQTT (8883). 4. Implement MQTT topic-level access control. 5. Place MQTT broker in isolated IoT VLAN.

title: Network Misconfiguration: RDP Permitted on Non-Standard Ports
description: Remote Desktop Protocol is permitted on non-standard ports (not 3389), suggesting an attempt to obscure RDP exposure. Security by obscurity does not reduce the actual risk.
impact: RDP running on non-standard ports is discovered by modern port scanners within minutes. The underlying RDP vulnerabilities and risks remain identical regardless of port number.
remediation_brief: 1. Treat RDP on non-standard ports with the same urgency as standard-port RDP. 2. Implement proper access controls (VPN, specific source IPs) rather than port obfuscation. 3. Consider replacing RDP with a zero-trust remote access solution.

title: Firewall: Cato WAN Firewall: Any-Any Permit Rule
description: A WAN firewall rule permits all traffic with no source, destination, or service restrictions across SD-WAN sites.
impact: Unrestricted site-to-site traffic bypasses intended network segmentation, allowing lateral movement between all connected sites.
remediation_brief: Replace any-any rules with specific site-to-site policies. Define explicit allowed traffic per application and direction.

title: Firewall: Cato Internet Firewall: Outbound Any-Any Permit
description: Internet-bound traffic is permitted without application or destination restriction, bypassing CASB and URL filtering controls.
impact: Users can reach any internet destination on any port, enabling data exfiltration and access to malicious infrastructure.
remediation_brief: Enable Cato CASB and URL Filtering. Define explicit application allow-lists for internet access. Block all non-approved traffic by default.

title: Firewall: Cato: No Identity-Based Policy — All Rules Use IP/Network Only
description: All firewall rules use IP addresses or network objects with no user or group identity conditions, missing the zero-trust identity layer.
impact: Any device with a matching IP can traverse permitted paths regardless of user identity, reducing the effectiveness of the SASE model.
remediation_brief: Migrate rules to identity-based policies using Cato's user/group identity conditions where possible.

title: Firewall: Cloudflare Gateway: No Default Block on Network Policy
description: No default-deny network policy exists in Cloudflare Gateway. Traffic not matching any explicit rule is passed through.
impact: Traffic not matching any explicit rule is permitted by default, allowing access to unclassified destinations and services.
remediation_brief: Add a catch-all network policy at the lowest priority that blocks all unmatched traffic.

title: Firewall: Cloudflare Gateway: DNS Security Policy Not Configured
description: No DNS security policies are present. Malicious domain blocking, DoH restrictions, and DNS-based threat intelligence are disabled.
impact: Users can resolve malicious domains, access phishing sites, and malware can use any DNS server for C2 communication.
remediation_brief: Enable Cloudflare Gateway DNS filtering. Add policies to block known malware, phishing, and C2 categories.

title: Firewall: Cloudflare Gateway: Unrestricted SSH/RDP in Network Policy
description: A network policy permits SSH or RDP from any source without identity conditions in Cloudflare Gateway.
impact: Any user or device matching the network policy can access SSH/RDP endpoints without additional identity verification, defeating zero-trust principles.
remediation_brief: Add user/group identity conditions to all SSH/RDP rules. Consider migrating to Cloudflare Access for zero-trust remote access.

title: Firewall: Executive Env: Guest Network Not Isolated from Corporate
description: Guest/visitor wireless or network segment can communicate with corporate resources. Executive environments are high-value targets and guests must have zero access to internal segments.
impact: A threat actor, journalist, or corporate spy posing as a visitor could pivot from the guest network to executive communications, email systems, or board-level documents.
remediation_brief: 1. Isolate guest VLAN with deny-all to all corporate subnets. 2. Permit only internet-bound traffic from guest segment. 3. Implement client isolation on guest wireless. 4. Log all guest traffic to a SIEM.

title: Firewall: Executive Env: Personal IoT Devices Reachable from Corporate Network
description: Rules permit traffic to/from IP ranges or ports associated with consumer IoT devices (smart TVs, streaming, home assistants). These devices typically have poor security hygiene and no patch cadence.
impact: Nation-state actors routinely compromise executive IoT devices for intelligence gathering. Cross-segment access creates a pivot path to executive communications and data.
remediation_brief: 1. Create a dedicated IoT VLAN with no route to corporate. 2. Restrict IoT segment to internet-only with content filtering. 3. Block known IoT management ports (8883, 1883, 8888) from corporate. 4. Implement network access control (NAC) to enforce device placement.

title: Firewall: Executive Env: AV/Conferencing Ports Exposed Internally Without Restriction
description: Audio/visual and conferencing equipment ports (Crestron, AMX, Extron, Zoom Rooms hardware) are reachable from all internal segments. These devices are rarely patched and frequently have default credentials.
impact: AV equipment in executive boardrooms and conference rooms can be compromised via network access, enabling audio/video eavesdropping on confidential meetings.
remediation_brief: 1. Place AV equipment on a dedicated AV VLAN. 2. Restrict access to AV management ports to AV management workstations only. 3. Block Crestron (41794/41796), Extron (23/80), AMX (1319) from general users. 4. Enable logging on all rules touching the AV segment.

title: Broken Access Control: Executive Env: No Zero-Trust Access Control for VPN/Remote Access
description: Remote access to the executive environment relies on traditional VPN without identity-aware, device-posture-based controls. Executive accounts are high-value phishing targets.
impact: Compromised VPN credentials grant full network access without posture validation. Executive accounts with VPN access are primary targets for credential theft and phishing campaigns.
remediation_brief: 1. Implement zero-trust network access (ZTNA) for all executive remote connections. 2. Require MFA with phishing-resistant methods (FIDO2/hardware token) for all access. 3. Enforce device posture checks before granting access. 4. Log and alert on all executive remote access sessions.

title: Firewall: Executive Env: Logging Disabled on Rules Covering Executive Subnets
description: Permit rules covering identified executive subnets have logging disabled, creating a forensic blind spot in the highest-value segment of the network.
impact: Without logging on executive network segments, security teams cannot detect or investigate threats targeting the most sensitive users and data in the organisation.
remediation_brief: Enable logging on ALL rules that permit traffic to or from executive subnets. Route logs to immutable SIEM storage. Set alerts for anomalous connection patterns.

title: Firewall: Firewall Rule Permits Traffic to Known Malicious IP ({ip})
description: A firewall rule permits traffic with a source or destination address that is flagged as KNOWN MALICIOUS by multiple threat-intelligence sources. The IP is confirmed as malicious infrastructure (C2, botnet node, compromised host, or hijacked network).
impact: This rule allows network traffic to/from an IP address confirmed as malicious infrastructure. Active communication with this IP may indicate an ongoing compromise, data exfiltration, or command-and-control activity.
remediation_brief: 1. Immediately add a deny rule for the malicious IP above this permit rule. 2. Investigate firewall logs for any traffic to/from the IP. 3. If traffic occurred, treat as a potential incident — isolate affected hosts and begin forensic analysis. 4. Review the rule to determine if it can be narrowed.

title: Firewall: Firewall Rule Permits Traffic to Suspected Malicious IP ({ip})
description: A firewall rule permits traffic with a source or destination address flagged as SUSPECTED malicious by threat-intelligence sources. The IP has been observed in attack activity, scanning, or brute-force attempts but is not yet confirmed as malicious.
impact: This rule allows traffic to/from an IP reported as suspicious by multiple threat-intelligence sources. While not confirmed malicious, the IP has been observed in attack activity, scanning, or brute-force attempts. Permitting traffic increases exposure to potential threats.
remediation_brief: 1. Review whether traffic to/from the IP is expected and business-justified. 2. If not, add a deny rule above the permit. 3. Monitor traffic to/from the IP for anomalous patterns. 4. Subscribe to threat-intel updates for the IP.

title: Firewall: Firewall Rule Blocks Known Malicious IP ({ip})
description: A firewall rule correctly denies traffic with a source or destination address that is flagged as KNOWN MALICIOUS by threat-intelligence sources. The deny rule is actively blocking malicious traffic.
impact: Positive observation: the firewall is actively blocking traffic to/from a confirmed malicious IP. This indicates effective threat-intel integration in the firewall policy.
remediation_brief: No action required — the deny rule is correctly blocking the malicious IP. Ensure this rule remains in place and is not overridden by a broader permit rule above it in the policy.

title: Active Directory: Kerberoastable Accounts
description: {...} user account(s) have Service Principal Names (SPNs) set, making them vulnerable to Kerberoasting attacks. An attacker with any domain user credential can request TGS tickets for these accounts and crack them offline.
impact: Kerberoasting allows any authenticated domain user to request service tickets for SPN-bearing accounts and attempt offline password cracking. If the account password is weak, the attacker obtains the cleartext credential. Privileged service accounts (e.g., SQL service accounts in Domain Admins) are especially high-value targets.
remediation_brief: Set strong, complex passwords (25+ characters) on all accounts with SPNs. Migrate service accounts to Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) which rotate passwords automatically. Remove unnecessary SPNs. Monitor for anomalous TGS-REQ activity (Event ID 4769).

title: Active Directory: AS-REP Roastable Accounts
description: {...} account(s) have Kerberos pre-authentication disabled (DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH flag). These accounts are vulnerable to AS-REP roasting, allowing offline password cracking without any prior authentication.
impact: AS-REP roasting is more dangerous than Kerberoasting because it does not require any valid domain credentials to execute. An attacker can request encrypted AS-REP messages for these accounts from outside the domain and crack them offline. This is a common initial access technique in Active Directory attacks.
remediation_brief: Enable Kerberos pre-authentication on all accounts: clear the 'Do not require Kerberos preauthentication' checkbox in account properties. No legitimate scenario requires this flag for standard user accounts. Audit accounts regularly for this flag. Monitor for anomalous AS-REQ traffic (Event ID 4768 with pre-auth type 0).

title: Active Directory: Unconstrained Delegation
description: {...} non-domain-controller account(s) are configured for unconstrained Kerberos delegation. These systems can impersonate any user that authenticates to them, including domain administrators.
impact: Unconstrained delegation allows a compromised server to reuse any user's Kerberos TGT that was forwarded during authentication. An attacker who compromises a server with unconstrained delegation can capture domain admin TGTs and use them to fully compromise the domain. This is a critical privilege escalation path in Active Directory environments.
remediation_brief: Replace unconstrained delegation with constrained delegation or resource-based constrained delegation (RBCD). Add privileged accounts to the Protected Users group or mark them as 'Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated'. Only Domain Controllers should have unconstrained delegation.

title: Policy: Weak Domain Password Policy
description: The domain password policy does not meet security best practices. Minimum password length, complexity requirements, or password history may be insufficient, allowing users to set weak or commonly guessed passwords.
impact: A weak domain password policy applies to all domain user accounts. Short passwords without complexity requirements can be cracked rapidly via offline attacks against NTDS.dit or captured hashes. The domain password policy is the single most impactful password control in the environment.
remediation_brief: Increase minimum password length to 12+ characters (14+ for privileged accounts). Enable complexity requirements. Set maximum password age to 60-90 days. Enforce at least 12 passwords of history. Deploy Fine-Grained Password Policies (PSOs) for privileged tiers. Implement Azure AD Password Protection for banned password lists.

title: Active Directory: LDAP Signing Not Enforced
description: LDAP signing is set to '{...}' instead of 'Require signing'. This allows LDAP traffic to be transmitted unsigned, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks.
impact: Without enforced LDAP signing, an attacker can perform LDAP relay attacks, intercepting and modifying LDAP queries and responses. This can be used to escalate privileges, modify group memberships, or reset passwords via LDAP relay combined with NTLM relay techniques (e.g., ntlmrelayx).
remediation_brief: Set 'Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements' to 'Require signing' via Group Policy. Also enable LDAP channel binding. Test thoroughly before enforcement as it may break legacy applications using simple LDAP binds.

title: Authentication: Kerberos DES Encryption Enabled
description: The domain supports weak Kerberos encryption types: {...}. DES and RC4 are cryptographically broken and should not be used for Kerberos authentication.
impact: DES-encrypted Kerberos tickets can be cracked trivially. RC4-HMAC (NTLM-based) is vulnerable to Kerberoasting offline cracking and overpass-the-hash attacks. Allowing weak encryption types downgrades the security of the entire Kerberos infrastructure.
remediation_brief: Disable DES and RC4 encryption types in the domain. Set msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes to support only AES128 (0x08) and AES256 (0x10). Test thoroughly — legacy systems (especially pre-2008 R2) may require RC4. Migrate legacy systems before disabling.

title: Active Directory: RBCD Configured
description: {...} account(s) have Resource-Based Constrained Delegation configured (msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity). RBCD allows specified principals to impersonate users to the target service.
impact: RBCD is a common privilege escalation vector. If an attacker can write to the msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity attribute of a target (via WRITE permission on the computer object), they can configure RBCD to impersonate any user (including Domain Admin) to that target's services. This is the basis of the RBCD/S4U2Self/S4U2Proxy attack chain.
remediation_brief: Review all RBCD configurations for legitimacy. Ensure that only authorized principals have WRITE access to computer objects' msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity attribute. Monitor changes to this attribute via Event ID 5136. Remove unnecessary RBCD configurations.

title: Active Directory: Domain Functional Level Outdated
description: The Active Directory domain or forest functional level is below the current recommended level for the installed domain controller OS version. Outdated functional levels prevent the use of modern security features such as Protected Users group, Authentication Policies, and Kerberos armoring.
impact: Outdated functional levels prevent the use of modern Active Directory security features including: Protected Users group (2012 R2+), Authentication Policies and Silos (2012 R2+), gMSA improvements, Kerberos armoring (FAST), and AES-only Kerberos enforcement. Older levels also correspond to operating systems that may be end-of-life.
remediation_brief: Raise the domain and forest functional levels after ensuring all Domain Controllers are running a supported Windows Server version. This is a one-way operation — test in a lab environment first. Target at minimum Windows Server 2016 functional level.

title: Active Directory: AdminSDHolder Orphaned Accounts
description: {...} account(s) have AdminCount=1 set but are not current members of any privileged group. These are orphaned AdminSDHolder protections from former privilege.
impact: Orphaned AdminSDHolder flags indicate accounts that were previously in privileged groups. The AdminCount flag persists after removal, and the AdminSDHolder ACL propagation may have left non-standard permissions. Attackers target these accounts as they may retain residual privileges or weaker ACLs.
remediation_brief: Clear the AdminCount attribute on accounts no longer in privileged groups. Reset the ACL on these accounts to inherit from the parent OU. Use the AdminSDHolder cleanup script to automate this process. Monitor AdminCount changes with Event ID 5136.

title: Active Directory: LAPS Not Deployed
description: Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) is not deployed on this system or in the domain. Without LAPS, local administrator passwords are typically identical across all machines in the domain, or are never rotated, or both.
impact: Shared local administrator passwords are the single most common lateral movement enabler in Active Directory environments. If one machine is compromised and its local admin password is recovered (via SAM dump, mimikatz, or other means), the same password grants admin access to every other machine in the domain. LAPS solves this by setting a unique, randomly generated password on each machine and rotating it automatically.
remediation_brief: Deploy LAPS (or Windows LAPS in Server 2025/Windows 11). Steps: 1) Extend the AD schema for LAPS attributes (ms-Mcs-AdmPwd, ms-Mcs-AdmPwdExpirationTime or Windows LAPS equivalents), 2) Install the LAPS CSE (Client-Side Extension) via GPO or SCCM, 3) Configure the LAPS GPO with password complexity, length (14+ chars), and age (30 days), 4) Set ACLs on the OU to restrict who can read the LAPS password (authorized helpdesk/admin groups only).

title: Active Directory: krbtgt Key Not Rotated
description: The krbtgt account password has not been changed in an extended period (typically 180+ days). The krbtgt account is used to encrypt all Kerberos Ticket Granting Tickets (TGTs) in the domain. If its key material is compromised, an attacker can forge Golden Tickets.
impact: A compromised krbtgt key enables Golden Ticket attacks, granting the attacker unrestricted access to any resource in the domain for the lifetime of the key. Kerberos maintains two most-recent krbtgt key versions — rotating the password invalidates the oldest one. Microsoft recommends rotating the krbtgt password at least every 180 days, and immediately after any suspected domain compromise.

mitre_attack.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Golden Ticket

remediation_brief: Rotate the krbtgt password using the Microsoft krbtgt reset script or manually via PowerShell (Reset-KrbtgtPassword). IMPORTANT: The krbtgt password must be reset TWICE (with a sufficient interval between resets, at least equal to the maximum ticket lifetime — typically 10 hours) to invalidate all existing TGTs. Schedule regular rotation every 180 days. After a suspected compromise, reset immediately (twice).

title: Account Management: Stale Domain Accounts
description: Domain user accounts were found that have not logged in for an extended period (90+ days) and are still enabled. Stale accounts represent dormant attack surface that attackers can target without triggering alerts tied to active users.
impact: Stale accounts are attractive targets for attackers because their compromise is less likely to be noticed — no legitimate user will report unexpected activity. These accounts may retain their original (potentially weak) passwords, group memberships, and access permissions. If any stale account has privileged access, it presents an unmonitored path to escalation.
