remediation_brief: Implement a regular account review process (at least quarterly). Disable accounts inactive for 90+ days. Delete accounts inactive for 180+ days after confirming they are no longer needed. Automate with PowerShell: Search-ADAccount -AccountInactive -TimeSpan 90.00:00:00 | Disable-ADAccount. Audit disabled accounts for sensitive group memberships before deletion.

title: Active Directory: SID History Abuse Risk
description: User or group accounts with non-empty SID History attributes were found. SID History is a legitimate migration feature that preserves access to resources in a source domain after migration. However, SID History can be abused to inject arbitrary SIDs (including Domain Admins) into a user's token.
impact: An attacker who can modify the SID History attribute can inject the SID of a privileged group (e.g., Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins) into their own or another account's SID History. The injected SID is included in the user's Kerberos tickets and PAC, granting access to all resources the injected SID has permission to. This is a stealthy persistence technique because the user's group memberships appear normal.
remediation_brief: Audit all accounts with SID History: Get-ADUser -Filter 'SIDHistory -like "*"' -Properties SIDHistory | Select Name,SIDHistory. Remove SID History entries after domain migration is complete and verified: Set-ADUser -Identity <user> -Remove @{SIDHistory=<SID>}. Enable SID filtering on all trusts to prevent cross-domain SID History abuse. Monitor Event ID 4765 (SID History added) and Event ID 4766 (SID History add attempt failed).

title: Active Directory: LAPS Weak Password Policy
description: Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) is deployed but configured with a weak password policy. The password length is below 20 characters, complexity is not enforced, or the rotation interval exceeds 30 days.
impact: Weak LAPS configuration reduces the effectiveness of local admin password management. Short passwords can be brute-forced if the LAPS attribute is compromised. Long rotation intervals extend the window of exposure for a compromised password. Both undermine LAPS' purpose of limiting lateral movement via shared local admin credentials.
remediation_brief: Configure LAPS GPO with: password length >= 20 characters, complexity enabled (uppercase, lowercase, digits, special characters), and password age <= 30 days. Use the LAPS Configuration tab in Group Policy Management or configure via registry: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft Services\AdmPwd.

title: Active Directory: LAPS Password Readable by Non-Administrators
description: The LAPS managed password attribute (ms-Mcs-AdmPwd) is readable by accounts beyond the intended administrators. Non-admin groups or all authenticated users can read local admin passwords managed by LAPS.
impact: LAPS stores local admin passwords in a confidential AD attribute. If the ACL on this attribute grants read access to non-administrators, any compromised domain account can harvest local admin passwords for all LAPS-managed computers, enabling widespread lateral movement.
remediation_brief: Audit and restrict the ACL on the ms-Mcs-AdmPwd attribute. Use 'Find-AdmPwdExtendedRights' from the LAPS PowerShell module to identify which principals can read the attribute. Remove read permissions from all groups except designated LAPS administrators. Use Set-AdmPwdReadPasswordPermission to grant access only to specific admin groups.

title: Active Directory: Fine-Grained Password Policies Not Deployed
description: No Fine-Grained Password Policies (Password Settings Objects / PSOs) are defined in Active Directory. The domain relies solely on the Default Domain Policy for password requirements, which applies uniformly to all users regardless of their privilege level.
impact: Without FGPPs, privileged accounts (Domain Admins, service accounts, helpdesk staff) use the same password requirements as standard users. High-privilege accounts should have stronger password policies (longer minimums, shorter expiry). A single policy cannot adequately protect the most sensitive accounts.
remediation_brief: Create Fine-Grained Password Policies (PSOs) for privileged account tiers. At minimum, create a PSO for Domain Admins and Tier-0 service accounts requiring 20+ character passwords, and another for Tier-1 privileged users requiring 15+ characters. Use Active Directory Administrative Center or New-ADFineGrainedPasswordPolicy. Requires domain functional level 2008+.

title: Active Directory: Group Managed Service Accounts Not Utilized
description: No Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSAs) are deployed in this Active Directory domain. Service accounts are likely using traditional accounts with static, manually-managed passwords that may not be rotated regularly.
impact: Traditional service accounts with static passwords are prime targets for Kerberoasting, credential theft, and password spraying. gMSAs provide automatic 120-character password rotation managed by AD itself, eliminating the risk of stale service account passwords. Without gMSAs, service account compromise provides persistent access until the password is manually changed.
remediation_brief: Deploy Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSAs) to replace traditional service accounts. Prerequisites: create a KDS Root Key (Add-KdsRootKey), domain functional level 2012+. Create gMSAs via New-ADServiceAccount -DNSHostName ... -ManagedPasswordIntervalInDays 30 -PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword <group>. Migrate services to use gMSA accounts.

title: ADCS: ESC1 - Misconfigured Certificate Template
description: A certificate template allows enrollees to specify a Subject Alternative Name (SAN) in the certificate request, AND low-privileged users can enroll, AND the template has an EKU that permits authentication (Client Authentication, PKINIT, Smart Card Logon, or any purpose). This is the ESC1 attack vector identified by SpecterOps.
impact: Any low-privileged domain user can request a certificate with an arbitrary SAN (e.g., specifying a Domain Admin UPN). This certificate can then be used for Kerberos authentication as the impersonated user, achieving complete domain compromise without needing to know the target user's password. This is the most commonly exploited ADCS vulnerability.
remediation_brief: Disable 'Supply in the request' option on the Subject Name tab of vulnerable certificate templates. Instead, configure 'Build from Active Directory information'. Restrict enrollment permissions to only the users/groups that require the template. Remove unnecessary EKUs (especially 'Any Purpose'). Consider removing the template entirely if not operationally required. Audit with: certutil -v -template | findstr /i 'CT_FLAG_ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT'.

title: ADCS: ESC2 - Overly Permissive Template
description: A certificate template has an Extended Key Usage (EKU) of 'Any Purpose' (OID 2.5.29.37.0) or no EKU at all (which is equivalent to any purpose), AND low-privileged users can enroll. Certificates with Any Purpose or no EKU restrictions can be used for any purpose including client authentication, code signing, and subordinate CA issuance.
impact: A certificate with 'Any Purpose' or no EKU can be used for client authentication (impersonating any user), code signing (creating trusted malicious software), or even as a subordinate CA certificate (issuing arbitrary certificates). The combination of unrestricted EKU and broad enrollment permissions creates a powerful attack vector for domain compromise.
remediation_brief: Replace 'Any Purpose' EKU with specific, required EKUs only (e.g., Client Authentication only if that is the purpose). Remove templates with no EKU unless operationally justified. Restrict enrollment permissions to the minimum required groups. Audit all templates for overly broad EKU settings using certipy or Certutil.

title: ADCS: ESC3 - Enrollment Agent Template
description: A certificate template with the Certificate Request Agent EKU (OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.311.20.2.1) allows low-privileged users to enroll. An Enrollment Agent certificate enables the holder to request certificates on behalf of other users, including privileged accounts.
impact: An attacker can first obtain an Enrollment Agent certificate, then use it to request certificates for any other user in the domain (e.g., Domain Admins) using a second template that allows enrollment by enrollment agents. This two-step attack achieves domain compromise by impersonating any user via certificate-based authentication.
remediation_brief: Restrict enrollment permissions on Enrollment Agent templates to only authorized Certificate Enrollment administrators. Configure enrollment restrictions on the CA: right-click CA > Properties > Enrollment Agents tab to restrict which enrollment agents can enroll for which templates and users. Consider disabling the Enrollment Agent template if not operationally required.

title: ADCS: ESC4 - Vulnerable Template ACL
description: A certificate template's access control list (ACL) grants write permissions (WriteDACL, WriteOwner, WriteProperty, or GenericWrite) to low-privileged users or groups. This allows an attacker to modify the template configuration to introduce ESC1-ESC3 conditions.
impact: An attacker with write access to a certificate template can modify it to enable ESC1 (add CT_FLAG_ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT), change EKUs to 'Any Purpose', or enable enrollment for their own account. After modification, they exploit the newly created ESC1/ESC2/ESC3 condition for domain compromise. The template modification itself may go unnoticed without specific ADCS auditing.
remediation_brief: Audit all certificate template ACLs and remove write permissions for non-administrative groups. Only Enterprise Admins, Domain Admins, and designated PKI administrators should have write access to templates. Use: certutil -v -template | Select-String 'Allow.*Write'. Review and tighten ACLs via certtmpl.msc. Enable ADCS auditing to detect template modifications.

title: ADCS: ESC6 - EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2
description: The Certificate Authority has the EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 flag enabled. This CA-level configuration allows ANY certificate requester to specify an arbitrary Subject Alternative Name (SAN) in their request, regardless of template settings. This effectively makes every authentication template on this CA vulnerable to ESC1.
impact: With this flag enabled, any domain user who can enroll in any template with an authentication EKU can specify an arbitrary SAN, impersonating any user in the domain including Domain Admins. This is a CA-wide misconfiguration that bypasses per-template SAN controls — fixing individual templates does not mitigate this issue. A single CA with this flag compromises the entire domain.
remediation_brief: Disable the EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 flag on the CA: certutil -config "CA\CAName" -setreg policy\EditFlags -EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2. Restart the CA service: net stop certsvc && net start certsvc. Verify: certutil -config "CA\CAName" -getreg policy\EditFlags — the output should NOT include EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2. After disabling, audit all recently issued certificates for suspicious SAN values.

title: ADCS: ESC8 - NTLM Relay to HTTP Enrollment
description: The AD Certificate Services web enrollment endpoint is accessible over HTTP (not HTTPS) and/or does not enforce Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA). This allows NTLM relay attacks where a coerced machine account authentication (e.g., via PetitPotam, PrinterBug) can be relayed to the enrollment endpoint to request a certificate as the machine.
impact: An attacker can coerce a domain controller to authenticate to their machine (using PetitPotam, PrinterBug, or similar), then relay that authentication to the ADCS HTTP enrollment endpoint to obtain a certificate as the DC's machine account. This certificate allows the attacker to authenticate as the DC, enabling DCSync to extract all domain credentials. This is a full domain compromise path.
remediation_brief: Enable HTTPS on all ADCS web enrollment endpoints and disable HTTP. Enable Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA) in IIS: IIS Manager > Authentication > Windows Authentication > Advanced Settings > Extended Protection = Required. Alternatively, disable the web enrollment role entirely if not required and use certreq or autoenrollment instead. Install patches for PetitPotam (CVE-2021-36942). Enable NTLM relay mitigations: enable SMB signing, LDAP signing, and channel binding.

title: Browser: Malicious Extension Detected ({browser})
description: One or more browser extensions match known malicious extensions in the threat intelligence database. These extensions may be stealing credentials, injecting ads, or exfiltrating browsing data.
impact: Malicious browser extensions can intercept all web traffic including passwords, session tokens, banking credentials, and form data. They can inject content into pages, redirect searches, cryptomine, and exfiltrate browsing history. They persist across browser restarts and are often difficult for users to identify.
remediation_brief: Remove the malicious extension(s) immediately. Check other browsers on the system for the same extensions. Review browsing history for credential exposure. Force password resets for any accounts accessed while the extension was installed. Deploy browser extension whitelisting via Group Policy.

title: Browser: Proxy Configured ({browser})
description: A browser-level proxy configuration was detected, separate from system proxy settings. This proxy intercepts all browser traffic and may route it through an unintended intermediary.
impact: A browser-level proxy can intercept all HTTP/HTTPS traffic from the browser, including login credentials, session tokens, and sensitive data. Browser-level proxies may bypass system proxy settings, making them harder to detect. If the proxy is malicious, it enables credential theft and traffic manipulation.
remediation_brief: Verify the proxy configuration is authorized and expected. Compare with system proxy settings. If a browser-specific proxy is not required, remove it. Investigate whether malware or a malicious extension configured the proxy.

title: Browser: Suspicious Bookmark Detected ({browser})
description: One or more browser bookmarks link to domains or IPs associated with known malicious infrastructure in the threat intelligence database.
impact: Bookmarks to malicious domains may indicate the user regularly visits compromised or phishing sites. This could be a watering hole attack vector, a phishing landing page saved by a targeted user, or a bookmark planted by malware for persistence or redirection.
remediation_brief: Investigate each suspicious bookmark. Check if the user intentionally saved it or if it was created by malware. Review browser history for visits to the bookmarked URLs. Remove the bookmarks and block the domains at the DNS/proxy level. Scan the system for malware.

title: Certificate: Expired Certificate
description: One or more certificates in the local machine or current user certificate store have expired.
impact: Expired certificates cause service disruptions, authentication failures, and trust warnings. They may also indicate neglected systems or processes. Expired certificates used for code signing or SSL/TLS expose users to man-in-the-middle and substitution attacks.
remediation_brief: Renew or replace all expired certificates. Remove expired certificates that are no longer needed. Implement certificate lifecycle management with automated renewal alerts at 30, 14, and 7 days before expiry.

title: Certificate: Expiring Soon
description: One or more certificates will expire within the next 30 days.
impact: Certificates expiring soon risk service disruptions if not renewed in time. SSL/TLS certificate expiry causes browser warnings and connection failures. Authentication certificate expiry can lock out users.
remediation_brief: Renew expiring certificates before their expiry date. Use automated certificate management tools (ACME, internal CA auto-enrollment) where possible. Verify new certificates are properly installed and tested before the old ones expire.

title: Certificate: Self-Signed in Trust Store
description: Certificates using deprecated signature algorithms (SHA1) or insufficient key lengths (RSA < 2048 bits) were detected.
impact: SHA1 signatures are vulnerable to collision attacks, enabling certificate forgery. RSA keys shorter than 2048 bits can be factored with sufficient computational resources, compromising the certificate's security.
remediation_brief: Replace weak certificates with ones using SHA-256 or stronger signature algorithms and RSA 2048-bit or longer keys (or ECDSA P-256+). Update internal CA templates to enforce modern cryptographic standards.

title: Certificate: Weak Signature Algorithm
description: A self-signed certificate that is not from a well-known Certificate Authority was found in the Trusted Root Certification Authorities store.
impact: Unknown root certificates in the trusted store could enable man-in-the-middle attacks by allowing an attacker's CA to issue trusted certificates for any domain. This could be from legitimate enterprise CA deployment or from malware installing rogue roots.
remediation_brief: Review all non-standard root certificates. Verify each against the organization's internal CA infrastructure. Remove any certificates that cannot be accounted for. If a rogue root is found, investigate how it was installed and treat the system as potentially compromised.

title: Certificate: Weak Key Size
description: A certificate using a key size shorter than 2048 bits was detected. Keys shorter than 2048 bits are considered weak and can be factored with modern computing resources, compromising all protections the certificate provides.
impact: A weak key can be factored using distributed computing or cloud resources. 1024-bit RSA keys have been publicly factored, and NIST deprecated keys shorter than 2048 bits since 2013. An attacker who factors the key can forge signatures, decrypt traffic, and impersonate the certificate holder.
remediation_brief: Replace the certificate with one using at least a 2048-bit RSA key (3072-bit or 4096-bit recommended for long-lived certificates). For new deployments, consider ECDSA P-256 or P-384 keys which provide equivalent security at smaller sizes. Update the certificate on all services and endpoints.

title: Firewall: Profile Disabled
description: One or more Windows Firewall profiles (Domain, Private, or Public) are disabled, leaving network traffic unfiltered for those network types.
impact: With a firewall profile disabled, the system accepts all inbound connections on that network type, exposing services and ports that should be restricted. Attackers on the same network can directly reach services without firewall filtering.
remediation_brief: Develop a system hardening plan based on the CIS Benchmark for the specific Windows version. Prioritize Level 1 controls first as they have minimal operational impact. Implement changes through Group Policy for consistent deployment across endpoints.

title: Policy: Screen Lock Timeout Not Configured
description: The screen lock timeout (ScreenSaverGracePeriod or equivalent) is not configured or is set to a value greater than 15 minutes, allowing unattended sessions to remain accessible.
impact: Unattended workstations without automatic screen lock allow physical attackers to access active sessions with the authenticated user's full privileges, including domain credentials and cached tokens.
remediation_brief: Address the specific failing CIS controls, prioritizing those related to authentication, access control, and network security. Focus on Level 1 controls that have not been implemented. Use Group Policy to enforce configurations across the organization.

title: Network Hardening: NetBIOS over TCP/IP Enabled
description: NetBIOS over TCP/IP (NBT) is enabled on one or more network interfaces, exposing the legacy name resolution and session services on ports 137-139.
impact: NetBIOS enables name-squatting, NBNS poisoning, and session enumeration. Attackers on the local network can intercept name resolution queries to redirect traffic, harvest credentials via NTLM relay, and enumerate shares, users, and sessions.
remediation_brief: Remediate all DISA STIG Category I findings immediately. These represent the highest priority security issues. Apply STIG fixes via Group Policy or SCAP compliance tools. Document any findings requiring a Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) if immediate remediation is not possible.

title: Network Hardening: IPv6 Transition Technologies
description: IPv6 transition technologies (Teredo, ISATAP, 6to4) are enabled, creating encapsulated IPv6-over-IPv4 tunnels that may bypass network security controls.
impact: IPv6 transition protocols can tunnel traffic past IPv4-only firewalls and IDS/IPS systems. Attackers can use these tunnels for covert command-and-control channels or to bypass network segmentation. Teredo in particular operates over UDP and can traverse NAT.
remediation_brief: Plan remediation of DISA STIG Category II findings within 90 days. Prioritize those related to authentication and access control. Apply STIG fixes via Group Policy where possible for consistent deployment.

title: Service Hardening: Remote Registry Enabled
description: The Remote Registry service (RemoteRegistry) is enabled and/or running, allowing remote systems to read and modify the local Windows registry.
impact: Remote Registry access enables attackers with valid credentials to remotely query and modify registry keys for reconnaissance, persistence, and configuration changes. Attackers can read stored credentials, enumerate installed software, and plant persistence mechanisms without interactive logon.
remediation_brief: Use the hardening score as a baseline measurement and track improvements over time. Prioritize remediation of findings that contribute most to the score deficit. Establish a target hardening score and implement a continuous improvement program.

title: Credential Exposure: WiFi Passwords in Cleartext
description: Wireless network profiles on this system store passwords in cleartext. The 'netsh wlan show profiles key=clear' command can extract these credentials without elevated privileges on some Windows versions, or with local admin on others.
impact: An attacker with local access can extract stored WiFi passwords for all previously connected networks. These credentials may grant access to corporate wireless networks, enabling lateral movement or unauthorized network access from outside the physical premises.
remediation_brief: Configure WiFi profiles to not store passwords locally where possible. Use 802.1X/EAP certificate-based authentication instead of PSK. For WPA2-Personal/WPA3-Personal networks, limit local admin access and implement endpoint detection for credential harvesting tools. Remove saved profiles for networks no longer in use.

title: Credential Exposure: Saved Remote Sessions
description: Saved remote access session configurations were found on this system, potentially containing stored credentials. This includes PuTTY sessions (registry), WinSCP sessions (registry/ini), FileZilla sitemanager.xml entries, and/or saved .rdp files with password hashes.
impact: Stored remote session credentials provide an attacker with ready-made access paths to other systems. PuTTY and WinSCP may store passwords in reversible formats, FileZilla historically stored passwords in base64 (trivially decoded), and .rdp files may contain password hashes. Compromising these sessions enables lateral movement to additional hosts.
remediation_brief: Remove saved credentials from remote access tools. Configure PuTTY and WinSCP to use SSH key authentication instead of passwords. Delete FileZilla sitemanager.xml entries that contain passwords. Remove .rdp files with embedded credentials. Use a secrets manager or enterprise password vault for remote access credentials.

title: Credential Exposure: Credential Files on Disk
description: Files containing plaintext or easily reversible credentials were found on disk. This includes unattend.xml/autounattend.xml (deployment passwords), sysprep.xml/sysprep.inf files, web.config connection strings, applicationHost.config bindings, and/or McAfee SiteList.xml files.
impact: These files often contain local administrator passwords, database connection strings, service account credentials, or encryption keys in cleartext or trivially reversible formats. An attacker can use these credentials for privilege escalation, database access, or lateral movement. Deployment files (unattend.xml) frequently contain the initial administrator password used during Windows installation.
remediation_brief: Remove or securely delete all deployment files (unattend.xml, sysprep.xml) after provisioning. Encrypt connection strings in web.config using aspnet_regiis -pe. Replace cleartext passwords in applicationHost.config with encrypted alternatives. Audit the file system for credential remnants periodically using endpoint detection rules.

title: Credential Exposure: GPP cpassword Exposure
description: Group Policy Preferences (GPP) XML files containing the 'cpassword' attribute were found in SYSVOL. Microsoft published the AES-256 key used to encrypt these passwords in MSDN documentation, making all cpassword values trivially decryptable by any domain user.
impact: Any authenticated domain user can read SYSVOL and decrypt GPP passwords using the publicly known AES key. These passwords typically belong to local administrator accounts, service accounts, or scheduled task accounts configured via Group Policy. This is a well-known, trivially exploitable vulnerability that provides immediate privilege escalation in most Active Directory environments.
remediation_brief: Install MS14-025 (KB2962486) which prevents creation of new GPP passwords. Delete all existing GPP XML files in SYSVOL that contain cpassword attributes. Rotate all passwords that were stored in GPP. Migrate to LAPS or gMSA for local administrator password management. Search SYSVOL: Get-ChildItem -Path '\\domain\SYSVOL' -Recurse -Include Groups.xml,Services.xml,Scheduledtasks.xml,DataSources.xml,Printers.xml,Drives.xml | Select-String 'cpassword'.

title: Credential Exposure: Cloud Credential Files
description: Cloud provider credential files were found on this system. This includes AWS credentials (~/.aws/credentials), Azure profiles (~/.azure/), and/or GCP service account key JSON files. These files contain access keys, tokens, or private keys that authenticate to cloud services.
impact: Compromised cloud credentials can grant an attacker access to cloud infrastructure, including compute instances, storage buckets, databases, and IAM controls. Depending on the permissions associated with the credentials, this can lead to data exfiltration, resource hijacking (cryptomining), or full cloud account compromise. Cloud credentials are frequently over-provisioned with excessive permissions.
remediation_brief: Remove long-lived cloud credential files from endpoints. Use short-lived tokens via IAM roles, instance profiles, or managed identities instead. For development machines, use aws-vault, Azure CLI managed identity, or workload identity federation. Rotate any credentials that were stored on disk. Implement cloud credential scanning in CI/CD pipelines.

title: Credential Exposure: Credential Manager Entries
description: Windows Credential Manager (Vault) contains stored credential entries. These may include web credentials, Windows credentials for network shares, and application-specific credentials protected by DPAPI.
impact: While Credential Manager entries are protected by DPAPI (tied to the user's logon session), they can be decrypted by any process running as that user. If an attacker gains user-level access, they can extract all Vault credentials using tools like mimikatz or built-in vaultcmd commands. This finding is informational — the presence of stored credentials is expected behavior.

mitre_attack.name: Credentials from Password Stores: Windows Credential Manager

remediation_brief: Review stored credentials periodically and remove entries for systems or services no longer accessed. Educate users not to save domain credentials in Credential Manager for sensitive systems. Implement Credential Guard to protect LSASS-derived credentials from extraction.

title: Credential Exposure: DPAPI Master Key Accessible
description: DPAPI (Data Protection API) master key material was found to be accessible on this system. DPAPI protects user credentials, browser passwords, WiFi keys, and other sensitive data. If an attacker can access the master key or derive it from the user's password, all DPAPI-protected secrets can be decrypted.
impact: DPAPI is the underlying encryption mechanism for Windows Credential Manager, browser saved passwords (Chrome, Edge), WiFi passwords, and many application secrets. An attacker with access to the DPAPI master key (stored in %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Protect\) and knowledge of the user's password can decrypt all DPAPI-protected data, providing access to a wide range of stored credentials.

mitre_attack.name: Credentials from Password Stores: Windows Credential Manager

remediation_brief: Implement Credential Guard to protect DPAPI master keys with virtualization-based security. Enforce strong passwords to make DPAPI key derivation computationally expensive. Restrict local admin access to limit offline DPAPI attacks. Use hardware-backed credential storage (TPM, smart cards) for the most sensitive credentials.

title: Credential Exposure: KeePass Database Found
description: KeePass password database files (.kdbx) were found on this system. While KeePass databases are encrypted, their presence indicates this system stores a password vault that may be targeted by attackers for credential harvesting.
impact: KeePass databases, if protected by a weak master password, can be cracked offline. CVE-2023-32784 demonstrated that KeePass master passwords could be recovered from process memory. Additionally, KeePass plugin loading, trigger mechanisms, and configuration file manipulation have been used for credential theft. The database itself is a high-value target for exfiltration.

mitre_attack.name: Credentials from Password Stores: Password Managers

remediation_brief: Ensure KeePass databases use strong master passwords (20+ characters) combined with key files. Keep KeePass updated to the latest version. Restrict KeePass plugin loading to signed/approved plugins. Consider migrating to an enterprise password manager with centralized audit logging and MFA enforcement.

title: Credential Exposure: SSH Private Keys Found
description: SSH private key files were found on this system. These keys may provide passwordless authentication to remote systems (Linux servers, network devices, cloud instances). Keys without passphrases are immediately usable by anyone who can read them.
impact: SSH private keys provide direct authentication to remote systems without requiring a password. If a key has no passphrase (or a weak one), an attacker can immediately use it for lateral movement. Keys in authorized_keys on target systems often have broad permissions. A single compromised SSH key can provide access to many systems in the environment.
remediation_brief: Ensure all SSH private keys are protected with strong passphrases. Use ssh-agent for key caching rather than storing unprotected keys. Implement SSH certificate-based authentication for managed environments. Audit and rotate SSH keys regularly. Remove keys for systems no longer accessed. Consider hardware-backed keys (FIDO2/PIV).

title: Credential Exposure: Auto-Logon Credentials in Registry
description: Windows auto-logon is enabled via the AutoAdminLogon registry key. When DefaultPassword is present in the Winlogon registry key, the password is stored in cleartext and readable by any local user. Even without DefaultPassword, auto-logon credentials stored in LSA Secrets can be extracted with administrative access.
impact: Auto-logon credentials allow anyone with physical or remote console access to bypass the Windows login screen entirely. When DefaultPassword is set in the registry, any local user or process can read the plaintext password. Even without a visible password, auto-logon stored in LSA Secrets can be extracted with tools like Mimikatz.
remediation_brief: Disable auto-logon by setting AutoAdminLogon to 0 and removing DefaultPassword from HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon. If auto-logon is required for kiosk scenarios, use Autologon.exe from Sysinternals (encrypts the password in LSA Secrets) and restrict physical/remote access to the system.

title: Event Log: Brute Force Attack Detected
description: Brute-force login activity detected with multiple failed authentication attempts from the same source within the past 7 days. Sources with more than 10 failures indicate automated credential guessing attacks targeting the system.
impact: Sustained brute-force attacks may eventually succeed, especially against accounts with weak or reused passwords. Successful compromise grants the attacker interactive access to the system and may lead to lateral movement, privilege escalation, and data exfiltration.
remediation_brief: Implement account lockout policies (5-10 attempts), enable multi-factor authentication, and block offending source IPs at the firewall. Investigate targeted accounts for compromise indicators. Consider implementing Azure AD Smart Lockout for adaptive protection.

title: Event Log: Account Lockouts Detected
description: Account lockout events (Event ID 4740) were detected in the security event log, indicating accounts are being locked due to repeated failed authentication. Lockouts may be caused by brute-force attacks, misconfigured services, or stale cached credentials.
impact: Account lockouts from brute-force attempts confirm active credential attacks against the system. Service account lockouts can cause application outages and business disruption.
remediation_brief: Investigate the source of lockouts for each affected account. For user accounts, verify no credential compromise occurred. For service accounts, check for stale cached credentials in scheduled tasks, services, or mapped drives. Consider migrating to Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA).

title: Event Log: Security Log Cleared
description: Event log clearing events detected (Event ID 1102/104). Clearing security logs destroys forensic evidence and is a strong indicator of attacker activity or insider threat attempting to cover their tracks.
impact: Cleared security logs eliminate the audit trail of authentication events, privilege escalation, and policy changes, preventing incident investigation and regulatory compliance verification. This is a common anti-forensics technique.
owasp_web: A09:2021 - Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
remediation_brief: Investigate the account that cleared the logs for compromise. Configure event log forwarding to a SIEM to preserve logs centrally. Restrict log management permissions to dedicated admin accounts. Enable alerting on Event ID 1102.

title: Event Log: Suspicious PowerShell Activity
description: PowerShell events contain suspicious patterns including encoded commands (-EncodedCommand), download cradles (Invoke-WebRequest/IEX), AMSI bypass attempts, or known offensive tool invocations such as Mimikatz or PowerView.
impact: Suspicious PowerShell activity may indicate post-exploitation activity, malware execution, or attacker reconnaissance. PowerShell is the most commonly abused living-off-the-land tool on Windows systems.
remediation_brief: Investigate each suspicious PowerShell event. Check the executing user and originating process. Enable PowerShell ScriptBlock Logging, Transcription, and Constrained Language Mode. Consider deploying AppLocker or WDAC to restrict PowerShell usage to authorized administrators.

title: Event Log: New Service Installations
description: New service installation events (Event ID 7045/4697) recorded in event logs. Service installations are a common persistence mechanism used by malware and attackers to maintain access that survives reboots.
impact: Attackers install malicious services to maintain persistent access. Services run with elevated privileges and can be configured to start automatically, ensuring the attacker's code runs at every boot.
owasp_web: A09:2021 - Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
remediation_brief: Review each new service installation for legitimacy. Verify the service executable path, signing status, and the account used for installation. Remove unauthorized services and investigate how they were installed.

title: Event Log: User Account Created
description: User account creation events (Event ID 4720) detected in security event logs. Account creation outside of normal provisioning workflows may indicate persistence or unauthorized access by an attacker.
impact: Attackers create local accounts to maintain persistent access. Unauthorized accounts may be added to privileged groups to escalate privileges and maintain a foothold on the compromised system.
owasp_web: A09:2021 - Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
remediation_brief: Verify each account creation was authorized through the proper provisioning workflow. Remove unauthorized accounts. Monitor for group membership changes (Event ID 4732) on newly created accounts.

title: System Hardening: UAC Disabled
description: User Account Control (UAC) is completely disabled on this endpoint. The registry value EnableLUA under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System is set to 0.
impact: All applications run with full administrative privileges without prompting. Malware and exploit payloads execute with elevated privileges immediately upon infection, greatly increasing the severity of any compromise.
remediation_brief: Re-enable UAC by setting the EnableLUA registry value to 1 at HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System. Set ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin to at least 2 (prompt for consent on secure desktop). Apply via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > User Account Control.

title: System Hardening: UAC Prompt Behavior Weak
description: The UAC elevation prompt for administrators is configured to auto-elevate without prompting (ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin is 0) or to prompt on a non-secure desktop.
impact: Weak UAC prompt settings allow malware to silently elevate privileges through auto-elevation or intercept elevation prompts on the interactive desktop, enabling privilege escalation without user awareness.
remediation_brief: Configure ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin to 2 (prompt for consent on the secure desktop) via Group Policy or registry. Also ensure PromptOnSecureDesktop is set to 1 to prevent interception of the elevation dialog by malicious software.

title: Network Hardening: SMBv1 Protocol Enabled
description: The deprecated SMBv1 protocol is enabled on this endpoint, either as a server or client component.
impact: SMBv1 has known critical vulnerabilities including EternalBlue (MS17-010) and lacks modern security features. It enables remote code execution, credential relay attacks, and was the primary propagation vector for WannaCry and NotPetya ransomware.
remediation_brief: Disable SMBv1 by running: Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol. For Server: Remove-WindowsFeature FS-SMB1. Alternatively set HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters\SMB1 to 0. Verify no legacy applications or devices require SMBv1 before disabling.

title: System Hardening: SMB Signing Not Required
description: SMB message signing is not required on this endpoint, allowing unsigned SMB communications.
impact: Without mandatory SMB signing, an attacker in a man-in-the-middle position can intercept and modify SMB traffic, perform relay attacks (NTLM relay), and hijack authenticated SMB sessions to access file shares or execute commands on other systems.
remediation_brief: Enable mandatory SMB signing by setting RequireSecuritySignature to 1 at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters and LanmanWorkstation\Parameters. Apply via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > Microsoft network server/client: Digitally sign communications (always).

title: Authentication: NTLMv1 Authentication Allowed
description: The LAN Manager authentication level allows NTLMv1 responses, a weak authentication protocol that is trivially crackable.
impact: NTLMv1 hashes can be cracked in seconds using rainbow tables or GPU-accelerated attacks, exposing user passwords. An attacker capturing NTLMv1 traffic on the network can recover plaintext credentials for lateral movement.
remediation_brief: Set LmCompatibilityLevel to 5 (Send NTLMv2 response only. Refuse LM & NTLM) at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa. Apply via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > Network security: LAN Manager authentication level. Test thoroughly as legacy devices may require NTLMv1.

title: Authentication: LM Password Hashes Stored
description: The system is configured to store LAN Manager (LM) hash values for passwords, a severely weak hash format.
impact: LM hashes split passwords into two 7-character halves, are case-insensitive, and use DES without salt. They can be cracked in minutes even for complex passwords, giving an attacker who obtains the SAM database or captures authentication traffic immediate access to plaintext passwords.
remediation_brief: Set NoLMHash to 1 at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa to prevent storage of LM hashes. Apply via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > Network security: Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change. Force all users to change passwords after enabling.

title: System Hardening: AutoRun Enabled
description: AutoRun/AutoPlay is enabled, allowing automatic execution of programs from removable media and network drives.
impact: Malware can be automatically executed when a USB drive, CD/DVD, or network share is accessed. This is a classic initial access vector used by worms (Conficker) and targeted attacks using planted USB devices.
remediation_brief: Set NoDriveTypeAutoRun to 255 (0xFF) at HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\Explorer to disable AutoRun on all drive types. Apply via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > AutoPlay Policies > Turn off Autoplay (All drives).

title: Credential Exposure: WDigest Plaintext Credentials
description: WDigest authentication is configured to store plaintext credentials in memory (UseLogonCredential set to 1 at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest).
impact: An attacker who achieves local administrator access can use tools like Mimikatz to extract plaintext passwords from LSASS process memory for all currently logged-in users, including domain administrators. This enables immediate lateral movement without any cracking.
remediation_brief: Set UseLogonCredential to 0 at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest. On Windows 8.1/Server 2012 R2 and later with KB2871997 installed, WDigest plaintext caching is disabled by default. Verify the registry value is explicitly set to 0 to prevent re-enablement by malware.

title: System Hardening: LSA Protection Not Enabled
description: Local Security Authority (LSA) protection is not enabled. The RunAsPPL registry value is not set to 1 at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa.
impact: Without LSA protection, the LSASS process can be accessed by any process running as local administrator. Attackers can dump credentials from LSASS memory using standard tools, bypassing most endpoint security controls.
remediation_brief: Enable LSA protection by setting RunAsPPL to 1 at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa. A system restart is required. Test application compatibility first as some security products may not function with PPL enabled. On Windows 11 22H2+, LSA protection is enabled by default.

title: System Hardening: Credential Guard Not Enabled
description: Windows Defender Credential Guard (Virtualization Based Security for credential isolation) is not enabled on this endpoint.
impact: Without Credential Guard, NTLM hashes and Kerberos TGTs stored in LSASS memory can be extracted by tools running as local administrator. Credential Guard isolates these secrets in a hardware-backed virtual enclave that even kernel-level attackers cannot access.
remediation_brief: Enable Credential Guard by setting EnableVirtualizationBasedSecurity to 1 at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\DeviceGuard and RequirePlatformSecurityFeatures to 1 or 3. Prerequisites: UEFI firmware, Secure Boot, TPM 2.0, and 64-bit Windows 10/11 Enterprise or Server 2016+. Apply via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > System > Device Guard.

title: Network Hardening: LLMNR Enabled
description: Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution (LLMNR) is enabled, allowing unauthenticated name resolution on the local network.
impact: An attacker on the local network can respond to LLMNR queries to capture NTLMv2 hashes from connecting clients using tools like Responder. These hashes can be cracked offline or relayed to other services for unauthorized access.
remediation_brief: Disable LLMNR via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Network > DNS Client > Turn off multicast name resolution. Set EnableMulticast to 0 at HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\DNSClient. Ensure proper DNS infrastructure is in place as a replacement.

title: Network Hardening: WPAD Enabled
description: Web Proxy Auto-Discovery (WPAD) protocol is enabled, allowing automatic proxy configuration via DNS or DHCP.
impact: An attacker can poison WPAD queries via LLMNR/NBNS or rogue DHCP to redirect all HTTP traffic through a malicious proxy, enabling credential interception, session hijacking, and man-in-the-middle attacks on all web traffic.
remediation_brief: Disable the WinHTTP Auto-Proxy Service (WinHttpAutoProxySvc) and set its startup to Disabled. In Internet Options, uncheck 'Automatically detect settings'. If proxy auto-configuration is needed, use explicit PAC file URLs rather than WPAD discovery.

title: Monitoring: PowerShell Script Block Logging Disabled
description: PowerShell script block logging is not enabled, preventing the recording of PowerShell script content in Windows Event Logs.
impact: Without script block logging, PowerShell-based attacks (obfuscated download cradles, in-memory execution, AMSI bypasses) leave no forensic evidence. Incident response teams cannot determine what malicious PowerShell commands were executed.
owasp_web: A09:2021 - Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
remediation_brief: Enable PowerShell script block logging via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows PowerShell > Turn on PowerShell Script Block Logging. Set EnableScriptBlockLogging to 1 at HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging.

title: Monitoring: PowerShell Module Logging Disabled
description: PowerShell module logging is not enabled, which would record pipeline execution details for specified modules.
impact: Module logging provides a detailed record of which PowerShell cmdlets and functions were invoked. Without it, forensic investigators have reduced visibility into the specific operations performed during an attack.
owasp_web: A09:2021 - Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
remediation_brief: Enable PowerShell module logging via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows PowerShell > Turn on Module Logging. Configure the module names to log (use * for all modules).

title: Monitoring: PowerShell Transcription Disabled
description: PowerShell transcription (recording of all PowerShell input and output to text files) is not enabled.
impact: Transcription provides a complete record of interactive and scripted PowerShell sessions including output. Without it, defenders lose a valuable forensic data source for investigating PowerShell-based attacks.
owasp_web: A09:2021 - Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
remediation_brief: Enable PowerShell transcription via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows PowerShell > Turn on PowerShell Transcription. Configure the output directory to a secured file share for centralized collection. Ensure adequate disk space and proper NTFS permissions on the transcript directory.

title: System Hardening: PowerShell v2 Engine Available
description: The PowerShell v2 engine is still installed as a Windows feature, providing a downgrade path that bypasses modern logging and security controls.
impact: Attackers can invoke PowerShell v2 (powershell -version 2) to bypass AMSI, script block logging, constrained language mode, and other security features that only exist in PowerShell v5+. This is a well-documented defense evasion technique.
remediation_brief: Remove the PowerShell v2 engine: Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName MicrosoftWindowsPowerShellV2Root. For Server: Remove-WindowsFeature PowerShell-V2. Verify no applications depend on PowerShell v2 before removal.

title: Endpoint Protection: Windows Defender Disabled
description: Windows Defender Antivirus is completely disabled or not running on this endpoint with no alternative antimalware solution detected.
impact: Without antimalware protection, all known malware including commodity threats, ransomware, and trojans can execute without detection. The system has no real-time file scanning, web filtering, or behavior monitoring.
remediation_brief: Re-enable Windows Defender by removing any Group Policy that disables it (DisableAntiSpyware registry key), starting the WinDefend service, and ensuring real-time protection is turned on. If a third-party antivirus is intended, verify it is properly installed and running. Ensure at minimum one antimalware solution is active at all times.

title: Endpoint Protection: Defender Exclusions Present
description: Windows Defender has file, folder, process, or extension exclusions configured that exempt certain paths or processes from scanning.
impact: Attackers frequently target known exclusion paths to stage and execute malware. Common exclusion paths like temp directories, development folders, or application paths become safe havens for malicious payloads that will never be scanned.
remediation_brief: Review all Windows Defender exclusions and remove any that are not strictly necessary for application compatibility. Document the business justification for each remaining exclusion. Avoid broad exclusions (entire drives, common directories). Monitor excluded paths for suspicious file creation via separate detection mechanisms.

title: Endpoint Protection: Defender Real-Time Protection Off
description: Windows Defender is installed but real-time protection is turned off, leaving the system without active file scanning.
impact: Files downloaded, copied, or created are not scanned until a manual or scheduled scan occurs. Malware can execute immediately upon arrival without triggering any detection, potentially running for hours or days before a scheduled scan.
remediation_brief: Enable real-time protection in Windows Security settings or via PowerShell: Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $false. If Group Policy is preventing this, update the policy to allow real-time protection. Verify protection is active with Get-MpComputerStatus.

title: Remote Desktop: RDP Without NLA
description: Remote Desktop Protocol is enabled without requiring Network Level Authentication (NLA), allowing unauthenticated users to reach the RDP login screen.
impact: Without NLA, attackers can establish RDP sessions without credentials, consuming server resources (DoS) and reaching the Windows login screen where they can attempt credential attacks. This also exposes the system to pre-authentication RDP vulnerabilities like BlueKeep.
remediation_brief: Enable NLA for Remote Desktop by setting UserAuthentication to 1 at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp. Apply via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Remote Desktop Services > Remote Desktop Session Host > Security > Require user authentication for remote connections by using Network Level Authentication.

title: System Hardening: DEP Not System-Wide
description: Data Execution Prevention (DEP) is not configured to protect all programs, only essential Windows programs and services.
impact: Without system-wide DEP, buffer overflow exploits can execute shellcode in data memory regions. DEP prevents code execution from non-executable memory pages, making many common exploitation techniques significantly harder.
remediation_brief: Configure DEP to protect all programs by running: bcdedit /set nx AlwaysOn. Alternatively, configure via System Properties > Advanced > Performance Settings > Data Execution Prevention > Turn on DEP for all programs and services except those I select. Add specific exceptions only for applications that are confirmed incompatible.

title: Access Control: Anonymous Named Pipe Access
description: Anonymous (null session) access to named pipes is permitted, allowing unauthenticated users to connect to specific named pipes on the system.
impact: Attackers can enumerate sensitive information through named pipes without authentication, including user lists, group memberships, share lists, and security policies. This information aids in planning targeted credential attacks and privilege escalation.
remediation_brief: Clear the NullSessionPipes registry value at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters and set RestrictNullSessAccess to 1. Apply via Group Policy: Network access: Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares (Enabled).

title: Access Control: Null Session Access
description: The system allows null session (anonymous) connections for SAM enumeration and share enumeration.
impact: Attackers can connect without credentials to enumerate all user accounts, groups, and network shares. This provides a complete map of the attack surface and user accounts to target for password spraying or brute force attacks.
remediation_brief: Set RestrictAnonymousSAM to 1 and RestrictAnonymous to 1 at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa. Apply via Group Policy: Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts (Enabled) and Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares (Enabled).

title: Policy: Audit Policy Insufficient
description: The Windows audit policy does not log critical security events. Key audit categories such as logon events, privilege use, object access, or policy changes are not configured for success and/or failure auditing.
impact: Without comprehensive audit logging, security incidents go undetected and uninvestigated. Login attempts, privilege escalation, file access, and policy changes occur without any record, severely impacting incident response and forensic capabilities.
owasp_web: A09:2021 - Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
remediation_brief: Configure advanced audit policy via Group Policy to log at minimum: Logon/Logoff (Success+Failure), Account Logon (Success+Failure), Privilege Use (Success+Failure), Object Access (Failure), Policy Change (Success+Failure), System (Success+Failure). Use auditpol to verify: auditpol /get /category:*.

title: Service Hardening: Print Spooler Running
description: The Print Spooler service is running on a server where printing functionality is likely not required.
impact: The Print Spooler service has been the target of multiple critical vulnerabilities including PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-34527) enabling remote code execution and privilege escalation. Running it on servers unnecessarily increases the attack surface.
remediation_brief: Disable the Print Spooler service on servers that do not need printing: Stop-Service -Name Spooler -Force; Set-Service -Name Spooler -StartupType Disabled. On domain controllers, the Spooler should always be disabled as it exposes the DC to coercion attacks via the MS-RPRN protocol.

title: Endpoint Protection: Application Whitelisting Not Configured
description: Neither AppLocker nor Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) is configured on this system. Without application whitelisting, any executable, script, or DLL can run without restriction.
impact: Without application control, an attacker can execute arbitrary malware, scripts, and tools on the system without restriction. Application whitelisting is consistently rated as one of the most effective endpoint security controls by ACSC Essential Eight, NIST, and CIS. Its absence significantly increases the attack surface for malware execution, lateral movement tools, and post-exploitation frameworks.
remediation_brief: Implement AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC). Start in audit mode to identify legitimate applications, then switch to enforce mode. At minimum, implement script rules to block unauthorized script execution. For WDAC: create a base policy with Microsoft recommended block rules, then supplement with organization-specific allow rules. For AppLocker: configure default rules plus explicit allow rules for approved applications.

title: System Hardening: HVCI Not Enabled
description: Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity (HVCI / Memory Integrity) is not enabled on this system. HVCI uses virtualization-based security (VBS) to protect the Windows kernel code integrity verification process, preventing kernel-mode code injection and driver-based attacks.
impact: Without HVCI, the kernel is vulnerable to code injection attacks via malicious drivers, kernel exploits, and rootkits. HVCI prevents unsigned or improperly signed kernel-mode code from executing, significantly raising the bar for kernel-level attacks. Its absence leaves the system vulnerable to bootkit/rootkit installations and kernel-mode exploit payloads.
remediation_brief: Enable HVCI via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > System > Device Guard > Turn On Virtualization Based Security > Virtualization Based Protection of Code Integrity = Enabled with UEFI lock. Alternatively, enable via Windows Security > Device Security > Core isolation > Memory integrity. Prerequisites: compatible CPU with virtualization extensions (Intel VT-x/AMD-V), UEFI firmware, Secure Boot enabled.

title: System Hardening: CredSSP Delegation Enabled
description: Credential Security Support Provider (CredSSP) delegation is enabled, allowing this system to forward user credentials to remote servers. The AllowFreshCredentials or AllowFreshCredentialsDomain policies permit credential delegation to specified or all remote hosts.
impact: CredSSP delegation sends the user's cleartext credentials to the remote server. If the remote server is compromised, these credentials are immediately available to the attacker. CredSSP delegation to '*' (all servers) is especially dangerous as it enables credential forwarding to any host, including attacker-controlled machines. This defeats the purpose of Restricted Admin mode and other credential protection mechanisms.

mitre_attack.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Application Access Token

remediation_brief: Disable CredSSP delegation via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > System > Credentials Delegation > Allow delegating fresh credentials = Disabled. If CredSSP is required for specific administrative tasks, restrict delegation to specific trusted servers only (never use '*'). Apply CVE-2018-0886 patches. Consider using Remote Credential Guard instead of CredSSP for RDP sessions.

title: Endpoint Protection: AMSI Not Registered
description: No Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) provider is registered on this system. AMSI is a Windows interface that allows applications to send content (scripts, macro code, .NET assemblies) to the installed antimalware solution for scanning before execution.
impact: Without AMSI, script-based attacks (PowerShell, VBScript, JScript, .NET) can execute malicious code without real-time scanning. AMSI is the primary defense against fileless malware, obfuscated scripts, and in-memory attacks. Its absence or deregistration is a common attacker technique (T1562.001) to disable defenses before deploying payloads.

mitre_attack.name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools

remediation_brief: Verify that Windows Defender or a third-party antimalware solution with AMSI support is installed and active. Check AMSI provider registration: reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\AMSI\Providers" /s. If no providers are listed, reinstall or re-register the antimalware solution. If AMSI was deliberately tampered with, investigate as a potential compromise indicator.

title: System Hardening: .NET Framework v2/v3.5 Installed
description: .NET Framework version 2.0 or 3.5 is installed on this system. These legacy .NET versions include the CLR v2 runtime which has weaker security controls than CLR v4 and can be leveraged by attackers to bypass application-level security restrictions.
impact: The .NET CLR v2 runtime can be invoked by PowerShell v2 and other tools to bypass AMSI, script block logging, constrained language mode, and other security controls that are only enforced in CLR v4. Attackers specifically target legacy .NET to downgrade the runtime and evade security monitoring. If .NET 2.0/3.5 is not required by any application, it represents unnecessary attack surface.
remediation_brief: Remove .NET Framework 3.5 (includes 2.0 and 3.0) if no application requires it: Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName NetFx3. On Server: Remove-WindowsFeature NET-Framework-Core. Before removing, verify no application dependencies by auditing installed software and testing in a pre-production environment.

title: System Hardening: PS Constrained Language Not Enforced
description: PowerShell is running in Full Language Mode rather than Constrained Language Mode (CLM). Full Language Mode allows unrestricted access to .NET types, COM objects, and Win32 APIs, enabling powerful post-exploitation capabilities.
impact: Full Language Mode enables attackers to load arbitrary .NET assemblies, invoke Win32 APIs via P/Invoke or Add-Type, create COM objects, and execute complex exploitation frameworks (Invoke-Mimikatz, PowerView, etc.) entirely in memory. Constrained Language Mode blocks these capabilities while preserving administrative scripting functionality.
remediation_brief: Enforce Constrained Language Mode via WDAC/AppLocker code integrity policies (the most robust method — CLM activates automatically when UMCI is enforced). Alternatively, set the __PSLockdownPolicy environment variable to 4 (system-wide), though this is less robust than WDAC enforcement. Test with administrative scripts first — CLM restricts .NET and COM access that some admin scripts require.

title: System Hardening: ASR Rules Not Configured
description: Windows Defender Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules are not configured or are set to audit-only mode. ASR rules block specific behaviors commonly used by malware, such as Office macros creating child processes, obfuscated scripts, credential theft from LSASS, and untrusted USB process execution.
impact: Without ASR rules, the system lacks behavioral protection against common attack techniques: Office macro malware, script-based attacks, credential dumping, ransomware file encryption patterns, and lateral movement techniques. ASR rules are one of the most effective free security controls available on Windows 10/11 and Server 2016+.
remediation_brief: Enable ASR rules via Group Policy or Intune. Recommended rules to enable in block mode: Block Office apps from creating child processes (D4F940AB-401B-4EFC-AADC-AD5F3C50688A), Block credential stealing from LSASS (9e6c4e1f-7d60-472f-ba1a-a39ef669e4b2), Block executable content from email/webmail (BE9BA2D9-53EA-4CDC-84E5-9B1EEEE46550), Use advanced protection against ransomware (c1db55ab-c21a-4637-bb3f-a12568109d35). Start in audit mode for 2 weeks, then switch to block.

title: Endpoint Protection: Controlled Folder Access Not Enabled
description: Windows Defender Controlled Folder Access is not enabled. This feature protects designated folders (Documents, Desktop, Pictures, etc.) from unauthorized modification by untrusted applications, serving as anti-ransomware protection.
impact: Without Controlled Folder Access, ransomware and destructive malware can freely encrypt or delete files in user profile folders and other protected locations. CFA provides a last line of defense against ransomware by blocking unauthorized write operations, even from elevated processes, unless the application is explicitly whitelisted.
remediation_brief: Enable Controlled Folder Access via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Microsoft Defender Antivirus > Microsoft Defender Exploit Guard > Controlled Folder Access > Configure Controlled folder access = Enabled (Block mode). Alternatively: Set-MpPreference -EnableControlledFolderAccess Enabled. Whitelist legitimate applications that need write access to protected folders.

title: Endpoint Protection: Network Protection Not Enabled
description: Windows Defender Network Protection is not enabled. Network Protection extends SmartScreen capabilities to block outbound connections to low-reputation or malicious domains and IP addresses, protecting against phishing, exploit hosting sites, and command-and-control infrastructure.
impact: Without Network Protection, the system can establish connections to known-malicious domains, phishing sites, and C2 infrastructure without being blocked. This feature provides network-layer defense against web-based threats and can prevent initial access (drive-by downloads, phishing), malware download, and C2 communication.
remediation_brief: Enable Network Protection via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Microsoft Defender Antivirus > Microsoft Defender Exploit Guard > Network Protection > Prevent users and apps from accessing dangerous websites = Enabled (Block mode). Alternatively: Set-MpPreference -EnableNetworkProtection Enabled. Start in audit mode to identify false positives before enforcing.

title: Endpoint Protection: Exploit Protection Not Configured
description: Windows Exploit Protection (successor to EMET) process mitigations are not configured. Exploit Protection applies per-process exploit mitigations such as DEP, ASLR, CFG (Control Flow Guard), heap integrity validation, and image load restrictions to protect against memory corruption exploits.
impact: Without process-level exploit mitigations, applications are more vulnerable to memory corruption exploits (buffer overflows, use-after-free, ROP chains). Exploit Protection mitigations make exploit development significantly harder and can prevent known exploitation techniques from succeeding, even against unpatched vulnerabilities.
remediation_brief: Configure Exploit Protection system-wide and per-application: Windows Security > App & browser control > Exploit protection settings. Enable for high-risk applications (browsers, Office, PDF readers, Java). Key mitigations: DEP (AlwaysOn), ASLR (ForceRelocateImages, BottomUp), CFG (enabled), SEHOP (enabled). Deploy via Group Policy using an XML configuration file: Set-ProcessMitigation -PolicyFilePath exploit-protection-settings.xml.

title: Network Hardening: SMB Client Signing Not Required
description: Outbound SMB connections from this host do not require packet signing. An attacker on the local network can intercept and relay SMB authentication to other targets.
impact: Without client-side signing, NTLM relay attacks are possible. An attacker poisons name resolution (LLMNR/NBT-NS), intercepts this machine's outbound SMB authentication, and relays it to another host to execute commands or access shares.
remediation_brief: Set RequireSecuritySignature to 1 under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanWorkstation\Parameters.

title: Access Control: Anonymous SAM Account Enumeration Allowed
description: Unauthenticated users can enumerate local user accounts through the SAM database. RestrictAnonymousSAM is not enabled.
impact: An attacker can retrieve the full list of local user accounts without any credentials, providing a target list for password spraying and brute force attacks.
remediation_brief: Set RestrictAnonymousSAM to 1 under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa.

title: System Hardening: Built-in Administrator Exempt from UAC
description: The built-in Administrator account (RID 500) runs all processes with full elevated privileges without UAC prompts. FilterAdministratorToken is not enabled.
impact: Any process launched by the RID-500 Administrator account runs with unrestricted administrative privileges. If an attacker obtains these credentials, post-exploitation is immediate with no elevation prompt barrier.
remediation_brief: Set FilterAdministratorToken to 1 under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System. Rename the built-in Administrator account.

title: Authentication: Blank Passwords Permitted for Network Logon
description: Accounts with empty passwords can authenticate over the network (SMB, RDP, WinRM). LimitBlankPasswordUse is disabled.
impact: An attacker who discovers any account with no password set can authenticate remotely. On domain controllers this grants access to SYSVOL, NETLOGON, and potentially administrative shares.
remediation_brief: Set LimitBlankPasswordUse to 1 under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa. Audit all local and domain accounts to ensure no accounts have empty passwords.

title: Access Control: Anonymous Users Included in Everyone Group
description: The Everyone security group includes anonymous (unauthenticated) connections. Any resource with Everyone permissions is accessible without credentials.
impact: Shares, files, and objects granted to Everyone become accessible to null-session connections. This effectively removes the authentication boundary for any Everyone-permissioned resource on the system.
remediation_brief: Set EveryoneIncludesAnonymous to 0 under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa. Review all resources with Everyone permissions.

title: Remote Desktop: Weak RDP Transport Encryption
description: Remote Desktop is configured with weak or legacy transport encryption. Sessions can be intercepted or downgraded by an on-path attacker.
impact: SecurityLayer=0 uses legacy RDP encryption (RC4-based, no server certificate validation). Low MinEncryptionLevel allows 56-bit or 40-bit session keys. An on-path attacker can intercept keystrokes, screen content, and credentials.
remediation_brief: Set SecurityLayer to 2 (TLS) and MinEncryptionLevel to 3 (High) under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp.

title: Monitoring: Critical Audit Subcategories Disabled
description: Security-critical audit subcategories are not configured. Events in these categories are not being logged, preventing detection and forensic investigation.
impact: Without subcategory auditing for logon events, credential validation, account management, and process creation, the system cannot detect brute force attacks, pass-the-hash, unauthorized account changes, or malicious process execution.
remediation_brief: Enable Advanced Audit Policy via Group Policy for: Logon, User Account Management, Credential Validation, Process Creation, and Audit Policy Change subcategories.

title: Privilege Escalation: Sensitive User Rights Assigned to Non-Default Accounts
description: Sensitive user rights (SeDebugPrivilege, SeLoadDriverPrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege, etc.) are assigned to accounts beyond the operating system defaults. These rights enable credential theft, kernel-level access, or file system bypass.
impact: SeDebugPrivilege allows dumping LSASS memory to extract all cached credentials. SeLoadDriverPrivilege allows loading a malicious kernel driver. SeBackupPrivilege allows reading any file on the system regardless of ACLs, including SAM and SYSTEM registry hives.
remediation_brief: Review User Rights Assignment in Group Policy. Remove non-essential accounts from sensitive privileges. Only SYSTEM, LOCAL SERVICE, and Administrators should hold SeDebugPrivilege, SeLoadDriverPrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege, and SeTcbPrivilege.

title: Monitoring: Advanced Audit Policy Overridden by Legacy Settings
description: Advanced Audit Policy subcategory settings are being silently overridden by legacy basic audit policy. Granular audit configurations may not be taking effect.
impact: Without SCENoApplyLegacyAuditPolicy enabled, basic audit policy takes precedence over Advanced Audit Policy subcategory settings. Administrators who configure granular auditing may not realize their settings are being ignored, creating a false sense of security.
remediation_brief: Set SCENoApplyLegacyAuditPolicy to 1 under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa and use only Advanced Audit Policy Configuration in Group Policy.

title: SMB Signing Bypass: Re-Authentication Identity Check Missing
description: SMB signing is enforced but the server does not verify that a re-authenticating session belongs to the same identity. An attacker who opens a signed session with their own credentials can re-authenticate it using a relayed privileged identity, retaining their signing key while gaining the victim's privileges.
impact: SMB signing alone does not prevent relay attacks on this host. An attacker with network position and the ability to coerce authentication (LLMNR/mDNS poisoning, PetitPotam, PrinterBug) can relay privileged credentials even against signing-enforced targets. Domain Controllers are the highest-value target for this technique.
remediation_brief: Install KB5124008 (September 2026 cumulative update) or later. This update adds a same-identity check on SMB session re-authentication. Verify with: NetExec reauth_swap module or patchcheck.py from the reauthx toolkit.
Enable SMB encryption: Set-SmbServerConfiguration -EncryptData $true. For per-share encryption: Set-SmbShare -Name <share> -EncryptData $true.
title: Network Hardening: SMB Encryption Not Enabled
description: SMB traffic encryption is not enabled on the server. All file share and IPC traffic is transmitted in cleartext on the wire.
impact: Without SMB encryption, an attacker with network access can capture file contents, credentials in transit, and sensitive data from shared folders using passive sniffing.

remediation_brief: Enable RejectUnencryptedAccess: Set-SmbServerConfiguration -RejectUnencryptedAccess $true. Verify all clients support SMB3 encryption before enabling.
title: Network Hardening: SMB Unencrypted Access Not Rejected
description: SMB encryption is enabled but the server does not reject connections from clients that do not support encryption.
impact: Clients that do not support SMB3 encryption can still connect with unencrypted SMB2/SMB3, negating the encryption policy for those sessions.

remediation_brief: Enable WEC: wecutil qc. Configure subscriptions via Group Policy (Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Event Forwarding).
title: Monitoring: Windows Event Forwarding Not Active
description: The Windows Event Collector (WEC) service is not running. Event forwarding subscriptions cannot receive events.
impact: Without WEF, security events remain on individual endpoints and are lost when disk space runs out or when an attacker clears local logs. Centralised collection is critical for SIEM-based detection and incident response.

remediation_brief: Create WEF subscriptions using wecutil cs <subscription.xml> or via Group Policy. Forward at minimum: Security log, Sysmon, PowerShell, and AppLocker events.
title: Monitoring: No WEF Subscriptions Configured
description: The Windows Event Collector service is running but no event subscriptions are configured.
impact: WEC is enabled but has no subscriptions to forward events to a collector. Security events are not being centralised.

remediation_brief: Configure Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > System > Removable Storage Access. At minimum deny write and execute access to removable disks.
title: System Hardening: Removable Storage Policy Not Restrictive
description: Removable storage access is not restricted. Write and/or execute access to removable media is allowed.
impact: Unrestricted removable storage allows data exfiltration via USB drives and introduces malware risk from infected media. Write access enables an insider to copy sensitive data; execute access enables auto-launched payloads.

remediation_brief: Enable 'Special Logon' auditing via: auditpol /set /subcategory:"Special Logon" /success:enable /failure:enable.
title: Monitoring: Special Logon Events Not Audited
description: The audit subcategory 'Logon/Logoff > Special Logon' is not configured. Recommended: Success.
impact: Without auditing Special Logon events, the security team lacks visibility into this activity category, which may hinder forensic investigation and threat detection.

remediation_brief: Enable 'Account Lockout' auditing via: auditpol /set /subcategory:"Account Lockout" /success:enable /failure:enable.
title: Monitoring: Account Lockout Events Not Audited
description: The audit subcategory 'Logon/Logoff > Account Lockout' is not configured. Recommended: Failure.
impact: Without auditing Account Lockout events, the security team lacks visibility into this activity category, which may hinder forensic investigation and threat detection.

remediation_brief: Enable 'Removable Storage' auditing via: auditpol /set /subcategory:"Removable Storage" /success:enable /failure:enable.
title: Monitoring: Removable Storage Access Not Audited
description: The audit subcategory 'Object Access > Removable Storage' is not configured. Recommended: Success,Failure.
impact: Without auditing Removable Storage events, the security team lacks visibility into this activity category, which may hinder forensic investigation and threat detection.

remediation_brief: Enable Tamper Protection via the Windows Security app or Intune. It cannot be enabled via Group Policy by design.
title: Endpoint Protection: Defender Tamper Protection Disabled
description: Windows Defender Tamper Protection is disabled. Malware or an attacker can disable Defender protections programmatically.
impact: Without Tamper Protection, an attacker with admin access can disable Defender via PowerShell, registry edits, or the sc command. Ransomware routinely disables AV before encrypting.

remediation_brief: Enable cloud protection: Set-MpPreference -MAPSReporting Advanced.
title: Endpoint Protection: Defender Cloud Protection Disabled
