description: Defender cloud-delivered protection is disabled. The endpoint relies solely on local signature definitions.
impact: Cloud protection provides rapid response to zero-day threats through cloud-based machine learning. Without it, detection depends on local definitions which may be hours behind.

remediation_brief: Update definitions: Update-MpSignature. Investigate why automatic updates are failing.
title: Endpoint Protection: Defender Definitions Outdated
description: Antimalware definitions are outdated (more than 7 days old). Current threats may not be detected.
impact: Outdated antivirus definitions miss newly discovered malware signatures. Threat actors routinely test payloads against current definitions, so stale definitions significantly reduce detection rates.

remediation_brief: Re-enable the disabled antivirus product. Investigate why it was disabled.
title: Endpoint Protection: Antivirus Product Disabled
description: Installed antivirus product(s) are disabled. A disabled AV provides zero endpoint protection.
impact: A disabled antivirus product provides zero protection. This may indicate tampering by malware or an attacker.

remediation_brief: Re-enable all sub-protections via PowerShell: Set-MpPreference -DisableBehaviorMonitoring $false -DisableIOAVProtection $false -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $false.
title: Endpoint Protection: Defender Sub-Protections Disabled
description: One or more Defender real-time sub-protections are disabled (behavior monitoring, IOAV, or on-access protection).
impact: Disabling behaviour monitoring, IOAV, or on-access protection weakens the overall Defender posture even when real-time protection shows as enabled.

remediation_brief: Enable DNS-over-HTTPS in Windows 11+: Settings > Network > DNS server assignment > Encrypted preferred. For older systems, deploy a local encrypted DNS proxy.
title: Network Hardening: DNS Client Security Not Configured
description: DNS client security gaps: Neither DNS-over-HTTPS nor DNS-over-TLS is enabled; DNSSEC validation is not enabled.
impact: Without encrypted DNS (DoH/DoT), all DNS queries are visible to network observers, leaking browsing activity and internal hostnames. Without DNSSEC validation, DNS responses can be spoofed to redirect traffic to attacker-controlled servers.

remediation_brief: Apply the CIS Windows benchmark using Group Policy or a configuration management tool. Start with Level 1 settings, then evaluate Level 2 settings for applicability.
title: Compliance: CIS Benchmark Baseline Deviations
description: Multiple settings deviate from the CIS Windows benchmark baseline.
impact: CIS benchmarks represent industry-consensus hardening standards. Multiple deviations indicate the system has not been hardened according to best practices, increasing the overall attack surface.

title: Network: Suspicious Outbound Connection
description: The Windows Firewall is disabled for the Domain network profile.
impact: All inbound and outbound traffic is unfiltered when connected to a domain network. Any service listening on any port is exposed to all hosts on the network, enabling lateral movement and direct exploitation.
remediation_brief: Enable the Windows Firewall for the Domain profile via Group Policy or PowerShell: Set-NetFirewallProfile -Profile Domain -Enabled True. Review and configure appropriate inbound/outbound rules before enabling to avoid disrupting legitimate services.

title: Network: High-Risk Port Exposed
description: The Windows Firewall is disabled for the Private network profile.
impact: All network traffic is unfiltered when connected to private networks. Services and ports that should be restricted are accessible to all devices on the local network segment.
remediation_brief: Enable the Windows Firewall for the Private profile: Set-NetFirewallProfile -Profile Private -Enabled True.

title: Network: Proxy Configured
description: The Windows Firewall is disabled for the Public network profile, the most exposed profile.
impact: When connected to any public or untrusted network (airports, hotels, coffee shops), all services are exposed without any filtering. This is the highest-risk firewall misconfiguration as public networks are inherently hostile.
remediation_brief: Immediately enable the Windows Firewall for the Public profile: Set-NetFirewallProfile -Profile Public -Enabled True. The Public profile should have the most restrictive ruleset with all inbound connections blocked by default.

title: Network: External DNS on Domain Host
description: A high-risk network port is listening on this endpoint (e.g., 445/SMB, 135-139/RPC, 3389/RDP, 23/Telnet, 21/FTP, 1433/MSSQL, 3306/MySQL, 5432/PostgreSQL).
impact: High-risk ports are frequent targets for automated scanning and exploitation. Exposed database ports enable direct SQL injection and credential brute-forcing. Exposed management ports enable remote administration attacks.
remediation_brief: Close or restrict access to unnecessary high-risk ports using Windows Firewall rules. For required services, restrict inbound access to specific authorized IP ranges. Consider using IPsec or VPN for administrative access to sensitive services.

title: Persistence: WMI Event Subscription
description: Active WMI event subscriptions (EventFilter + EventConsumer + FilterToConsumerBinding) were found on this system. WMI subscriptions execute automatically in response to system events and survive reboots, making them a powerful persistence mechanism.
impact: WMI event subscriptions run with SYSTEM privileges and are difficult to detect through standard monitoring. An attacker can use them to execute malicious scripts or binaries when specific events occur (user logon, process creation, time-based triggers). WMI persistence is used by APT groups and is notoriously resistant to removal — it survives reinstallation of applications and many cleanup procedures.

mitre_attack.name: Event Triggered Execution: Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription

remediation_brief: Review all WMI event subscriptions: Get-WMIObject -Namespace root\Subscription -Class __EventFilter; Get-WMIObject -Namespace root\Subscription -Class __EventConsumer; Get-WMIObject -Namespace root\Subscription -Class __FilterToConsumerBinding. Remove any unknown or suspicious subscriptions. Deploy Sysmon with WMI monitoring (Event IDs 19-21). Implement WMI activity logging via Group Policy.

title: Persistence: COM Object Hijacking
description: COM object registrations in the HKCU registry hive override HKLM registrations for CLSIDs that are loaded by privileged processes. This COM object hijacking technique allows a user-level modification to cause a privileged process to load an attacker-controlled DLL.
impact: COM hijacking is a stealthy persistence and privilege escalation technique. When a legitimate, privileged application loads a hijacked CLSID, it executes the attacker's DLL with the application's privileges. This survives reboots, is difficult to detect without specific monitoring, and blends with normal COM activity. Many legitimate Windows processes load COM objects during startup.

mitre_attack.name: Event Triggered Execution: Component Object Model Hijacking

remediation_brief: Audit HKCU\Software\Classes\CLSID for entries that shadow HKLM CLSID registrations. Remove unauthorized CLSID overrides. Deploy Sysmon with registry monitoring (Event IDs 12-14) targeting CLSID paths. Implement application whitelisting (AppLocker/WDAC) to prevent loading of unauthorized DLLs from user-writable locations.

title: Persistence: AppInit_DLLs Configured
description: The AppInit_DLLs registry value is configured with one or more DLL paths. Windows loads any DLL listed in AppInit_DLLs into every process that loads user32.dll — which includes virtually all GUI applications. This mechanism is a well-known persistence and injection technique.
impact: DLLs specified in AppInit_DLLs are loaded into every GUI process on the system, providing system-wide code injection. An attacker can use this for keylogging, credential interception, API hooking, or persistent backdoor access. The injected DLL runs with the privileges of each host process, potentially including SYSTEM-level services.
remediation_brief: Clear the AppInit_DLLs registry value: reg delete "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows" /v AppInit_DLLs /f. Also clear the WOW64 key: reg delete "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Wow6432Node\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows" /v AppInit_DLLs /f. Set LoadAppInit_DLLs to 0 to disable the mechanism entirely. Enable Secure Boot and RequireSignedAppInit_DLLs to restrict to signed DLLs only.

title: Persistence: IFEO Debugger Set
description: Image File Execution Options (IFEO) registry entries have a 'Debugger' value set for one or more executables. This causes Windows to launch the specified debugger program instead of (or before) the target executable, effectively hijacking the execution of legitimate programs.
impact: An attacker can set an IFEO debugger entry for commonly used programs (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, taskmgr.exe) to redirect their execution to a malicious binary. This is a stealthy persistence mechanism that activates whenever the legitimate program is launched. It is also used to prevent security tools from running by redirecting them to an empty program or a kill command.

mitre_attack.name: Event Triggered Execution: Image File Execution Options Injection

remediation_brief: Audit IFEO registry entries: reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options" /s /v Debugger. Remove any unauthorized Debugger values. Deploy Sysmon with registry monitoring (Event IDs 12-14) targeting IFEO keys. Legitimate IFEO uses include application compatibility shims — verify with the application vendor before removing.

title: Persistence: Accessibility Feature Modified
description: One or more Windows accessibility feature binaries (sethc.exe, utilman.exe, osk.exe, narrator.exe, magnify.exe, DisplaySwitch.exe) have been modified or replaced. The modification timestamp does not align with the OS installation date or last Windows Update, indicating potential tampering.
impact: Replacing accessibility binaries with cmd.exe or a backdoor is a classic persistence technique that provides SYSTEM-level command prompt access from the Windows login screen — before any user has authenticated. An attacker can press Shift five times (sethc.exe), Win+U (utilman.exe), or similar shortcuts to trigger the backdoor. This survives reboots, user password changes, and most remediation attempts short of restoring the original binaries.
remediation_brief: Restore original accessibility binaries from a known-good source or Windows installation media: sfc /scannow or DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth. Verify file hashes against Microsoft published hashes. Investigate as a potential compromise — this finding indicates the system may have been backdoored. Deploy file integrity monitoring on %SystemRoot%\System32\sethc.exe, utilman.exe, osk.exe, narrator.exe, magnify.exe, DisplaySwitch.exe.

title: Persistence: Print Monitor DLL
description: Custom print monitor DLLs were found registered in the system. Print monitors are loaded by the Print Spooler service (spoolsv.exe) which runs as SYSTEM. An unauthorized print monitor DLL provides persistent, SYSTEM-level code execution.
impact: Print monitor DLLs are loaded by the spoolsv.exe service at startup and run with SYSTEM privileges. An attacker who registers a malicious DLL as a print monitor achieves persistence that survives reboots and is difficult to detect — the DLL appears as a legitimate print subsystem component. This technique is used by APT groups for long-term persistence.

mitre_attack.name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Port Monitors

remediation_brief: Audit print monitor registry entries: reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Monitors" /s. Compare against known legitimate monitors (Standard TCP/IP Port, WSD Port, USB Monitor, Local Port). Remove any unknown or suspicious monitor entries. Verify DLL signatures for all registered monitor DLLs. Deploy Sysmon with registry monitoring on the Print\Monitors key.

title: Persistence: LSA Authentication Package Modified
description: Non-default authentication packages or security support providers (SSPs) are registered in the LSA registry configuration. LSA authentication packages are loaded by lsass.exe at boot and run with SYSTEM privileges. Unauthorized packages can intercept credentials during authentication.
impact: A malicious LSA authentication package runs inside lsass.exe with SYSTEM privileges and intercepts every authentication event on the system. This allows credential harvesting of all user passwords (including domain admin) in cleartext as they authenticate. This is one of the most powerful persistence mechanisms available, used by advanced threat actors and tools like mimilib.

mitre_attack.name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Authentication Package

remediation_brief: Audit LSA registry entries: reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa" /v "Authentication Packages" and "Security Packages". Default values are 'msv1_0' for Authentication Packages and '' (empty) or 'kerberos msv1_0 schannel wdigest tspkg pku2u' for Security Packages. Remove any unauthorized entries. Enable LSA Protection (RunAsPPL) to prevent unauthorized DLL loading into lsass.exe. Enable Credential Guard for additional protection. Investigate as potential compromise.

title: Persistence: Suspicious Scheduled Task Detected
description: One or more scheduled tasks were identified with suspicious characteristics: executing from temporary directories, user profile paths, or using interpreters (PowerShell, cmd, mshta, wscript, cscript, rundll32) with encoded or obfuscated arguments.
impact: Scheduled tasks are a common persistence mechanism for malware and threat actors. Suspicious tasks can execute arbitrary code at system boot, user logon, or on a recurring schedule, maintaining persistent access even after the initial compromise vector is remediated.
remediation_brief: Investigate each flagged scheduled task. Remove tasks that are not legitimate. For legitimate tasks, move executables to protected directories (Program Files). Restrict scheduled task creation via GPO to administrators only. Monitor Task Scheduler event logs (Event IDs 106, 140, 141) for unauthorized task creation.

title: Privilege Escalation: AlwaysInstallElevated Enabled
description: The AlwaysInstallElevated policy is enabled in both HKLM and HKCU registry hives. This Windows Installer policy allows any user to install MSI packages with SYSTEM-level privileges, regardless of the user's actual privilege level.
impact: Any standard user can create a malicious MSI package (e.g., using msfvenom) and install it with SYSTEM privileges. This is a trivial, reliable privilege escalation path that requires no exploitation of software vulnerabilities — only the misconfiguration itself. Tools like PowerUp, WinPEAS, and Metasploit all check for and exploit this setting.
remediation_brief: Disable AlwaysInstallElevated by setting both registry values to 0: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer\AlwaysInstallElevated=0 and HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer\AlwaysInstallElevated=0. Apply via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows Installer > Always install with elevated privileges = Disabled.

title: Privilege Escalation: Modifiable Service Binary
description: One or more Windows service executables reside in directories that are writable by non-administrative users, or the service binary file itself has permissive ACLs. This allows a standard user to replace the service binary with a malicious one.
impact: An attacker can replace or modify a service binary that runs as SYSTEM or a privileged account. On the next service restart (or system reboot), the attacker's code executes with the service account's privileges, typically SYSTEM. This is a reliable privilege escalation technique that persists across reboots.

mitre_attack.name: Hijack Execution Flow: Services File Permissions Weakness

remediation_brief: Audit and correct file system permissions on all service binary paths. Service executables should be owned by Administrators/SYSTEM with write access restricted to Administrators only. Use icacls to verify: icacls "C:\path\to\service.exe". Install services only in protected directories (C:\Program Files\). Remove write permissions for Users/Authenticated Users groups on service binary paths.

title: Privilege Escalation: DLL Search Order Hijacking
description: One or more directories in the system PATH are writable by non-administrative users. Windows DLL search order loads DLLs from the application directory first, then the system directory, then each PATH directory in order. A writable PATH directory allows an attacker to place a malicious DLL that will be loaded by legitimate applications.
impact: An attacker can place a crafted DLL in a writable PATH directory with the same name as a DLL that a privileged application expects to load. When the application runs, it loads the attacker's DLL instead, executing arbitrary code with the application's privileges. This is particularly dangerous for services and scheduled tasks running as SYSTEM.

mitre_attack.name: Hijack Execution Flow: DLL Search Order Hijacking

remediation_brief: Audit all directories in the system PATH and remove write permissions for non-administrative users. Remove unnecessary directories from PATH. Enable SafeDllSearchMode (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\SafeDllSearchMode=1). Consider implementing Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) to restrict DLL loading to signed binaries.

title: Privilege Escalation: Dangerous Token Privileges
description: The current process or service accounts hold dangerous Windows token privileges. SeImpersonatePrivilege and SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege enable token impersonation attacks (Potato family exploits). SeDebugPrivilege allows debugging any process including LSASS. SeBackupPrivilege/SeRestorePrivilege bypass file ACLs. SeTcbPrivilege acts as part of the operating system.
impact: Token impersonation privileges (SeImpersonate, SeAssignPrimaryToken) enable immediate SYSTEM-level privilege escalation via tools like JuicyPotato, PrintSpoofer, RoguePotato, or GodPotato. SeDebugPrivilege allows LSASS memory dumping for credential extraction. These privileges are commonly held by IIS application pool accounts, SQL Server service accounts, and other service identities.
remediation_brief: Review and minimize token privileges assigned to service accounts. Remove SeImpersonatePrivilege and SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege from service accounts where not operationally required. Use Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) with minimal privileges. Audit User Rights Assignments via: secpol.msc > Local Policies > User Rights Assignment. Consider running services in Windows containers or AppContainers which restrict available privileges.

title: Privilege Escalation: Unquoted Service Path
description: One or more Windows services have unquoted executable paths containing spaces, AND at least one intermediate directory in the path is writable by non-administrative users. Windows resolves unquoted paths by trying each space-delimited segment as a potential executable.
impact: An attacker can place an executable at a space-boundary in the unquoted path. For example, if the service path is 'C:\Program Files\Some Service\service.exe' (unquoted), placing 'C:\Program.exe' or 'C:\Program Files\Some.exe' in a writable directory causes it to execute with the service's privileges. This requires both the unquoted path AND a writable intermediate directory to be exploitable.

mitre_attack.name: Hijack Execution Flow: Path Interception by Unquoted Path

remediation_brief: Quote all service binary paths that contain spaces. Fix via registry: reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\<ServiceName>" /v ImagePath /t REG_EXPAND_SZ /d '"C:\Program Files\...\service.exe"' /f. Additionally, restrict write permissions on all intermediate directories in service paths. Identify all unquoted paths: wmic service get name,pathname | findstr /i /v "C:\Windows" | findstr /i "  ".

title: Access Control: Named Pipe Permission Weakness
description: Named pipes on this system have overly permissive access controls, allowing non-administrative users to read, write, or impersonate connections on pipes used by privileged services.
impact: Improperly secured named pipes can be exploited for privilege escalation or lateral movement. An attacker can connect to a weakly-permissioned pipe to capture or relay authentication tokens, inject commands into service communication channels, or impersonate the pipe server's identity. Named pipe impersonation is a core technique in several Potato-family privilege escalation exploits.
remediation_brief: Audit named pipe ACLs using pipelist.exe (Sysinternals) and accesschk.exe. Restrict pipe permissions to the minimum required identities. Remove write/connect access for Authenticated Users and Everyone groups on privileged service pipes. Implement pipe security descriptors in service configurations.

title: Process: Known Malicious Process Detected
description: One or more running processes match known malicious software signatures in the threat intelligence database. This is a strong indicator of active system compromise requiring immediate incident response.
impact: Known malicious processes indicate active malware execution. Depending on the malware type (RAT, keylogger, cryptominer, ransomware dropper), the attacker may have full remote access, be exfiltrating data, or preparing for destructive action. The system should be considered compromised.
remediation_brief: Immediately isolate the system from the network. Capture memory and disk images for forensic analysis before remediation. Identify the malware family and check for persistence mechanisms (scheduled tasks, services, registry run keys, WMI subscriptions). Re-image the system after forensics are complete.

title: Process: Running from Temporary Directory
description: One or more processes are executing from temporary directories (%TEMP%, %TMP%, C:\Windows\Temp). Legitimate software rarely runs from temp folders; this pattern is a strong indicator of malware, dropper activity, or exploitation payload execution.
impact: Malware commonly stages and executes from temporary directories because they are user-writable, loosely monitored, and files there are expected to be transient. Ransomware droppers, fileless malware stagers, and post-exploitation payloads frequently use temp paths as their execution location.
remediation_brief: Investigate each process: check file hash against VirusTotal, examine parent process chain, check for associated network connections. Implement AppLocker or WDAC policies to block executable execution from temp directories. Enable Windows Defender ASR rules to block execution from temp paths.

title: Process: No Executable Path
description: One or more running processes have no associated executable path on disk. This may indicate fileless malware executing entirely from memory, process hollowing, or a process whose binary was deleted after execution.
impact: Processes without a disk-backed executable path can indicate fileless malware executing entirely from memory, process hollowing (where a legitimate process is replaced in memory with malicious code), or an attacker who deleted the binary after launching it to hinder forensic analysis.
remediation_brief: Investigate each process: capture a memory dump for forensic analysis, check the parent process chain for suspicious lineage, examine loaded DLLs and handles. Implement Sysmon with process creation logging (Event ID 1) to capture full command lines and parent process details.

title: Process: SYSTEM Process in User-Writable Path
description: One or more processes are running as SYSTEM from user-writable locations (Users, AppData, Downloads, ProgramData, Temp). Legitimate SYSTEM processes run from protected directories (System32, Program Files). This is a strong indicator of privilege escalation or malware with elevated privileges.
impact: A process running as SYSTEM from a user-writable directory indicates successful privilege escalation. The attacker has achieved the highest local privilege level and can install rootkits, create backdoor accounts, modify security settings, access any file on the system, and pivot to other systems.
remediation_brief: Immediately investigate: capture memory and disk forensics, identify the privilege escalation vector (service binary hijacking, DLL search order hijacking, unquoted service path). Fix the underlying vulnerability. Deploy WDAC/AppLocker to prevent execution from user-writable paths.

title: Remote Access: Unauthorized RMT Detected
description: A remote management tool (TeamViewer, AnyDesk, LogMeIn, ConnectWise, Splashtop, etc.) was detected that is not part of the organization's approved toolset.
impact: Unauthorized remote access tools create unmonitored backdoors into the network. They bypass VPN, firewall, and network security controls by tunneling through standard HTTPS. Attackers frequently install these tools for persistent remote access.
remediation_brief: Remove unauthorized remote management tools and block their installation via application control policies. If the tool was installed by an attacker, initiate incident response. Maintain an approved remote access solution with centralized logging and multi-factor authentication.

title: Remote Desktop: RDP Enabled
description: Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) is enabled on this system. RDP exposes the system to brute-force attacks, credential stuffing, and known RDP vulnerabilities including BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708) and DejaBlue.
impact: An attacker who gains RDP access obtains full interactive control of the system. Without NLA, unauthenticated attackers can reach the login screen and exploit pre-authentication vulnerabilities.
remediation_brief: Disable RDP if not required. If required, enforce Network Level Authentication (NLA), restrict access via firewall rules to authorized IP ranges, use an RDP gateway, and enable account lockout policies.

title: Service Hardening: WinRM Running
description: Windows Remote Management (WinRM) is running on this system. WinRM allows remote command execution via PowerShell remoting and is a common lateral movement vector used by attackers.
impact: An attacker with valid credentials can use WinRM to execute arbitrary commands remotely. If basic authentication or unencrypted traffic is allowed, credentials may be captured in transit.
remediation_brief: Disable WinRM if not required. If required, enforce HTTPS transport, disable basic authentication, configure TrustedHosts to restrict connections, and monitor WinRM event logs for unauthorized access.

title: Service Hardening: SSH Server Enabled
description: An SSH server (OpenSSH) is running on this Windows system. SSH on Windows endpoints is uncommon and may indicate unauthorized installation, developer tools, or a persistence mechanism installed by an attacker.
impact: SSH provides encrypted remote shell access that can be used for lateral movement, tunneling, and persistent access. On Windows endpoints, SSH is rarely business-justified and represents an additional attack surface.
remediation_brief: Disable the OpenSSH Server Windows feature if not required. If required, enforce key-based authentication, disable password login, and restrict access via firewall rules to authorized source IPs.

title: Service Hardening: Multiple RMT Tools
description: The OpenSSH Server service is running on this Windows endpoint, providing SSH remote access.
impact: OpenSSH on Windows provides command-line remote access. While potentially legitimate for administration, it adds an additional remote access vector that should be documented and monitored.
remediation_brief: If OpenSSH is authorized, ensure it is configured securely: disable root login, use key-based authentication, limit allowed users, and monitor SSH logs. If not authorized, disable the sshd service.

title: EOL Software: End-of-Life Software Installed
description: Software that has reached end-of-life and no longer receives security updates is installed on this endpoint.
impact: EOL software accumulates unpatched vulnerabilities over time with no vendor fixes available. Publicly known exploits continue to work indefinitely. This represents a permanent and growing security gap.
remediation_brief: Upgrade or replace end-of-life software with supported versions. If no replacement is available, implement compensating controls (network isolation, application whitelisting) and document the risk acceptance.

title: Software: Remote Access Software
description: An installed software version is known to contain security vulnerabilities with available updates.
impact: Running known-vulnerable software versions exposes the system to exploits targeting those specific vulnerabilities. Attackers routinely scan for known vulnerable software versions using automated tools.
remediation_brief: Update the software to the latest patched version. If updates are not immediately possible, implement compensating controls such as network segmentation and application-level monitoring. Prioritize based on CVSS score and network exposure.

title: Software: Suspicious Startup Item
description: Development tools (compilers, debuggers, IDEs, scripting language interpreters beyond what the system requires) are installed on a production system.
impact: Development tools enable an attacker to compile and run custom tools directly on the compromised system, create sophisticated payloads, and debug security controls. Their presence on production systems violates hardening baselines.
remediation_brief: Remove development tools from production systems. If development work is needed, use separate development environments. Document any exceptions with business justification and compensating controls.

title: Software: P2P/Torrent Software
description: Software not included in the organization's approved software list was detected. This finding requires per-engagement policy configuration.
impact: Unauthorized software may introduce vulnerabilities, licensing issues, or compliance violations. It may also indicate shadow IT or user-installed tools that bypass change management.
remediation_brief: Review unauthorized software with the system owner to determine if it should be added to the approved list or removed. Implement application control policies (AppLocker, WDAC) to prevent installation of unapproved software.

title: Software: Known Vulnerable Software Installed
description: Installed software matches known vulnerable versions with published CVEs or documented security defects. These versions have public exploits or well-documented attack paths.
impact: An attacker can exploit known vulnerabilities in installed software to gain unauthorized access, execute arbitrary code, or escalate privileges. Public exploit code and automated exploit frameworks (Metasploit, Nuclei) make exploitation straightforward.
remediation_brief: Update all identified software to the latest patched version. Where an update is not possible, implement compensating controls: restrict network access to the service, deploy WAF rules, enable exploit prevention features, and increase monitoring.

title: Service Hardening: High-Risk Services Running
description: High-risk services are actively running, including services that transmit credentials in cleartext (Telnet), allow remote registry manipulation, or expose SNMP information with default community strings.
impact: Telnet transmits all data including credentials in cleartext. Remote Registry allows attackers to read and modify registry settings remotely. SNMP with default community strings enables full network reconnaissance. FTP transmits credentials in cleartext.
remediation_brief: Disable unnecessary high-risk services. Replace Telnet with SSH. Replace SNMP v1/v2c with v3 using authentication and encryption. Disable Remote Registry unless required by a specific management tool.

title: Service Hardening: Unnecessary Services Running
description: Unnecessary or legacy services are actively running. While individually low-risk, each running service expands the system's attack surface.
impact: Legacy services like SSDP, UPnP, Computer Browser, and Telephony are rarely needed on servers and can be exploited for reconnaissance, denial of service, or as pivot points in chained attacks.
remediation_brief: Review each identified service and disable any that are not required for the system's operational role. Set unnecessary services to Disabled startup type.

title: Service Hardening: Services Running Under User Accounts
description: Services are running under domain or local user accounts rather than standard service accounts (LocalSystem, LocalService, NetworkService). These credentials are cached in memory and may have excessive privileges.
impact: Service account credentials cached in LSASS memory are extractable via Mimikatz or comsvcs.dll MiniDump. If the service account has domain admin or other elevated privileges, compromising this host yields those credentials. Service accounts often have weak, non-rotating passwords.
remediation_brief: Migrate services to Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA). For services requiring a user account: enforce minimum privileges, rotate passwords regularly, deny interactive logon, and exclude from privileged groups.

title: Software: Network Tunnel or Bypass Tool Installed
description: Network tunneling or overlay network software is installed. These tools create encrypted channels that can bypass firewall rules, IDS/IPS inspection, and network segmentation controls.
impact: Tools like cloudflared, ngrok, ZeroTier, Tailscale, and Chisel create encrypted outbound tunnels that bypass perimeter security. An attacker can use them to establish persistent command-and-control channels or expose internal services to the internet without firewall approval.
remediation_brief: Remove unauthorized tunnel software. If operationally required (e.g., Cloudflare Tunnel), document the business justification, restrict access, and monitor. Block known tunnel endpoints at the firewall. Deploy application control policies.

title: Software: Development or Diagnostic Tools on Production Server
description: Development, diagnostic, or offensive security tools are installed on a production server. These tools lower the post-exploitation barrier by providing compilers, packet analyzers, or debuggers an attacker can use directly.
impact: Installed compilers can build custom malware on-target. Packet analyzers capture credentials in transit. Debuggers dump process memory including cached credentials from LSASS. These tools eliminate the need for an attacker to upload their own tooling, avoiding endpoint detection.
remediation_brief: Remove development, diagnostic, and security tools from production servers. Development should occur in isolated environments. If tools are required operationally, document the justification and restrict access via file system ACLs.

title: Software: Software Installed Without Version Information
description: Software packages are installed with no version information in the Windows registry. This prevents vulnerability assessment and may indicate manually installed, sideloaded, or malicious software.
impact: Software without version metadata cannot be checked against vulnerability databases (CVE, NVD). Sideloaded applications and malware that registers itself in the Uninstall registry key often omit version data, making them invisible to patch management and vulnerability scanners.
remediation_brief: Investigate software with missing version information. Remove unauthorized or unrecognized software. Enforce software installation policies that require standard packaging with version metadata.

title: Authentication: SQL Server Mixed Authentication
description: SQL Server is configured with mixed authentication mode, allowing both Windows and SQL Server authentication. SQL authentication transmits credentials that may be weaker and harder to audit than Windows/Kerberos authentication.
impact: Mixed mode enables SQL logins (like 'sa') which are frequently targeted by brute-force attacks. SQL passwords are not subject to Active Directory password policies, may be stored in application config files, and bypass centralized authentication controls.
remediation_brief: Switch to Windows Authentication mode unless SQL authentication is strictly required. If mixed mode must remain, disable the 'sa' account, enforce strong passwords on all SQL logins, and enable SQL Server Audit for login events.

title: Service Hardening: IIS Default Site
description: IIS is running with the default web site active. The default site exposes server information, may serve default pages, and typically lacks application-specific hardening that production deployments require.
impact: The default IIS site reveals the web server platform, may expose debug pages or sample applications, and often lacks proper access controls. Attackers use default sites to fingerprint the server and find known vulnerabilities.
remediation_brief: Remove or stop the 'Default Web Site' if it is not needed. For production sites, create named sites with specific bindings and remove all default content, sample applications, and documentation.

title: Service Hardening: Unnecessary Server Roles
description: Server roles (DHCP, DNS, AD DS, Hyper-V, IIS, etc.) are installed on this workstation. Server roles on workstations expand the attack surface with services not intended for endpoint use.
impact: Each server role introduces additional listening services, open ports, and potential vulnerabilities. On a workstation, these roles are rarely monitored or patched with the same rigor as production servers.
remediation_brief: Remove unnecessary server roles via Server Manager or DISM. Workstations should not run server infrastructure services unless specifically authorized and hardened.

title: Service Hardening: Web Server on Workstation
description: A web server (IIS, Apache, Nginx, XAMPP, WAMP, etc.) is running on this workstation. Web servers on endpoints are often development installations with default configurations and no hardening.
impact: Web servers on workstations are typically unmonitored, lack WAF protection, may expose sensitive development data, and are frequently misconfigured with directory listing, debug modes, or default credentials enabled.
remediation_brief: Remove web server software from workstations. Use dedicated servers or containerized development environments. If a local dev server is required, ensure it binds only to localhost (127.0.0.1).

title: EOL Software: End-of-Life Windows Version
description: The Windows operating system version running on this endpoint has reached end-of-life and no longer receives security updates from Microsoft.
impact: An attacker can exploit publicly disclosed vulnerabilities that will never be patched, leading to full system compromise. The organization also faces compliance violations as most frameworks require supported software.
remediation_brief: Upgrade the operating system to a currently supported version of Windows that receives regular security updates. For Windows Server environments, plan a migration path to Server 2019 or later. For desktop systems, upgrade to Windows 10 22H2 or Windows 11. Coordinate with application owners to verify compatibility before migration.

title: Patch Management: Missing Critical Updates
description: The endpoint has critical or important security updates pending installation, leaving known vulnerabilities unpatched.
impact: Attackers can exploit publicly known vulnerabilities with available patches. Delayed patching is one of the most common vectors for ransomware and lateral movement within enterprise networks.
remediation_brief: Install all pending critical and important security updates immediately. Configure Windows Update or WSUS to automatically download and install security updates on a regular schedule. Establish a patch management process with a maximum 30-day window for critical updates and 90 days for important updates.

title: Patch Management: Windows Update Disabled
description: The Windows Update service (wuauserv) is disabled or stopped, preventing automatic security update installation.
impact: Without the update service running, the system will not receive security patches, accumulating vulnerabilities over time. This creates a growing attack surface that adversaries can exploit.
remediation_brief: Enable the Windows Update service by setting its startup type to Automatic and starting the service. Verify that Group Policy is not overriding this setting. If WSUS or SCCM is used for update management, ensure the client agent is properly configured and communicating with the update server.

title: Patch Management: WSUS Not Configured
description: No Windows Server Update Services (WSUS) or equivalent centralized update management solution is configured for this endpoint.
impact: Without centralized update management, there is no visibility into the patch compliance status of this endpoint. Updates depend on individual machine settings, making enterprise-wide patch compliance difficult to enforce and verify.
remediation_brief: Configure a centralized update management solution such as WSUS, SCCM, or Intune. Point this endpoint to the organization's WSUS server via Group Policy (Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows Update > Specify intranet Microsoft update service location).

title: Patch Management: System Uptime Exceeds 90 Days
description: The system has been running for over 90 days without a reboot, which may indicate that kernel-level patches requiring a restart have not been applied.
impact: Many Windows security updates require a system restart to take effect. Extended uptime suggests these updates have been downloaded but not fully installed, leaving kernel-level vulnerabilities unpatched.
remediation_brief: Schedule a maintenance window to restart the system and apply any pending updates that require a reboot. Establish a regular reboot schedule aligned with the organization's patch management cycle, typically monthly following Patch Tuesday.

title: Patch Management: No Backup Configured
description: No Windows backup solution (Windows Server Backup, System Restore, or third-party backup) is configured on this endpoint.
impact: Without backups, data loss from ransomware, hardware failure, or accidental deletion is unrecoverable. This significantly increases the business impact of any destructive attack or system failure.
remediation_brief: Configure Windows Server Backup or a third-party backup solution to perform regular system state and data backups. Store backups on a separate, isolated storage target. Test backup restoration procedures regularly to ensure recoverability.

title: Patch Management: Last Backup Over 30 Days
description: The most recent backup on this system is older than 30 days, indicating that backup jobs may have failed or been disabled.
impact: A stale backup means up to 30+ days of data would be lost in a disaster recovery scenario. Critical business data, configuration changes, and system state captured after the last backup cannot be restored.
remediation_brief: Investigate why backups have not completed recently. Check backup job schedules, storage target availability, and backup service health. Resume regular backup operations and configure alerting for backup failures.

title: System Hardening: BitLocker Not Enabled
description: BitLocker Drive Encryption is not enabled on one or more fixed drives, leaving data at rest unprotected.
impact: If the device is stolen or a hard drive is physically removed, all data on unencrypted volumes is accessible without authentication. This includes cached credentials, local databases, documents, and application data.
remediation_brief: Enable BitLocker Drive Encryption on all fixed drives. Use TPM+PIN for pre-boot authentication where possible. Store recovery keys in Active Directory or a centralized key management solution. For systems without TPM, use USB key-based or password-based protectors.

title: System Hardening: TPM Not Available
description: No Trusted Platform Module (TPM) is available or the TPM is not in a ready state on this endpoint.
impact: Without a functional TPM, hardware-rooted security features such as BitLocker with TPM-based protectors, Credential Guard, and Measured Boot cannot be used. The system must rely on software-only security mechanisms which are more susceptible to tampering.
remediation_brief: If the hardware supports TPM, enable it in the BIOS/UEFI firmware settings and initialize it through the TPM Management console (tpm.msc). For virtual machines, enable virtual TPM through the hypervisor. If the hardware does not support TPM, consider hardware replacement during the next refresh cycle.

title: System Hardening: Secure Boot Not Enabled
description: UEFI Secure Boot is not enabled on this endpoint, allowing unsigned or tampered boot components to execute during system startup.
impact: An attacker with physical access or kernel-level privileges can install a bootkit or rootkit that loads before the operating system, persisting across reinstalls and evading all OS-level security controls including antivirus and EDR.
remediation_brief: Enable Secure Boot in the system's UEFI firmware settings. Ensure the operating system was installed in UEFI mode (not legacy BIOS). Verify that all boot components (bootloader, kernel, drivers) are properly signed. Note that enabling Secure Boot on a legacy BIOS-installed system requires OS reinstallation in UEFI mode.

title: Monitoring: Sysmon Not Installed
description: Sysmon (System Monitor) is not installed on this system. Sysmon provides detailed telemetry about process creation, network connections, file creation, registry modifications, WMI events, and other security-relevant activities that are essential for threat detection and incident response.
impact: Without Sysmon, the system lacks granular visibility into process execution (with command lines and parent process chains), network connections per-process, file creation timestamps and hashes, registry modifications, WMI activity, and named pipe operations. This severely limits the ability to detect and investigate malicious activity, lateral movement, and persistence mechanisms. Native Windows event logs lack the detail that Sysmon provides.
owasp_web: A09:2021 - Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
remediation_brief: Install Sysmon from Microsoft Sysinternals: sysmon64.exe -accepteula -i sysmonconfig.xml. Use a community-maintained configuration such as SwiftOnSecurity/sysmon-config or olafhartong/sysmon-modular as a starting point. Key event types to enable: Process creation (Event 1), Network connection (Event 3), File creation (Event 11), Registry modification (Event 13), WMI events (Events 19-21). Forward Sysmon logs to a SIEM for detection and alerting.

title: Service Hardening: PrintNightmare Vulnerable
description: The system is vulnerable to PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-34527 / CVE-2021-1675). The Print Spooler service is running AND the RestrictDriverInstallationToAdministrators registry key is not set to 1, or the NoWarningNoElevationOnInstall / UpdatePromptSettings Point-and-Print restriction keys are configured unsafely.
impact: PrintNightmare allows any authenticated user (local or remote) to execute arbitrary code with SYSTEM privileges by exploiting the Print Spooler service's driver installation functionality. This vulnerability was actively exploited in the wild and provides reliable remote code execution. On domain controllers, it enables immediate domain compromise. Multiple exploit variants exist in public tooling.

mitre_attack.name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Print Processors

remediation_brief: 1) Install all PrintNightmare patches (KB5004945 and later cumulative updates). 2) Set RestrictDriverInstallationToAdministrators=1: reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Printers\PointAndPrint" /v RestrictDriverInstallationToAdministrators /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f. 3) Set NoWarningNoElevationOnInstall=0 and UpdatePromptSettings=0 in the same key. 4) On servers that do not need printing, disable the Print Spooler service entirely: Stop-Service Spooler; Set-Service Spooler -StartupType Disabled. 5) On domain controllers, always disable Print Spooler.

title: Network Hardening: DNS Zone Transfer Allowed
description: The DNS server role is installed and zone transfers (AXFR) are allowed to any requestor, or are not restricted to specific secondary DNS servers. This allows any host to download the complete contents of DNS zones, including all hostnames, IP addresses, and service records.
impact: Unrestricted DNS zone transfers expose the entire internal DNS namespace to any attacker who can reach the DNS server. This provides a complete map of internal hosts, services, domain controllers, and other infrastructure without triggering typical detection mechanisms. The information enables targeted attacks against specific systems and services identified through the zone data.
remediation_brief: Restrict zone transfers to authorized secondary DNS servers only. In DNS Manager: right-click zone > Properties > Zone Transfers > uncheck 'Allow zone transfers' or select 'Only to the following servers' and list authorized secondaries. For AD-integrated zones, consider disabling zone transfers entirely and relying on AD replication. Verify with: nslookup > set type=AXFR > ls -d <domain>.

Update the Sysmon configuration to include all critical event types. Use a comprehensive config like SwiftOnSecurity/sysmon-config or olafhartong/sysmon-modular as a baseline. Deploy with: sysmon -c <config.xml>.
title: Monitoring: Sysmon Configuration Incomplete
description: Sysmon is installed but critical event categories are not present in the active configuration.
impact: Sysmon is installed but not logging critical event categories needed for threat detection. Missing categories mean gaps in visibility for process creation, network connections, remote thread injection, or registry modifications — core telemetry for detecting adversary tradecraft.

title: Account Management: Built-in Administrator Enabled
description: The built-in Administrator account (RID 500) is enabled on this endpoint.
impact: The built-in Administrator is a well-known target for brute force attacks and cannot be locked out by default. If compromised, it provides full system control. Attackers specifically target this account during password spraying and pass-the-hash attacks.
remediation_brief: Disable the built-in Administrator account and create named individual admin accounts. If the built-in account must remain enabled for emergency access, rename it and set a complex password stored in a password vault. Consider implementing LAPS for local admin password management.

title: Account Management: Guest Account Enabled
description: The built-in Guest account is enabled on this endpoint, allowing unauthenticated or minimally-authenticated access.
impact: The Guest account provides a foothold for unauthenticated access to the system. Even with limited privileges, it can be used for local enumeration, accessing public shares, and as a stepping stone for privilege escalation.
remediation_brief: Disable the Guest account immediately: net user Guest /active:no. Verify via Group Policy that it remains disabled.

title: Account Management: Password Never Expires
description: One or more interactive user accounts have the 'Password never expires' flag set.
impact: Passwords that never expire may remain unchanged for years, increasing the window for compromise through credential theft or brute force. Compliance frameworks universally require periodic password rotation.
remediation_brief: Remove the 'Password never expires' flag from interactive user accounts. Implement a maximum password age policy (60-90 days). Service accounts should use managed service accounts (gMSA) or be documented with compensating controls if password expiry would break functionality.

title: Account Management: Excessive Local Administrators
description: The local Administrators group contains more than 3 members, indicating excessive administrative access.
impact: Each local administrator account is a potential credential for full system compromise. Excessive admin accounts increase the attack surface for pass-the-hash, credential theft, and privilege abuse. Lateral movement is easier when admin credentials are widespread.
remediation_brief: Review the local Administrators group and remove unnecessary members. Implement the principle of least privilege using standard user accounts for daily operations. Consider implementing LAPS and just-in-time admin access solutions.

title: Policy: Weak Password Policy
description: The local password policy does not meet security baselines: minimum length is less than 8 characters and/or password complexity requirements are disabled.
impact: Weak password policies allow users to set easily guessable passwords. Short passwords without complexity requirements can be cracked in seconds using modern hardware, making brute force and dictionary attacks trivially successful.
remediation_brief: Set minimum password length to at least 12 characters and enable complexity requirements. Configure via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Account Policies > Password Policy. Consider implementing a password filter or Azure AD Password Protection to block common passwords.

title: Authentication: Account Lockout Not Configured
description: The account lockout threshold is set to 0 (disabled), allowing unlimited failed login attempts without locking the account.
impact: Without account lockout, attackers can perform unlimited password guessing attacks against all accounts without triggering any lockout defense. Password spraying and brute force attacks can continue indefinitely.
remediation_brief: Configure account lockout policy: set lockout threshold to 5-10 failed attempts, lockout duration to 30 minutes, and reset counter after 30 minutes. Apply via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Account Policies > Account Lockout Policy.

title: Wireless Reconnection Successful
description: The wireless interface successfully disconnected from and reconnected to the target SSID within the expected time window. The SSID association was confirmed by polling the interface state.
remediation: No action required. This is an expected operational event confirming normal wireless stack behaviour.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
remediation_brief: Review and harden configuration per security best practices and CIS benchmarks. Disable unnecessary features and apply least functionality.

title: Wireless Reconnection Failed or Timed Out
description: The reconnect command was issued but the interface did not confirm association with the target SSID within the 20-second polling window. This may indicate a weak signal, aggressive rate-limiting of (re)association requests by the AP, or a WPA Enterprise authentication delay.
remediation: Verify the device remains within AP range. Check whether the access point enforces re-association rate limits or client flood protection. Investigate whether WPA Enterprise RADIUS timeout is causing delays.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
remediation_brief: Review and harden configuration per security best practices and CIS benchmarks. Disable unnecessary features and apply least functionality.

title: SSID Mismatch After Reconnect
description: After issuing the reconnect command for the target SSID, the interface associated with a different SSID. This may indicate the presence of a rogue access point with a stronger signal, or unintended roaming to an adjacent network.
remediation: Investigate whether a rogue AP broadcasting the same or similar SSID is present. Confirm that the wireless client prefers the intended BSSID. Consider enabling BSSID-pinning or 802.11w Management Frame Protection.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
remediation_brief: Review and harden configuration per security best practices and CIS benchmarks. Disable unnecessary features and apply least functionality.

title: Wireless Interface Not Found
description: The specified or auto-detected wireless interface could not be found on the system. The tool is unable to perform any disconnect/reconnect operations.
remediation: Verify the wireless adapter is physically connected and recognised by the OS. Run 'iw dev' (Linux) or 'airport -I' (macOS) to confirm available interfaces. Ensure the correct interface name is passed via --interface.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
remediation_brief: Review and harden configuration per security best practices and CIS benchmarks. Disable unnecessary features and apply least functionality.

title: Target Network Not Available
description: The interface is not currently associated with the expected SSID at the start of a cycle. The target network may be temporarily unavailable, out of range, or the interface has roamed to a different network.
remediation: Confirm the device is in range of the target AP. Check whether the AP has de-authenticated the client. Investigate AP availability or DHCP lease expiry causing loss of association.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
remediation_brief: Review and harden configuration per security best practices and CIS benchmarks. Disable unnecessary features and apply least functionality.

title: Cycle Completed Successfully
description: A full disconnect/reconnect cycle completed without error. Both the disconnect and reconnect commands succeeded, and the association with the target SSID was confirmed.
remediation: No action required. Normal operational event.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
remediation_brief: Review and harden configuration per security best practices and CIS benchmarks. Disable unnecessary features and apply least functionality.

title: Maximum Cycle Count Reached
description: The configured maximum number of disconnect/reconnect cycles has been reached. The tool has exited normally.
remediation: No action required. Re-run with a higher --count value or 0 for continuous operation if additional testing cycles are needed.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
remediation_brief: Review and harden configuration per security best practices and CIS benchmarks. Disable unnecessary features and apply least functionality.

title: Disconnect Command Returned Non-Zero Exit Code
description: The OS wireless disconnect command (iw, wpa_cli, nmcli, or airport) returned a non-zero exit code. The interface may not have cleanly disassociated before the reconnect attempt.
remediation: Verify that the process has sufficient privileges (sudo). Confirm the wireless stack is responsive. On Linux, check whether wpa_supplicant is running and accessible via the DBUS interface.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
remediation_brief: Review and harden configuration per security best practices and CIS benchmarks. Disable unnecessary features and apply least functionality.

title: Reconnect Command Returned Non-Zero Exit Code
description: The OS wireless reconnect command returned a non-zero exit code. The network may not have been joined. This may indicate the SSID is not in the system's known network profiles, or that the wireless daemon rejected the connection attempt.
remediation: Confirm the SSID has a saved connection profile (NetworkManager connection or wpa_supplicant configuration block). On macOS, ensure the network was previously joined and is in the keychain.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
remediation_brief: Review and harden configuration per security best practices and CIS benchmarks. Disable unnecessary features and apply least functionality.

title: Dry-Run Cycle Completed (Simulated)
description: A cycle completed in dry-run mode. No actual wireless commands were issued. This confirms the timing logic and argument parsing are functioning correctly.
remediation: No action required. Remove --dry-run for live testing.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
remediation_brief: Review and harden configuration per security best practices and CIS benchmarks. Disable unnecessary features and apply least functionality.

title: Privilege Escalation Required for Wireless Commands
description: Wireless management commands (iw, nmcli, airport) require elevated privileges. The tool invokes these via sudo. If passwordless sudo is not configured, interactive prompts may interrupt automated testing.
remediation: Configure passwordless sudo for the specific wireless commands used by drift (e.g., /usr/bin/iw, /usr/sbin/nmcli, /usr/bin/wpa_cli) in /etc/sudoers.d/drift.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
remediation_brief: Review and harden configuration per security best practices and CIS benchmarks. Disable unnecessary features and apply least functionality.

title: Interface Auto-Detection Fallback Used
description: The wireless interface was not explicitly specified. The tool fell back to parsing /proc/net/wireless or airport output to determine the active interface. The selected interface may not be the intended test adapter.
remediation: Specify the intended interface explicitly using --interface to avoid ambiguity in multi-adapter environments.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
remediation_brief: Review and harden configuration per security best practices and CIS benchmarks. Disable unnecessary features and apply least functionality.

title: Azure Storage: Azure Storage Account allows HTTP: {name}
description: Azure storage account does not enforce HTTPS-only. Data in transit may traverse plaintext.
impact: Attackers on-path can intercept blob/queue/file data and Shared Access Signatures. SAS tokens captured this way grant persistent access until their expiry.
remediation_brief: az storage account update --name <name> --https-only true

title: Azure Storage: Azure Storage Account publicly accessible: {name}
description: Storage account network ACL defaults to Allow with no IP restrictions configured.
impact: Blob endpoints are reachable from the entire internet. Authentication still applies, but any leaked SAS, key, or AD token is immediately exploitable from any source.
remediation_brief: az storage account update --default-action Deny + add specific IP/VNet rules.

title: Azure Key Vault: Azure Key Vault soft-delete disabled: {name}
description: Soft-delete is not enabled on this Key Vault — accidental deletions cannot be recovered within the retention window.
impact: An attacker (or careless operator) who deletes a key, secret, or certificate causes permanent loss; downstream applications that depend on the material break and cannot be restored.
remediation_brief: az keyvault update --name <kv> --enable-soft-delete true

title: Azure Key Vault: Azure Key Vault purge-protection disabled: {name}
description: Purge-protection is disabled — soft-deleted keys / secrets can be immediately purged by an attacker with delete permission.
impact: Attacker with Contributor or Key Vault Contributor can soft-delete then immediately purge, bypassing the soft-delete grace window and destroying evidence.
remediation_brief: az keyvault update --name <kv> --enable-purge-protection true

title: Azure VM: Azure VM OS disk unencrypted: {name}
description: Azure Disk Encryption is disabled on the OS disk.
impact: If the underlying VHD is exfiltrated (snapshot abuse, storage-account compromise), the OS volume can be mounted offline and credentials, keys, and data extracted.
remediation_brief: az vm encryption enable --resource-group <rg> --name <vm> --disk-encryption-keyvault <kv-id>

title: GCS: GCS bucket uniform access disabled: {name}
description: Uniform bucket-level access is disabled; legacy per-object ACLs are in effect.
impact: Object ACLs can grant unintended public-read or all-authenticated-users access bypassing IAM policy. Inventory of object ACLs is hard to audit at scale.
remediation_brief: gcloud storage buckets update gs://<bucket> --uniform-bucket-level-access

title: GCE: GCE instance uses default service account: {name}
description: Compute instance is attached to the default Compute Engine service account.
impact: Default SA is granted Editor by default in legacy projects and supplies broad scopes (cloud-platform). Workload compromise becomes project-wide compromise.
remediation_brief: Create a least-privilege custom SA and re-attach: gcloud compute instances set-service-account.

title: GCE: GCE instance has public IP: {name}
description: Compute instance has an external IP configured.
impact: Direct internet exposure increases attack surface; ensure firewall rules and IAP/Cloud Armor are in place. INFO unless the workload has no internet-egress requirement.
remediation_brief: If unneeded, remove the access-config: gcloud compute instances delete-access-config.

title: GCP: GCP project-level {role} granted to {member}
description: Project-level owner or editor role granted to a user / service account.
impact: Owner/editor at project scope can disable logging, modify any resource, and pivot to other resources. Lateral movement is trivial within the project boundary.
remediation_brief: Replace with narrower predefined or custom roles scoped to specific resources.

title: S3 bucket missing public access block: {name}
description: No S3 public access block configured — objects may be publicly accessible via ACLs or bucket policies.
impact: Without a public access block, misconfigured bucket policies or object ACLs can expose sensitive data to the entire internet. An attacker can enumerate and download objects without authentication.
remediation_brief: aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket <name> --public-access-block-configuration BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true
category: S3 bucket missing public access block

title: S3 bucket incomplete public access block: {name}
description: Not all four public access block settings are enabled on the S3 bucket.
impact: Partial public access block leaves gaps that can be exploited to make objects or the bucket policy public. An attacker who gains write access to the bucket policy or ACLs can bypass the incomplete protections.
remediation_brief: Enable all four public access block settings: BlockPublicAcls, IgnorePublicAcls, BlockPublicPolicy, RestrictPublicBuckets.
category: S3 bucket incomplete public access block

title: S3 bucket versioning disabled: {name}
description: Versioning is not enabled on the S3 bucket — accidental deletions or overwrites are unrecoverable.
impact: Without versioning, a compromised credential or accidental deletion permanently destroys data. Ransomware actors who gain S3 write access can overwrite objects with no recovery path.
remediation_brief: aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket <name> --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled

title: S3 bucket default encryption not configured: {name}
description: No default server-side encryption configured on the S3 bucket.
impact: Objects uploaded without explicit encryption headers are stored in plaintext. If the underlying storage is compromised or snapshots are exfiltrated, data is readable without decryption.
remediation_brief: Enable SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS default encryption on the bucket.
category: S3 bucket default encryption not configured

title: S3 bucket access logging disabled: {name}
description: Server access logging is not enabled on the S3 bucket — access patterns are not auditable.
impact: Without access logs, unauthorized access or data exfiltration from the bucket cannot be detected or investigated after the fact. Incident response is severely hampered.
owasp_web: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
remediation_brief: Enable server access logging to a dedicated logging bucket.

title: S3 bucket policy is public: {name}
description: The S3 bucket policy evaluates as public — objects may be accessible to anyone on the internet.
impact: Any anonymous internet user can list and download objects from the bucket. Sensitive data (PII, credentials, backups, intellectual property) is fully exposed. This is a common root cause of major data breaches.
remediation_brief: Review and restrict the bucket policy. Enable S3 Block Public Access at the account level.

title: S3 bucket MFA Delete not enabled: {name}
description: MFA Delete is not enabled — versioned objects can be permanently deleted without MFA authentication.
impact: An attacker with DeleteObject permission can permanently remove object versions and delete markers, destroying data and audit trails even when versioning is enabled. MFA Delete would require a second factor for these destructive operations.
remediation_brief: Enable MFA Delete via aws s3api put-bucket-versioning with an MFA device.
category: S3 bucket MFA Delete not enabled

title: EC2 instance with public IP: {name}
description: EC2 instance has a public IP address assigned, making it directly reachable from the internet.
impact: Direct internet exposure increases the attack surface. If security groups or NACLs are misconfigured, services running on the instance become accessible to attackers worldwide.
remediation_brief: Remove the public IP if internet access is not required. Use a NAT gateway or VPN for outbound connectivity.

title: EBS volume unencrypted: {volume_id}
description: EBS volume is not encrypted at rest.
impact: If the underlying EBS snapshot is shared, copied to another account, or the physical media is decommissioned, data is readable without decryption. Credentials, keys, and sensitive application data stored on the volume are exposed.
remediation_brief: Create an encrypted snapshot of the volume and replace it with an encrypted copy.

title: Security group {sg_name} ({sg_id}) exposes sensitive ports to 0.0.0.0/0
aliases: SG exposes sensitive ports to internet
description: Security group inbound rule allows 0.0.0.0/0 access to sensitive ports (SSH, RDP, databases, etc.).
impact: Sensitive management and database ports are accessible from any IP address on the internet. Attackers can brute-force credentials, exploit known vulnerabilities, or exfiltrate data from exposed database services.
remediation_brief: Restrict the source CIDR to known IP ranges or use a bastion host / VPN.

title: Security group {sg_name} ({sg_id}) allows all ports from 0.0.0.0/0
aliases: SG allows all ports from any IP
description: Security group inbound rule allows unrestricted access (all ports, 0-65535) from any IP address.
impact: Every service on every port of associated instances is exposed to the entire internet. This is functionally equivalent to no firewall and allows attackers to discover and exploit any running service.
remediation_brief: Remove the 0.0.0.0/0 all-port rule. Apply least-privilege rules scoped to specific ports and source CIDRs.

title: EC2 instance IMDSv2 not enforced: {name}
description: EC2 instance does not require IMDSv2 (HttpTokens != required). IMDSv1 is vulnerable to SSRF-based credential theft.
impact: An attacker who achieves SSRF on the instance can query the IMDSv1 endpoint (http://169.254.169.254) to steal IAM role credentials, pivot to other AWS services, and escalate privileges across the account.
remediation_brief: aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-options --instance-id <id> --http-tokens required --http-endpoint enabled

title: EC2 instance user data contains secrets: {name}
description: EC2 instance user data contains secret-like environment variables or values (passwords, API keys, tokens). Anyone with ec2:DescribeInstanceAttribute permission can read these.
impact: Secrets in user data are accessible to any IAM principal with DescribeInstanceAttribute permission and are logged in CloudTrail. Compromised credentials grant direct access to the systems or services they protect.
remediation_brief: Move secrets to AWS Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store (SecureString). Reference them in user data by ARN/name, not value.
category: EC2 instance user data contains secrets

title: IAM user without MFA: {username}
description: IAM user has no MFA device configured.
impact: Without MFA, a compromised password (phishing, credential stuffing, breach reuse) gives an attacker full access to the user's AWS permissions. MFA is the primary defense against credential-based account takeover.
remediation_brief: Enable virtual MFA (TOTP) or hardware MFA for this IAM user.

title: IAM user has AdministratorAccess: {username}
description: IAM user has the AdministratorAccess managed policy directly attached, granting unrestricted access to all AWS services and resources.
impact: Compromise of this user's credentials grants the attacker full control of the AWS account: they can create resources, exfiltrate all data, disable logging, delete backups, and pivot to connected accounts.
remediation_brief: Remove direct AdministratorAccess. Use role assumption with least-privilege policies and require MFA for role assumption.

title: IAM access key older than 90 days: {username}/{key_id}
description: IAM access key is older than 90 days and should be rotated.
impact: Long-lived access keys have a wider window for compromise through code leaks, log exposure, or insider threats. Stale keys often belong to forgotten integrations with overly broad permissions.
remediation_brief: Rotate the access key: create a new key, update consuming applications, then deactivate and delete the old key.
category: IAM access key older than 90 days

title: IAM: Root account has active access keys
description: The AWS root account has access keys configured. Root keys should never exist — they grant unrestricted, irrevocable access.
impact: Root credentials cannot be scoped by IAM policies or SCPs. Compromise gives an attacker absolute control: they can close the account, change billing, bypass all IAM controls, and destroy all resources.
remediation_brief: Delete all root account access keys immediately. Use IAM users and roles for all programmatic access.

title: IAM: Password policy does not meet complexity requirements
aliases: IAM: Account password policy not configured
description: The IAM account password policy is absent or does not enforce adequate complexity (minimum length >= 14, symbols, numbers, upper and lowercase).
impact: Weak password policies allow users to set easily guessable passwords, increasing susceptibility to brute-force and credential-stuffing attacks against the AWS console.
remediation_brief: aws iam update-account-password-policy --minimum-password-length 14 --require-symbols --require-numbers --require-uppercase-characters --require-lowercase-characters

title: IAM server certificate expired: {cert_name}
description: IAM server certificate has expired.
impact: Expired certificates cause TLS errors or silent fallback to unencrypted connections. Services relying on the certificate may become unavailable or transmit data in plaintext.
remediation_brief: Replace or delete the expired IAM server certificate. Migrate to ACM for automatic renewal where possible.

title: IAM: Root account without MFA
description: The AWS root account does not have MFA enabled. The root account has unrestricted access to all AWS services and resources.
impact: Without MFA, a compromised root password grants complete account takeover — including the ability to delete all resources, exfiltrate all data, and lock out all other users. Root access cannot be restricted by IAM policies.
remediation_brief: Enable MFA on the root account: AWS Console → My Security Credentials → MFA → Activate MFA. Use a hardware FIDO2 key for strongest protection.

title: Orphaned IAM user: {uname}
description: IAM user has no console password, no active access keys, and no MFA. This appears to be an unused or orphaned account.
impact: Orphaned accounts increase attack surface — if credentials are later enabled without proper controls, the account becomes a pivot point. Dormant accounts also indicate poor identity lifecycle management.
remediation_brief: Delete the unused IAM user or activate credentials if the account is still needed. Implement a periodic IAM user review process.

title: IAM user has overly-permissive policy: {uname} ({pol_name})
description: An IAM user has a full-access managed policy directly attached, violating the principle of least privilege.
