description: The server presents a self-signed TLS certificate that is not issued by a trusted Certificate Authority. Self-signed certificates are not validated by browsers or TLS clients by default, indicating the service may not be production-hardened or is using a private PKI without proper trust distribution.
impact: Users must manually trust the certificate or bypass browser warnings, which normalizes ignoring TLS errors and makes man-in-the-middle attacks feasible. A self-signed certificate on an internet-facing service suggests it may be a development, staging, or unmaintained system with weaker security controls.
remediation_brief: Replace the self-signed certificate with one issued by a trusted public Certificate Authority (e.g. Let's Encrypt, DigiCert). If a private CA is required, ensure its root certificate is distributed to all intended clients.

title: SSL/TLS Certificate: TLS Certificate Hostname Mismatch
description: The TLS certificate presented by the server does not match the hostname being accessed. The certificate's Common Name (CN) and Subject Alternative Name (SAN) entries do not include the domain name used to reach the service. This may indicate a misconfiguration, a shared certificate, or a reused certificate from a different service.
impact: Browsers and TLS clients will reject the connection or display warnings, which users may bypass. A hostname mismatch can indicate the service was deployed hastily, is using a certificate intended for another domain, or is sharing infrastructure with other services — all of which leak information about the environment.
remediation_brief: Ensure the TLS certificate's Common Name (CN) or Subject Alternative Name (SAN) entries include all hostnames the server is accessed by. Reissue the certificate with the correct domain names if needed.

title: SSL/TLS Certificate: Revoked TLS Certificate Detected
description: The TLS certificate presented by the server has been revoked by its issuing Certificate Authority. Certificate revocation typically occurs due to key compromise, CA compromise, or administrative decommission. A revoked certificate should not be trusted for any purpose.
impact: A revoked certificate may indicate that the private key was compromised, potentially allowing an attacker to impersonate the server. Clients that check CRL/OCSP will reject the connection, but not all clients perform revocation checking, leaving some users vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks using the compromised key.
remediation_brief: Replace the revoked certificate immediately with a new certificate from a trusted CA. Investigate the reason for revocation — if key compromise is suspected, generate a new key pair. Rotate any credentials or secrets that may have been exposed.

title: Enumeration: TLS Certificate SAN Enumeration
description: The TLS certificate presented by the server contains multiple Subject Alternative Name (SAN) entries, revealing additional hostnames and services hosted on this infrastructure. SAN enumeration is a passive reconnaissance technique that exposes the scope of services behind a single certificate.
impact: An attacker can enumerate additional attack surface by reviewing SAN entries, discovering internal hostnames, staging environments, or related services that may have weaker security controls. Shared certificates also indicate infrastructure relationships between the listed domains.

mitre_attack.name: Search Open Technical Databases: Digital Certificates

remediation_brief: Review SAN entries to ensure no unintended hostnames (internal names, staging environments, decommissioned services) are exposed. Use separate certificates for services that should not be associated publicly.

title: Discovery: Ivanti Cloud Services Appliance (CSA) Detected
description: The TLS certificate fingerprint identifies this host as an Ivanti Cloud Services Appliance (CSA). Ivanti CSA has been the target of multiple critical actively-exploited zero-day vulnerabilities including path traversal (CVE-2024-8963), SQL injection (CVE-2024-9379), OS command injection (CVE-2024-8190), and another OS command injection (CVE-2024-9380).
impact: An attacker can chain these vulnerabilities to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution on the CSA appliance. Successful exploitation provides full administrative access to the appliance and the ability to pivot into the internal network. CISA has issued emergency directives for these vulnerabilities.
remediation_brief: Verify the Ivanti CSA is running the latest patched firmware version. Apply all available security patches immediately. If running CSA 4.6, migrate to CSA 5.0 as version 4.6 has reached end-of-life. Monitor CISA KEV catalogue for new Ivanti advisories.

title: Discovery: Pulse Secure / Ivanti Connect Secure VPN Detected
description: The TLS certificate fingerprint identifies this host as a Pulse Secure / Ivanti Connect Secure VPN appliance. This product line has been the target of critical zero-day exploitation including authentication bypass (CVE-2023-46805) and command injection (CVE-2024-21887), which were chained for unauthenticated RCE.
impact: An attacker can exploit known vulnerabilities to bypass authentication and execute arbitrary commands on the VPN appliance, gaining access to the internal network. VPN appliances are high-value targets as they provide direct access to corporate networks and are internet-facing by design.
remediation_brief: Verify the Ivanti Connect Secure appliance is running the latest patched firmware. Apply vendor mitigation XML and patches as directed by Ivanti advisories. Run the Ivanti Integrity Checker Tool (ICT) to detect signs of compromise. Consider factory-resetting the appliance if compromise is suspected.

title: Discovery: F5 BIG-IP Detected
description: The TLS certificate fingerprint identifies this host as an F5 BIG-IP appliance. F5 BIG-IP has had critical remote code execution vulnerabilities including CVE-2023-46747 (authentication bypass to RCE) and CVE-2022-1388 (iControl REST unauthenticated RCE).
impact: An attacker exploiting known F5 BIG-IP vulnerabilities can achieve unauthenticated remote code execution with root privileges on the appliance. As a load balancer/ADC, BIG-IP sits in a privileged network position with visibility into all traffic it proxies, including credentials and session tokens.
remediation_brief: Verify the F5 BIG-IP is running the latest patched firmware version. Restrict management interface access to trusted networks only. Disable iControl REST on external interfaces if not required.

title: Discovery: Citrix NetScaler / ADC Detected
description: The TLS certificate fingerprint identifies this host as a Citrix NetScaler or ADC appliance. Citrix ADC has been the target of critical zero-day exploitation including CVE-2023-4966 ('Citrix Bleed', session token leakage) and CVE-2023-3519 (unauthenticated RCE).
impact: An attacker can exploit Citrix Bleed (CVE-2023-4966) to steal valid session tokens without authentication, bypassing MFA and gaining access to internal resources. CVE-2023-3519 allows unauthenticated remote code execution on the appliance itself. Both were widely exploited in the wild by ransomware operators.
remediation_brief: Apply Citrix security patches immediately. After patching Citrix Bleed, terminate all active sessions and rotate all credentials — the patch does not invalidate stolen session tokens. Run Citrix-provided IoC scanning tools to check for compromise.

title: Discovery: Fortinet FortiGate Detected
description: The TLS certificate fingerprint identifies this host as a Fortinet appliance (FortiGate, FortiWeb, or FortiOS-based). FortiOS has been the target of critical zero-day exploitation including CVE-2024-21762 (out-of-bound write in SSL VPN) and CVE-2023-27997 (heap buffer overflow in SSL VPN, 'XORtigate').
impact: An attacker can exploit known FortiOS vulnerabilities to achieve pre-authentication remote code execution on the firewall appliance. As a perimeter firewall/VPN, FortiGate sits at the network boundary with full visibility into traffic and provides a pivot point into the internal network.
remediation_brief: Verify the Fortinet appliance is running the latest patched FortiOS firmware. Disable SSL VPN if not required. Restrict management interfaces to trusted networks. Enable logging and monitor for indicators of compromise.

title: Discovery: Palo Alto Networks Detected
description: The TLS certificate fingerprint identifies this host as a Palo Alto Networks appliance. PAN-OS has been the target of critical zero-day exploitation including CVE-2024-3400 (GlobalProtect command injection with CVSS 10.0), which was actively exploited before a patch was available.
impact: An attacker can exploit CVE-2024-3400 to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution with root privileges on the firewall through the GlobalProtect gateway. As a next-generation firewall, Palo Alto devices provide full network visibility and can be used to intercept traffic, modify firewall rules, or pivot into the internal network.
remediation_brief: Verify the Palo Alto appliance is running the latest patched PAN-OS version. Apply hotfixes for CVE-2024-3400 immediately. Restrict management interface access and disable unused GlobalProtect portals. Monitor for indicators of compromise using Palo Alto's threat prevention signatures.

title: Discovery: SonicWall Detected
description: The TLS certificate fingerprint identifies this host as a SonicWall appliance. SonicWall has had critical vulnerabilities including CVE-2024-40766 (improper access control in SonicOS management and SSLVPN) which was actively exploited by ransomware operators.
impact: An attacker can exploit known SonicWall vulnerabilities to gain unauthorized access to the firewall management interface or VPN services. SonicWall appliances are perimeter security devices and their compromise provides direct access to the internal network.
remediation_brief: Verify the SonicWall appliance is running the latest patched firmware version. Restrict SSLVPN and management interface access. Enable MFA for all VPN connections. Monitor for unauthorized access attempts.

title: Discovery: Cisco ASA Detected
description: The TLS certificate fingerprint identifies this host as a Cisco Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA). Cisco ASA is a widely-deployed firewall/VPN platform that has had numerous critical vulnerabilities over its lifetime, including path traversal, authentication bypass, and remote code execution flaws.
impact: A Cisco ASA appliance at the network perimeter provides firewall, VPN, and NAT services. Its compromise gives an attacker the ability to modify access control rules, intercept VPN traffic, and pivot into the internal network. ASA's WebVPN and AnyConnect components have historically been targeted.
remediation_brief: Verify the Cisco ASA is running the latest patched firmware version. Restrict management access to trusted networks. Disable unused VPN profiles and WebVPN features. Monitor syslog for unauthorized access attempts.

title: Discovery: VMware vSphere / ESXi Detected
description: The TLS certificate fingerprint identifies this host as a VMware vSphere, vCenter, or ESXi host. VMware hypervisor products have been targeted by critical vulnerabilities and are high-value targets for ransomware operators who encrypt entire virtual machine datastores.
impact: Compromise of a VMware hypervisor gives an attacker control over all virtual machines running on it, including the ability to access VM disks, snapshot memory, and intercept network traffic between VMs. ESXi-targeting ransomware (e.g. ESXiArgs) can encrypt entire datastores, taking down all hosted services simultaneously.
remediation_brief: Verify VMware ESXi/vCenter is running the latest patched version. Restrict management interfaces (port 443, 902) to a dedicated management VLAN. Disable SSH on ESXi hosts unless actively needed. Enable lockdown mode on ESXi hosts.

title: Discovery: Sophos Firewall Detected
description: The TLS certificate fingerprint identifies this host as a Sophos firewall appliance (XG Firewall, Sophos Firewall OS, or legacy Cyberoam). Sophos firewalls have had critical vulnerabilities including SQL injection and code injection flaws in their user portal and management interfaces.
impact: An attacker exploiting Sophos firewall vulnerabilities can gain unauthorized access to the firewall management interface, modify security policies, and potentially achieve remote code execution. As a perimeter device, compromise provides a pivot point into the internal network and visibility into all traversing traffic.
remediation_brief: Verify the Sophos firewall is running the latest firmware version. Disable the User Portal on WAN-facing interfaces if not required. Restrict management access to trusted internal networks only. Enable automatic hotfix installation.

title: Information Disclosure: Technology Stack Identified (Wappalyzer)
description: Webanalyze (Wappalyzer engine) identified the technology stack running on the target web application. Technologies detected may include web servers, application frameworks, CMS platforms, JavaScript libraries, analytics tools, CDNs, and other components. Each identified technology can be checked against known vulnerability databases for version-specific issues.
impact: Technology fingerprinting reveals the exact software stack in use, enabling targeted vulnerability research. An attacker can search for CVEs, default credentials, and known misconfigurations specific to each detected technology and version. Identifying the CMS, framework, and server version narrows the attack surface to known weaknesses.

mitre_attack.name: Gather Victim Host Information: Client Configurations

remediation_brief: Ensure all identified technologies are running their latest patched versions. Remove version information from HTTP response headers where possible (e.g. ServerTokens Prod, server_tokens off). Remove unused technologies and frameworks to reduce attack surface.

title: Discovery: Hidden HTTP Parameters Discovered
description: arjun discovered hidden HTTP parameters that are not present in crawled forms, links, or visible page elements. These parameters are accepted by the server but not publicly advertised, potentially exposing additional attack surface for injection, authentication bypass, or information disclosure.
impact: Hidden parameters may accept unexpected input that bypasses client-side validation. An attacker who discovers hidden debug, admin, or configuration parameters can probe them for injection vulnerabilities, privilege escalation, or information disclosure. These parameters are often less hardened than publicly documented ones because developers assume they are not discoverable.
remediation_brief: Review all discovered hidden parameters for security implications. Remove any debug, test, or administrative parameters from production deployments. Ensure all accepted parameters are documented and subject to the same input validation and authorization controls as public parameters.

title: Information Disclosure: Security-Sensitive Hidden Parameter
description: arjun discovered a hidden HTTP parameter with a security-sensitive name pattern (such as admin, debug, test, secret, token, key, or password). These parameters suggest debug functionality, authentication bypasses, or configuration controls that should not be accessible in production.
impact: Security-sensitive hidden parameters frequently enable debug modes, expose verbose error output, bypass authentication, or reveal API keys and tokens. An attacker who discovers a 'debug=true' parameter may gain access to stack traces, internal paths, and database queries. Parameters named 'token' or 'key' may accept forged credentials.
remediation_brief: Remove all debug, test, and administrative parameters from production deployments. If debug functionality is required, gate it behind strong authentication and restrict access to authorized personnel. Audit parameter names for sensitive patterns during code review.

title: Injection: Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) — SSTImap Confirmed
description: SSTImap confirmed that the target application is vulnerable to Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI). User-supplied input is rendered directly within a server-side template engine without proper sanitization, allowing an attacker to inject template directives that execute arbitrary code on the server.
impact: A confirmed SSTI vulnerability allows full remote code execution (RCE) on the server. An attacker can read/write arbitrary files, exfiltrate database credentials, pivot to internal networks, and fully compromise the application server. SSTI is one of the highest-impact web vulnerabilities because template engines run with the full privileges of the application process.
remediation_brief: Use sandboxed template engines that restrict template directives to safe operations. Never pass user input directly into template rendering functions. Use template engines' built-in auto-escaping features. If dynamic templates are required, use a strict allowlist of permitted template operations and sanitize all input before rendering.

title: Injection: SSTI — Template Engine Identified
description: SSTImap identified the template engine in use on the target application (e.g., Jinja2, Twig, Freemarker, Mako, Velocity, Smarty) but was unable to achieve code execution. The engine may have sandboxing or input filtering that prevents exploitation, but the presence of a detectable engine suggests user input reaches the template layer.
impact: Template engine identification narrows the attack surface for targeted exploitation. Even if SSTImap could not achieve RCE, manual techniques or future bypass discoveries may succeed. The detection confirms that user input interacts with the template engine, which is a prerequisite for SSTI attacks.
remediation_brief: Ensure the template engine is properly sandboxed with restricted directive capabilities. Verify that user input does not reach template rendering functions. Apply input sanitization and output encoding at the template layer.

title: Injection: OS Command Injection — commix Confirmed
description: commix confirmed that the target application is vulnerable to OS command injection. User-supplied input is incorporated into operating system commands without proper sanitization, allowing an attacker to execute arbitrary system commands on the underlying server with the privileges of the web application process.
impact: Confirmed OS command injection allows full remote code execution. An attacker can read/write files, dump databases, install backdoors, establish reverse shells, pivot to internal networks, and fully compromise the server. This is a maximum-severity vulnerability that provides complete control over the affected system.
remediation_brief: Use parameterized OS commands or language-native APIs instead of shell execution. Never concatenate user input into shell commands. Apply strict input validation with allowlists for expected parameter values. Use subprocess calls with argument arrays instead of shell=True. Implement the principle of least privilege for the web application process.

title: Injection: Blind Command Injection (Time-Based) — commix
description: commix detected blind OS command injection via time-based techniques. The application's response time varied when time-delay payloads (e.g., sleep) were injected, indicating that user input is incorporated into operating system commands. While output is not directly reflected, the time-delay confirmation proves command execution occurs on the server.
impact: Blind command injection is exploitable for full remote code execution even though command output is not returned in the response. An attacker can exfiltrate data character-by-character via time-based inference, establish out-of-band channels (DNS, HTTP callbacks), or write webshells to achieve interactive access. The impact is equivalent to confirmed command injection, with only exploitation complexity increased.
remediation_brief: Use parameterized OS commands or language-native APIs instead of shell execution. Never concatenate user input into shell commands. Apply strict input validation with allowlists. Use subprocess calls with argument arrays instead of shell=True.

title: Web Vulnerability: Web Cache Poisoning
description: toxicache confirmed that the web cache can be poisoned. An unkeyed input (such as an HTTP header not included in the cache key) is reflected in the cached response. An attacker can send a request with a malicious header value, which gets cached and then served to all subsequent users requesting the same URL.
impact: Web cache poisoning allows an attacker to serve malicious content to all users of the affected URL via the CDN or reverse proxy cache. This can be used for stored XSS (injecting JavaScript via unkeyed headers), phishing (redirecting users to attacker-controlled pages), denial of service (caching error responses), and defacement. The attack scales to all users because the poisoned response is served from cache.
remediation_brief: Configure the cache to key on all security-relevant headers. Remove or normalize unkeyed headers before caching. Implement cache-control headers (no-store for sensitive pages). Validate and sanitize all input reflected in responses, including HTTP headers. Use Vary headers to include all inputs that affect the response.

title: Web Vulnerability: Web Cache Deception
description: toxicache detected that the web cache serves incorrect content to users due to path confusion or misconfigured caching rules. An attacker can craft URLs that cause the cache to store authenticated or personalized content and serve it to other users, or serve static content in place of dynamic responses.
impact: Web cache deception can expose authenticated content (account pages, API responses with tokens, personal data) to unauthenticated users. An attacker tricks a victim into visiting a crafted URL that caches their authenticated response, then retrieves that cached content. This can leak session tokens, personal information, and CSRF tokens.
remediation_brief: Configure proper cache rules per content type. Never cache authenticated or personalized responses. Set Cache-Control: no-store on all dynamic/authenticated pages. Normalize URL paths before cache key generation to prevent path confusion attacks.

title: Web Misconfiguration: Unkeyed Header in Cache Response
description: toxicache detected that the web cache does not include a specific HTTP header in its cache key, but the header's value is reflected in the cached response. This means the header could potentially be used for cache poisoning if an exploitable reflection point is found.
impact: An unkeyed header that is reflected in the response is a prerequisite for web cache poisoning. While this finding alone does not confirm exploitation, it indicates that the cache configuration does not properly account for all inputs that influence the response. This is the foundation for cache poisoning attacks that can lead to stored XSS, phishing, or defacement at scale.
remediation_brief: Include all security-relevant HTTP headers in the cache key configuration. Review cache configuration to ensure that any header whose value appears in responses is either included in the cache key or stripped before caching.

title: Session: Session Token Exposed in URL
description: Session-related parameter(s) appear in the URL query string. Tokens in URLs leak through browser history, Referer headers, proxy logs, and server access logs.
impact: An attacker who obtains the URL (via Referer header, shared link, browser history, or proxy logs) gains immediate authenticated access to the victim's session without needing to compromise cookies or credentials directly.
remediation_brief: Transmit session tokens only via cookies (with Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite attributes) or Authorization headers. Never embed session identifiers in URL query parameters or path segments.

title: Session: Session Token in Page Links
description: Page links embed session tokens in URL query parameters within href attributes, leaking tokens through Referer headers when users navigate to external sites.
impact: Session tokens are transmitted to third-party servers via Referer headers when users click external links, allowing third parties or network observers to hijack user sessions.
remediation_brief: Remove session tokens from all hyperlinks. Use cookie-based session management exclusively. Set Referrer-Policy to no-referrer or same-origin.

title: Cookies: Overly Broad Cookie Domain Scope
description: Session cookies are scoped to a parent domain rather than the application's specific hostname, allowing any subdomain under the parent to read these cookies.
impact: A compromised sibling application on any subdomain under the parent domain can read and replay session cookies, enabling cross-application session hijacking without attacking the target directly.
remediation_brief: Set the cookie Domain attribute to the exact hostname of the application. Avoid using parent domain cookies unless required for cross-subdomain SSO.

title: Cookies: Cookie Path Scoped to Root
description: Session cookies use Path=/ while the application resides at a subpath. Other applications on the same hostname can read these cookies.
impact: Other applications sharing the same hostname (common in shared hosting or multi-tenant environments) can access session cookies, creating a cross-application information disclosure risk.
remediation_brief: Set the cookie Path attribute to the application's base URL path to limit cookie visibility to the application's URL space.

title: JWT: JWT Algorithm None Accepted
description: A JWT token uses algorithm 'none', meaning the token has no signature verification. Any attacker can forge arbitrary tokens with any claims.
impact: Complete authentication bypass. An attacker can craft JWTs with arbitrary claims (admin roles, any user identity) without needing the signing key, gaining unrestricted access to all application functionality.

mitre_attack.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Application Access Token

remediation_brief: Enforce a strong signing algorithm (RS256, ES256) server-side. Reject tokens with alg=none. Use an allowlist of accepted algorithms.

title: JWT: JWT Missing Expiration Claim
description: A JWT token has no 'exp' (expiration) claim. Without expiration, a stolen token remains valid indefinitely.
impact: A stolen or leaked JWT can be replayed indefinitely since it never expires, giving an attacker persistent unauthorized access until the signing key is rotated or the token is explicitly blacklisted.

mitre_attack.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Application Access Token

remediation_brief: Include an 'exp' claim in all JWTs with a reasonable lifetime (15 minutes for access tokens, hours for refresh tokens). Validate expiration server-side on every request.

title: JWT: JWT Excessive Lifetime
description: A JWT token has an excessively long lifetime (>24 hours). Long-lived tokens increase the window for token theft and replay attacks.
impact: Extended token lifetimes give attackers a wider window to intercept, steal, and reuse tokens. If a token is compromised, the attacker maintains access for the full remaining lifetime without needing to re-authenticate.
remediation_brief: Reduce JWT lifetime to 15-60 minutes for access tokens. Use refresh tokens for session continuity. Implement token revocation for compromised tokens.

title: Information Disclosure: JWT Contains Sensitive Data
description: A JWT payload contains sensitive fields (passwords, SSNs, credit card numbers). JWT payloads are base64url-encoded (not encrypted) and readable by anyone with access to the token.
impact: Sensitive information embedded in the JWT is exposed to anyone who intercepts the token (via logs, browser storage, network capture, or Referer headers). This is a direct data exposure vulnerability since JWTs are not encrypted by default.
owasp_api: API3:2023 Broken Object Property Level Authorization
remediation_brief: Remove sensitive data from JWT payloads. Store sensitive data server-side and reference it by ID. Use JWE (encrypted JWT) if payload confidentiality is required.

title: JWT: JWT Missing Audience Claim
description: A JWT token has no 'aud' (audience) claim. Without audience restriction, tokens intended for one service may be replayed against a different service that shares the same signing key.
impact: Tokens can be cross-replayed between services that share signing infrastructure. An attacker with a token from a lower-privilege service can replay it against a higher-privilege service if no audience validation is performed.
remediation_brief: Include an 'aud' claim in all JWTs identifying the intended recipient. Validate the audience server-side and reject tokens with unexpected audience values.

title: Session: Session Persists After Password Change
aliases: Session Not Invalidated on Password Change
Password Change Does Not Revoke Sessions
description: Existing sessions remain valid after a password change. If an attacker has compromised a session, changing the password does not revoke their access.
impact: A user who changes their password to recover from a compromise cannot fully revoke attacker access. The compromised session persists, and the attacker retains authenticated access until natural session expiry.
remediation_brief: Invalidate all existing sessions for the user when their password is changed. Force re-authentication on all devices.

title: Session: Excessive Session Cookie Lifetime
description: A session cookie has an excessively long lifetime (>30 days), increasing the window for session hijacking via stolen cookies.
impact: Extremely long-lived session cookies remain valid for weeks or months, giving attackers an extended window to exploit stolen cookies. Even if the user logs out from one device, the cookie on another compromised device remains usable.
remediation_brief: Set session cookie Max-Age/Expires to a reasonable duration (4-8 hours for standard apps, shorter for sensitive apps). Implement absolute server-side session timeout independent of cookie expiry.

title: Missing Security Header: Missing Referrer-Policy With External Links
description: The authenticated page contains external links but no Referrer-Policy header is set. Browsers default to sending the full URL as the Referer header when users click external links, potentially leaking session tokens or sensitive URL parameters.
impact: Session tokens, CSRF tokens, or other sensitive URL parameters are transmitted to third-party servers via the Referer header when users click external links. Third parties can use leaked tokens for session hijacking.
remediation_brief: Set Referrer-Policy header to 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin' or 'no-referrer' to prevent URL leakage. Apply via HTTP header or <meta> tag.

title: Misconfigured Security Header: Mixed Content on Authenticated Page
description: The authenticated HTTPS page loads resources over plain HTTP. Mixed content allows a network attacker to inject malicious resources into the authenticated page via MITM.
impact: A network-positioned attacker can modify HTTP-loaded resources (scripts, styles, images) in transit, injecting malicious content into the authenticated HTTPS page. This can lead to session hijacking, credential theft, or arbitrary code execution in the user's browser context.
remediation_brief: Load all resources over HTTPS. Use Content-Security-Policy: upgrade-insecure-requests to automatically upgrade HTTP to HTTPS.

title: Session: Potential Session Puzzling
description: The same session cookie name is assigned different values across functionally distinct paths (login, registration, password reset, profile). This may indicate session variable overloading where authentication state from one context can be leveraged in another.
impact: An attacker may exploit session puzzling to escalate privileges by initiating a session in one security context (e.g. password reset flow) and presenting it to another context (e.g. authenticated dashboard) where the session variables carry unintended authority.
remediation_brief: Use separate session variables for each functional context (authentication, registration, password reset). Regenerate session IDs at each privilege boundary. Do not reuse session objects across security contexts.

title: Web Misconfiguration: IIS Tilde Shortname Vulnerability
description: The IIS web server processes 8.3 short filename (tilde) requests, confirmed by differential response analysis. When the server receives a request containing the *~1* wildcard pattern, it responds differently (e.g. 404 vs 501) depending on whether the pattern matches an existing short filename, confirming the server interprets tilde shortname syntax.
impact: This misconfiguration enables an attacker to perform brute-force enumeration of the first six characters of all files and directories on the web server using 8.3 short filename patterns. This can reveal backup files, configuration files, source code, hidden administrative paths, and other resources not intended to be publicly accessible.
remediation_brief: Disable 8.3 filename generation via `fsutil behavior set disable8dot3 1` and restart IIS. Note that existing short names persist until the files are recreated; to remove them, copy files to a new directory and delete the originals.

title: Enumeration: IIS Tilde Directory Enumeration
description: Active brute-force enumeration of IIS 8.3 short filenames recovered actual file and directory names from the web server. The shortscan tool exploited the confirmed tilde shortname vulnerability to recover the first six characters of files and directories on disk.
impact: An attacker has successfully enumerated file and directory names on the server, potentially revealing backup files (e.g. web~1.bak), configuration files, source code files, database dumps, or hidden administrative directories. These discoveries can be used to directly access sensitive resources or to inform further targeted attacks against the application.
remediation_brief: Disable 8.3 filename generation: `fsutil behavior set disable8dot3 1` then restart IIS. Existing short names persist until files are recreated. Review all enumerated names for sensitive files and restrict access to any exposed administrative or backup paths. Consider renaming or removing sensitive files that were discovered.

title: Debug Endpoint Exposed
remediation_brief: Remove debug endpoints from production deployments. Restrict access to any legitimate admin endpoints by IP allowlist and authentication.
description: A debug or administrative endpoint was found publicly accessible. These endpoints may expose configuration data, heap dumps, environment variables, or allow remote code execution.
impact: An attacker could leverage this to gain significant unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate sensitive data from affected systems. Exposed information aids attacker reconnaissance and reveals sensitive system details.
_x_remediation: Remove debug endpoints from production deployments. Restrict access to any legitimate admin endpoints by IP allowlist and authentication.

title: Debug Endpoint Exposed: {path}
remediation_brief: Remove or restrict access to sensitive information. Disable verbose errors, directory listings, and unnecessary headers.
description: fracture detected: <value>. This finding indicates a security concern that requires review.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Exposed information aids attacker reconnaissance and reveals sensitive system details.

title: Weak Cryptography: JWE PBES2 Low Iteration Count ({p2c})
description: The JWE token uses PBES2 password-based key wrapping with a dangerously low PBKDF2 iteration count (p2c). OWASP 2023 recommends at least 210,000 iterations for PBKDF2-SHA512; NIST SP 800-132 sets a floor of 10,000. Low iteration counts allow an attacker who captures a JWE token to brute-force the encryption password offline at high speed using commodity hardware.
impact: An attacker who intercepts or retrieves a JWE token can recover the encryption password via offline brute-force. With the password, the attacker can decrypt any token encrypted with the same password, potentially exposing session data, authentication claims, or sensitive payload content. The low iteration count reduces the attack cost from computationally infeasible to practical with consumer GPUs.
remediation_brief: Increase the PBES2 iteration count (p2c) to at least 210,000 per OWASP 2023 guidance for PBKDF2-SHA512. Consider migrating from password-based encryption (PBES2) to direct key wrapping (A256KW) or asymmetric key wrapping (RSA-OAEP) to eliminate brute-force risk entirely.

title: Weak Cryptography: JWE Compression Before Encryption ({zip})
description: The JWE token applies compression (typically DEFLATE) before encryption. Compression before encryption can enable CRIME/BREACH-style oracle attacks when an attacker can influence part of the plaintext and observe ciphertext length changes.
impact: In specific scenarios where an attacker can inject controlled content into the token payload and observe the resulting ciphertext size, the compression oracle leaks information about adjacent plaintext bytes. This can lead to byte-by-byte recovery of secrets (session tokens, CSRF tokens) embedded in the encrypted payload. Exploitability depends heavily on the application architecture.
remediation_brief: Remove compression from JWE tokens (remove the 'zip' header parameter). If compression is required for payload size, ensure no attacker-controlled data enters the encrypted payload to prevent oracle attacks.

title: Weak Cryptography: JWE Uses Password-Based Encryption (PBES2)
description: The application uses password-based encryption (PBES2) for JWE tokens. PBES2 derives the encryption key from a shared password via PBKDF2, making the token's confidentiality dependent on password strength and iteration count. Direct key wrapping (A256KW) or asymmetric key wrapping (RSA-OAEP, ECDH-ES) are preferred for server-to-server token exchange.
impact: The security of all encrypted tokens depends on a single shared password. If the password is weak, reused, or compromised through any channel, all past and future tokens encrypted with it are exposed. Password-based schemes also introduce brute-force attack surface that key-based wrapping eliminates entirely.
remediation_brief: Migrate from password-based encryption (PBES2) to direct key wrapping (A256KW) or asymmetric key wrapping (RSA-OAEP, ECDH-ES+A256KW). If PBES2 must be retained, ensure the password has at least 128 bits of entropy and the iteration count meets current OWASP guidance (210,000+ for SHA-512).

title: Broken Access Control: Cross-Role Discovery — Role-Exclusive Endpoint (Tentative)
description: During multi-role testing, a role's authenticated crawl discovered an endpoint that is not accessible to other tested roles. The discovering role receives HTTP 200 while one or more other roles receive HTTP 401 or 403. This access pattern may indicate broken function-level authorization (BFLA) where access controls are inconsistent across roles, or it may represent legitimate role-specific functionality where different roles have intentionally different feature sets within the scope of their responsibilities.
impact: If this represents a genuine access control gap, an attacker who compromises the discovering role's credentials gains access to functionality that other roles cannot reach, potentially bypassing intended authorization boundaries. If the pattern is by design (role-specific functionality), there is no security impact. Manual review is required to distinguish between the two scenarios.
remediation_brief: Verify whether this role-exclusive access pattern is by design. If the endpoint should be accessible to all authenticated roles, implement consistent role-based authorization. If role-specific, document the intended access policy and ensure it aligns with the principle of least privilege. Review function-level access controls to confirm they enforce the intended authorization model.

title: AI/ML Service Detected: {service_name}
description: A nuclei template tagged with AI/ML-related keywords identified an AI or machine learning service running on the target. This includes LLM inference servers (Ollama, vLLM, LiteLLM), ML platforms (MLflow, TorchServe, Triton), AI web interfaces (Gradio, Streamlit, ComfyUI), and cloud AI services (Bedrock, SageMaker). AI services are vulnerable to a distinct class of attacks including prompt injection, training data extraction, model theft, and output manipulation.
impact: An exposed AI/ML service significantly expands the attack surface. Prompt injection attacks can bypass safety guardrails to exfiltrate data, execute unauthorized actions via tool-use APIs, or manipulate model outputs. Unprotected inference endpoints may allow model abuse, resource exhaustion, or extraction of proprietary model weights and training data. AI services running on default configurations often lack authentication, rate limiting, and input validation.
remediation_brief: Review AI/ML service exposure. Restrict access to authorized clients only via network controls and authentication. Conduct specialized AI security testing with tools like pAIn to evaluate prompt injection, data exfiltration, and model abuse vectors.

description: The SSH service is configured with one or more weaknesses including weak ciphers/MACs, SSHv1 support, permitted root login, or password-based authentication, increasing exposure to brute-force and protocol-level attacks.

_x_remediation: Harden sshd_config to disable SSHv1, restrict ciphers and MACs to strong algorithms, disable root login, disable password authentication, and require public-key authentication only.

title: SMB Signing Disabled or Not Required
remediation_brief: Enable and require SMB signing via Group Policy (RequireSecuritySignature=1) on all Windows systems to prevent NTLM relay attacks.
description: SMB packet signing is not enforced on the server, allowing an attacker positioned between client and server to relay or tamper with SMB authentication and data.
impact: An attacker could leverage this to gain significant unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate sensitive data from affected systems. Network-level vulnerabilities may allow traffic interception, lateral movement, or unauthorized service access.
_x_remediation: Enable and require SMB signing via Group Policy (RequireSecuritySignature=1) on all Windows systems to prevent NTLM relay attacks.

title: Directory Listing Enabled

title: CAN Replay Attack
remediation_brief: Implement SecOC (Secure Onboard Communication, ISO 21434 / AUTOSAR) for safety-critical CAN signals to add freshness counters and message authentication codes. Apply a CAN firewall or gateway to rate-limit and filter frames by ID and frequency. Physically restrict access to OBD-II ports and CAN bus connectors. Log and alert on unexpected frame repetition patterns.
description: A previously captured CAN frame was successfully replayed and accepted as a legitimate message by one or more nodes on the bus. CAN provides no built-in authentication or sequence numbering, meaning any captured frame can be retransmitted at will to reproduce an action — such as unlocking a door, disabling a safety system, or triggering an actuator — without knowledge of the originating system. This class of attack is particularly dangerous in automotive and industrial control environments where CAN commands directly affect physical state.
impact: An attacker could exploit this to gain full system compromise, execute arbitrary code, or obtain complete unauthorized access to sensitive data and systems. Input validation failures may allow injection attacks, data manipulation, or unauthorized code execution.
_x_remediation: Implement SecOC (Secure Onboard Communication, ISO 21434 / AUTOSAR) for safety-critical CAN signals to add freshness counters and message authentication codes. Apply a CAN firewall or gateway to rate-limit and filter frames by ID and frequency. Physically restrict access to OBD-II ports and CAN bus connectors. Log and alert on unexpected frame repetition patterns.

title: SSL/TLS Vulnerability: BEAST
remediation_brief: Disable TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 on the server; accept only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3. Prefer AEAD cipher suites (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) over CBC modes. If TLS 1.0 must remain enabled for legacy clients, configure server-side mitigation by preferring RC4 (deprecated) or — better — use TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV and enforce cipher order.
description: The TLS server accepts TLS 1.0 connections using CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) cipher suites, making it susceptible to the BEAST (Browser Exploit Against SSL/TLS) attack. BEAST exploits a chosen-plaintext vulnerability in the way TLS 1.0 initialises IV values for CBC, allowing an attacker with MITM position and the ability to inject chosen plaintext to perform a blockwise chosen-boundary attack and recover session cookies or other short secrets. While practical exploitation requires both network position and JavaScript injection into the victim's browser, the condition is easily avoided by disabling TLS 1.0.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Weak cryptographic implementations may allow interception, decryption, or forgery of protected communications.
_x_remediation: Disable TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 on the server; accept only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3. Prefer AEAD cipher suites (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) over CBC modes. If TLS 1.0 must remain enabled for legacy clients, configure server-side mitigation by preferring RC4 (deprecated) or — better — use TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV and enforce cipher order.

title: SSL/TLS Vulnerability: LUCKY13
remediation_brief: Migrate to TLS 1.3 or configure TLS 1.2 to use only AEAD cipher suites (AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM, CHACHA20-POLY1305), which do not use MAC-then-encrypt and are inherently immune to LUCKY13. Remove all CBC cipher suites from the server's cipher preference list.
description: The TLS configuration accepts CBC cipher suites that are vulnerable to the LUCKY13 timing side-channel attack. LUCKY13 exploits a timing discrepancy in the MAC verification step of MAC-then-encrypt CBC cipher suites: the number of compression function calls differs based on where padding ends, allowing a statistical timing oracle to decrypt TLS records byte by byte. The attack requires many connections and precise timing measurements but has been demonstrated against real-world TLS stacks including OpenSSL.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Weak cryptographic implementations may allow interception, decryption, or forgery of protected communications.
_x_remediation: Migrate to TLS 1.3 or configure TLS 1.2 to use only AEAD cipher suites (AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM, CHACHA20-POLY1305), which do not use MAC-then-encrypt and are inherently immune to LUCKY13. Remove all CBC cipher suites from the server's cipher preference list.

title: SSL/TLS Vulnerability: SWEET32
remediation_brief: Disable all 3DES and Blowfish cipher suites from the server configuration. Ensure no cipher suite using DES, 3DES, IDEA, or Blowfish appears in the negotiated cipher list. Prefer 128-bit or 256-bit block ciphers (AES-GCM). Upgrade to TLS 1.3 where possible to eliminate legacy cipher negotiation entirely.
description: The TLS server negotiates cipher suites using 64-bit block ciphers such as 3DES (Triple-DES) or Blowfish, making it vulnerable to the SWEET32 birthday attack. After approximately 2^32 blocks (~32 GB of data over a single TLS session), the birthday bound is reached and an attacker can exploit block collisions in CBC mode to recover plaintext. While 32 GB may seem large, long-lived TLS sessions — such as those in web applications with keep-alive or WebSocket connections — can reach this volume in hours.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Weak cryptographic implementations may allow interception, decryption, or forgery of protected communications.
_x_remediation: Disable all 3DES and Blowfish cipher suites from the server configuration. Ensure no cipher suite using DES, 3DES, IDEA, or Blowfish appears in the negotiated cipher list. Prefer 128-bit or 256-bit block ciphers (AES-GCM). Upgrade to TLS 1.3 where possible to eliminate legacy cipher negotiation entirely.

title: SSL/TLS Certificate: Expiring Soon
remediation_brief: Renew the certificate immediately to restore a full validity window. Implement automated certificate renewal using the ACME protocol (Let's Encrypt with certbot, acme.sh, or Caddy) to eliminate manual renewal dependency. Configure monitoring alerts when certificate expiry is within 30 and 14 days.
description: The server's TLS certificate has a remaining validity of fewer than 30 days, placing it at imminent risk of expiry. Upon expiry, browser and client connections will be rejected with a certificate trust error, causing a service outage that appears indistinguishable from a site being down. In environments without automated certificate renewal, short expiry windows frequently result in user-facing downtime and may indicate a weak certificate lifecycle management process.
impact: An attacker could use this information or weakness for reconnaissance or to facilitate more targeted attacks against the organization. Weak cryptographic implementations may allow interception, decryption, or forgery of protected communications.
_x_remediation: Renew the certificate immediately to restore a full validity window. Implement automated certificate renewal using the ACME protocol (Let's Encrypt with certbot, acme.sh, or Caddy) to eliminate manual renewal dependency. Configure monitoring alerts when certificate expiry is within 30 and 14 days.

title: SSL/TLS - Overly Long Certificate Expiry
remediation_brief: Reissue the certificate with a validity period of 398 days or fewer. Transition to automated ACME-based 90-day renewal (Let's Encrypt) to align with current CA/B Forum best practices and reduce reliance on long-lived credentials.
description: The TLS certificate has a validity period exceeding 398 days, in violation of the CA/Browser Forum baseline requirements adopted by all major browsers since September 2020. Certificates with excessively long lifetimes present elevated risk: compromised private keys or mis-issuance cannot be remediated without active revocation (which is poorly enforced by clients), and the certificate may outlive the cryptographic assumptions under which it was issued. Major browsers now hard-fail on certificates exceeding 398 days issued after the policy effective date.
impact: An attacker could use this information or weakness for reconnaissance or to facilitate more targeted attacks against the organization. Weak cryptographic implementations may allow interception, decryption, or forgery of protected communications.

title: FTP Bounce Attack Possible
remediation_brief: Configure the FTP server to reject PORT commands where the specified IP address does not match the client's source address (disable FTP bounce in daemon configuration). Consider migrating from FTP to SFTP or FTPS. Apply firewall rules to restrict outbound connections from the FTP server to known-good destination addresses.
description: The FTP server accepts the PORT command with arbitrary destination IP addresses, enabling FTP bounce attacks. In a bounce attack, an attacker directs the FTP server to open a data connection to a third-party host on any specified port, effectively using the FTP server as a TCP proxy to port-scan internal hosts, bypass egress filtering, or connect to services that would otherwise reject connections from the attacker's source address. This technique can also be used to transfer files to or from third-party machines without direct connectivity.
impact: An attacker could leverage this to gain significant unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate sensitive data from affected systems. Network-level vulnerabilities may allow traffic interception, lateral movement, or unauthorized service access.
_x_remediation: Configure the FTP server to reject PORT commands where the specified IP address does not match the client's source address (disable FTP bounce in daemon configuration). title: NFS Insecure Export Options
remediation_brief: Audit /etc/exports and apply root_squash, all_squash, and nosuid to all exports. Remove no_root_squash unless there is a documented and approved use case. description: One or more NFS exports are configured with insecure options that increase the risk of unauthorised access or privilege escalation. Common insecure settings include no_root_squash (which allows root on the client to act as root on the server), rw on broad CIDR ranges, no_all_squash, or insecure (allowing connections from non-privileged ports). A client with rw and no_root_squash access can write arbitrary files — including SUID binaries or SSH authorised_keys entries — that enable full host compromise.
impact: An attacker could leverage this to gain significant unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate sensitive data from affected systems. Network-level vulnerabilities may allow traffic interception, lateral movement, or unauthorized service access.

title: Missing Secure Cookie Attribute: HttpOnly
remediation_brief: Set the HttpOnly flag on all session, authentication, and sensitive cookies in the application or web server configuration. This flag prevents client-side scripts from accessing the cookie value while still allowing the browser to include it in HTTP requests.
description: A session or sensitive cookie was identified without the HttpOnly attribute. Without this flag, the cookie value is accessible to JavaScript running in the page context, making it directly extractable by any cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability on the same domain. An attacker who finds a reflected or stored XSS flaw can trivially read the session cookie via document.cookie and hijack the authenticated session without needing to exploit the TLS layer.
impact: An attacker could use this information or weakness for reconnaissance or to facilitate more targeted attacks against the organization.
_x_remediation: Set the HttpOnly flag on all session, authentication, and sensitive cookies in the application or web server configuration. This flag prevents client-side scripts from accessing the cookie value while still allowing the browser to include it in HTTP requests.

title: Missing Secure Cookie Attribute: Secure
remediation_brief: Set the Secure flag on all session, authentication, and sensitive cookies. Combined with a site-wide HTTPS redirect and HSTS, this ensures cookies are never transmitted over unencrypted channels.
description: A session or sensitive cookie was identified without the Secure attribute. Without this flag, the browser will transmit the cookie over both HTTPS and plaintext HTTP connections. If the application supports or redirects through any HTTP endpoint — even briefly — the session cookie will be included in the cleartext request and is visible to network attackers. This condition is commonly exploited via SSL stripping attacks that downgrade HTTPS to HTTP before the Secure cookie check takes effect.
impact: An attacker could use this information or weakness for reconnaissance or to facilitate more targeted attacks against the organization.
_x_remediation: Set the Secure flag on all session, authentication, and sensitive cookies. Combined with a site-wide HTTPS redirect and HSTS, this ensures cookies are never transmitted over unencrypted channels.

title: Missing Secure Cookie Attribute: SameSite
remediation_brief: Set SameSite=Strict for cookies used in purely same-origin contexts, or SameSite=Lax as a minimum to prevent cookie transmission in cross-origin subresource requests while allowing top-level navigations. Avoid SameSite=None unless the cookie must be shared in cross-site embedded contexts, in which case the Secure attribute is also mandatory.
description: A session or sensitive cookie was identified without a SameSite attribute. Cookies without SameSite are sent by the browser in all cross-site requests, including those initiated by third-party web pages. This exposes the application to cross-site request forgery (CSRF) attacks, where an attacker's page silently makes authenticated requests to the target application using the victim's browser-stored session cookie, potentially triggering state-changing actions without user consent.
impact: An attacker could use this information or weakness for reconnaissance or to facilitate more targeted attacks against the organization.
_x_remediation: Set SameSite=Strict for cookies used in purely same-origin contexts, or SameSite=Lax as a minimum to prevent cookie transmission in cross-origin subresource requests while allowing top-level navigations. Avoid SameSite=None unless the cookie must be shared in cross-site embedded contexts, in which case the Secure attribute is also mandatory.

title: Misconfigured Secure Cookie Attribute: SameSite
remediation_brief: If SameSite=None is required for cross-site embedding, the Secure attribute must also be present. Evaluate whether SameSite=Strict is appropriate; if so, upgrade from Lax to Strict. Review all state-changing endpoints to confirm they are protected by either SameSite=Strict or an additional CSRF token mechanism.
description: A session or sensitive cookie was identified with the SameSite attribute set to an insecure value. Setting SameSite=None without also setting the Secure attribute causes the cookie to be rejected by modern browsers or sent over HTTP, while SameSite=Lax may be insufficient for applications requiring CSRF protection on all state-changing requests that can be triggered via cross-origin navigations. Misconfigured SameSite values indicate an incomplete implementation of the cookie security policy.
impact: An attacker could use this information or weakness for reconnaissance or to facilitate more targeted attacks against the organization.
_x_remediation: If SameSite=None is required for cross-site embedding, the Secure attribute must also be present. Evaluate whether SameSite=Strict is appropriate; if so, upgrade from Lax to Strict. Review all state-changing endpoints to confirm they are protected by either SameSite=Strict or an additional CSRF token mechanism.

title: Serial Port Allows Remote Access
remediation_brief: Password-protect the serial console in device firmware and configure an inactivity timeout. Disable network bridging of serial interfaces unless strictly required; if required, protect access with authenticated VPN and firewall rules. In production firmware builds, disable UART console output and bootloader access entirely or require a hardware-present jumper to unlock.
description: A serial console interface is accessible to an unauthenticated party via an exposed physical connector, a network-bridged serial server, or a serial-over-LAN (SOL) interface that is reachable from the assessment network. impact: An attacker could exploit this to gain full system compromise, execute arbitrary code, or obtain complete unauthorized access to sensitive data and systems. Physical security weaknesses may allow unauthorized hardware access, data extraction, or device manipulation.
_x_remediation: Password-protect the serial console in device firmware and configure an inactivity timeout. title: SSL/TLS Vulnerability: Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160)
remediation_brief: Upgrade OpenSSL to 1.0.1g or later (or 1.0.2 / 1.1.0+ for current branches). After patching, rotate all TLS private keys and certificates, revoke the old certificates, invalidate all active sessions, and reset any passwords that may have been in server memory during the exposure window. Verify remediation by re-running the Heartbleed check.
description: The target is running a version of OpenSSL affected by CVE-2014-0160 (Heartbleed). The TLS heartbeat extension implementation in OpenSSL 1.0.1 through 1.0.1f fails to validate the length field in the heartbeat request, allowing an unauthenticated remote attacker to read up to 64 kilobytes of server memory per request without leaving a trace in standard access logs. Repeated requests allow an attacker to recover private TLS keys, session tokens, passwords, and other secrets from server memory over time.
impact: An attacker could exploit this to gain full system compromise, execute arbitrary code, or obtain complete unauthorized access to sensitive data and systems. Weak cryptographic implementations may allow interception, decryption, or forgery of protected communications.
_x_remediation: Upgrade OpenSSL to 1.0.1g or later (or 1.0.2 / 1.1.0+ for current branches). title: Bluetooth Device Discovered
remediation_brief: Reconcile every discovered radio against the authorised asset inventory; disable or shield Bluetooth interfaces that are not required.
description: A Bluetooth (BR/EDR or BLE) device was detected during zero-knowledge scanning, along with its advertising data (address, address type, RSSI, name, service UUIDs, manufacturer data).
impact: Confirms a live wireless attack surface and provides the address and advertised metadata needed to target every subsequent enumeration, pairing, and exploitation test.
_x_remediation: Reconcile every discovered radio against the authorised asset inventory; disable or shield Bluetooth interfaces that are not required.

title: BLE GATT Service Enumerated
remediation_brief: Where the GATT layout itself is sensitive, require an encrypted, bonded link before service discovery is permitted.
description: The GATT server of a BLE device was enumerated without prior knowledge, revealing its services, characteristics, handles and properties (read/write/notify).
impact: Discloses device function and defines the read/write/subscribe attack surface; unauthenticated enumeration is the first step toward characteristic abuse.
_x_remediation: Where the GATT layout itself is sensitive, require an encrypted, bonded link before service discovery is permitted.

title: Classic Bluetooth SDP Service Enumerated
remediation_brief: Disable unused BR/EDR profiles; restrict SDP exposure and require authentication for sensitive services.
description: Classic Bluetooth (BR/EDR) SDP service records were enumerated (RFCOMM/L2CAP channels, profiles such as SPP/DUN/PAN).
impact: Exposed SDP records widen the BR/EDR attack surface and can reveal legacy profiles (PAN/BNEP, DUN) with their own vulnerability history.
_x_remediation: Disable unused BR/EDR profiles; restrict SDP exposure and require authentication for sensitive services.

title: Static or Public Bluetooth Address — Device Trackable
remediation_brief: Enable LE Privacy with frequently-rotating Resolvable Private Addresses; distribute the IRK only to bonded peers.
description: The device advertises with a Public or Static-Random Bluetooth address that does not rotate, rather than a rotating Resolvable Private Address (RPA).
impact: A stable address lets any passive listener track and correlate a body-worn or clinical device (and by extension a patient) across time and location, and leaks the OUI/vendor.
_x_remediation: Enable LE Privacy with frequently-rotating Resolvable Private Addresses; distribute the IRK only to bonded peers.

title: Sensitive Identifier Broadcast in Advertising Data
remediation_brief: Remove serials and patient identifiers from the advertised device name and manufacturer data; expose per-unit IDs only via an authenticated, bonded GATT read; consider BT 5.4 Encrypted Advertising Data.
description: The device broadcasts a serial number, patient identifier, or other per-unit token in its advertising name or manufacturer-specific data, in the clear.
impact: A stable unique identifier in advertising defeats address privacy (the string becomes the tracking key) and discloses asset/patient information to any passive listener in range.
_x_remediation: Remove serials and patient identifiers from the advertised device name and manufacturer data; expose per-unit IDs only via an authenticated, bonded GATT read; consider BT 5.4 Encrypted Advertising Data.

title: Just Works Pairing — No MITM Protection
remediation_brief: Provision real IO capability and set the MITM bit (LESC Numeric Comparison or Passkey Entry); where no IO exists, use OOB pairing or an app-layer authenticated channel.
description: The device negotiated Just Works pairing (SMP MITM-protection bit = 0, or an IO capability of NoInputNoOutput on either side), which provides no man-in-the-middle protection.
impact: An active attacker in radio range can interpose during pairing and relay or modify the entire connection, because Just Works authenticates neither party.
_x_remediation: Provision real IO capability and set the MITM bit (LESC Numeric Comparison or Passkey Entry); where no IO exists, use OOB pairing or an app-layer authenticated channel.

title: LE Legacy Pairing — Passively Decryptable
remediation_brief: Require LE Secure Connections (ECDH P-256); reject SC=0 on any hardware that supports LESC (BLE 4.2+).
description: The device negotiated LE Legacy pairing (SMP Secure Connections bit = 0). Legacy derives the session key from a weak Temporary Key (Just Works TK=0; Passkey Entry TK is a ~20-bit value).
impact: A passively-sniffed pairing can be decrypted offline with crackle, recovering the Long-Term Key and all past and future bonded traffic for that pair.
_x_remediation: Require LE Secure Connections (ECDH P-256); reject SC=0 on any hardware that supports LESC (BLE 4.2+).

title: Static or Reused BLE Passkey
remediation_brief: Use a fresh, random, per-pairing passkey that is never hard-coded, printed, or reused across units; prefer Numeric Comparison or OOB where the UI allows.
description: The device authenticates LE Secure Connections pairing with a static or reused 6-digit passkey — printed on the enclosure, embedded in firmware/manual, or identical across units — rather than a fresh random per-pairing value.
impact: A hard-coded or shared passkey defeats the MITM protection of LESC Passkey Entry: anyone who can read the printed/documented value can complete an authenticated man-in-the-middle relay, reducing LESC to Just Works in practice.
_x_remediation: Use a fresh, random, per-pairing passkey that is never hard-coded, printed, or reused across units; prefer Numeric Comparison or OOB where the UI allows.

title: Bluetooth Pairing Method Confusion
remediation_brief: Pin the negotiated association model, present an unambiguous 'enter' vs 'compare' UI, and prefer OOB pairing.
description: A man-in-the-middle can negotiate Numeric Comparison with one device and Passkey Entry with the other in the same ceremony; both use a 6-digit value, so the user reads the number one device shows and enters it into the other, completing a stable MITM even under LESC.
impact: Defeats the highest LESC/MITM security level via the human factor (CERT VU#534195): the attacker holds a persistent interposed position while both devices report a successful pairing.
_x_remediation: Pin the negotiated association model, present an unambiguous 'enter' vs 'compare' UI, and prefer OOB pairing.

title: Bluetooth Pairing Security Downgrade Accepted
remediation_brief: Enforce a security floor (SC=1, MITM for sensitive functions, 16-byte key) and abort pairing on any weaker offer; re-verify the negotiated level before exposing sensitive GATT.
description: The device completed pairing after a forced downgrade offer (Secure Connections cleared, IO capability set to NoInputNoOutput, and/or a reduced key size), instead of aborting.
impact: A device that silently accepts SC=0 / Just Works / a short key when it can support stronger security is exploitable via an active downgrade man-in-the-middle in range.
_x_remediation: Enforce a security floor (SC=1, MITM for sensitive functions, 16-byte key) and abort pairing on any weaker offer; re-verify the negotiated level before exposing sensitive GATT.

title: Short Bluetooth Encryption Key Negotiated
remediation_brief: Enforce a 16-byte encryption key floor and abort pairing/connection on any shorter negotiated size.
description: The device negotiated a maximum encryption key size below 16 bytes (BLE floor is 7). Short keys reduce brute-force cost and are the BLE analogue of the KNOB attack.
impact: A negotiated key near the 7-byte floor allows an attacker to brute-force the session key and decrypt or inject traffic.
_x_remediation: Enforce a 16-byte encryption key floor and abort pairing/connection on any shorter negotiated size.

title: Bluetooth Vulnerability: ECDH Public Key Not Validated (CVE-2018-5383)
remediation_brief: Update to post-2018 firmware/OS that mandates ECDH public-key on-curve validation.
description: The pairing stack does not validate the peer's ECDH public key (Y-coordinate) during Secure Simple Pairing / LE Secure Connections, allowing a fixed-coordinate invalid-curve attack.
impact: An in-range MITM present during pairing can force the shared secret into a small subgroup and recover the session key (~50% per attempt, retryable), fully compromising the session.
_x_remediation: Update to post-2018 firmware/OS that mandates ECDH public-key on-curve validation.

title: Bluetooth Vulnerability: KNOB — Encryption Key Entropy Downgrade (CVE-2019-9506)
remediation_brief: Patch the host to enforce a minimum encryption key entropy (>=7 octets BR/EDR, 16 for LESC) and abort shorter negotiations.
description: The BR/EDR encryption key-entropy negotiation (LMP) is not integrity-protected, letting a MITM force both devices to a 1-byte (8-bit) key.
impact: The reduced-entropy key is brute-forced in real time, allowing an in-range attacker with no pairing or user interaction to decrypt and inject traffic on the link.
_x_remediation: Patch the host to enforce a minimum encryption key entropy (>=7 octets BR/EDR, 16 for LESC) and abort shorter negotiations.

title: Bluetooth Vulnerability: BLUFFS — Forward/Future Secrecy Weakness (CVE-2023-24023)
remediation_brief: Reject low negotiated key lengths, adopt the SIG key-derivation fix, and operate in Secure Connections Only mode.
description: Weaknesses in BR/EDR session-key derivation (Core Spec 4.2-5.4) permit unilateral, repeatable session-key derivation, breaking forward and future secrecy; combined with key-length downgrade it enables MITM and impersonation across sessions.
impact: An in-range attacker can force reuse of a weak session key, decrypting captured traffic and impersonating a device across multiple sessions.
_x_remediation: Reject low negotiated key lengths, adopt the SIG key-derivation fix, and operate in Secure Connections Only mode.

title: Bluetooth Vulnerability: BIAS — Impersonation (CVE-2020-10135)
remediation_brief: Enable Secure Connections Only mode and require mutual authentication in both directions.
description: BR/EDR authentication does not mandate mutual authentication; via role-switch and SC-to-legacy downgrade an attacker impersonates a previously-paired master or slave without possessing the link key.
impact: An attacker in range who knows the victim BD_ADDR can impersonate a trusted, previously-bonded device without any key material.
_x_remediation: Enable Secure Connections Only mode and require mutual authentication in both directions.

title: Bluetooth Vulnerability: BLURtooth — Cross-Transport Key Overwrite (CVE-2020-15802)
remediation_brief: Apply BT 5.1 CTKD restrictions that forbid overwriting authenticated keys or downgrading key strength.
description: In dual-mode devices supporting Cross-Transport Key Derivation (spec 4.2/5.0 before 5.1), an unauthenticated attacker in range can trigger CTKD to overwrite an authenticated bonding key with an unauthenticated or lower-entropy one.
impact: The paired relationship can be silently weakened without user interaction, enabling MITM on a link the user believes is securely bonded.
_x_remediation: Apply BT 5.1 CTKD restrictions that forbid overwriting authenticated keys or downgrading key strength.

title: Bluetooth Vulnerability: BLESA — BLE Reconnection Spoofing (CVE-2020-9770)
remediation_brief: Enforce mandatory authenticated and encrypted reconnection before accepting any data from a previously-bonded peer.
description: BLE reconnection authentication is optional and often not enforced by the client, so a central accepts spoofed data from an impersonated peripheral without re-authentication after the first bonding.
impact: An attacker spoofing the peripheral BD_ADDR can feed forged data (e.g. medical telemetry) to the consuming device on reconnect, with no user interaction.
_x_remediation: Enforce mandatory authenticated and encrypted reconnection before accepting any data from a previously-bonded peer.

title: Unauthenticated GATT Characteristic Read
remediation_brief: Set encryption/authentication-required permissions on sensitive characteristics; gate PHI behind LESC-authenticated bonding.
description: One or more GATT characteristics returned data over an unpaired, unencrypted link (ATT Read Response with a value and no 0x05/0x0F/0x08 security error).
impact: Any listener in range can read the exposed data with no credential; where it is PHI, telemetry, or configuration the confidentiality impact is severe.
_x_remediation: Set encryption/authentication-required permissions on sensitive characteristics; gate PHI behind LESC-authenticated bonding.

title: Unauthenticated GATT Characteristic Write
remediation_brief: Require an authenticated, encrypted, bonded link (LESC + MITM) for all writes; add application-layer authorization (signed / challenge-response commands) to control points and OTA.
description: A GATT write to a device characteristic succeeded over an unpaired, unencrypted link (ATT Write Response with no security error).
impact: Unauthenticated write access permits configuration change, actuation, factory reset, or firmware/OTA abuse with no credential — the highest-impact GATT finding, and safety-critical on a medical device.
_x_remediation: Require an authenticated, encrypted, bonded link (LESC + MITM) for all writes; add application-layer authorization (signed / challenge-response commands) to control points and OTA.

title: Unauthenticated GATT Notification/Indication Stream
remediation_brief: Require encryption on the CCCD and its source characteristic; do not start notifications before authenticated bonding.
description: On an unpaired link the device granted a large ATT MTU and started notifications/indications after a CCCD write, streaming data without authentication.
impact: Sensitive telemetry or PHI is exposed to any in-range listener without pairing; a large pre-auth MTU on a sensitive stream aggravates the leak.
_x_remediation: Require encryption on the CCCD and its source characteristic; do not start notifications before authenticated bonding.

title: SweynTooth BLE SoC Vulnerability Surface
remediation_brief: Update the BLE controller firmware/SDK to a patched release; where the SoC is end-of-life, apply architectural mitigations (restrict pairing, disable unused profiles, physical/RF controls).
description: The device's BLE System-on-Chip belongs to a vendor/part with known SweynTooth firmware vulnerabilities in the Link Layer, L2CAP, SMP or ATT (crash, deadlock, or the Telink Zero-LTK Installation security bypass).
impact: Depending on the SoC and SDK version, an in-range attacker can crash or deadlock the device (DoS, may require power-cycle) or, on affected Telink parts, install an all-zero LTK for arbitrary read/write — safety-relevant per FDA/CISA advisory ICS-ALERT-20-063-01.
_x_remediation: Update the BLE controller firmware/SDK to a patched release; where the SoC is end-of-life, apply architectural mitigations (restrict pairing, disable unused profiles, physical/RF controls).

title: BrakTooth BR/EDR SoC Vulnerability Surface
remediation_brief: Update the Bluetooth controller firmware to a patched release; for end-of-life SoCs, disable unused profiles, restrict connectability, and apply physical/RF controls.
description: The device's BR/EDR System-on-Chip belongs to a vendor/part with known BrakTooth LMP/Baseband vulnerabilities (V1-V16), ranging from crashes and deadlocks to Espressif ESP32 arbitrary code execution.
impact: An in-range attacker can crash, deadlock, or (on ESP32) execute code on the controller; several affected parts (e.g. TI CC2564C, Qualcomm CSR8811/8510) were 'no fix planned', leaving only architectural mitigation.
_x_remediation: Update the Bluetooth controller firmware to a patched release; for end-of-life SoCs, disable unused profiles, restrict connectability, and apply physical/RF controls.

title: BleedingTooth Linux BlueZ Kernel Vulnerability Surface
remediation_brief: Patch the kernel to 5.9+ (or vendor backport); set CONFIG_BT_HS=n to remove the A2MP path; rfkill unused radios.
description: The Linux host behind the Bluetooth controller runs an unpatched BlueZ kernel (< 5.9), exposing the BleedingTooth family: BadKarma (L2CAP heap type-confusion), BadChoice (info leak), BadVibes (BLE ext-advertising heap overflow).
impact: BadKarma chains to zero-click kernel remote code execution over BR/EDR from radio range; BadVibes needs only that the victim is scanning, with no BD_ADDR required.
_x_remediation: Patch the kernel to 5.9+ (or vendor backport); set CONFIG_BT_HS=n to remove the A2MP path; rfkill unused radios.

title: BlueBorne Bluetooth Stack Vulnerability Surface
remediation_brief: Apply the 2017-09+ vendor security patches; disable Bluetooth when unused.
description: The host Bluetooth stack (Linux BlueZ, Android, Windows, or old iOS) predates the 2017 BlueBorne patches, exposing SDP/BNEP/L2CAP flaws that require only that Bluetooth is powered on.
impact: An attacker in range can achieve remote code execution or MITM with no pairing and no user interaction; 'non-discoverable' is not a mitigation because the address is recoverable by sniffing.
_x_remediation: Apply the 2017-09+ vendor security patches; disable Bluetooth when unused.

title: LE Secure Connections Confirmed (Passively Uncrackable)
remediation_brief: Maintain LESC; additionally verify per-pairing random passkeys, no debug keys, and rejection of downgrade offers.
description: The device completed LE Secure Connections pairing (ECDH P-256), confirmed on the wire by the Pairing Public Key / DHKey Check PDUs and/or a crackle result of 'LE Secure Connections'.
impact: Positive assurance that the session key never crosses the air and the pairing is not passively crackable; residual risk shifts to implementation flaws (static passkey, debug keys, downgrade acceptance).
_x_remediation: Maintain LESC; additionally verify per-pairing random passkeys, no debug keys, and rejection of downgrade offers.

title: BlueSmack / L2CAP Echo Denial of Service
