description: osift detected: Social Security pattern detected:. This finding indicates a security concern that requires review.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Exposed information aids attacker reconnaissance and reveals sensitive system details.

title: DNS Information: DNS: DMARC record found
description: A DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance) record was found for the domain. DMARC instructs receiving mail servers on how to handle messages that fail SPF and DKIM validation checks.
impact: A properly configured DMARC record instructs receiving mail servers to reject or quarantine spoofed emails. While this is a positive security control, the DMARC policy details reveal the organization's email authentication architecture and reporting endpoints, which inform phishing campaign design.
remediation_brief: Ensure DMARC policy is set to 'reject' (p=reject) for maximum protection against email spoofing. Configure aggregate and forensic reporting endpoints to monitor policy violations.

title: DNS: Missing CAA Record
aliases: DNS Information: DNS: Missing CAA Record
description: No CAA record found. Without CAA, any public Certificate Authority can issue TLS certificates for this domain.
impact: Any Certificate Authority can issue TLS certificates for this domain. An attacker who compromises a CA's validation process — or uses a permissive CA — can obtain a valid certificate and use it for man-in-the-middle attacks or impersonation.
remediation_brief: Publish a CAA DNS record restricting certificate issuance to your authorized CA(s), e.g. 0 issue "letsencrypt.org".

title: DNS Information: nslookup forward lookup: {record_summary}
description: Forward DNS lookup enumeration was performed, revealing mail exchange (MX), name server (NS), text (TXT), and other DNS records for the domain.
impact: DNS record enumeration reveals mail servers, nameservers, SPF policies, and other infrastructure details that map the organization's digital footprint. An attacker uses this data to identify email providers, hosting relationships, and security mechanisms that inform subsequent attack phases.

mitre_attack.name: Search Open Technical Databases: DNS/Passive DNS

remediation_brief: Review DNS records for unnecessary information disclosure. Ensure SPF, DKIM, and DMARC are properly configured. Consider restricting zone transfers and minimizing publicly exposed DNS records.

title: DNS Vulnerability: Typosquatting Domain Detected
description: One or more domains visually or typographically similar to the target domain were detected with active DNS resolution, indicating potential typosquatting infrastructure.
impact: Typosquatting domains that resolve to active infrastructure can be used for phishing, credential harvesting, or malware distribution targeting the organization's users and customers. An attacker registers domains visually similar to the legitimate domain to intercept mistyped URLs or craft convincing phishing campaigns.
remediation_brief: Monitor for typosquatting domains using automated tools (dnstwist). Consider registering common misspellings of the domain proactively. Implement DMARC to prevent spoofed emails from look-alike domains. Establish a domain takedown process with registrars.

title: DNS Information: DNS: A Record
description: A record maps a domain to an IPv4 address, revealing the IP infrastructure behind a hostname.
impact: Exposing A records allows attackers to identify hosting providers, colocated services, and network topology for targeted attacks.

mitre_attack.name: Search Open Technical Databases: DNS/Passive DNS

remediation_brief: Minimize unnecessary A records. Use CDN or proxy services to obscure origin server IPs where appropriate.

title: DNS Information: DNS: AAAA Record
description: AAAA record maps a domain to an IPv6 address, revealing dual-stack infrastructure.
impact: IPv6 records can expose additional attack surface on hosts that may have different firewall rules or monitoring than their IPv4 counterparts.

mitre_attack.name: Search Open Technical Databases: DNS/Passive DNS

remediation_brief: Ensure IPv6 hosts have equivalent security controls to IPv4. Remove AAAA records for services not intentionally dual-stacked.

title: DNS Information: DNS: MX Record
description: MX record identifies the mail servers responsible for accepting email for the domain.
impact: Attackers use MX records to identify email infrastructure, target mail servers for exploitation, and craft phishing campaigns that mimic legitimate mail routing.

mitre_attack.name: Search Open Technical Databases: DNS/Passive DNS

remediation_brief: Ensure MX records point only to authorized mail servers. Implement SPF, DKIM, and DMARC. Remove MX records for domains that do not send or receive email.

title: DNS Information: DNS: NS Record
description: NS record identifies the authoritative nameservers for the domain.
impact: Knowledge of nameservers enables DNS cache poisoning attempts, zone transfer attacks, and helps map the organization's DNS infrastructure and hosting relationships.

mitre_attack.name: Search Open Technical Databases: DNS/Passive DNS

remediation_brief: Use reputable DNS providers with DNSSEC support. Restrict zone transfers to authorized secondaries. Monitor for unauthorized NS record changes.

title: DNS Information: DNS: TXT Record
description: TXT records contain arbitrary text data including SPF policies, DKIM keys, domain verification tokens, and service configuration.
impact: TXT records can leak internal service configurations, reveal third-party integrations (Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, etc.), and expose verification tokens that may enable service takeover.

mitre_attack.name: Search Open Technical Databases: DNS/Passive DNS

remediation_brief: Audit TXT records regularly. Remove obsolete verification tokens. Ensure SPF records use restrictive policies (-all). Implement DKIM and DMARC.

title: DNS Information: DNS: SOA Record
description: SOA record contains the primary nameserver, responsible party email, and zone serial/refresh parameters.
impact: SOA records reveal the primary DNS administrator's contact, zone update frequency, and infrastructure details useful for social engineering and timing attacks around zone refreshes.

mitre_attack.name: Search Open Technical Databases: DNS/Passive DNS

remediation_brief: Ensure SOA contact email does not expose internal personnel. Use reasonable TTL and refresh values.

title: DNS Information: DNS: CNAME Record
description: CNAME record creates an alias from one domain to another canonical name.
impact: CNAME records can reveal internal naming conventions, third-party service dependencies, and may be vulnerable to subdomain takeover if the canonical target is decommissioned.

mitre_attack.name: Search Open Technical Databases: DNS/Passive DNS

remediation_brief: Regularly audit CNAME records for dangling references. Remove CNAMEs pointing to decommissioned services to prevent subdomain takeover.

title: CI/CD Security: Workflow Injection Vulnerability
aliases: CI/CD Security: GitHub Actions: Workflow Injection Vulnerability
description: gato identified a GitHub Actions workflow that uses unsanitized expression substitution (${{ }}) with attacker-controlled input (such as issue titles, PR bodies, or commit messages). This allows an attacker to inject arbitrary code that executes in the workflow runner context.
impact: Workflow injection allows an attacker to execute arbitrary code in the CI/CD environment. This can lead to secret exfiltration (GitHub tokens, deployment keys, API credentials), supply chain compromise (modifying build artifacts), lateral movement to other repositories, and persistent access via self-hosted runner compromise.

mitre_attack.name: Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain

remediation_brief: Use intermediate environment variables instead of direct expression substitution in workflow run steps. Replace ${{ github.event.issue.title }} with an env: block that assigns the value to an environment variable, then reference the variable in the script. Use actions/github-script with the github context object instead of shell interpolation.

title: CI/CD Security: Secret Exfiltration Path
aliases: CI/CD Security: GitHub Actions: Secret Exfiltration Path
description: gato identified a workflow configuration where secrets are accessible to jobs or steps that process untrusted input. An attacker who can trigger the workflow (via PR, issue, or fork) may be able to exfiltrate secrets through environment variables, workflow artifacts, or out-of-band channels.
impact: Secret exfiltration from CI/CD pipelines can expose deployment credentials, cloud provider keys, signing certificates, and API tokens. Compromised secrets enable lateral movement to production environments, supply chain attacks via signed releases, and persistent access to organizational infrastructure.

mitre_attack.name: Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain

remediation_brief: Restrict secrets to specific jobs using environment-level scoping. Use OIDC tokens instead of long-lived credentials for cloud authentication. Require approval for workflows triggered by external contributors. Avoid passing secrets to steps that handle untrusted input.

title: CI/CD Security: Overly Permissive Permissions
aliases: CI/CD Security: GitHub Actions: Overly Permissive Permissions
description: gato identified a GitHub Actions workflow with overly permissive GITHUB_TOKEN permissions (such as write-all, admin, or contents: write). Workflows should follow the principle of least privilege and request only the minimum permissions required for their function.
impact: Overly permissive workflow tokens increase the blast radius if the workflow is compromised. A write-all token can modify repository contents, create releases, manage issues/PRs, push to protected branches, and modify repository settings. If combined with a workflow injection, an attacker gains full repository control.
remediation_brief: Apply least-privilege permissions to all workflows. Use the permissions: key at the workflow or job level to request only required scopes (e.g., contents: read, issues: write). Avoid write-all or admin permissions.

title: CI/CD Security: Self-Hosted Runner Risk
aliases: GitHub Actions Runner on Public Repo
CI/CD Security: GitHub Actions: Self-Hosted Runner Risk
description: gato identified self-hosted GitHub Actions runners configured on a public repository. Self-hosted runners in public repos are dangerous because any user can submit a pull request that triggers a workflow run on the runner, potentially executing arbitrary code in the organization's infrastructure.
impact: Self-hosted runners on public repos allow any GitHub user to execute code on the organization's infrastructure by submitting a crafted pull request. This can lead to lateral movement into internal networks, credential theft from the runner environment, persistence via runner modification, and access to other repositories that share the same runner group.

mitre_attack.name: Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain

remediation_brief: Use ephemeral/disposable runners for public repositories. Restrict self-hosted runners to private repos only. If self-hosted runners must be used on public repos, enable the 'Require approval for all outside collaborators' setting and use separate runner groups with restricted repository access.

title: CI/CD Security: Audit Complete — No Issues
aliases: CI/CD Security: GitHub Actions: Audit Complete — No Issues
description: gato completed a security audit of the target organization's GitHub Actions workflows and found no injection vulnerabilities, secret exfiltration paths, excessive permissions, or self-hosted runner risks.
impact: No security issues were identified in the GitHub Actions configuration. This is a positive finding indicating that CI/CD workflows follow security best practices for the areas audited.
remediation_brief: No remediation required. Continue to audit workflows periodically, especially when new workflows are added or existing ones are modified.

title: Authentication Bypass: CDN/WAF Bypass: Origin IP Exposed
description: hakoriginfinder discovered the origin server IP address behind the CDN/WAF. The origin IP responds to HTTP requests directly, bypassing all CDN/WAF protections (rate limiting, DDoS mitigation, WAF rules, geo-blocking, bot detection). The origin was confirmed by matching response characteristics to the target domain.
impact: Direct access to the origin server bypasses all CDN/WAF security controls. An attacker can launch DDoS attacks directly against the origin, exploit web application vulnerabilities without WAF interference, bypass rate limiting and bot detection, and circumvent geo-blocking or IP-based access controls. The origin server may also expose internal services or management interfaces not intended to be publicly accessible.

mitre_attack.name: Gather Victim Network Information: IP Addresses

remediation_brief: Restrict the origin server firewall to accept connections only from CDN/WAF edge IP ranges. Use the CDN provider's published IP lists (e.g., Cloudflare IPs, AWS CloudFront IPs) in firewall rules. Block all direct access to the origin from non-CDN sources. Consider using authenticated origin pulls (mTLS between CDN and origin).

title: Authentication Bypass: CDN/WAF Bypass: Potential Origin IP
description: hakoriginfinder identified an IP address that may be the origin server behind the CDN/WAF. The IP responded to HTTP requests with content that partially matches the target domain (e.g., 2xx/3xx status code with related content). Further verification is needed to confirm this is the actual origin.
impact: If this IP is confirmed as the origin server, an attacker can bypass all CDN/WAF protections. Even as a candidate, it reveals infrastructure information that narrows the attack surface and may identify related services, staging environments, or development servers.

mitre_attack.name: Gather Victim Network Information: IP Addresses

remediation_brief: Verify whether this IP is the actual origin server. If confirmed, restrict its firewall to accept connections only from CDN edge IPs. If it is a staging or development server, ensure it is not publicly accessible.

title: Authentication Bypass: CDN/WAF Bypass: No Origin Exposure
description: hakoriginfinder scanned for the origin server IP behind the CDN/WAF and found no exposed origin IPs. The CDN/WAF appears to properly protect the origin server from direct access.
impact: The CDN/WAF is correctly protecting the origin server. No direct access paths were discovered during the scan.
remediation_brief: No remediation required. Continue to ensure origin server firewall restricts access to CDN edge IPs only.

title: Discovery: Historical Endpoints Discovered
description: waymore discovered historical endpoints for the target domain across multiple web archive sources (Wayback Machine, Common Crawl, VirusTotal, URLScan.io, AlienVault OTX). These URLs represent the domain's historical web presence and may include endpoints that are no longer publicly linked but still accessible.
impact: Historical endpoints can reveal previously accessible admin panels, configuration pages, backup files, development endpoints, and API routes. Even if removed from the current site, these endpoints may still respond to requests. Archived URLs also reveal the application's evolution, naming conventions, and internal structure.

mitre_attack.name: Search Open Technical Databases: Scan Databases

remediation_brief: Review discovered endpoints and remove or restrict access to any that should not be publicly accessible. Implement proper authentication and authorization controls on all endpoints.

title: Information Disclosure: Sensitive Historical URL Discovered
description: waymore discovered historical URLs matching security-sensitive patterns (admin, config, debug, backup, test, internal, setup, install, phpinfo, .env, wp-admin, phpmyadmin) in web archive data. These URLs may indicate administrative interfaces, configuration files, or backup resources that were previously accessible and may still respond to requests.
impact: Sensitive historical URLs may reveal admin panels that still respond, configuration files with credentials, database backups, installation wizards that can be replayed, debug pages with verbose error output, and internal API documentation. These represent high-value targets for an attacker who can access them directly.

mitre_attack.name: Search Open Technical Databases: Scan Databases

remediation_brief: Remove sensitive endpoints from production. Add authentication to admin panels. Delete backup and configuration files from web-accessible directories. Disable debug/install/setup endpoints in production. Request removal of sensitive cached pages from web archives where possible.

title: Discovery: Historical API Endpoint
description: waymore discovered API endpoints in web archive data (/api/, /v1/, /v2/, /graphql, /rest/, /ws/, /webhook). These endpoints may represent current or deprecated API surfaces that can be probed for authentication bypasses, information disclosure, or injection vulnerabilities.
impact: Historical API endpoints reveal the application's API structure, versioning scheme, and endpoint naming conventions. Deprecated API versions may lack security controls applied to current versions. API endpoints are high-value targets for authentication bypass, injection, and data exfiltration.

mitre_attack.name: Search Open Technical Databases: Scan Databases

remediation_brief: Decommission deprecated API versions. Ensure all API endpoints require proper authentication and authorization. Maintain an up-to-date API inventory and remove endpoints that are no longer needed.

title: Information Disclosure: Document Metadata: Internal Username Leaked
description: exiftool extracted an internal username from the Author or Creator metadata field of a publicly accessible document. This username may correspond to an internal Active Directory account, email address, or application login credential.
impact: Leaked usernames enable targeted phishing, credential stuffing, and password spraying attacks. Internal usernames often follow predictable patterns (first.last, flast) that allow enumeration of additional accounts. Combined with other OSINT, usernames can be used for social engineering or to identify high-value targets (executives, administrators).

mitre_attack.name: Gather Victim Identity Information: Employee Names
Gather Victim Host Information: Client Configurations

remediation_brief: Strip metadata from all documents before publishing. Use document management policies that automatically remove Author, Creator, and other identifying metadata fields. Configure document creation tools to use generic or organizational names instead of personal usernames.

title: Information Disclosure: Document Metadata: Software Version Disclosed
description: exiftool extracted the software name and version from the Creator or Producer metadata field of a publicly accessible document. This reveals the specific applications used to create or modify the document, including version numbers that may be checked against known vulnerability databases.
impact: Software version disclosure enables targeted vulnerability research. An attacker who knows the exact version of Microsoft Office, Adobe Acrobat, or other document creation tools can search for version-specific CVEs, craft targeted exploits, and identify outdated software that may be vulnerable to known attacks.

mitre_attack.name: Gather Victim Host Information: Client Configurations

remediation_brief: Strip metadata from documents before publishing. This is informational and does not require urgent remediation.

title: Information Disclosure: Document Metadata: Internal File Path Leaked
description: exiftool extracted an internal file system path (such as C:\Users\jsmith\Documents\... or /home/admin/reports/...) from a publicly accessible document's metadata. This reveals the internal directory structure, operating system, and potentially the username of the document creator.
impact: Internal file paths reveal the organization's operating system, directory structure, username conventions, and internal project names. This information assists in crafting targeted phishing payloads, identifying high-value targets, and planning post-exploitation activities. Path structures can also reveal development vs. production environments.

mitre_attack.name: Gather Victim Host Information: Client Configurations

remediation_brief: Strip metadata from all documents before publishing. Use metadata removal tools (exiftool -all=, mat2) as part of the document publishing workflow. Configure document templates to avoid embedding local file paths.

title: Information Disclosure: Document Metadata: Email Address Leaked
description: exiftool extracted an email address from the metadata of a publicly accessible document. This email may belong to the document's author, reviewer, or the organization's document management system.
impact: Email addresses extracted from document metadata can be used for targeted phishing, social engineering, and email-based attacks. They may also reveal internal email naming conventions that allow enumeration of additional email addresses across the organization.

mitre_attack.name: Gather Victim Identity Information: Email Addresses

remediation_brief: Strip metadata from documents before publishing. This is informational — email addresses may already be publicly available through other channels.

title: Information Disclosure: Document Metadata: GPS Coordinates Leaked
description: exiftool extracted GPS coordinates from the EXIF metadata of a publicly accessible image or document. This reveals the physical location where the photo was taken or the document was created, which may include office locations, employee residences, or sensitive facility coordinates.
impact: GPS coordinates in publicly accessible documents can reveal office locations, data center addresses, employee home locations, and other sensitive physical locations. This information enables physical surveillance, social engineering, and targeted attacks against specific facilities. For individuals, leaked GPS data from personal photos represents a privacy violation.

mitre_attack.name: Gather Victim Org Information: Determine Physical Locations

remediation_brief: Strip EXIF GPS data from all images and documents before publishing. Configure mobile devices and cameras to disable GPS tagging. Use metadata removal tools (exiftool -gps:all=, mat2) as part of the content publishing workflow.

title: Information Disclosure: Document Metadata: Audit Summary
description: exiftool completed a metadata audit of publicly accessible documents found during reconnaissance. This finding summarizes the total number of documents analyzed, metadata fields extracted, and categories of information discovered across all scanned documents.
impact: This is a summary finding providing an overview of the document metadata analysis. Individual findings for specific metadata disclosures (usernames, software versions, file paths, GPS data) are reported separately.
remediation_brief: Review individual document metadata findings for specific remediation actions. Implement organization-wide metadata stripping policies for all publicly published documents.

title: Known Vulnerable: Known Vuln on Service
description: A known vulnerability was identified on an internet-facing service via passive reconnaissance (Shodan, Censys, or similar). The vulnerability is associated with the detected service version or banner.
impact: An attacker can exploit the known vulnerability to gain unauthorized access, execute code, or escalate privileges on the affected service. The exposure is amplified because the vulnerability is publicly documented and exploit code may be available.
remediation_brief: Patch or upgrade the affected service to a version that addresses the vulnerability. If patching is not immediately possible, restrict network access to the service via firewall rules or VPN.

title: Known Vulnerable: Known CVE on Service
description: A specific CVE was matched to an internet-facing service via passive scanning engines (Shodan, Censys, FullHunt, ZoomEye, Netlas). The CVE is associated with the detected service version or technology stack.
impact: An attacker with knowledge of the CVE can craft targeted exploits against the service. Public exploit code or Metasploit modules may be available, reducing the skill barrier for exploitation.
remediation_brief: Apply the vendor-issued patch or upgrade the software to a non-vulnerable version. Review the CVE advisory for specific mitigations if a patch is not available.

title: Enumeration: Cloud Platform Identified via CNAME
description: DNS CNAME records reveal that subdomains resolve to third-party cloud or SaaS platforms (e.g., AWS CloudFront, Azure, Heroku, Shopify). This maps the organization's cloud infrastructure footprint.
impact: An attacker can use cloud platform identification to focus reconnaissance on platform-specific attack vectors (subdomain takeover, misconfigured S3 buckets, exposed API gateways).
remediation_brief: Review CNAME mappings for accuracy. Ensure all pointed-to cloud resources are actively managed and not abandoned (which could allow subdomain takeover).

title: Enumeration: Mail Infrastructure Identified via SPF
description: SPF (Sender Policy Framework) DNS records reveal the organization's authorized mail sending infrastructure, including third-party email service providers.
impact: An attacker can use SPF record data to map authorized mail infrastructure and identify potential targets for impersonation or relay attacks.
remediation_brief: Ensure SPF records are accurate and use '-all' (hard fail) rather than '~all' (soft fail). Remove references to decommissioned mail infrastructure.

title: Enumeration: SaaS Platform Identified via DNS TXT
description: DNS TXT records (domain verification, site verification) reveal third-party SaaS platforms integrated with the organization (e.g., Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Salesforce, HubSpot).
impact: An attacker can use SaaS platform identification to craft targeted phishing campaigns or focus on platform-specific API exploitation.
remediation_brief: Audit DNS TXT records periodically. Remove verification records for SaaS platforms no longer in use.

title: Information Disclosure: Non-Production Infrastructure Exposed via CNAME
description: DNS CNAME records expose non-production infrastructure (staging, dev, test, UAT, QA environments) to the public internet.
impact: An attacker can target non-production environments which often have weaker security controls, default credentials, or debug features enabled. Compromise of non-production systems can provide access to production data or lateral movement paths.
remediation_brief: Restrict DNS resolution of non-production environments to internal networks. Use split-horizon DNS or remove public CNAME records for non-production hosts.

title: Discovery: Network Infrastructure Concentration
description: Analysis of the organization's DNS and IP address space reveals concentration of infrastructure in a small number of hosting providers, ASNs, or IP ranges.
impact: High concentration of infrastructure in a single provider increases the blast radius of provider-level incidents (outages, security breaches). An attacker can focus efforts on a single provider's attack surface.
remediation_brief: Document infrastructure concentration risk. Consider diversifying hosting across multiple providers for critical services.

title: Threat Intel: Indicator of Compromise Detected
description: VirusTotal analysis flagged the target domain or associated infrastructure with indicators of compromise (IoC). Multiple security vendors have flagged the asset as malicious or associated with malicious activity.
impact: The presence of IoCs indicates the domain or infrastructure may already be compromised, used for malware distribution, or associated with command-and-control activity. Immediate investigation is required.
remediation_brief: Investigate the flagged asset immediately. Cross-reference with internal logs for evidence of compromise. If confirmed, initiate incident response procedures.

title: Threat Intel: Domain Flagged Malicious
description: Threat intelligence sources (VirusTotal, URLScan, AlienVault OTX) have flagged the target domain as malicious or associated with malicious activity.
impact: A domain flagged as malicious may be actively used for phishing, malware distribution, or C2 operations. This could indicate compromise or abuse of the organization's domain.
remediation_brief: Investigate the domain flagging. Check for unauthorized DNS changes, compromised web applications, or rogue content. Request delisting from threat intelligence vendors after remediation.

title: Threat Intel: IP Address Flagged Malicious
description: Threat intelligence sources have flagged an IP address associated with the target as malicious. The IP may be listed in blocklists or associated with known attack campaigns.
impact: A flagged IP address may indicate the infrastructure is compromised and being used for attacks, or that the IP was previously used by malicious actors and retains a negative reputation.
remediation_brief: Investigate the IP flagging. Check hosting infrastructure for compromise. If the IP is shared hosting, consider dedicated IP allocation. Request delisting after remediation.

title: Threat Intel: Malicious URL Detected
description: URLScan or similar services detected specific URLs under the target domain that are associated with malicious content, phishing kits, or malware delivery.
impact: Malicious URLs indicate active compromise of web infrastructure. Visitors to these URLs may be exposed to malware, credential theft, or drive-by downloads.
remediation_brief: Immediately investigate and remove malicious content. Review web server access logs. Scan for web shells or unauthorized modifications. Implement file integrity monitoring.

title: Threat Intel: Domain Referenced in Threat Pulses
description: AlienVault OTX threat intelligence pulses reference the target domain in connection with threat campaigns, malware analysis, or security research.
impact: References in threat pulses may indicate the domain is a known target, has been previously compromised, or is associated with threat actor infrastructure.
remediation_brief: Review the specific OTX pulses for context. Cross-reference with internal security logs. Assess whether the references indicate current or historical risk.

title: Threat Intel: Malware Samples Associated with Domain
description: VirusTotal or similar platforms have identified malware samples that reference or communicate with the target domain.
impact: Malware association indicates the domain may be used as a C2 server, malware distribution point, or data exfiltration destination. This represents active or recent compromise.
remediation_brief: Investigate immediately. Review DNS logs for communications with known malware infrastructure. Scan internal endpoints for the identified malware samples. Initiate incident response if compromise is confirmed.

title: Threat Intel: IP Referenced in Threat Pulses
description: AlienVault OTX threat intelligence pulses reference an IP address associated with the target in connection with threat campaigns or security research.
impact: IP references in threat pulses may indicate the infrastructure has been targeted, compromised, or is collocated with threat actor resources.
remediation_brief: Review the specific OTX pulses for context. Verify IP ownership and usage. Cross-reference with firewall and IDS logs for suspicious activity.

title: Threat Intel: IntelligenceX Leak Data Found
description: IntelligenceX search identified leaked data associated with the target domain, including potential credentials, email addresses, or sensitive documents found in paste sites, data breaches, or dark web sources.
impact: Leaked credentials can be used for credential stuffing or targeted attacks. Exposed documents may reveal sensitive business information, internal infrastructure details, or employee personal data.
remediation_brief: Identify affected accounts and force password resets. Implement MFA across all exposed services. Monitor for unauthorized access using the leaked credentials.

title: Discovery: Internet-Wide Scan Engine Match
description: The target's infrastructure was identified in internet-wide scan engines (Shodan, Censys, ZoomEye, FOFA, Netlas). These engines index publicly accessible services and their banners.
impact: Presence in scan engines confirms the services are publicly accessible and their banners/versions are indexed. Attackers routinely use these engines to identify vulnerable targets at scale.
remediation_brief: Review indexed services for necessity of public exposure. Implement banner hardening to reduce information leakage. Consider rate-limiting or blocking scan engine IP ranges for non-public services.

title: DNS Information: DKIM Selectors Identified
description: DNS enumeration identified DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) selectors configured for the domain. DKIM selectors reveal which email services are authorized to sign outbound mail.
impact: While DKIM is a positive security control, knowledge of selectors can help an attacker understand which email platforms are in use and potentially craft more convincing phishing emails.
remediation_brief: Ensure DKIM keys use at least 2048-bit RSA. Rotate DKIM keys periodically. Remove selectors for decommissioned email services.

title: Enumeration: Social Media Profile Identified
description: Username enumeration tools (maigret) identified social media and platform profiles associated with target usernames across 3,000+ platforms.
impact: Social media profiles can be used for social engineering, impersonation attacks, and gathering personal information about employees. Profile data may reveal organizational structure and communication patterns.
remediation_brief: Review identified profiles for appropriateness. Implement social media security awareness training. Consider monitoring for impersonation accounts.

title: Discovery: HTML Form Discovered
description: Web crawling identified HTML forms on the target's web applications. Forms represent potential input vectors for injection attacks.
impact: HTML forms are primary input vectors for web application attacks including XSS, SQL injection, CSRF, and parameter manipulation. Each form represents a potential attack surface.
remediation_brief: Ensure all forms implement proper input validation, CSRF tokens, and output encoding. Review form actions for sensitive operations that require authentication.

title: Information Disclosure: Credential Breach with Password
description: HaveIBeenPwned or similar breach databases contain credentials for the target domain with plaintext or hashed passwords exposed. The breach includes usable credential material.
impact: Exposed passwords enable direct credential stuffing attacks against the organization's services. If employees reuse passwords, attackers can gain unauthorized access to email, VPN, cloud services, and internal applications.
remediation_brief: Force immediate password resets for all affected accounts. Implement MFA on all externally accessible services. Check for credential reuse across systems. Enroll affected users in breach notification monitoring.

title: Information Disclosure: Credential Breach Detected
description: HaveIBeenPwned or similar breach databases contain records for the target domain. The breach data may include email addresses, usernames, and associated metadata, but no plaintext passwords.
impact: Breach records confirm that employee email addresses are circulating in public breach datasets. Attackers use this data for targeted phishing, credential stuffing with common passwords, and social engineering.
remediation_brief: Notify affected users. Enforce password changes for affected accounts. Implement MFA. Monitor for unauthorized access attempts targeting the breached accounts.

title: Information Disclosure: Sensitive Code Exposure
description: GitDorker or similar GitHub dorking tools identified public repositories containing code that references the target domain with potentially sensitive content (API keys, secrets, configuration files, internal URLs).
impact: Exposed source code and secrets in public repositories can be used to gain unauthorized access to APIs, internal systems, and cloud resources. Secrets in code are immediately exploitable.
remediation_brief: Revoke and rotate all exposed secrets immediately. Remove or make private the affected repositories. Implement pre-commit hooks and CI/CD secret scanning to prevent future leaks.

title: DNS: Permissive SPF Record (+all)
remediation_brief: Replace '+all' with '-all' or '~all' in the SPF record. Enumerate all authorized senders with 'include:' and 'ip4:'/'ip6:' mechanisms.
description: SPF record uses '+all', allowing any server to send mail as this domain.
impact: This completely negates SPF protection. Any host on the internet can send email that passes SPF checks for this domain, enabling trivial phishing and business-email-compromise attacks with no detectable authentication failure.

title: DNS: SPF Softfail Policy (~all)
remediation_brief: Upgrade the SPF record's '~all' to '-all' (hardfail) once all legitimate senders are enumerated.
description: SPF record uses '~all' (softfail). Mail from unauthorised sources is flagged but not rejected.
impact: Spoofed email from this domain may reach recipients' inboxes, albeit with a softfail indicator. Some mail servers ignore softfail, so phishing messages can still succeed, especially when DMARC is absent or set to p=none.

title: DNS: SPF Neutral Policy (?all)
remediation_brief: Replace '?all' with '-all' and enumerate authorized senders.
description: SPF record uses '?all' (neutral), providing no meaningful protection against spoofing.
impact: A neutral SPF result tells receivers nothing about unauthorised senders. It is functionally equivalent to having no SPF record and provides zero protection against email spoofing.

title: DNS: Missing SPF All Mechanism
remediation_brief: Add an explicit '-all' or '~all' mechanism at the end of the SPF record.
description: SPF record has no 'all' mechanism. Receiving servers may treat unlisted senders inconsistently.
impact: Without an explicit 'all' mechanism, different receiving servers apply different default policies to unlisted senders — some accept, some softfail, some reject. This inconsistency means spoofed mail delivery is unpredictable but not prevented.

title: DNS: SPF Record Present
remediation_brief: Informational — SPF is correctly configured. Periodically review the record to ensure new senders are included.
description: SPF record present with a strict policy. Authorized senders are enumerated.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.

title: DNS: DMARC Policy: Monitor Only
remediation_brief: After reviewing RUA aggregate reports and confirming all legitimate senders align with SPF/DKIM, escalate the DMARC policy to 'p=quarantine' and then 'p=reject'.
description: DMARC policy is 'p=none' (monitor only). Spoofed emails are reported but not blocked.
impact: While DMARC aggregate reports (RUA) are collected, failing messages still reach recipients. An attacker can spoof email from this domain and the messages will be delivered, albeit with a DMARC fail indicator. The domain is in monitoring mode and not yet enforcing.

title: DNS: DMARC Policy: Quarantine
remediation_brief: Upgrade DMARC policy from 'p=quarantine' to 'p=reject' for maximum spoofing protection.
description: DMARC policy is 'p=quarantine'. Spoofed messages are sent to spam/quarantine.
impact: Spoofed messages are quarantined rather than rejected outright. An attacker's forged emails will land in recipients' spam folders, where they could still be read. Full protection requires p=reject.

title: DNS: DMARC Policy: Reject
remediation_brief: Informational — DMARC is at the strongest enforcement level. Continue monitoring RUA reports for legitimate senders that fail alignment.
description: DMARC policy is 'p=reject' — optimal configuration. Spoofed messages are rejected outright.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.

title: DNS: DMARC Record Present
remediation_brief: Informational — DMARC record is published. Verify the policy level meets organizational requirements.
description: DMARC record present with a recognized policy.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.

title: DNS: DMARC Subdomain Policy: Monitor Only
remediation_brief: Set sp=quarantine or sp=reject in the DMARC record to extend enforcement to subdomains.
description: DMARC subdomain policy is 'sp=none' while the apex policy is stricter. Subdomains can still be spoofed.
impact: An attacker can spoof email from any subdomain (e.g. hr.example.com, it.example.com) because the subdomain-specific policy overrides the apex domain's enforcement. This is a common oversight that leaves a wide spoofing surface.

title: DNS: Missing CAA Issuewild
remediation_brief: Add a CAA record with the 'issuewild' tag restricting wildcard certificate issuance to authorized CAs.
description: CAA record restricts apex certificate issuance but has no 'issuewild' tag. Wildcard certificates may be issued by any CA.
impact: Although apex certificate issuance is restricted, a CA not in the permitted list can still issue wildcard certificates (*.example.com). An attacker who exploits a CA validation flaw can obtain a wildcard certificate covering all subdomains.

title: DNS: CAA Record Present
remediation_brief: Informational — CAA is correctly configured with both issue and issuewild restrictions.
description: CAA record restricts certificate issuance to specified CAs, including wildcard coverage.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.

title: DNS: Missing DNSSEC
remediation_brief: Enable DNSSEC at the domain registrar. Sign the zone and publish DS records in the parent zone.
description: DNSSEC is not enabled. DNS responses can be forged via cache poisoning or MITM.
impact: Without DNSSEC, an attacker positioned on the network path can forge DNS responses, redirecting users to malicious servers. This enables credential theft, malware delivery, and man-in-the-middle attacks against any service that relies on DNS resolution for this domain.

title: DNS: DNSSEC Enabled
remediation_brief: Informational — DNSSEC is active. Periodically verify key rotation and DS record alignment with the parent zone.
description: DNSSEC is enabled. DNS responses are cryptographically signed.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.

title: DNS: DKIM Record Present
remediation_brief: Informational — DKIM is configured. Verify key strength (≥2048-bit RSA or Ed25519) and monitor for selector rotation.
description: DKIM public key(s) found on one or more selectors.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.

title: DNS: DKIM Revoked Key
remediation_brief: Confirm the revocation is deliberate and that no active mail flows depend on the revoked selector. Update the signing configuration to use a current selector.
description: One or more DKIM selectors have an empty public key (p=), indicating intentional revocation.
impact: A revoked DKIM key means messages signed with that selector will fail DKIM validation. If mail flows still depend on the revoked selector, legitimate email may be rejected or flagged, and DMARC alignment may fail.

title: DNS: Weak DKIM Key
remediation_brief: Rotate DKIM keys to at least 2048-bit RSA or Ed25519. Publish the new public key and update the signing configuration.
description: One or more DKIM selectors use an RSA key shorter than 2048 bits.
impact: RSA keys below 2048 bits can be factored with modern hardware. An attacker who recovers the private key can sign forged email that passes DKIM validation, enabling authenticated phishing from this domain.

title: DNS: Missing MTA-STS Policy
remediation_brief: Publish an MTA-STS policy: create a well-known file at https://mta-sts.<domain>/.well-known/mta-sts.txt and a _mta-sts.<domain> TXT record.
description: No MTA-STS policy found. MTA-STS forces SMTP connections to use TLS, preventing downgrade attacks on inbound mail.
impact: Without MTA-STS, an attacker on the network path between sending and receiving mail servers can strip STARTTLS via a downgrade attack, intercepting email in cleartext. Sensitive communications (credentials, invoices, PII) are exposed.

title: DNS: MTA-STS Policy Present
remediation_brief: Informational — MTA-STS is configured. Periodically verify the policy file and max_age are current.
description: MTA-STS policy record present. Inbound SMTP connections are required to use TLS.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.

title: DNS: Missing TLS-RPT Record
remediation_brief: Publish a _smtp._tls.<domain> TXT record specifying an rua= address to receive TLS failure reports (RFC 8460).
description: No TLS-RPT reporting record found. TLS-RPT delivers aggregate reports about STARTTLS failures.
impact: Without TLS-RPT, the domain owner has no visibility into STARTTLS failures on inbound mail. Downgrade attacks, certificate errors, and misconfigured sending servers go undetected, leaving mail delivery issues and potential interception invisible.

title: DNS: TLS-RPT Record Present
remediation_brief: Informational — TLS-RPT is configured. Periodically review reports for STARTTLS failures.
description: TLS-RPT reporting record present. Aggregate TLS failure reports are delivered.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.

title: DNS: BIMI Record Present
remediation_brief: Informational — BIMI is configured. Ensure the Verified Mark Certificate (VMC) is current and the SVG logo meets BIMI requirements.
description: BIMI (Brand Indicators for Message Identification) record found. The domain publishes a brand logo for authenticated email.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.

title: Relay Established Successfully
description: A pivot relay session was established between pivot-client and pivot-agent. Authentication, TLS handshake, and network profile activation all succeeded. Scanner traffic can now reach the target CIDR.
remediation: No action required. Operational success event. Ensure the session is deactivated cleanly after scanning completes.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening.
remediation_brief: Implement secure session management with proper timeout, regeneration, and invalidation. Use secure cookie flags.

title: Authentication Failed — Invalid HMAC Token
description: The AUTH message sent by a connecting client contained an HMAC-SHA256 digest that did not match the expected value for the provided nonce and shared secret. The connection was rejected.
remediation: Verify that security.auth_token matches exactly on both agent and client configurations (including whitespace). For chained profiles, ensure upstream.auth_token matches the upstream relay's token.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening.
remediation_brief: Remove hardcoded secrets from code and config. Implement a secrets management solution with rotation policies.

title: Replay Attack Detected — Nonce Already Used
description: An AUTH message was received with a nonce that has been used in a previous authentication attempt within the current session. This is indicative of a replay attack — a captured AUTH message being retransmitted.
remediation: Investigate the source IP of the replayed authentication attempt. Verify TLS is enforced end-to-end (no MitM). Rotate auth_token and regenerate TLS certificates if compromise is suspected.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Input validation failures may allow injection attacks, data manipulation, or unauthorized code execution.
remediation_brief: Implement proper input validation, output encoding, and parameterized queries. Apply security headers and content security policies.

title: TLS Handshake Failed
description: The TLS handshake between pivot-client and pivot-agent failed. Possible causes: certificate not trusted by the client's CA bundle, CN/SAN mismatch, expired certificate, or unsupported TLS version.
remediation: 1. Ensure ca.crt on the client was generated by the same CA that signed agent.crt. 2. Confirm security.tls.server_hostname in client config matches CN/SAN in agent.crt. 3. Check certificate expiry. 4. Verify TLS 1.2+ is supported on both sides.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening. Weak cryptographic implementations may allow interception, decryption, or forgery of protected communications.
remediation_brief: Update cryptographic configurations to current standards. Disable deprecated protocols and cipher suites. Ensure certificates are valid and properly configured.

title: Unauthorised Connection Attempt — IP Not in Allowlist
description: A connection was received from a source IP that is not present in security.allowed_peers. The connection was rejected after TLS handshake but before authentication, minimising information leakage.
remediation: Review allowed_peers in the agent configuration. If the source IP is legitimate, add it to the allowlist. Investigate unexpected connection sources.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening. Weak cryptographic implementations may allow interception, decryption, or forgery of protected communications.
remediation_brief: Update cryptographic configurations to current standards. Disable deprecated protocols and cipher suites. Ensure certificates are valid and properly configured.

title: iptables Rule Applied Successfully
description: iptables FORWARD and MASQUERADE rules were successfully installed on the relay device for a network profile. IP forwarding is active. Scanner traffic will be NATted to the relay's LAN IP.
remediation: No action required. Verify rule cleanup occurs on session deactivation.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening. Network-level vulnerabilities may allow traffic interception, lateral movement, or unauthorized service access.
remediation_brief: Restrict network access using firewalls and segmentation. Disable unnecessary services and protocols. Implement network monitoring.

title: iptables Rule Cleanup Completed
description: All iptables rules installed for a relay session were removed successfully. ip_forward was reset to its pre-session value if no other sessions are active. Relay state is fully clean.
remediation: No action required. Verify with: sudo iptables -L FORWARD -n -v and sudo iptables -t nat -L POSTROUTING -n -v
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening.
remediation_brief: Implement secure session management with proper timeout, regeneration, and invalidation. Use secure cookie flags.

title: Relay Chain Established
description: A multi-hop relay chain was successfully established. The current agent spawned an internal chain_connector (pivot-client) to a downstream relay and received network profile activation confirmation. All intermediate routes are active.
remediation: No action required. Operational success event. Verify end-to-end connectivity with a test scan before the full engagement.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening. Network-level vulnerabilities may allow traffic interception, lateral movement, or unauthorized service access.
remediation_brief: Restrict network access using firewalls and segmentation. Disable unnecessary services and protocols. Implement network monitoring.

title: Connection to Upstream Relay Failed
description: A chained relay attempted to connect to its configured upstream relay (pivot-agent at upstream.host) but failed. The chain is broken and the target network is unreachable.
remediation: 1. Verify the upstream relay is running and reachable from the current relay device. 2. Check upstream.host and upstream.port in the profile configuration. 3. Verify auth_token, TLS certs, and network routing between relay nodes.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening. Network-level vulnerabilities may allow traffic interception, lateral movement, or unauthorized service access.
remediation_brief: Restrict network access using firewalls and segmentation. Disable unnecessary services and protocols. Implement network monitoring.

title: Certificate Validation Failed — Agent Certificate Not Trusted
description: The pivot-client rejected the agent's TLS certificate because it could not be validated against the configured CA bundle. This may indicate a certificate mismatch or a potential MitM attack.
remediation: Verify cafile on the client points to the CA that signed the agent's certificate. Re-generate certificates with tools/pivot-gen-certs.sh if needed. Never set verify_hostname: false in production.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening. Weak cryptographic implementations may allow interception, decryption, or forgery of protected communications.
remediation_brief: Update cryptographic configurations to current standards. Disable deprecated protocols and cipher suites. Ensure certificates are valid and properly configured.

title: mTLS Client Certificate Required
description: The agent is configured with require_client_cert: true (mutual TLS). Clients must present a valid certificate signed by the agent's CA in addition to HMAC token authentication.
remediation: Generate a client certificate with tools/pivot-gen-certs.sh and configure certfile/keyfile in the client's TLS configuration block.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening. Weak cryptographic implementations may allow interception, decryption, or forgery of protected communications.
remediation_brief: Update cryptographic configurations to current standards. Disable deprecated protocols and cipher suites. Ensure certificates are valid and properly configured.

title: HMAC Verification Failed — Token Mismatch
description: The HMAC-SHA256 digest computed from the client's nonce and the stored shared secret did not match the digest provided in the AUTH message. Authentication was denied. Constant-time comparison was used to prevent timing oracle attacks.
remediation: Verify auth_token values match exactly on both sides. If mismatches persist after verifying configs, investigate for tampering or MitM. Rotate the shared secret.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening. Weak cryptographic implementations may allow interception, decryption, or forgery of protected communications.
remediation_brief: Update cryptographic configurations to current standards. Disable deprecated protocols and cipher suites. Ensure certificates are valid and properly configured.

title: iptables Rule Application Failed
description: The agent could not install required iptables FORWARD or MASQUERADE rules. This prevents traffic forwarding to the target network. The relay session is non-functional.
remediation: Ensure pivot-agent is running as root or with CAP_NET_ADMIN + CAP_NET_RAW. Verify iptables is installed: which iptables. Check: sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening. Network-level vulnerabilities may allow traffic interception, lateral movement, or unauthorized service access.

title: Route Installation Failed on Scanner
description: pivot-client failed to install the OS route for the target CIDR on the scanner machine. The scanner cannot reach the target network even though the relay session is active.
remediation: Run pivot-client with sudo. On Linux: verify ip command is available. On macOS: verify route command is available and sudo rights are granted.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening.
remediation_brief: Implement secure session management with proper timeout, regeneration, and invalidation. Use secure cookie flags.

title: Session Expired — Heartbeat Timeout
description: The relay session was closed because no HEARTBEAT message was received from the client within the configured heartbeat_timeout period. The client may have crashed or the network path was interrupted.
remediation: Ensure pivot-client is running and the network path between client and agent remains stable. Adjust heartbeat_interval and heartbeat_timeout in the config if the network is lossy.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system.
remediation_brief: Implement secure session management with proper timeout, regeneration, and invalidation. Use secure cookie flags.

title: Maximum Concurrent Sessions Reached
description: A new connection was rejected because the agent has reached session.max_sessions. No additional relay clients can connect until an existing session is released.
remediation: Increase session.max_sessions in the agent config if additional concurrent connections are needed. Verify that existing sessions are not stuck.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system.
remediation_brief: Implement secure session management with proper timeout, regeneration, and invalidation. Use secure cookie flags.

title: sysctl ip_forward Activation Failed
description: The agent could not set net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 via sysctl. Without IP forwarding enabled, traffic cannot be relayed between the VPN and LAN interfaces.
remediation: Run pivot-agent as root. Manually verify: sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward. In some hardened environments, sysctl may be locked — consult system configuration.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening.
remediation_brief: Apply system hardening baselines (CIS, DISA STIG). Disable unnecessary services, features, and accounts.

title: Clean Session Deactivation Completed
description: The pivot-client sent a DEACTIVATE message and the agent responded with DEACTIVATE_RESPONSE. iptables rules, kernel routes, and ip_forward were all cleaned up. Session state is fully removed.
remediation: No action required. Verify cleanup with: ip route show && iptables -L FORWARD -n -v
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system.
remediation_brief: Implement secure session management with proper timeout, regeneration, and invalidation. Use secure cookie flags.

title: Application is debuggable
description: android:debuggable=true allows attaching a debugger to the running app, enabling memory inspection, method interception, and data extraction.
impact: An attacker on a rooted device or via ADB can attach a debugger (jdb, LLDB) to the running process, inspect heap memory, modify variables at runtime, bypass authentication checks, and extract encryption keys or credentials from memory.
remediation_brief: Set android:debuggable=false in the AndroidManifest.xml for all release builds; use build variants to ensure debug flags never ship to production.

title: Application allows backup
description: android:allowBackup is true (or not explicitly set to false), allowing adb backup to extract application data including databases and shared preferences.
impact: An attacker with physical access or ADB access can extract the entire app sandbox via 'adb backup', obtaining databases, SharedPreferences, cached credentials, session tokens, and other sensitive files without root access.
remediation_brief: Set android:allowBackup=false in AndroidManifest.xml, or implement a BackupAgent that encrypts sensitive data before backup.

title: Cleartext traffic allowed
description: android:usesCleartextTraffic=true allows unencrypted HTTP connections globally from the application.
impact: All network traffic from the app can be sent over plaintext HTTP. An on-path attacker (e.g. on public Wi-Fi) can intercept, read, and modify requests and responses including authentication credentials, session tokens, and personal data.
remediation_brief: Set android:usesCleartextTraffic=false in AndroidManifest.xml; use a network security config to scope any necessary cleartext exceptions to specific domains.

title: Exported {component_type} without permission: {name}
description: An Android component (activity, service, receiver, or provider) is exported and accessible by any app without requiring a custom permission.
impact: Any app on the device can invoke the exported component directly via an Intent. If the component handles sensitive operations (user data, transactions, internal APIs) without its own authentication, an attacker's app can abuse it to extract data or trigger privileged actions.
remediation_brief: Set android:exported=false on components that do not need to be externally accessible; add a custom permission with android:protectionLevel='signature' to restrict access.

title: Low minimum SDK version: API {version}
description: The application's minSdkVersion targets an Android API level below 24 (Android 7.0), which lacks several modern security features.
impact: Devices running older Android versions do not enforce network security config by default, lack file-based encryption, do not support scoped storage, and miss numerous security patches. The app's security posture is limited to the lowest supported platform.
remediation_brief: Raise minSdkVersion to at least API 24 (Android 7.0) to inherit network security config, file-based encryption, and other platform security features.

title: Excessive dangerous permissions ({count})
description: The application requests more than 10 Android dangerous (runtime) permissions, indicating an overly broad data-access footprint.
impact: Excessive permissions expand the attack surface: if the app is compromised, the attacker inherits access to camera, microphone, location, contacts, SMS, storage, and more. Users are less likely to scrutinize individual permission prompts when there are many.
remediation_brief: Audit all dangerous permission requests; remove any not strictly required by core functionality; apply the principle of least privilege.

title: Dangerous permission: {name}
description: The app requests a specific Android dangerous (runtime) permission, classified by Android as granting access to sensitive user data or device capabilities.
impact: Each dangerous permission grants access to a sensitive resource (camera, microphone, location, contacts, etc.). While individually justifiable, each adds to the app's data-access footprint and the potential impact if the app is compromised.
remediation_brief: Verify the permission is justified by the app's core functionality; request it just-in-time rather than at launch; remove if not essential.

title: Information Disclosure: Potential hard-coded secret: {label}
description: Pattern matching a known secret format (AWS access key, Google API key, private key, JWT, etc.) was found in the APK bundle (DEX, smali, or resource files).
impact: Hard-coded secrets in APKs are trivially recoverable via decompilation (jadx, apktool). If valid in production they grant the attacker the same privileges as the app, often including server-side API access, cloud resource manipulation, or payment processing.
remediation_brief: Rotate the exposed secret immediately; remove from the APK; fetch credentials via an authenticated server call at runtime.

title: Network Security Config: base config allows cleartext traffic
description: The network_security_config.xml base-config element has cleartextTrafficPermitted='true', allowing unencrypted HTTP connections to all domains by default.
impact: All HTTP traffic from the app is unencrypted. An on-path attacker can intercept, read, and modify every request and response, including credentials, session tokens, and personal data. This overrides Android's default HTTPS-only behaviour on API 28+.
remediation_brief: Set cleartextTrafficPermitted='false' in the base-config; use domain-config exceptions only for domains that genuinely require HTTP and are on a migration path.

title: Network Security Config: domain config trusts user-installed certificates
description: A domain-config in network_security_config.xml includes a trust-anchors element with certificates src='user', causing the app to trust user-installed CA certificates for that domain.
impact: An attacker who installs their own CA certificate on the device (via social engineering, MDM, or physical access) can perform a man-in-the-middle attack against the configured domain. All HTTPS traffic to that domain can be intercepted and decrypted.
remediation_brief: Remove certificates src='user' from trust-anchors in production builds; trust only system CAs or pin specific certificates.

title: Network Security Config: domain permits cleartext traffic
description: A domain-config in network_security_config.xml permits cleartext traffic (cleartextTrafficPermitted='true') for a specific domain with includeSubdomains='true'.
impact: HTTP traffic to the specified domain and all its subdomains is unencrypted and subject to interception. While scoped to a specific domain, any subdomain matching the pattern inherits the cleartext exception, broadening the exposure.
remediation_brief: Migrate the domain to HTTPS and remove the cleartext exception; if HTTP is temporarily necessary, scope the domain-config to the narrowest domain without includeSubdomains.

title: Code Analysis: WebView JavaScript enabled
description: The application calls WebSettings.setJavaScriptEnabled(true), enabling JavaScript execution inside a WebView.
impact: If the WebView loads content from untrusted sources, an attacker can inject malicious JavaScript (XSS) to steal cookies, session tokens, or local storage data and relay it to an external server.
remediation_brief: Disable JavaScript in WebViews that display untrusted content; validate and sanitize all data loaded via loadUrl/loadData.

title: Code Analysis: WebView file access enabled
description: The application calls WebSettings.setAllowFileAccess(true), allowing the WebView to read local files via file:// URIs.
impact: Combined with JavaScript execution, an attacker exploiting an XSS vulnerability can read local app files (databases, SharedPreferences, cached credentials) via file:// and exfiltrate them.
remediation_brief: Set setAllowFileAccess(false) unless file access is explicitly required; scope to specific paths if needed.

title: Code Analysis: WebView universal file URL access
description: The application calls WebSettings.setAllowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs(true), allowing file:// pages to access content from any origin.
impact: An attacker who can write a local file (e.g. via a download or cache poisoning) can load it in the WebView and use JavaScript to read content from any other origin, including the app's own sandbox files and HTTPS endpoints.
remediation_brief: Set setAllowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs(false) (default since API 16); never enable for production builds.

title: Code Analysis: JavaScript interface exposed
description: The application calls WebView.addJavascriptInterface(), exposing a Java object to JavaScript running inside the WebView.
impact: On API < 17, ALL public methods of the exposed object are callable from JavaScript, enabling arbitrary code execution via reflection. On API >= 17, only @JavascriptInterface methods are exposed, but bridge calls still execute with the app's full permissions.
remediation_brief: Limit exposed methods; validate all input from JavaScript bridge calls; require minSdkVersion >= 17.

title: Code Analysis: WebView debugging enabled
description: The application enables WebView remote debugging via WebView.setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled(true).
impact: On a rooted/USB-debuggable device, Chrome DevTools can connect to the WebView to inspect page content, execute arbitrary JavaScript, intercept network traffic, and extract sensitive data displayed in the WebView.
remediation_brief: Disable setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled in release builds; guard with BuildConfig.DEBUG check.

title: Code Analysis: Runtime.exec() command execution
description: The application invokes java.lang.Runtime.exec() to execute a system command.
impact: If user-controlled or externally influenced data reaches the command argument without sanitization, an attacker can inject arbitrary shell commands for execution with the app's UID and permissions.
remediation_brief: Avoid Runtime.exec(); if required, use fixed command strings with no user input concatenation.

title: Code Analysis: ProcessBuilder command execution
description: The application uses java.lang.ProcessBuilder to execute system commands.
impact: Same as Runtime.exec() — if attacker-controlled data influences the command or arguments, arbitrary command injection is possible.
remediation_brief: Avoid ProcessBuilder; if required, use fixed command strings without user input.

title: Code Analysis: Weak cryptographic algorithm
description: The application uses a known-weak cryptographic algorithm or mode (ECB, DES, 3DES) via javax.crypto.Cipher.getInstance().
impact: ECB mode leaks patterns in encrypted data; DES provides only 56-bit key strength. An attacker can exploit these weaknesses to decrypt stored secrets, authentication tokens, or user data.
remediation_brief: Use AES-256 with GCM or CBC mode and proper IV management; avoid ECB mode and DES/3DES entirely.

title: Code Analysis: SecureRandom seeded predictably
description: The application calls SecureRandom.setSeed(), which on certain Android versions can replace OS entropy with a developer-supplied (possibly predictable) seed.
impact: A predictable random number generator can allow an attacker to predict session tokens, encryption keys, nonces, or OTPs, leading to authentication bypass or data decryption.
remediation_brief: Do not call setSeed(); let the default constructor provide OS entropy. Use new SecureRandom() directly.

title: Code Analysis: Direct SQL query construction
description: The application constructs SQL queries directly via SQLiteDatabase.rawQuery() or execSQL() with a String argument rather than parameterized queries.
impact: If user input is concatenated into the SQL string, an attacker can inject arbitrary SQL to read, modify, or delete database contents, bypassing authentication or exfiltrating stored secrets.
remediation_brief: Use parameterized queries (selectionArgs in rawQuery, bindArgs in execSQL) instead of string concatenation.

title: Code Analysis: World-readable/writable file mode
description: The application creates files with MODE_WORLD_READABLE or MODE_WORLD_WRITABLE, making them accessible to all apps on the device.
impact: Any app on the device can read (or write) the file. If the file contains credentials, tokens, or personal data, an attacker's app can silently exfiltrate it. Writable files allow data injection or tampering.
remediation_brief: Use MODE_PRIVATE for all file creation; share data between apps via ContentProviders with proper permissions.

title: Code Analysis: Hostname verifier bypass
description: The application overrides or disables SSL hostname verification using ALLOW_ALL_HOSTNAME_VERIFIER or a custom HostnameVerifier that accepts all hostnames.
impact: An attacker with a valid certificate for ANY domain can perform a man-in-the-middle attack against the app's HTTPS connections. All traffic can be intercepted even though TLS is nominally in use.
remediation_brief: Use the default HostnameVerifier; do not override with ALLOW_ALL or a permissive custom verifier.

title: Code Analysis: Data written to clipboard
description: The application writes data to the system clipboard via ClipboardManager.setPrimaryClip().
impact: On Android < 10 (API 29), any app can read the clipboard at any time without user interaction. If the app copies passwords, tokens, or PII, a malicious background app can harvest them silently.
remediation_brief: Avoid writing sensitive data to the clipboard; if necessary, clear it after a short timeout.

title: Code Analysis: Excessive logging
description: The application contains an excessive number of android.util.Log calls (debug, verbose, info, error), indicating verbose logging in the release build.
impact: Log output is written to logcat, which on rooted devices or via ADB is readable by any process. Sensitive data (tokens, credentials, PII, internal URLs, error details) logged at any level can be captured by an attacker.
remediation_brief: Remove or guard verbose/debug logging in release builds; use ProGuard/R8 rules to strip Log.d/v/i calls.

title: Third-party tracker SDK detected: {tracker_name}
description: The APK bundles a known third-party tracker or analytics SDK, identified by its package path in the DEX/smali code.
impact: Tracker SDKs collect user behaviour data (screen views, events, device identifiers) and transmit it to external servers. This may violate user privacy expectations and regulatory requirements (GDPR, CCPA) if consent is not properly obtained.
remediation_brief: Audit tracker SDKs for data collection scope; ensure user consent is obtained; provide opt-out mechanisms.

title: Excessive third-party trackers detected ({count})
description: The APK bundles more than 5 distinct third-party tracker or analytics SDKs.
impact: Each tracker SDK collects and transmits user data independently, compounding privacy exposure. Multiple trackers increase the attack surface (each is a dependency that may have vulnerabilities) and the volume of data leaving the device.
remediation_brief: Review and remove unnecessary tracker SDKs; consolidate analytics to the fewest providers that meet business requirements.

title: Protection: Anti-debug mechanism detected
description: The app implements anti-debugging checks (e.g. isDebuggerConnected(), ptrace self-trace) to detect runtime analysis.
impact: Anti-debug mechanisms are a positive security control that makes dynamic analysis harder for attackers. Their presence indicates the developer has invested in runtime integrity protection.
remediation_brief: No remediation needed — this is a positive security control. Consider strengthening with multi-layered detection.

title: Protection: Anti-emulator detection found
description: The app checks for emulator/virtual-machine indicators (Build.FINGERPRINT, Build.MODEL, goldfish, generic) to detect analysis environments.
impact: Anti-emulator checks are a positive security control that prevents automated analysis in emulators. Their presence indicates the developer is protecting against sandbox-based malware analysis or dynamic testing.
remediation_brief: No remediation needed — this is a positive security control.

title: Protection: Packer/obfuscator detected: {name}
description: The APK is protected by a code packer or obfuscator (e.g. DexGuard, Bangcle, ProGuard/R8, Tencent, Secneo).
impact: Packers and obfuscators make reverse engineering harder and slow down attackers. Their presence is a positive indicator of investment in intellectual property protection and anti-tampering.
remediation_brief: No remediation needed — this is a positive security control.

title: Protection: No code obfuscation detected
description: The APK does not appear to use code obfuscation (no ProGuard/R8 mapping, no known packer signatures, readable class and method names).
impact: Without obfuscation, an attacker can decompile the APK (via jadx or apktool) and read the source code almost as clearly as the original, making it trivial to discover business logic, API endpoints, hardcoded secrets, and vulnerability patterns.
remediation_brief: Enable ProGuard/R8 in the release build configuration; consider DexGuard or similar commercial obfuscators for sensitive applications.

title: Firebase Realtime Database URL exposed
description: A Firebase Realtime Database URL (*.firebaseio.com) was found in the APK. If database security rules are misconfigured, the database may be publicly readable or writable.
impact: An attacker can attempt to access the Firebase database directly from a browser or tool. If rules allow unauthenticated reads, all stored data (user records, messages, configurations) is exposed. If writes are allowed, the attacker can inject or delete data.
remediation_brief: Enforce Firebase Security Rules requiring authentication for all reads and writes; use role-based access control.

title: Firebase Storage URL exposed
description: A Firebase Cloud Storage URL (firebasestorage.googleapis.com) was found in the APK.
impact: If storage security rules are misconfigured, an attacker can list, download, or upload files to the bucket without authentication, potentially accessing user-uploaded content or injecting malicious files.
