remediation_brief: Enforce Firebase Storage security rules requiring authentication; restrict file types and sizes; use per-user storage paths.

title: Firebase configuration file (google-services.json) present
description: The APK contains a google-services.json (or GoogleService-Info.plist) file with Firebase project configuration, including project ID, API key, and storage bucket.
impact: While the API key alone cannot authenticate, the configuration reveals the Firebase project ID and bucket names, enabling targeted probing of database rules and storage permissions.
remediation_brief: Ensure Firebase security rules are properly configured; restrict API key usage via Google Cloud Console.

title: Firebase Remote Config usage detected
description: The APK references Firebase Remote Config classes, indicating the app fetches configuration values from Firebase at runtime.
impact: Remote Config values can influence app behaviour. If the Firebase project is compromised, an attacker could modify remote config to change app behaviour, redirect traffic, or enable hidden features.
remediation_brief: Validate remote config values on the client before acting on them; use Firebase App Check to restrict access.

title: APK uses only JAR signing (v1) — Janus vulnerability
description: The APK is signed only with the v1 (JAR) scheme and lacks v2/v3 APK Signature Scheme protection, making it vulnerable to the Janus vulnerability (CVE-2017-13156).
impact: An attacker can prepend a DEX file to a v1-only-signed APK. Android's installer verifies v1 (which only checks the ZIP entries) while the runtime loads the prepended DEX. This allows code injection into a legitimately signed app without breaking the signature.

mitre_attack.name: Modify OS Kernel or Boot Partition

remediation_brief: Enable APK Signature Scheme v2 (and v3 if targeting API 28+) in your build configuration; both v1+v2 should be enabled for backward compatibility.

title: APK certificate uses weak signing algorithm
description: The APK signing certificate uses a weak hash algorithm (SHA1withRSA, MD5withRSA) that is vulnerable to collision attacks.
impact: A weak signing hash allows an attacker to potentially generate a second certificate with the same hash, enabling signature forgery. While practical collision attacks against SHA-1 have been demonstrated, exploiting this in APK signing is complex but feasible for a resourced attacker.
remediation_brief: Re-sign the APK with a certificate using SHA256withRSA or SHA384withRSA.

title: APK signing certificate expired or expiring soon
description: The APK signing certificate has expired or will expire within 90 days.
impact: An expired certificate prevents app updates from being installed through the Play Store or sideloading, as Android requires consistent signing across versions. The developer may be forced to issue a new signing identity, breaking update paths for existing users.
remediation_brief: Generate a new signing certificate with a long validity period (25+ years is standard for Android); use Play App Signing for key management.

title: APK signed with debug certificate
description: The APK is signed with an Android debug certificate (CN=Android Debug, typically from ~/.android/debug.keystore), which is a default keystore shared across developer machines.
impact: The debug keystore password is publicly known ("android"). Any developer can sign an app with the same debug key and produce a matching package signature. This allows an attacker to create a malicious update that Android's installer accepts as legitimate.
remediation_brief: Sign release builds with a dedicated release keystore; never distribute debug-signed APKs outside development.

title: APK signing information
description: Summary of the APK signing certificate details including Common Name, organization, validity period, key algorithm, and which APK Signature Scheme versions are present.
impact: Informational. The signing certificate details are used to evaluate the overall signing posture of the application.
remediation_brief: Review certificate details for appropriate key length (RSA 2048+), algorithm (SHA256+), and validity period.

title: Browsable activity with deep link: {activity_name}
description: An activity declares an intent filter with the BROWSABLE category, registering a deep link scheme (custom scheme:// or https:// App Link) that can be invoked from a browser or another app.
impact: Deep links allow external invocation of specific app screens. If the receiving activity does not validate parameters, an attacker can craft a malicious link that triggers unintended actions (account linking, data display, state changes) when the user clicks it.
remediation_brief: Validate all deep link parameters; require re-authentication for sensitive actions; prefer App Links (verified HTTPS) over custom schemes.

title: Unprotected browsable activity: {activity_name}
description: A browsable activity is exported without a custom permission, meaning any app or web page can invoke it with arbitrary parameters via its deep link.
impact: An attacker can craft a link (in a phishing email, web page, or malicious app) that opens the unprotected activity with attacker-controlled parameters. This can be used to bypass navigation flows, inject data into forms, or trigger privileged operations without user consent.
remediation_brief: Validate all incoming Intent data; require user confirmation for sensitive actions; use App Links with digital asset verification.

title: Behaviour: SMS sending capability
description: The app uses SmsManager API (sendTextMessage/sendMultipartTextMessage) and declares the SEND_SMS permission, giving it the ability to send SMS messages programmatically.
impact: If the app is compromised, the SMS capability can be used to send premium-rate messages (billing fraud), exfiltrate data via SMS, or participate in SMS-based social engineering campaigns — all transparent to the user.
remediation_brief: Verify SMS capability is justified by core functionality; remove SEND_SMS permission if not essential.

title: Behaviour: Phone call initiation capability
description: The app uses Intent.ACTION_CALL or TelecomManager APIs with the CALL_PHONE permission, allowing it to initiate phone calls without user interaction via the dialer.
impact: A compromised app with direct call capability can silently dial premium-rate numbers (billing fraud) or be used for harassment. ACTION_CALL bypasses the dialer UI entirely.
remediation_brief: Use ACTION_DIAL instead of ACTION_CALL to require user confirmation; remove CALL_PHONE permission if not essential.

title: Behaviour: Contact access capability
description: The app accesses the contacts database (ContactsContract provider) with READ_CONTACTS or WRITE_CONTACTS permission.
impact: Contact data is highly sensitive PII. A compromised app with contacts access can exfiltrate the user's entire address book (names, phone numbers, emails, photos), which is a common technique used by spyware and social engineering platforms.
remediation_brief: Verify contacts access is justified; remove READ_CONTACTS/WRITE_CONTACTS if not essential; minimize data read.

title: Behaviour: Location tracking capability
description: The app actively tracks the user's location via requestLocationUpdates, getLastKnownLocation, or FusedLocationProviderClient with fine or coarse location permissions.
impact: Location data reveals the user's physical movements, home and work addresses, and daily patterns. A compromised app with location tracking can surveil the user in real time or build a historical location profile.
remediation_brief: Verify location tracking is justified; use coarse location when fine is not needed; minimize tracking duration; remove if not essential.

title: Behaviour: Camera capture capability
description: The app accesses the device camera via Camera API, CameraManager, or ACTION_IMAGE_CAPTURE with the CAMERA permission.
impact: A compromised app with camera access can silently capture photos or video of the user's surroundings, constituting covert surveillance. This is a high-sensitivity permission often targeted by spyware.
remediation_brief: Verify camera access is justified; remove CAMERA permission if not essential; use ACTION_IMAGE_CAPTURE for one-shot photos.

title: Behaviour: Audio recording capability
description: The app uses MediaRecorder, AudioRecord, or similar APIs with the RECORD_AUDIO permission, giving it the ability to capture audio from the device microphone.
impact: A compromised app with audio recording capability can silently record conversations, meetings, and ambient audio, constituting covert surveillance. This is among the most sensitive permissions on mobile devices.
remediation_brief: Verify audio recording is justified; remove RECORD_AUDIO permission if not essential; consider push-to-talk patterns to limit recording duration.

title: Dynamic: SSL pinning bypass — vulnerable (Android)
description: Frida SSL pinning bypass succeeded on Android target, indicating the app does not implement certificate pinning or its implementation is bypassable.
impact: An attacker can position a proxy between the app and its server to intercept, read, and modify all HTTPS traffic including authentication tokens and sensitive data.
remediation_brief: Implement certificate pinning using TrustKit, OkHttp CertificatePinner, or network_security_config with pin-set.

title: Dynamic: Root detection bypass — vulnerable (Android)
description: Frida root detection bypass succeeded; the app does not adequately detect a rooted environment or its checks are easily bypassed.
impact: An attacker on a rooted device can hook runtime methods, extract credentials from memory, bypass payment flows, and tamper with app logic without the app detecting the hostile environment.

mitre_attack.name: Modify OS Kernel or Boot Partition

remediation_brief: Implement multi-layered root detection (SafetyNet/Play Integrity, file-based, property-based) with obfuscation.

title: Dynamic: Data storage monitoring — insecure storage detected (Android)
description: Frida data storage hooks captured SharedPreferences writes or SQLite queries containing potentially sensitive data.
impact: Sensitive data stored in SharedPreferences or SQLite in plaintext can be extracted from a rooted device or from adb backup if allowBackup is true.
remediation_brief: Encrypt sensitive data at rest using EncryptedSharedPreferences or SQLCipher; avoid storing secrets locally.

title: Dynamic: Weak cryptographic API usage detected (Android)
description: Frida crypto hooks observed the app using deprecated or weak cryptographic transforms (DES, ECB mode, MD5, SHA1 for integrity).
impact: Weak cryptography can be broken by an attacker to decrypt stored data, forge tokens, or bypass integrity checks.
remediation_brief: Replace weak algorithms with AES-256-GCM for encryption and SHA-256+ for hashing; avoid ECB mode.

title: Dynamic: WebView security issue detected (Android)
description: Frida WebView hooks detected WebView debug mode enabled or JavaScript enabled in a WebView that loads external content.
impact: Debug-enabled WebViews allow Chrome DevTools attachment on rooted devices. JavaScript-enabled WebViews loading external content are susceptible to XSS and data exfiltration.
remediation_brief: Disable setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled in production; restrict JavaScript to trusted content only.

title: Dynamic: SSL pinning bypass — vulnerable (iOS)
description: Frida SSL pinning bypass succeeded on iOS target via SSLSetSessionOption or NSURLSession hooks.
impact: Same as Android: all HTTPS traffic can be intercepted, including tokens and PII.
remediation_brief: Implement TrustKit or URLSessionDelegate-based certificate pinning.

title: Dynamic: Jailbreak detection bypass — vulnerable (iOS)
description: Frida jailbreak detection bypass succeeded; the app does not detect or adequately prevent running on a jailbroken device.
impact: On a jailbroken device an attacker can hook Objective-C methods, dump the keychain, bypass payment logic, and modify runtime behaviour.
remediation_brief: Implement multi-layered jailbreak detection (file-based, dylib injection, Cydia checks) with runtime integrity validation.

title: Dynamic: Keychain monitoring — insecure keychain usage (iOS)
description: Frida keychain hooks detected SecItemAdd/SecItemCopyMatching activity, indicating keychain usage that may store sensitive items with weak access controls.
impact: Keychain items with kSecAttrAccessibleAlways or without access-group restrictions can be extracted by a jailbroken-device attacker or from an iTunes backup.
remediation_brief: Use kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly for sensitive items; set access groups explicitly.

title: Root/Jailbreak Detection Present
description: The application implements root/jailbreak detection, as identified by Frida hooking known detection methods during instrumentation.
impact: Informational — this is a positive security control. The detection was noted during bypass for testing purposes. Verify that it covers all detection vectors and is resistant to bypass.
remediation_brief: N/A — informational. Verify detection covers file checks, binary presence, system properties, and native integrity. Test with multiple bypass tools.

title: SSL Certificate Pinning Implemented
description: The application implements SSL certificate pinning, as identified by Frida intercepting pinning validation methods during instrumentation.
impact: Informational — this is a positive security control. Pinning was bypassed for MITM analysis. Verify that the implementation is resistant to common bypass techniques.
remediation_brief: N/A — informational. Verify pinning is implemented in native code, covers all TLS connections, and includes backup pins for certificate rotation.

title: Missing Screenshot Protection on Sensitive Screens
description: Frida instrumentation detected that the app does not implement FLAG_SECURE (Android) or screenshot prevention (iOS) on sensitive screens.
impact: Sensitive data on screen can be captured via screenshots, screen recording, or the recent-apps thumbnail. Accessibility-enabled malware can capture screen content silently.
remediation_brief: Set FLAG_SECURE on Activities displaying sensitive data (Android). On iOS, overlay a blur in applicationWillResignActive. Apply to login, payment, profile, and settings screens.

title: Network Security: App Transport Security Arbitrary Loads Allowed
description: NSAllowsArbitraryLoads=true disables ATS globally; non-HTTPS connections are permitted.
impact: The app may communicate with backends over plaintext HTTP; an on-path attacker can read or modify any unencrypted traffic, including authentication tokens.
remediation_brief: Remove NSAllowsArbitraryLoads or scope to specific domains via NSExceptionDomains.

title: Network Security: ATS Exception Allows HTTP for {dom}
description: Per-domain NSExceptionAllowsInsecureHTTPLoads exception bypasses ATS for the listed domain.
impact: Traffic to the excepted domain is plaintext and subject to interception. Acceptable only for legacy backends you control and have committed to migrating.
remediation_brief: Migrate the backend to HTTPS and remove the exception.

title: Attack Surface: Custom URL Scheme Registered: {sch}://
description: Custom URL scheme allows any app on the device to invoke this app with arbitrary parameters.
impact: If deep-link handlers don't validate parameters or enforce authentication, a malicious app could trigger sensitive actions (password change, in-app purchase, etc.). Verify each handler.
remediation_brief: Validate every parameter; require re-authentication for sensitive actions; prefer Universal Links over custom schemes where possible.

title: Build Configuration: get-task-allow Enabled (Debuggable Binary)
description: The binary's entitlements set get-task-allow=true, allowing debuggers to attach.
impact: An attacker on a jailbroken device can attach lldb to the running process and read memory, dump keychain items, or modify runtime behaviour. Should never ship in App Store builds.
remediation_brief: Set get-task-allow=false in the production entitlements file before signing.

title: Build Configuration: Wildcard Application-Identifier in Entitlements
description: Wildcard provisioning profile (e.g. com.example.*) used in entitlements.
impact: Keychain access groups and shared containers are scoped wider than intended; other apps signed with the same wildcard can read shared keychain entries.
remediation_brief: Use specific bundle-identifier provisioning profiles in production.

title: Information Disclosure: Potential hard-coded secret: {label}
description: Pattern matching a known secret format (AWS access key, Google API key, private key, …) was found in the bundle.
impact: Hard-coded secrets in client binaries are trivially recoverable by anyone with the IPA. If valid in production they grant the attacker the same privileges as the app, often including server-side actions the user is not authorised for.
remediation_brief: Rotate the exposed secret; remove from the bundle; fetch via authenticated server call.

title: Binary Security: NX (No-Execute) Bit Not Confirmed
description: The iOS binary Mach-O header does not include the MH_NO_HEAP_EXECUTION flag, indicating that the NX (No eXecute) heap protection may not be enforced.
impact: Without NX heap protection an attacker who achieves a heap overflow can place shellcode on the heap and execute it directly, simplifying exploitation of memory-corruption vulnerabilities.
remediation_brief: Compile the binary with standard Xcode settings that enable NX and heap protection; avoid disabling MH_NO_HEAP_EXECUTION.

title: Binary Security: PIE (Position Independent Executable) Not Enabled
description: The iOS binary Mach-O header does not include the MH_PIE flag. Without PIE, Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) cannot randomize the binary's load address.
impact: An attacker exploiting a memory-corruption bug can predict code and data addresses reliably, making ROP chains and return-to-libc attacks significantly easier. All App Store binaries are expected to be PIE.
remediation_brief: Recompile the binary as a Position Independent Executable (PIE); in Xcode ensure 'Generate Position-Dependent Code' is set to NO.

title: Binary Security: Stack Canary (Stack Protector) Missing
description: The iOS binary does not import ___stack_chk_fail or ___stack_chk_guard symbols, indicating that stack smashing protection (-fstack-protector) is not compiled in.
impact: Without stack canaries, a buffer overflow on the stack can silently overwrite the return address and redirect execution. Stack canaries detect such corruption before the function returns, making exploitation materially harder.
remediation_brief: Compile with -fstack-protector-all (Xcode default for release builds); verify ___stack_chk_fail appears in the symbol table.

title: Binary Security: ARC (Automatic Reference Counting) Not Enabled
description: The iOS binary does not import _objc_release, indicating that Automatic Reference Counting (ARC) is not enabled for the Objective-C codebase.
impact: Manual memory management without ARC is prone to use-after-free, double-free, and dangling-pointer vulnerabilities. An attacker who triggers such a bug can achieve arbitrary code execution.
remediation_brief: Enable ARC for all Objective-C source files (Xcode: Objective-C Automatic Reference Counting = YES); migrate any manual retain/release code.

title: Binary Security: RPATH Load Command Present in Binary
description: The Mach-O binary contains one or more LC_RPATH load commands that define runtime library search paths.
impact: While RPATH is commonly used for framework loading, a writable or user-controllable RPATH entry on a jailbroken device could allow dylib injection. Review paths to ensure none are attacker-writable.
remediation_brief: Audit LC_RPATH entries; remove any that point to writable or non-standard paths; use @rpath/@executable_path relative references.

title: Binary Security: Code Signature Missing or Invalid
description: The codesign utility reports that the main binary lacks a valid code signature.
impact: An unsigned binary cannot be verified for integrity or publisher identity. On a jailbroken device an attacker could replace or patch the binary without detection. Unsigned apps are rejected by the App Store.
remediation_brief: Sign the binary with a valid Apple Developer certificate before distribution.

title: Binary Security: Binary Not Encrypted (FairPlay DRM Absent)
description: The LC_ENCRYPTION_INFO / LC_ENCRYPTION_INFO_64 load command shows cryptid=0, meaning the binary is not encrypted with Apple's FairPlay DRM.
impact: An unencrypted binary can be directly disassembled and reverse-engineered without a decryption step. This lowers the bar for extracting proprietary algorithms, API keys, and business logic.
remediation_brief: Distribute the app through the App Store (which applies FairPlay encryption automatically); for enterprise distribution consider additional code-obfuscation tools.

title: Information Disclosure: Debug Symbols Not Stripped from Binary
description: The nm utility reports that the binary still contains symbol names, indicating debug symbols have not been stripped for the release build.
impact: Debug symbols reveal internal class names, method names, and data structures, significantly aiding reverse engineering. While not directly exploitable, they lower the cost of discovering vulnerabilities.
remediation_brief: Enable Strip Linked Product and Strip Debug Symbols During Copy in Xcode release build settings; run 'strip' on the binary before packaging.

title: Binary Security: Insecure C API Usage Detected
description: The iOS binary imports potentially dangerous C standard library functions (e.g. strcpy, strcat, sprintf, gets, memcpy) that are known sources of buffer overflow vulnerabilities.
impact: Use of unsafe C string and memory functions without bounds checking can lead to stack and heap buffer overflows. An attacker who controls the input to these functions can achieve arbitrary code execution.
remediation_brief: Replace unsafe C functions with bounds-checked alternatives: strlcpy/strlcat instead of strcpy/strcat, snprintf instead of sprintf, fgets instead of gets, memcpy_s or explicit length checks.

title: Information Disclosure: NSLog Usage Detected in Binary
description: The iOS binary imports _NSLog, which writes to the system console log. Production builds should not log sensitive data.
impact: NSLog output is readable by any app on a jailbroken device and by anyone with physical access via Xcode or Console.app. Sensitive data (tokens, passwords, PII) logged via NSLog is exposed to other processes and forensic extraction.
remediation_brief: Remove or guard NSLog calls in release builds; use os_log with appropriate privacy levels or a logging framework that strips debug logs from production.

title: Binary Security: malloc Used Without calloc (Uninitialized Memory Risk)
description: The binary imports _malloc but does not import _calloc. malloc returns uninitialized memory, which can leak sensitive data if not explicitly zeroed.
impact: Uninitialized heap memory may contain residual data from previous allocations (passwords, tokens, keys). If the application reads these bytes before writing, it may inadvertently process or expose stale secrets. Using calloc instead auto-zeros allocated memory.
remediation_brief: Prefer calloc over malloc for security-sensitive allocations; alternatively memset allocated buffers to zero immediately after malloc.

title: Framework Binary Weakness: {check}
description: A bundled framework or dylib binary is missing a standard exploit mitigation (stack canary or ARC). The same protections required of the main binary apply to all embedded code.
impact: A vulnerability in a bundled framework without stack canaries or ARC is as exploitable as one in the main binary. Third-party frameworks are a common attack surface because they are less frequently audited.
remediation_brief: Rebuild or obtain updated versions of bundled frameworks compiled with -fstack-protector-all and ARC enabled; contact the framework vendor if source is unavailable.

title: iOS Permission: {permission_key}
description: The application's Info.plist declares a privacy-sensitive usage description key, requesting access to a protected resource (camera, microphone, location, contacts, etc.).
impact: Each privacy permission grants the app access to sensitive user data. While individually justifiable, the combination of permissions defines the app's data reach. An attacker who compromises the app inherits all granted permissions.
remediation_brief: Verify each permission is justified by the app's core functionality; remove any permissions not strictly necessary; request permissions just-in-time rather than at launch.

title: iOS Permission: Excessive Permissions
description: The application requests more than 6 sensitive iOS privacy permissions, indicating a broad data-access footprint that exceeds what most single-purpose apps require.
impact: An app with excessive permissions exposes a wider attack surface: if compromised, the attacker gains access to camera, microphone, location, contacts, health data, and more simultaneously. Users and reviewers should question whether every permission is essential.
remediation_brief: Audit all declared usage-description keys in Info.plist; remove permissions not essential to core functionality; apply the principle of least privilege.

title: Exported Activities Without Permission ({count})
description: Exported activity components are accessible to any app on the device without a permission check, as confirmed by successful 'am start' invocation.
impact: A malicious app can launch these activities directly, potentially bypassing the app's normal navigation flow, authentication screens, or input validation. This can expose internal functionality not intended for external access.
remediation_brief: Set android:exported="false" or protect with a signature-level permission. Validate all input received via Intent extras in exported activities.

title: Exported Services Without Permission ({count})
description: Exported service components are accessible to any app without permission, as confirmed by successful 'am startservice' invocation.
impact: A malicious app can bind to or start these services, potentially triggering privileged operations, data processing, or background tasks on behalf of the attacker.
remediation_brief: Set android:exported="false" or protect with a signature-level permission. Validate Intent data in onStartCommand/onBind.

title: Unprotected Content Provider: {name}
description: An exported content provider responds to queries without requiring a permission, allowing any app on the device to read its data.
impact: A malicious app can query the content provider and extract all stored data, which may include user records, authentication state, internal application data, or cached API responses.
remediation_brief: Add a read/write permission with android:protectionLevel="signature". Set android:exported="false" if external access is not needed.

title: SQL Injection in Content Provider: {name}
description: The exported content provider is vulnerable to SQL injection — fuzz payloads returned data instead of errors, indicating unsanitised input is passed directly into SQL queries.
impact: An attacker can extract or modify all data stored by the provider via crafted SQL payloads. This may include authentication tokens, user data, and internal application state. In some cases, file-system access is possible via SQLite's ATTACH DATABASE.
remediation_brief: Use parameterised queries (selectionArgs) in the ContentProvider's query/insert/update/delete methods. Never concatenate user input into SQL strings.

title: Injectable Broadcast Receivers ({count})
description: Exported broadcast receivers accepted intents from an unprivileged caller without requiring a permission, as confirmed by 'am broadcast' testing.
impact: Malicious apps can trigger these receivers with crafted intents to manipulate application behavior, bypass controls, trigger unintended actions, or exfiltrate data via extras in the broadcast result.
remediation_brief: Set android:exported="false" or require a signature-level permission. Validate all data received in onReceive() before acting on it.

title: Custom URL Scheme Deep Links ({count})
description: The app registers custom URL schemes that can be hijacked by a malicious app registering the same scheme on the device.
impact: On Android, any app can register the same scheme and intercept deep links. On iOS, URL schemes are first-come-first-served. A malicious app can intercept OAuth callbacks, authentication tokens, or navigation URLs passed via deep links.
remediation_brief: Migrate to App Links (Android) or Universal Links (iOS) which use domain verification and cannot be hijacked. Never pass sensitive data (tokens, credentials) in custom URL scheme parameters.

title: Deep Link Input Validation Issues ({count})
description: Deep link fuzz payloads (javascript:, file://, path traversal, XSS, SSTI, open redirect) were accepted without error, indicating insufficient input validation.
impact: An attacker can craft deep links that trigger XSS in WebViews, local file access, server-side template injection, or open-redirect attacks. This is exploitable via phishing links, QR codes, or malicious apps.
remediation_brief: Validate and sanitise all deep link parameters against a strict allowlist. Reject javascript: and file: schemes. Use a URL parser and verify the host/path before routing.

title: Custom URL Schemes ({count})
description: The iOS app registers custom URL schemes via CFBundleURLTypes. These schemes are first-come-first-served on the device and can be claimed by other apps.
impact: A malicious app installed before the target can claim the scheme and intercept OAuth callbacks, tokens, or sensitive navigation data. Universal Links should be preferred.
remediation_brief: Migrate to Universal Links (Associated Domains) which use HTTPS domain verification and cannot be hijacked. Do not pass tokens or credentials in custom URL scheme parameters.

title: Sensitive Data in Pasteboard
description: The device pasteboard contains sensitive data (tokens, credentials, PII) after app usage. Other apps can read this data.
impact: On iOS before 14 and Android before API 30, any app can read the clipboard silently. Even on newer versions, clipboard access notifications may not prevent data theft by malicious apps that act immediately.
remediation_brief: Clear the pasteboard after paste operations. Use UIPasteboard with localOnly and expirationDate on iOS. Use ClipboardManager.clearPrimaryClip() on Android.

title: Authentication Token Leaked in Logs
description: JWT tokens, bearer tokens, OAuth tokens, or Firebase/cloud tokens were found in the application's runtime logs.
impact: Application logs can be read via ADB or by any app on older Android (pre-API 16). Leaked auth tokens enable session hijacking — an attacker can replay the token to impersonate the user.
owasp_web: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
remediation_brief: Never log authentication tokens. Use ProGuard/R8 to strip Log.d/Log.v in release builds. Replace token values with masked placeholders in debug logs.

title: API Key Exposed in Logs
description: API keys or client secrets were found in the application's runtime logs.
impact: Logged API keys can be extracted via ADB by any user with device access. Compromised keys grant direct access to the app's backend APIs with the app's privilege level.
owasp_web: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
remediation_brief: Remove API key logging from all code paths. Use build-type log filtering to strip debug logs from release builds.

title: Password Leaked in Logs
description: User passwords or credentials were found in the application's runtime logs.
impact: Anyone with ADB access can read the password from logs. If the user reuses passwords, this becomes a credential-stuffing vector across all their accounts.
owasp_web: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
remediation_brief: Never log passwords or credentials at any log level. Audit all log statements in authentication flows. Use ProGuard/R8 to strip debug logging in release builds.

title: PII Exposed in Logs
description: Personally identifiable information (email addresses, phone numbers, SSNs, credit card numbers) was found in application runtime logs.
impact: PII in logs can be extracted by any user with device/ADB access. This violates data protection regulations and exposes users to identity theft, phishing, and fraud.
owasp_web: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
remediation_brief: Mask or redact PII in all log statements. Log only identifiers or hashed values when referencing user data. Review logging in user profile, payment, and registration flows.

title: Internal URL Exposed in Logs
description: Internal/private IP addresses or URLs (10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x) were found in the application's runtime logs.
impact: Internal network topology information aids reconnaissance for network-layer attacks. An attacker learns internal IP ranges, service ports, and API paths that should not be externally visible.
remediation_brief: Remove internal URLs from log output. Use environment-aware logging that masks backend URLs in release builds.

title: Sensitive Stack Trace in Logs
description: Stack traces referencing sensitive framework classes (javax.crypto, SecurityKeystore, CCCrypt, BiometricPrompt, SQLCipher, etc.) appear in the runtime logs.
impact: Stack traces reveal internal implementation details — which crypto libraries, keystore wrappers, and security mechanisms the app uses. This aids targeted attack development against specific implementations.
remediation_brief: Catch exceptions at security boundaries and log a generic error. Never log full stack traces in production. Use a crash reporting service that redacts sensitive frames.

title: Verbose Logging Enabled in Production
description: Over 40% of the app's log output consists of verbose (V) or debug (D) level entries, indicating debug logging was not stripped from the production build.
impact: Verbose logging increases the attack surface for information disclosure. Debug logs often contain variable values, method parameters, and internal state that aid reverse engineering and vulnerability discovery.
remediation_brief: Use ProGuard/R8 to remove Log.d() and Log.v() calls from release builds. Use a logging framework with build-type-aware filtering (Timber, OSLog).

title: JWT Token Found in Process Memory
description: JWT tokens were found persisting in the application's process memory via memory dump analysis.
impact: An attacker with root access can dump process memory and extract valid JWT tokens for session hijacking. JWTs in memory after logout indicate the app does not zero sensitive data.
remediation_brief: Zero out token values immediately after use. Use short-lived tokens. Avoid caching tokens in Java String objects (use char[] and zero). In native code, use memset_s/SecureZeroMemory.

title: Bearer Token Found in Process Memory
description: Bearer authentication tokens were found in the application's process memory.
impact: Extracted bearer tokens can be replayed to authenticate as the user. If the token has no expiry or is long-lived, the window for session hijacking is indefinite.
remediation_brief: Zero token memory after use. Use char[] instead of String in Java/Kotlin. Implement token rotation and short expiry.

title: API Key Found in Process Memory
description: API keys or client secrets were found in the application's process memory.
impact: API keys extracted from memory grant direct access to backend services. Unlike session tokens, API keys often do not expire and can be used indefinitely until rotated.
remediation_brief: Load keys into secure enclaves when possible. Zero memory after use. Use short-lived, per-session derived keys rather than long-lived API keys.

title: Password Found in Process Memory
description: User passwords were found in the application's process memory, indicating the app retains the plaintext password beyond the authentication moment.
impact: An attacker with root/memory-dump capability can extract the user's actual password — not just a token. This enables credential replay against any service where the user has an account.
remediation_brief: Use char[] for password handling and zero immediately after authentication. Never store the password — send it once to the server, receive a token, and discard it. Use SecureString equivalents.

title: Private Key Found in Process Memory
description: A PEM-encoded private key (RSA, EC, or DSA) was found in the application's process memory.
impact: A compromised private key enables impersonation of the app or server in TLS connections, forging of signed tokens, and decryption of past encrypted communications.
remediation_brief: Store private keys exclusively in Android Keystore or iOS Secure Enclave. Never load raw PEM into app memory. Use hardware-backed key operations that never expose the key material.

title: Credit Card Number in Process Memory
description: Credit card numbers (matching Visa, Mastercard, Amex, Discover patterns) were found in the application's process memory.
impact: Extracted card numbers enable financial fraud. This is a PCI DSS violation — cardholder data must never persist in cleartext memory beyond the immediate transaction.
remediation_brief: Use a PCI-compliant payment SDK that handles card data in its own isolated process. Never store card numbers in app memory — tokenise at the point of entry.

title: SSN Found in Process Memory
description: Social Security Numbers (XXX-XX-XXXX pattern) were found in the application's process memory.
impact: SSNs in memory can be extracted for identity theft. This is a compliance violation under multiple frameworks (HIPAA, state privacy laws).
remediation_brief: Never load full SSNs into app memory. Display only the last 4 digits. Use server-side tokenisation for SSN storage and transmission.

title: PIN/Passcode Found in Process Memory
description: PIN codes or passcodes were found in the application's process memory.
impact: PINs extracted from memory can be used to bypass app-level authentication, access locked features, or authorize transactions.
remediation_brief: Zero PIN memory immediately after verification. Use char[] and explicit zeroing. Do not cache PINs for convenience — use biometric authentication instead.

title: Sensitive Data in Clipboard
description: The device clipboard contains data matching sensitive patterns (tokens, passwords, PII) — accessible to all apps.
impact: Clipboard data is shared system-wide. On older Android and iOS, any app can read it silently. Sensitive data in the clipboard persists until overwritten and can be harvested by clipboard-monitoring malware.
remediation_brief: Clear clipboard after paste operations. On iOS, use UIPasteboard with localOnly and expirationDate. On Android, use ClipboardManager.clearPrimaryClip() after a timeout.

title: Cleartext HTTP Traffic to {host}
description: The mobile application sends HTTP (unencrypted) traffic to a backend host. All request and response data traverses the network in plaintext.
impact: An on-path attacker (shared Wi-Fi, compromised router, ISP-level) can read every byte of the communication — authentication tokens, personal data, API responses — and silently modify it in transit.
remediation_brief: Enforce HTTPS for all network communications. Implement HSTS on the server side and certificate pinning in the application.

title: Sensitive Data in URL ({pattern})
description: The request URL contains sensitive data (password, token, SSN, email, credit card, or API key) in its query parameters.
impact: URL query parameters are recorded in server access logs, browser history, proxy caches, HTTP referer headers, and analytics platforms. Credentials or PII in URLs are persistently exposed across multiple systems beyond the intended recipient.
owasp_api: API3:2023 Broken Object Property Level Authorization
remediation_brief: Move sensitive data from URL query parameters to request headers (e.g. Authorization) or POST request bodies. Enforce HTTPS for all endpoints.

title: Sensitive Data in {src} Body ({pattern})
description: The request or response body contains sensitive data such as SSNs, credit card numbers, email addresses, phone numbers, or plaintext passwords.
impact: Sensitive PII or credentials transmitted in API bodies may be logged, cached, or stored by intermediary systems. If the connection is intercepted, the data is immediately exploitable for identity theft or account takeover.
owasp_api: API3:2023 Broken Object Property Level Authorization
remediation_brief: Minimize sensitive data in API requests and responses. Use tokenization for PII, field-level encryption for stored credentials, and ensure HTTPS is enforced.

title: {header}: {host}
description: The server response is missing a security header (Strict-Transport-Security, Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options, or X-Frame-Options).
impact: Missing HSTS allows protocol-downgrade attacks; missing CSP permits XSS payload execution in WebViews; missing X-Content-Type-Options enables MIME-sniffing attacks; missing X-Frame-Options allows clickjacking.
remediation_brief: Configure the web server to include the missing security header in all responses. Enable HSTS with a minimum max-age of 31536000.

title: API Key/Token in Traffic ({key_type}): {host}
description: A recognizable API key or token pattern (AWS access key, Google API key, Firebase key, GitHub token, Slack token, Stripe key, Twilio key, or Bearer token) was detected in the intercepted traffic.
impact: Exposed API keys can be extracted by any attacker with network access and used to access cloud resources, make API calls, or escalate privileges in the associated service — often without rate-limiting or audit trail that points back to the attacker.
remediation_brief: Rotate the exposed key immediately. Replace long-lived API keys with short-lived, scoped tokens (e.g. OAuth2 client credentials). Never embed keys in client-side applications.

title: Insecure Cookie: {name} on {host}
description: A Set-Cookie response header is missing one or more of the Secure, HttpOnly, or SameSite flags.
impact: A cookie without the Secure flag is transmitted over HTTP and can be intercepted. Without HttpOnly, JavaScript (including XSS payloads in WebViews) can read it. Without SameSite, the cookie is sent on cross-origin requests enabling CSRF.
remediation_brief: Add the Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite=Strict (or Lax) flags to all session and sensitive cookies.

title: TLS Certificate Issue: {host}
description: The mitmproxy connection recorded a TLS error for the host, such as a self-signed certificate, expired certificate, or hostname mismatch.
impact: Certificate errors indicate the application may accept invalid certificates, making it vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks. An attacker on the network path can present their own certificate and intercept all encrypted traffic.
remediation_brief: Use valid certificates from a trusted Certificate Authority. Implement certificate pinning in the mobile application to reject unexpected certificates.

title: Third-Party Data Leakage: {tracker}
description: The application sends data to a known third-party analytics or advertising SDK (e.g. Google Analytics, Facebook SDK, Adjust, AppsFlyer, Crashlytics). The transmitted data may include device identifiers, location data, or user identifiers.
impact: Third-party SDKs transmit user data to external servers outside the application's control. This creates regulatory exposure (GDPR, CCPA), increases the attack surface via additional data stores, and may violate user privacy expectations if not disclosed.
remediation_brief: Review all data sent to third-party analytics and advertising SDKs. Minimize PII transmission, anonymize device and user identifiers, and disclose all third-party data sharing in the privacy policy.

title: Unencrypted Authentication: {host}
aliases: Credentials in URL on Auth Endpoint
description: An authentication-related request (login, signin, token, OAuth endpoint) was sent over plaintext HTTP, or credentials were found in the URL of an authentication endpoint.
impact: User credentials (username, password, session token) are transmitted in cleartext and visible to any network observer. An attacker can capture credentials for account takeover, or replay captured tokens to hijack active sessions.
remediation_brief: All authentication endpoints MUST use HTTPS. Redirect HTTP to HTTPS. Implement HSTS. Send credentials in the request body, never in URL parameters.

title: Deprecated TLS Version ({version}): {host}
description: The connection to the host was negotiated using a deprecated TLS version (TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, SSLv2, or SSLv3) that has known cryptographic vulnerabilities.
impact: Deprecated TLS versions are vulnerable to BEAST, POODLE, and other protocol-downgrade attacks that allow an attacker to decrypt traffic. Major browsers and compliance frameworks (PCI DSS) have deprecated these versions.
remediation_brief: Configure the server to support TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 only. Disable TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, SSLv2, and SSLv3.

title: Application is Debuggable
description: The android:debuggable flag is set to true in the manifest, allowing attachment of a debugger to the process for runtime inspection.
impact: An attacker can attach a debugger (JDWP) to the running process, set breakpoints on sensitive operations, inspect in-memory credentials, and modify execution flow at runtime. This effectively removes all application-layer security guarantees.
remediation_brief: Set android:debuggable=false in the release build manifest. Use ProGuard/R8 to strip debug symbols. Ensure the build pipeline never produces debuggable release APKs.

title: Application Allows Backup
description: The android:allowBackup flag is not explicitly set to false, enabling ADB backup extraction of the app's private data directory.
impact: An attacker with physical access or ADB connectivity can extract the entire app data directory via 'adb backup', capturing stored credentials, tokens, session data, and user files without root.
remediation_brief: Set android:allowBackup="false" in the manifest. If backup is required, implement android:fullBackupContent with a backup_rules.xml that excludes sensitive files.

title: Cleartext Traffic Allowed
description: android:usesCleartextTraffic is true, permitting the app to send unencrypted HTTP traffic to any host.
impact: Sensitive data transmitted over cleartext HTTP is vulnerable to interception by any on-path attacker. This includes network operators, rogue Wi-Fi access points, and compromised routers.
remediation_brief: Set android:usesCleartextTraffic="false" in the manifest. Use a Network Security Config to restrict cleartext to specific debug domains only.

title: Exported Components Without Permission Protection ({count})
description: One or more Android components (activities, services, receivers, providers) are exported without requiring a permission, meaning any app on the device can invoke them.
impact: Malicious apps can launch exported activities to bypass authentication, bind to exported services to trigger privileged operations, or query exported providers to exfiltrate data. This directly undermines the Android permission model.
remediation_brief: Set android:exported="false" on components that do not need to be accessible to other apps. For components that must be exported, protect them with a custom signature-level permission.

title: Dangerous Permission: {permission}
description: The app requests a dangerous Android permission that grants access to sensitive user data or device capabilities (SMS, call log, contacts, camera, microphone, location, storage, package install, overlay, settings).
impact: Over-permissioned apps increase the blast radius of any vulnerability. If the app is compromised, the attacker inherits every granted permission. Users who grant permissions for legitimate use unknowingly extend them to exploit code.
remediation_brief: Apply the principle of least privilege. Remove permissions not required for core functionality. Use runtime permission requests scoped to the minimum needed moment.

title: Network Security Config Allows Cleartext
description: The network_security_config.xml base-config permits cleartext traffic to all domains.
impact: All HTTP traffic from the app is allowed without restriction. An on-path attacker can intercept any request that doesn't explicitly use HTTPS, including API calls that may carry authentication tokens.
remediation_brief: Set cleartextTrafficPermitted="false" in the base-config element. Allow cleartext only to specific domains via domain-config for legitimate reasons.

title: Network Security Config Trusts User Certificates
description: The network_security_config.xml includes user-installed CA certificates in its trust anchors for one or more domains.
impact: User-installed certificates are typically added for development/testing MITM proxies. If present in a production build, any CA certificate the device owner installs is trusted, enabling trivial TLS interception without certificate pinning bypass.
remediation_brief: Remove user trust-anchors from production builds. Use build-type variants to enable user CA trust only in debug builds.

title: Embedded Secret: {type} ({count} instance(s))
description: Secrets (API keys, passwords, tokens, AWS keys, private keys, Firebase endpoints) were found embedded in the application binary or its bundled resources.
impact: Anyone who downloads the app can extract these secrets using standard reverse-engineering tools (apktool, jadx, Hopper). Compromised keys grant direct access to backend APIs, cloud infrastructure, or third-party services — often with the app's full privilege set.
remediation_brief: Move secrets to a secure backend or secrets manager. Use compile-time environment variables for build-specific keys. Rotate all discovered secrets immediately — they are considered compromised once published in a binary.

title: Third-Party Tracking SDKs Detected ({count})
description: The application bundles third-party tracking or analytics SDKs (Google Analytics, Firebase, Facebook, AppsFlyer, Adjust, etc.) that transmit user data to external parties.
impact: Tracking SDKs collect and transmit device identifiers, usage patterns, and sometimes PII to external servers. This may conflict with privacy regulations (GDPR, CCPA) and organizational data-handling policies.
remediation_brief: Review each SDK's data collection scope. Ensure privacy policy discloses all third-party data sharing. Implement consent flows and provide opt-out mechanisms where required.

title: App Transport Security Disabled
description: NSAllowsArbitraryLoads is set to YES in the Info.plist, globally disabling App Transport Security (ATS) and permitting cleartext HTTP connections.
impact: All network traffic from the app may be sent without TLS encryption. An attacker on the same network can intercept authentication tokens, API responses, and user data.
remediation_brief: Remove NSAllowsArbitraryLoads or set it to NO. Use NSExceptionDomains only for domains that genuinely require HTTP and are controlled by the organization.

title: Missing Root/Jailbreak Detection
description: The app runs without issue on a rooted/jailbroken device and does not detect or respond to the compromised device state.
impact: A rooted device removes OS sandboxing — an attacker can read any app's data, hook any method via Frida, intercept all traffic, and modify the runtime environment. Without detection, the app is unaware it operates in a hostile environment.

mitre_attack.name: Modify OS Kernel or Boot Partition

remediation_brief: Implement multi-layered root/jailbreak detection: file checks (/system/app/Superuser, /Applications/Cydia), binary presence (su, magisk), system property checks, SafetyNet/Play Integrity, and native code integrity verification.

title: Root/Jailbreak Detection Bypassable
description: The app's root/jailbreak detection was bypassed using Frida runtime hooks, indicating the detection logic relies on hookable methods.
impact: An attacker can use freely available Frida scripts to bypass root detection and run the app on a compromised device with full instrumentation capability. All subsequent protections that depend on root detection are also defeated.

mitre_attack.name: Modify OS Kernel or Boot Partition

remediation_brief: Implement detection in native code with integrity checks on the detection logic itself. Use multiple detection vectors concurrently. Integrate with server-side device attestation (Play Integrity / DeviceCheck).

title: No SSL Certificate Pinning Detected
description: The app does not implement SSL certificate pinning — Frida hooks detected no pinning validation in the TLS handshake path.
impact: Without pinning, a MITM attacker with a trusted CA certificate (rogue Wi-Fi, corporate proxy, compromised device) can intercept all HTTPS traffic including authentication tokens, API calls, and user data.
remediation_brief: Implement certificate pinning using OkHttp CertificatePinner (Android), NSURLSession pinnedCertificates (iOS), or TrustKit. Pin the leaf certificate or its SPKI hash.

title: SSL Certificate Pinning Bypassable
description: The app implements SSL pinning but it was bypassed using Frida hooks on the certificate validation methods.
impact: An attacker with Frida can intercept all HTTPS traffic despite pinning. This means the pinning implementation can be defeated by publicly available tooling, reducing it to a speed bump rather than a real defence.
remediation_brief: Move pinning validation to native code with integrity checks. Use multiple validation points. Combine with anti-instrumentation detection (Frida detection, ptrace checks).

title: No Anti-Debug / Frida Detection
description: Frida successfully attached to the running app process without triggering any anti-debug or anti-instrumentation response.
impact: An attacker can use Frida to hook any method, bypass any security check, extract runtime secrets, and monitor all function calls. Without anti-instrumentation, the app is fully transparent to runtime analysis.
remediation_brief: Detect Frida by checking for frida-server processes, scanning for frida-agent.so in /proc/self/maps, monitoring for D-Bus connections, and checking for default Frida listening ports (27042).

title: No Emulator Detection
description: The app runs on an Android emulator without restriction, as detected by hardware/model/qemu system properties.
impact: Emulators provide full control over the execution environment — network interception, filesystem access, memory inspection, and automated interaction are trivial. This lowers the barrier for dynamic analysis and reverse engineering.
remediation_brief: Detect emulator environments via system properties (ro.hardware, ro.kernel.qemu), build characteristics (goldfish, ranchu), and sensor availability. Restrict sensitive operations on detected emulators.

title: Screenshot Not Prevented
description: The app does not set FLAG_SECURE on sensitive screens — screenshots and screen recordings can capture displayed sensitive data.
impact: Malware with accessibility permissions can take screenshots silently. The recent-apps thumbnail also captures the screen content, visible to any app that can read it.
remediation_brief: Set FLAG_SECURE on Activities that display sensitive data. On iOS, overlay a blur or placeholder in applicationWillResignActive and viewWillDisappear.

title: App Leaks Sensitive Data to Clipboard
description: After app usage, the clipboard contains sensitive data (credentials, tokens, PII) that was not present before the app was used.
impact: The app actively writes sensitive data to the shared clipboard, where any other app can read it. This is a direct data leak vector that persists even after the app is backgrounded.
remediation_brief: Avoid copying sensitive data to the clipboard. If copy is necessary, clear the clipboard after a short timeout. Use custom copy controls with expiration.

title: No Code Integrity / Anti-Tampering
description: No runtime integrity verification was detected — the app does not use SafetyNet, Play Integrity API, or custom tamper-detection mechanisms.
impact: A repackaged or modified APK runs without restriction. An attacker can insert backdoors, disable security checks, or inject monitoring code and redistribute the modified app.

mitre_attack.name: Modify OS Kernel or Boot Partition

remediation_brief: Integrate Play Integrity API (Android) or DeviceCheck/App Attest (iOS). Implement signature verification at startup. Use native code with obfuscation for integrity checks.

title: Sensitive Data in Shared Preferences
description: Sensitive data (auth tokens, session tokens, API keys, refresh tokens) was found in plaintext SharedPreferences (Android) or NSUserDefaults/Preferences plist (iOS).
impact: SharedPreferences are stored as plaintext XML on disk. Any process with root access can read them. On older Android versions or rooted devices, this gives an attacker direct access to session tokens and API credentials without any additional exploitation.
remediation_brief: Store sensitive data in Android Keystore (EncryptedSharedPreferences) or iOS Keychain with appropriate access control flags. Never store authentication tokens in plaintext preferences.

title: Unencrypted SQLite Database
description: An unencrypted SQLite database in the app's data directory contains columns with sensitive data (password, token, session_id, api_key, secret, credit_card, ssn, etc.).
impact: The database can be extracted via ADB backup, root shell, or device imaging. All stored data is immediately readable in plaintext, including credentials and PII that may span the entire user base stored on the device.
remediation_brief: Encrypt the database using SQLCipher or Realm encryption. Derive the encryption key from the Android Keystore / iOS Keychain, not from a hardcoded value.

title: World-Readable File in App Data
description: Files in the app's data directory have world-readable permissions (o+r), allowing any app on the device to read them without root.
impact: A malicious app running unprivileged can read the contents of these files. If they contain tokens, session data, or user information, a co-installed app can silently exfiltrate them.
remediation_brief: Create files with MODE_PRIVATE (0600). Never use MODE_WORLD_READABLE or MODE_WORLD_WRITEABLE. Audit all file-creation code paths for correct permission flags.

title: Sensitive Data in Cache
description: Cache files in the app's cache directory contain sensitive data matching patterns for auth tokens, API keys, passwords, session tokens, or PII.
impact: Cache files may persist across app sessions and survive app updates. With root access, an attacker can read cached API responses, authentication tokens, or user data that the developer assumed was transient.
remediation_brief: Strip sensitive data from API responses before caching. Use encrypted cache or clear cache on logout. Set appropriate Cache-Control headers on sensitive API responses (no-store).

title: Session Data Persists After Logout
description: Sensitive data (tokens, session keys, credentials) persists in the app's data directory after the user logs out, as confirmed by pre/post-logout snapshot comparison.
impact: An attacker who gains device access after the user believes they have logged out can recover session tokens and re-authenticate without credentials. This defeats the purpose of the logout function entirely.
remediation_brief: On logout, clear all stored tokens (SharedPreferences, Keychain, SQLite). Invalidate server-side sessions. Wipe the app's cache directory. Verify by checking the data directory post-logout.

title: Credentials Stored in Plaintext
description: Plaintext passwords or credentials were found stored in the app's SharedPreferences, plists, or other on-disk files.
impact: Any local attacker (root, backup extraction, or device imaging) can read the user's credentials directly. If the user reuses passwords across services, this becomes a credential-stuffing vector.
remediation_brief: Never store passwords on-device. Use token-based authentication. If credential caching is required, store them in Android Keystore / iOS Keychain with biometric access gates.

title: Discovery: Live Host Discovered
remediation_brief: Document all discovered hosts and verify they are authorised to be present on the network segment.
description: A host responded to ICMP ping or TCP probe during phase 1 host discovery. The host is alive and will be included in subsequent scan phases.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening. Network-level vulnerabilities may allow traffic interception, lateral movement, or unauthorized service access.
_x_remediation: Document all discovered hosts and verify they are authorised to be present on the network segment.

title: Discovery: Open Port Discovered
remediation_brief: Review all open ports and close any that are not required for business operations.
description: An open TCP/UDP port was detected on a live host. The service listening on the port will be probed for version information and vulnerabilities.
impact: Each discovered open port represents a network service accessible to attackers. Identifying all open ports is a prerequisite for targeted service exploitation and provides the baseline for vulnerability assessment.
_x_remediation: Review all open ports and close any that are not required for business operations.

title: Insecure Protocol Detected: TLS 1.0 Enabled
remediation_brief: Disable TLS 1.0 on the server. Configure a minimum of TLS 1.2. Prefer TLS 1.3.
description: The server accepts TLS 1.0 connections. TLS 1.0 is deprecated due to known weaknesses including BEAST, POODLE, and weak cipher suites. PCI DSS 3.2+ requires disabling TLS 1.0.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Weak cryptographic implementations may allow interception, decryption, or forgery of protected communications.
_x_remediation: Disable TLS 1.0 on the server. Configure a minimum of TLS 1.2. Prefer TLS 1.3.

title: Insecure Protocol Detected: TLS 1.1 Enabled
remediation_brief: Disable TLS 1.1. Configure minimum TLS 1.2 with strong cipher suites.
description: The server accepts TLS 1.1 connections. TLS 1.1 is deprecated and does not support modern authenticated cipher suites.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Weak cryptographic implementations may allow interception, decryption, or forgery of protected communications.
_x_remediation: Disable TLS 1.1. Configure minimum TLS 1.2 with strong cipher suites.

title: Insecure Protocol Detected: SSLv2 Enabled
remediation_brief: Disable SSLv2 immediately. Configure modern TLS 1.2+ with authenticated encryption cipher suites.
description: The server accepts SSLv2 connections. SSLv2 is fundamentally broken and vulnerable to the DROWN attack (CVE-2016-0800), which can decrypt TLS 1.2 sessions.
impact: An attacker could exploit this to gain full system compromise, execute arbitrary code, or obtain complete unauthorized access to sensitive data and systems. Weak cryptographic implementations may allow interception, decryption, or forgery of protected communications.
_x_remediation: Disable SSLv2 immediately. Configure modern TLS 1.2+ with authenticated encryption cipher suites.

title: Insecure Protocol Detected: SSLv3 Enabled
remediation_brief: Disable SSLv3. Enable only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3.
description: The server accepts SSLv3 connections. SSLv3 is vulnerable to the POODLE attack (CVE-2014-3566), which allows decryption of CBC-encrypted TLS sessions.
impact: An attacker could leverage this to gain significant unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate sensitive data from affected systems. Weak cryptographic implementations may allow interception, decryption, or forgery of protected communications.
_x_remediation: Disable SSLv3. Enable only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3.

title: SSL/TLS Ciphers: Weak Cipher Suite Enabled
remediation_brief: Disable all weak cipher suites. Allow only AEAD ciphers (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) with 128-bit or greater key length.
description: The server supports cipher suites providing 64-bit or less symmetric encryption, export-grade key exchange, or null/anonymous authentication (RC4, DES, 3DES, EXPORT, aNULL, eNULL).
impact: An attacker could leverage this to gain significant unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate sensitive data from affected systems. Weak cryptographic implementations may allow interception, decryption, or forgery of protected communications.
_x_remediation: Disable all weak cipher suites. Allow only AEAD ciphers (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) with 128-bit or greater key length.

title: SSL/TLS Certificate: Self-Signed TLS Certificate
remediation_brief: Replace the self-signed certificate with one issued by a trusted CA. For internal services, deploy an internal PKI.
description: The server presents a self-signed certificate not issued by a trusted certificate authority. Clients cannot verify the server's identity, enabling MITM attacks.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Weak cryptographic implementations may allow interception, decryption, or forgery of protected communications.
_x_remediation: Replace the self-signed certificate with one issued by a trusted CA. For internal services, deploy an internal PKI.

title: SSL/TLS Certificate: Expired TLS Certificate
remediation_brief: Renew the certificate immediately. Implement automated certificate renewal (Let's Encrypt / ACME protocol).
description: The server's TLS certificate has passed its expiry date. Expired certificates are rejected by modern clients with a hard error, and indicate poor certificate lifecycle management.
impact: An attacker could leverage this to gain significant unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate sensitive data from affected systems. Weak cryptographic implementations may allow interception, decryption, or forgery of protected communications.
_x_remediation: Renew the certificate immediately. Implement automated certificate renewal (Let's Encrypt / ACME protocol).

title: SSL/TLS Vulnerability: TLS Heartbleed Vulnerability
remediation_brief: Upgrade OpenSSL to 1.0.1g or later. Revoke and replace server certificates and private keys. Invalidate all session tokens.
description: The server is vulnerable to Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160). An attacker can read up to 64 KB of server process memory per request, potentially exposing private keys, session tokens, and plaintext data.
impact: An attacker could exploit this to gain full system compromise, execute arbitrary code, or obtain complete unauthorized access to sensitive data and systems. Weak cryptographic implementations may allow interception, decryption, or forgery of protected communications.
_x_remediation: Upgrade OpenSSL to 1.0.1g or later. Revoke and replace server certificates and private keys. Invalidate all session tokens.

title: SMB Vulnerability: SMB Signing Not Required

mitre_attack.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle: LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay

remediation_brief: Enable and require SMB signing via Group Policy: 'Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always)'. Enable on all domain controllers and clients.
description: SMB packet signing is not required on this host. Without signing, relay attacks (NTLM relay) allow an attacker to authenticate as any user whose credentials can be intercepted.
impact: An attacker could leverage this to gain significant unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate sensitive data from affected systems. Network-level vulnerabilities may allow traffic interception, lateral movement, or unauthorized service access.
_x_remediation: Enable and require SMB signing via Group Policy: 'Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always)'. Enable on all domain controllers and clients.

title: SMB Vulnerability: SMB Share Accessible (No Authentication)
remediation_brief: Disable null session access. Remove guest accounts. Enforce authentication on all shares. Audit share permissions.
description: An SMB share is accessible without authentication (null session or guest access). Files and directories on the share are readable and potentially writable by unauthenticated users.
impact: An attacker could exploit this to gain full system compromise, execute arbitrary code, or obtain complete unauthorized access to sensitive data and systems. Network-level vulnerabilities may allow traffic interception, lateral movement, or unauthorized service access.
_x_remediation: Disable null session access. Remove guest accounts. Enforce authentication on all shares. Audit share permissions.

title: SMB Vulnerability: SMB Share Accessible (Authenticated)
remediation_brief: Apply least-privilege access controls to all SMB shares. Audit who has read/write access. Remove unnecessary shares.
description: An SMB share is accessible using provided credentials. The share may expose sensitive files, configuration data, or provide a foothold for lateral movement.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Network-level vulnerabilities may allow traffic interception, lateral movement, or unauthorized service access.
_x_remediation: Apply least-privilege access controls to all SMB shares. Audit who has read/write access. Remove unnecessary shares.

title: Credential Capture: LLMNR/NBT-NS Response Captured (Responder)

mitre_attack.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle: LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay

remediation_brief: Disable LLMNR and NBT-NS via Group Policy. Enable SMB signing. Deploy 802.1X port authentication. Monitor for LLMNR/NBT-NS traffic.
description: Responder captured an LLMNR or NBT-NS broadcast and responded with a poisoned answer. The victim host sent an NTLM authentication attempt to the attacker.
impact: An attacker could leverage this to gain significant unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate sensitive data from affected systems.
_x_remediation: Disable LLMNR and NBT-NS via Group Policy. Enable SMB signing. Deploy 802.1X port authentication. Monitor for LLMNR/NBT-NS traffic.

title: Credential Capture: NTLMv1 Hash Captured

mitre_attack.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle: LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay

remediation_brief: Disable NTLMv1 via Group Policy: 'Network security: LAN Manager authentication level' to 'Send NTLMv2 response only'. Disable LLMNR and NBT-NS.
description: An NTLMv1 authentication hash was captured via Responder poisoning. NTLMv1 is trivially crackable in seconds using rainbow tables or GPU brute force.
impact: An attacker could exploit this to gain full system compromise, execute arbitrary code, or obtain complete unauthorized access to sensitive data and systems.
_x_remediation: Disable NTLMv1 via Group Policy: 'Network security: LAN Manager authentication level' to 'Send NTLMv2 response only'. Disable LLMNR and NBT-NS.

title: Credential Capture: NTLMv2 Hash Captured
remediation_brief: Disable LLMNR and NBT-NS. Enforce SMB signing. Use Kerberos authentication in AD environments. Deploy a strong password policy.
description: An NTLMv2 authentication hash was captured via Responder poisoning. NTLMv2 hashes are crackable offline with GPU-accelerated password cracking tools.
impact: An attacker could leverage this to gain significant unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate sensitive data from affected systems. Weak or missing authentication allows unauthorized users to access protected resources.
_x_remediation: Disable LLMNR and NBT-NS. Enforce SMB signing. Use Kerberos authentication in AD environments. Deploy a strong password policy.

title: Information Disclosure: Web Server

impact: An attacker could use this information or weakness for reconnaissance or to facilitate more targeted attacks against the organization. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.

title: Information Disclosure: Directory Listing Enabled
remediation_brief: Disable directory listing on the web server. Add an index file to directories that must be accessible. Apache: Options -Indexes. nginx: autoindex off.
description: The web server returns a directory listing when no index file is present. File paths, names, and modification timestamps are exposed to unauthenticated users.

remediation_brief: Use parameterised queries or prepared statements. Apply input validation and output encoding. Deploy a WAF with SQLi signatures. Conduct a full application security review.

title: LDAP: LDAP Anonymous Bind Permitted

title: Active Directory: Kerberoastable Service Account Identified

title: Active Directory: AS-REP Roastable Account Identified

title: SMB Vulnerability: EternalBlue (MS17-010) — Host Confirmed Vulnerable
remediation_brief: Apply Microsoft security update MS17-010 immediately. Disable SMBv1 via PowerShell: Set-SmbServerConfiguration -EnableSMB1Protocol $false. Block port 445 at perimeter and between network segments. Verify patch status via WSUS or SCCM.
description: The target host has been positively confirmed as vulnerable to EternalBlue (MS17-010). The SMBv1 implementation in the Windows SMB server does not properly handle transaction requests, allowing an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code with SYSTEM privileges. This vulnerability was weaponised by the WannaCry and NotPetya ransomware families and remains one of the most widely exploited vulnerabilities in existence. Successful exploitation requires no credentials and provides complete control of the target host.
impact: An attacker could exploit this to gain full system compromise, execute arbitrary code, or obtain complete unauthorized access to sensitive data and systems. Network-level vulnerabilities may allow traffic interception, lateral movement, or unauthorized service access.
_x_remediation: Apply Microsoft security update MS17-010 immediately. Disable SMBv1 via PowerShell: Set-SmbServerConfiguration -EnableSMB1Protocol $false. Block port 445 at perimeter and between network segments. Verify patch status via WSUS or SCCM.
