title: SSH Vulnerability: {cve_id}
description: ssh-audit matched the SSH server's banner against its built-in CVE database and identified one or more known vulnerabilities affecting the running version of OpenSSH, Dropbear, or Tectia SSH. The CVE ID, CVSS score, and a short description are recorded in the finding Output field; full details are available in the saved ssh-audit JSON report.
impact: Depending on the specific CVE, an attacker may achieve remote code execution, authentication bypass, user enumeration, host-key spoofing, denial of service, or memory disclosure. Banner-matched CVEs are pre-exploit indicators — the host running an affected version is the necessary precondition for exploitation, even when no public PoC has been tested against this specific deployment.
remediation_brief: Patch the SSH server to a release that fixes the CVE. For OpenSSH, upgrade via the operating system package manager (apt / dnf / pkg / yum). For embedded SSH stacks (Dropbear, Tectia, network appliances), apply vendor firmware updates. Where patching is not immediately feasible, restrict SSH access to trusted source IPs via firewall and monitor authentication logs for exploit attempts.

title: SSH Configuration: Algorithm Hardening
description: ssh-audit reports informational-severity recommendations for the SSH server's algorithm configuration. These are not vulnerabilities but represent opportunities to harden the configuration further by adding modern algorithms or removing older but still-secure ones.
impact: No direct impact at this severity. Addressing these recommendations improves the long-term cryptographic posture of the SSH service and reduces the surface for future downgrade or algorithm-confusion attacks as cryptographic best-practice evolves.
remediation_brief: Review the ssh-audit recommendations in the Output field. Update sshd_config (or vendor-equivalent) to add the recommended modern algorithms (e.g. sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com, curve25519-sha256) and remove deprecated algorithms not required for legacy client compatibility. Restart sshd and re-run ssh-audit to confirm the recommendations have been resolved.

title: Unauthenticated Access: VNC: No Authentication Required
remediation_brief: Configure VNC to require strong authentication. Use VNC password authentication at minimum; prefer certificate-based or OS-integrated authentication. Restrict VNC access to trusted networks via firewall rules and VPN.
description: The VNC server accepts connections with security type 1 (None), allowing any remote user to connect without providing credentials. The RFB handshake confirms authentication is not enforced.
impact: An attacker gains full interactive desktop access to the host without any credentials, enabling complete control of the system including file access, application execution, and keystroke capture.

title: Discovery: VNC: Authentication Required But Accessible
remediation_brief: Restrict VNC access to trusted networks. Consider disabling VNC if not required or replacing with a more secure remote access solution.
description: A VNC service is accessible on the network and requires authentication. While authentication is enforced, the service is reachable for brute-force attacks.
impact: VNC is reachable on the network, providing a target for credential brute-force attacks and potential exploitation of VNC implementation vulnerabilities.

title: Unauthenticated Access: WinRM: No Authentication Required
remediation_brief: Configure WinRM to require authentication (Kerberos or NTLM). Restrict WinRM access via Windows Firewall or GPO to trusted management networks only.
description: The WinRM (Windows Remote Management) service responded to an unauthenticated SOAP/WS-Management request without requiring credentials, allowing remote command execution.
impact: An attacker can execute arbitrary commands on the Windows host remotely without credentials, enabling full system compromise, data exfiltration, and lateral movement.

title: Discovery: WinRM Service
remediation_brief: Restrict WinRM access to trusted management networks via firewall rules. Disable WinRM if not operationally required.
description: The WinRM service is active and responding on the network. Authentication is required but the service is reachable as an attack surface.
impact: WinRM exposure provides a lateral movement target for attackers with valid credentials. Authentication methods exposed in WWW-Authenticate may guide attack strategy.

title: Insecure Protocol Detected: WinRM (Cleartext)
remediation_brief: Configure WinRM to use HTTPS (port 5986) with a valid TLS certificate. Disable the HTTP listener on port 5985.
description: WinRM is running on port 5985 (HTTP) without TLS encryption. Administrative credentials are transmitted in cleartext or weakly encoded over the network.
impact: An attacker on the network path can intercept WinRM credentials via packet capture, enabling remote command execution on the managed host.

title: Insecure Protocol Detected: Telnet Service Exposed — Cleartext Protocol
remediation_brief: Disable Telnet and replace with SSH for remote administration. If Telnet is operationally required, restrict access to trusted networks and monitor sessions.
description: A Telnet service is exposed on the network. Telnet transmits all data including credentials in cleartext, making it trivially interceptable.
impact: All data transmitted via Telnet, including usernames and passwords, can be captured by any attacker with network access. This enables credential theft and subsequent unauthorized access.

title: Unauthenticated Access: Kubernetes API: Unauthenticated Access
remediation_brief: Enable RBAC and configure API server authentication (certificates, OIDC, or webhook). Restrict API access to authorized networks. Never expose the API server to untrusted networks.
description: The Kubernetes API server is accessible without authentication. Unauthenticated requests can list, create, and modify cluster resources including pods, secrets, and deployments.
impact: An attacker can fully compromise the Kubernetes cluster — deploying malicious containers, exfiltrating secrets (including cloud credentials and TLS keys), pivoting to other infrastructure, and achieving persistent backdoor access.

title: Unauthenticated Access: Kubelet API: Unauthenticated Access
remediation_brief: Enable kubelet authentication and authorization (--authentication-token-webhook, --authorization-mode=Webhook). Disable the read-only port (10255).
description: The Kubelet API on port 10250 is accessible without authentication, allowing direct interaction with containers running on the node.
impact: An attacker can list running pods, execute commands inside containers, and exfiltrate data from any container on the node without any credentials.

title: Discovery: Kubernetes API Endpoint Detected
remediation_brief: Ensure the Kubernetes API is not exposed to untrusted networks. Verify RBAC is properly configured.
description: A Kubernetes API endpoint was detected on the network. Authentication is enforced but the endpoint's presence confirms a Kubernetes deployment.
impact: Confirms Kubernetes infrastructure for further targeted attacks. Version information may aid CVE exploitation.

title: Unauthenticated Access: Rsync: Anonymous Module Access
remediation_brief: Configure rsync modules to require authentication (auth users + secrets file). Restrict access by IP via hosts allow/deny. Disable rsync if not required.
description: The rsync daemon allows anonymous listing and potentially read/write access to shared modules without authentication.
impact: An attacker can enumerate and download files from shared rsync modules, potentially accessing configuration files, credentials, source code, or sensitive data. Write access enables malware deployment.

title: Network Misconfiguration: Java RMI Registry Exposed
remediation_brief: Restrict RMI registry access to localhost or trusted networks via firewall rules. Implement JMX authentication. Use serialization filters (JEP 290) to prevent deserialization attacks.
description: A Java RMI registry is exposed on the network. The JRMI handshake was confirmed. Exposed RMI registries are vulnerable to deserialization attacks via ysoserial payloads.
impact: An attacker can exploit Java deserialization vulnerabilities to achieve remote code execution on the server. Exposed RMI registries are a well-known exploitation vector with readily available tooling.

title: Memcached: Unauthenticated Access
remediation_brief: Enable SASL authentication for Memcached. Bind to localhost or trusted interfaces only. Implement firewall rules to restrict access. Consider Memcached with TLS (1.5.13+).
description: Memcached is accessible without authentication. The 'stats' command returned data successfully, confirming no authentication is configured.
impact: An attacker can read and modify cached data (including session tokens, credentials, and application data), flush the cache to cause a denial of service, or use the server for DDoS amplification attacks.

title: Elasticsearch: Unauthenticated Access
remediation_brief: Enable Elasticsearch security features (X-Pack Security or OpenSearch Security). Configure TLS and role-based access control. Bind to localhost or trusted interfaces only.
description: Elasticsearch is accessible without authentication. Cluster health, indices, and all stored data can be queried and modified by any network-accessible client.
impact: An attacker can read, modify, or delete all indexed data which may include PII, credentials, logs, and business-critical information. The cluster can also be used as a data exfiltration staging point.

title: IoT: MQTT Broker: No Authentication Required
remediation_brief: Enable MQTT authentication with username/password or client certificates. Configure ACLs to restrict topic access per client. Enable TLS encryption.
description: The MQTT broker accepted a CONNECT packet without credentials (CONNACK return code 0x00), confirming no authentication is required.
impact: An attacker can subscribe to all topics to intercept sensitive IoT/SCADA telemetry data, and publish malicious messages to manipulate connected devices or trigger unsafe actuator commands.

title: IoT: MQTT Broker Detected
remediation_brief: Verify MQTT broker authentication and ACLs are properly configured. Ensure TLS is enabled for production deployments.
description: An MQTT broker was detected on the network. Authentication is enforced (CONNACK rejected unauthenticated connection).
impact: Confirms an MQTT deployment for further targeted testing. The broker may be part of IoT or SCADA infrastructure.

title: Authentication: Default Credentials Accepted
remediation_brief: Change or delete the default guest account immediately. Create named accounts with strong passwords and least-privilege permissions. Restrict management UI access to trusted networks.
description: The RabbitMQ management UI is accessible with default credentials (guest/guest). The management API returned cluster overview data confirming full administrative access.
impact: An attacker gains full administrative control of the message broker — able to read, modify, and delete message queues, create new users, access published messages containing potentially sensitive data, and disrupt message-dependent applications.

title: Admin Endpoint Exposed: RabbitMQ
remediation_brief: Restrict RabbitMQ management UI access to trusted management networks. Ensure strong authentication is configured.
description: The RabbitMQ management UI on port 15672 is accessible on the network. Default credentials were rejected, indicating custom authentication is in place.
impact: The management interface is a brute-force target. Successful authentication provides full administrative control of the message broker.

title: Discovery: AMQP Service Detected
remediation_brief: Verify AMQP authentication is properly configured. Restrict AMQP access to authorized clients only.
description: An AMQP service was detected on port 5672. The protocol header exchange confirmed the service accepts AMQP 0-9-1 connections.
impact: Confirms message broker infrastructure for further targeted testing.

title: Insecure Protocol Detected: POP3: STARTTLS Not Supported
remediation_brief: Enable STARTTLS on the POP3 server or migrate to POP3S (port 995). Ensure TLS 1.2+ with strong cipher suites.
description: The POP3 server on port 110 does not advertise STLS capability in its CAPA response, meaning email retrieval credentials are transmitted in cleartext.
impact: Email credentials transmitted over POP3 without TLS can be intercepted by any attacker on the network path, enabling unauthorized mailbox access.

title: Insecure Protocol Detected: IMAP: STARTTLS Not Supported
remediation_brief: Enable STARTTLS on the IMAP server or migrate to IMAPS (port 993). Ensure TLS 1.2+ with strong cipher suites.
description: The IMAP server on port 143 does not advertise STARTTLS capability in its CAPABILITY response, meaning email credentials are transmitted in cleartext.
impact: Email credentials transmitted over IMAP without TLS can be intercepted by any attacker on the network path, enabling unauthorized mailbox and email content access.

title: Information Disclosure: Cloud Metadata Endpoint Accessible
remediation_brief: Implement IMDSv2 (AWS) requiring session tokens. Block outbound access to 169.254.169.254 from application containers. Implement network policies restricting metadata endpoint access.
description: The cloud instance metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254) is accessible from an internal web service, indicating potential SSRF vulnerability or misconfigured network controls.
impact: An attacker can extract cloud IAM temporary credentials, enabling full compromise of the cloud environment — lateral movement to other cloud services, data exfiltration from S3/Blob/GCS, and privilege escalation.

title: Unauthenticated Access: Jenkins: Unauthenticated Groovy Console (RCE)

mitre_attack.name: Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain

remediation_brief: Immediately restrict access to the Jenkins Script Console (/script) by configuring authentication. Enable Jenkins security realm and authorization strategy. Restrict access by IP at the network level.
description: The Jenkins Groovy Script Console at /script is accessible without authentication, allowing execution of arbitrary Groovy code on the Jenkins server.
impact: An attacker achieves immediate remote code execution on the Jenkins server. This enables reading credentials from the Jenkins credential store, modifying CI/CD pipelines for supply chain attacks, pivoting to build targets, and establishing persistent backdoors.

title: Unauthenticated Access: Jenkins: Unauthenticated Management Console
remediation_brief: Configure Jenkins authentication and authorization. Restrict /manage access to authenticated administrators only. Enable a security realm.
description: The Jenkins management console at /manage is accessible without authentication, exposing system configuration, plugin management, and credential stores.
impact: An attacker can view and modify system configuration, install malicious plugins, access stored credentials, and manipulate build infrastructure.

title: Active Directory: Kerberoastable Service Accounts Identified
remediation_brief: Use Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) with automatically rotated 120-character passwords. For legacy SPNs, enforce 25+ character passwords. Use AES256 encryption for Kerberos tickets. Monitor for TGS-REQ anomalies.
description: Service accounts with registered Service Principal Names (SPNs) were identified via Kerberos TGS-REP ticket requests. The extracted TGS tickets are crackable offline.
impact: An attacker can request TGS tickets for SPN-registered service accounts and crack them offline with hashcat/john. Compromised service accounts often have elevated privileges, enabling domain privilege escalation.

title: LDAP: Anonymous Enumeration — Users and Groups Discovered
remediation_brief: Disable anonymous LDAP binds. Configure the domain controller to require authenticated binds (dsHeuristics). Implement network segmentation to restrict LDAP access to authorized clients.
description: LDAP anonymous bind is permitted and was used to enumerate Active Directory users, groups, and password policies. User/group data was extracted without credentials.
impact: An attacker obtains a complete user and group listing for targeted attacks: password spraying, social engineering, and identifying privileged accounts. Password policy details inform brute-force strategy.

title: SMB Vulnerability: SMBv3 Remote Code Execution (CVE-2020-0796)
remediation_brief: Apply Microsoft security update KB4551762 immediately. Disable SMBv3 compression as a temporary mitigation via PowerShell: Set-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters' DisableCompression -Type DWORD -Value 1.
description: The host is vulnerable to CVE-2020-0796 (SMBGhost), a buffer overflow in SMBv3 compression handling in Windows 10 (1903/1909) and Server 2019. Detected via nmap smb-vuln-cve-2020-0796 NSE script.
impact: An unauthenticated attacker can achieve remote code execution with SYSTEM privileges via a specially crafted SMBv3 compressed packet. This is a wormable vulnerability — no user interaction required.

title: Authentication: Default Credentials Accepted
remediation_brief: Change all FTP credentials from factory defaults to strong, unique passwords. Disable unnecessary FTP accounts. Consider replacing FTP with SFTP (SSH file transfer) for encrypted credential transmission.
description: The FTP service accepted well-known default or factory-set credentials, granting authenticated access to the file transfer service.
impact: An attacker with knowledge of default credentials can authenticate to the FTP service, potentially reading sensitive files, uploading malicious content, or using the server as a staging point for lateral movement. Default credentials are among the first things attackers test and are trivially discoverable.

title: Authentication: FTP Brute Force Protection Not Detected
remediation_brief: Configure the FTP server to enforce connection rate limiting and account lockout after a threshold of failed login attempts. Most FTP servers (vsftpd, ProFTPD, Pure-FTPd) support MaxLoginAttempts or equivalent directives. Consider fail2ban as an additional layer.
description: The FTP server did not exhibit rate limiting, account lockout, or connection throttling after multiple rapid failed login attempts.
impact: Without brute-force protection, an attacker can make unlimited credential guessing attempts against the FTP service at high speed. This significantly reduces the time required to compromise accounts through dictionary attacks or credential stuffing.

title: Information Disclosure: Internal IP in HTTP Response
aliases: RFC 1918 Address Leakage in HTTP Response
description: The HTTP response body or headers from a web service contain one or more RFC 1918 private IP addresses (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16). This reveals internal network topology to external observers.
impact: An attacker can map internal network topology, identify backend hosts behind load balancers or proxies, and use disclosed addresses to craft targeted attacks such as SSRF against internal hosts or lateral movement after initial compromise.
remediation_brief: Configure web servers and application frameworks to suppress internal IP addresses from HTTP responses. Review error pages, debug output, reverse proxy headers, and application-generated content for private address leakage.

title: Discovery: Default Webpage Detected
description: The website shows indicators of being outdated, abandoned, or unnecessary, such as old copyright dates, under-construction messages, or default server landing pages.
impact: Outdated websites may contain unpatched vulnerabilities, deprecated frameworks, or unnecessary attack surface that increases the organization's risk profile.
remediation_brief: Remove or decommission unnecessary websites. Update outdated content and frameworks. Replace default server pages with proper content or restrict access.

title: Unauthenticated Access: Unauthenticated Docker API Exposed
description: The Docker Engine API is accessible without authentication. Endpoints such as /v1.24/containers/json and /v1.24/images/json return data freely, allowing enumeration of all containers and images on the host.
impact: An attacker can create, start, stop, and delete containers, pull arbitrary images, mount the host filesystem via --privileged containers, read secrets and environment variables from running containers, and achieve full host-level remote code execution.
remediation_brief: Restrict Docker API access to localhost or trusted networks. Enable TLS client certificate authentication. Use Docker's built-in authorization plugins.

title: Authentication Bypass: PostgreSQL Trust Authentication Enabled
description: PostgreSQL accepts connections as user 'postgres' without requiring a password, indicating trust authentication is configured in pg_hba.conf for the connecting network.
impact: Full superuser database access to anyone who can reach the port, allowing data exfiltration, modification, deletion, and potential OS command execution via COPY TO PROGRAM or custom functions.
remediation_brief: Reconfigure pg_hba.conf to require md5, scram-sha-256, or certificate authentication for all connections. Remove any 'trust' entries for non-local connections.

title: Unauthenticated Access: Unauthenticated CouchDB Access
description: CouchDB allows unauthenticated access to the /_all_dbs endpoint, revealing the list of all databases on the server.
impact: An attacker can enumerate all databases, read sensitive data, modify or delete documents, and potentially achieve remote code execution via CouchDB's query server functionality.
remediation_brief: Configure CouchDB to require authentication for all endpoints. Set require_valid_user = true in the [chttpd] section of local.ini.

title: Unauthenticated Access: Grafana Unauthenticated API Access
description: Grafana allows unauthenticated access to API endpoints such as /api/org, exposing organization details, dashboards, and data sources.
impact: Attackers can view dashboards containing sensitive metrics, enumerate data source configurations (which may include database credentials), and access alerting rules. Anonymous API access can also be leveraged to discover internal infrastructure.
remediation_brief: Disable anonymous access in grafana.ini by setting [auth.anonymous] enabled = false. Implement authentication for all API endpoints.

title: Authentication: Default Credentials Accepted
description: Grafana accepts the default credentials admin:admin, granting full administrative access to the Grafana instance.
impact: Full administrative access to all dashboards, data sources (which may contain database credentials and API keys), alerting rules, user management, and the ability to install plugins that could provide further access to the underlying system.
remediation_brief: Change the default admin password immediately. Enforce strong password policies and consider implementing SSO/LDAP authentication.

title: Unauthenticated Access: Unauthenticated Kibana Access
description: Kibana exposes its /api/status endpoint without authentication, revealing version information and system status. Full unauthenticated access may also allow reading Elasticsearch indices.
impact: Attackers can read Elasticsearch indices containing logs, metrics, and potentially sensitive data. Version disclosure enables targeted vulnerability exploitation. Kibana Dev Tools can be used to execute arbitrary Elasticsearch queries.
remediation_brief: Enable X-Pack security or Elastic Stack security features. Configure authentication for all Kibana endpoints. Use a reverse proxy with authentication as an additional layer.

title: Unauthenticated Access: Cassandra Unauthenticated CQL Access
aliases: Cassandra Native Protocol Accessible Without Authentication
description: Cassandra CQL accepted a STARTUP frame and returned READY without requesting authentication, indicating the PasswordAuthenticator is not enabled.
impact: Unauthenticated read/write access to all keyspaces and tables. An attacker can exfiltrate data, modify records, create or drop keyspaces, and potentially affect cluster stability.
remediation_brief: Enable PasswordAuthenticator in cassandra.yaml. Create administrative users with strong passwords and configure role-based access control.

title: Sensitive File Exposed: Git Repository Exposed via Web
description: The web server exposes a .git directory. The /.git/HEAD file returns a valid Git ref, indicating the full repository is accessible.
impact: An attacker can reconstruct the complete source code repository including all commit history, which may contain hardcoded credentials, API keys, database connection strings, internal comments revealing business logic, and configuration for other internal systems.
remediation_brief: Block access to .git directories in the web server configuration (e.g., Apache: <DirectoryMatch "\.git"> Deny from all </DirectoryMatch>). Deploy without the .git directory or use .gitignore and deployment pipelines.

title: Web Misconfiguration: Unsafe Methods Enabled
description: The web server allows dangerous HTTP methods such as PUT, DELETE, MOVE, COPY, or PROPFIND as reported by the OPTIONS response Allow header.
impact: PUT can allow arbitrary file upload (including web shells), DELETE can remove files, MOVE/COPY enable WebDAV file manipulation, and PROPFIND discloses directory structure and metadata. These methods may enable remote code execution or data destruction.
remediation_brief: Disable unused HTTP methods in the web server configuration. For Apache: use LimitExcept directive. For Nginx: return 405 for non-GET/POST methods.

title: Web Misconfiguration: Unsafe Methods Enabled
description: The web server responds to HTTP TRACE requests by echoing the full request back, including all headers.
impact: The TRACE method can be exploited for Cross-Site Tracing (XST) attacks, which combine XSS with TRACE to steal HTTP authentication credentials and cookies even when HttpOnly is set.
remediation_brief: Disable the TRACE method in the web server configuration. Apache: TraceEnable Off. Nginx: does not support TRACE by default.

title: Sensitive File Exposed: {_status_label} Page Exposed
description: The Apache server-status or server-info page is publicly accessible, exposing detailed server information including version, uptime, active connections, client IPs, and request URIs.
impact: Reveals internal IP addresses, active request URIs (which may contain session tokens or API keys), client connections, server configuration details, and loaded modules. This information facilitates targeted exploitation.
remediation_brief: Restrict access to mod_status and mod_info via Apache configuration (<Location /server-status> Require local </Location>) or disable them entirely.

title: Information Disclosure: Internal Hostname in HTTP Response
description: The HTTP response contains internal hostnames matching common internal TLD patterns (.local, .internal, .corp, .lan, .intranet, .private, .home, .localdomain).
impact: Internal hostname disclosure reveals the internal naming convention, domain structure, environment names (dev/staging/prod), and infrastructure layout. This aids reconnaissance and social engineering attacks.
remediation_brief: Remove internal hostnames from HTTP response headers, error pages, and application output. Use generic external-facing hostnames.

title: Debug Endpoint Exposed: {_dbg_label}
description: A debug or management endpoint (e.g., /actuator, /actuator/env, /debug, /__debug__, /console) is accessible and returns diagnostic information.
impact: Debug endpoints expose environment variables (which may contain credentials and API keys), database connection strings, application configuration, stack traces, and internal application state. Spring Boot Actuator /env can reveal secrets; H2 Console at /console can enable SQL injection.
remediation_brief: Disable debug endpoints in production environments. For Spring Boot: restrict actuator endpoints via management.endpoints.web.exposure.include. For Django: set DEBUG=False.

title: Sensitive File Exposed: PHP Info Page Exposed
description: A phpinfo() page is accessible, exposing the complete PHP configuration including loaded modules, file paths, environment variables, and server details.
impact: phpinfo() reveals the full server configuration, PHP version, loaded extensions, environment variables (which may contain database passwords and API keys), file paths, and operating system details. This enables targeted exploitation of known PHP and module vulnerabilities.
remediation_brief: Remove phpinfo files from production servers. Disable the phpinfo() function via php.ini: disable_functions = phpinfo.

title: Information Disclosure: DNS Server Version Disclosed
aliases: DNS Server Version Disclosed via CHAOS Query
description: The DNS server discloses its version string via a CHAOS TXT query for version.bind.
impact: Software version disclosure enables attackers to identify known vulnerabilities for the specific DNS server version and craft targeted exploits. BIND version disclosure is a common reconnaissance target.
remediation_brief: Configure the DNS server to suppress or fake version responses. For BIND: options { version "none"; }; For PowerDNS: server-id and version-string settings.

title: Enumeration: SMTP Mailing List Enumeration via EXPN
description: The SMTP EXPN command is enabled and reveals mailing list membership, disclosing valid email addresses and group membership.
impact: EXPN reveals valid email addresses and organizational group membership, enabling targeted phishing campaigns, social engineering, and password-spray attacks. Combined with VRFY, it provides a comprehensive user enumeration capability.

mitre_attack.name: Gather Victim Identity Information: Email Addresses

remediation_brief: Disable the SMTP EXPN command or restrict it to authenticated sessions. In Postfix: smtpd_expansion_filter. In Sendmail: PrivacyOptions=noexpn.

title: SSL/TLS Certificate: Hostname Mismatch
description: The SSL/TLS certificate Common Name (CN) does not match the hostname used to connect, as reported by testssl.sh.
impact: A hostname mismatch causes browsers and clients to display security warnings. Users may learn to ignore these warnings, making them vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks. The mismatch may also indicate a misconfigured or reused certificate.
remediation_brief: Obtain a certificate that matches the server hostname in the CN or SAN fields. Use wildcard certificates for multiple subdomains.

title: Information Disclosure: Sensitive Path in robots.txt
description: The robots.txt file contains Disallow entries for potentially sensitive paths such as admin panels, backup directories, configuration files, or development endpoints.
impact: While robots.txt instructs well-behaved crawlers to skip listed paths, it simultaneously advertises them to attackers. Sensitive paths in robots.txt serve as a roadmap for targeted enumeration and exploitation.
remediation_brief: Review robots.txt entries for sensitive paths. Remove entries that disclose internal structure. Ensure listed paths require authentication regardless of robots.txt.

title: Information Disclosure: Internal Hostname in SAN
description: The SSL/TLS certificate includes internal hostnames in its Subject Alternative Names, matching patterns like .local, .internal, .corp, .lan, .intranet, .private.
impact: Internal hostnames in publicly accessible certificates disclose the internal naming scheme, domain structure, and potentially the existence of internal services. This aids network mapping and targeted attacks against internal infrastructure.
remediation_brief: Remove internal hostnames from the SAN list in certificates used on public-facing services. Use separate certificates for internal and external services.

title: Network Misconfiguration: UPnP/SSDP Service Responding
description: The UPnP/SSDP service responded to an M-SEARCH discovery request, revealing device information and service endpoints.
impact: UPnP can expose device details and allow port forwarding changes without authentication. SSDP has been used in large-scale DDoS amplification attacks. Device information aids targeted exploitation of known firmware vulnerabilities.
remediation_brief: Disable UPnP if not required. Restrict SSDP (UDP 1900) via firewall rules to trusted networks only. Disable UPnP on routers and IoT devices.

title: Unauthenticated Access: MongoDB Unauthenticated Access
description: MongoDB accepted an isMaster query via the native OP_QUERY protocol without requiring authentication, indicating authorization is not enabled.
impact: Full read/write access to all databases, allowing data exfiltration, modification, deletion, and user creation. MongoDB instances without auth have been widely targeted by ransomware campaigns that delete databases and demand payment.
remediation_brief: Enable authorization in mongod.conf (security.authorization: enabled). Create administrative users with strong passwords. Bind MongoDB to localhost or trusted interfaces only.

title: Information Disclosure: Directory Listing Enabled
description: The web server has directory listing enabled, displaying file names, sizes, and modification dates to anyone who requests a directory without an index file.
impact: Directory listings allow attackers to discover backup files, configuration files, source code, database dumps, and other sensitive content that would otherwise require blind enumeration.
remediation_brief: Disable directory listing in the web server configuration. Apache: Options -Indexes. Nginx: autoindex off.

title: SSL/TLS Forward Secrecy: Not Supported
description: The server does not offer any cipher suites with forward secrecy (ECDHE or DHE key exchange). Without forward secrecy, compromise of the server's private key allows retroactive decryption of all recorded past sessions.
impact: An attacker who obtains the server's private key (through theft, legal compulsion, or future cryptanalysis) can decrypt all previously captured TLS traffic. Forward secrecy ensures each session uses ephemeral keys that are discarded, making past sessions safe even if the long-term key is compromised.
remediation_brief: Configure the server to use only cipher suites that provide forward secrecy (ECDHE or DHE key exchange). Disable static RSA key exchange. TLSv1.3 mandates forward secrecy and should be preferred.

title: SSH Configuration: Password Authentication Enabled
remediation_brief: Disable PasswordAuthentication and ChallengeResponseAuthentication in /etc/ssh/sshd_config. Require public key authentication exclusively. CIS Benchmark and DISA STIG both mandate disabling password-based SSH login.
description: The SSH server accepts password-based authentication methods (password and/or keyboard-interactive) alongside public key authentication. Password authentication is susceptible to brute-force attacks and does not enforce multi-factor authentication.
impact: An attacker can attempt password brute-force attacks against the SSH service. Even with strong passwords, password authentication lacks the cryptographic assurance of key-based authentication and is incompatible with most MFA implementations. Compliance frameworks including CIS Benchmarks and DISA STIGs mandate public-key-only SSH authentication.

title: SSH Configuration: Password Authentication Only
remediation_brief: Enable public key authentication and disable PasswordAuthentication and ChallengeResponseAuthentication in /etc/ssh/sshd_config. Generate and deploy SSH key pairs for all authorized users. CIS Benchmark and DISA STIG both mandate public-key-only SSH login.
description: The SSH server accepts only password-based authentication methods (password and/or keyboard-interactive) with no public key authentication available. This is a significant security weakness — the server cannot accept key-based authentication at all, making brute-force the only barrier to unauthorized access.
impact: Without public key authentication, the SSH server relies entirely on password strength for security. An attacker can mount online brute-force or credential-stuffing attacks with no cryptographic barrier. The absence of public key support also prevents deployment of certificate-based or hardware-token SSH authentication. This configuration violates CIS Benchmark and DISA STIG requirements for SSH hardening.

title: Discovery: O365 Tenant Detected
description: The target domain uses Microsoft 365 / Azure AD for email and authentication. MX records point to *.protection.outlook.com or the OpenID configuration endpoint confirms an Azure AD tenant.
impact: Confirms the organization uses Microsoft 365, enabling targeted O365 account enumeration, credential spray, and phishing attacks against the tenant.

mitre_attack.name: Gather Victim Identity Information: Email Addresses

remediation_brief: Implement conditional access policies, enforce MFA, and configure Azure AD Smart Lockout to mitigate enumeration and credential spray attacks.

title: Enumeration: O365 Account Enumeration
description: Valid O365 user accounts were confirmed via Azure AD authentication endpoint enumeration. The endpoint returns different responses for valid and invalid accounts, allowing an attacker to confirm which email addresses correspond to active accounts.
impact: Confirmed valid accounts can be targeted with password spray attacks, credential stuffing, phishing campaigns, and social engineering. This significantly reduces the attacker's search space for credential-based attacks.

mitre_attack.name: Gather Victim Identity Information: Email Addresses

remediation_brief: Implement conditional access policies, enforce MFA on all accounts, configure Azure AD Smart Lockout, and disable legacy authentication protocols that bypass MFA. Monitor Azure AD sign-in logs for enumeration patterns.

title: Unauthenticated Access: Unauthenticated X11 Display Access
description: An X11 display server accepts connections without authentication. The service responded to either xdpyinfo queries or raw X11 protocol handshake without requiring XAUTH/MIT-MAGIC-COOKIE credentials.
impact: An attacker can capture screen contents in real-time, inject keystrokes and mouse events, monitor all user activity on the display, and potentially execute arbitrary commands through keystroke injection. This provides full visibility into and control over the user's desktop session.
remediation_brief: Disable remote X11 connections or enforce XAUTH/MIT-MAGIC-COOKIE authentication. Configure X11 to listen only on localhost (-nolisten tcp). Use SSH X11 forwarding instead of direct X11 connections. Apply firewall rules to block ports 6000-6063 from untrusted networks.

title: Discovery: X11 Display Detected (Authentication Required)
description: An X11 display server is running but requires authentication to connect. The X11 protocol handshake was rejected with an authentication-required response.
impact: The X11 service is exposed on the network but properly requires authentication. While the service itself is secured, exposure of X11 ports to untrusted networks increases the attack surface. If authentication credentials are weak or compromised, the display could be accessed remotely.
remediation_brief: Verify X11 is configured to listen only on localhost unless remote access is required. Use SSH X11 forwarding instead of direct connections. Apply firewall rules to restrict access to X11 ports.

title: Authentication: Default Credentials Accepted
description: brutespray confirmed that a network service accepts default or factory-preset credentials. The service responded with a successful authentication using a well-known username/password combination.
impact: An attacker can immediately authenticate to the service using widely-known default credentials. Depending on the service, this may provide full administrative access, ability to read/modify data, execute commands, pivot to other systems, or completely compromise the host. Default credentials are among the most commonly exploited vulnerabilities.
remediation_brief: Change all default credentials immediately. Implement strong, unique passwords for all service accounts. Deploy account lockout policies. Consider disabling unnecessary services entirely.

title: Authentication: Weak Credentials: {SERVICE}
description: brutespray confirmed that a network service accepts weak or easily guessable credentials. The service authenticated successfully with a non-default but weak username/password combination.
impact: An attacker can authenticate to the service using credentials that are easily guessable or present in common wordlists. This may provide unauthorized access to sensitive data, the ability to modify configurations, or a foothold for lateral movement within the network.
remediation_brief: Enforce strong password policies with minimum length, complexity, and rotation requirements. Implement account lockout after failed attempts. Deploy multi-factor authentication where possible.

title: OS Version Detected: {os} [Inferred]
description: Operating system inferred from software version analysis and port fingerprinting rather than direct nmap OS detection or SSH banner identification. Inference sources include IIS version to Windows Server edition mapping, SQL Server version correlation, OpenSSH banner to Linux distribution mapping, Cockpit version to RHEL mapping, Microsoft service software presence, VMware ESXi detection, and Windows-characteristic port combinations (RDP, SMB, MSRPC, WinRM).
impact: Accurate OS identification enables targeted vulnerability assessment, patch validation, and compliance scope determination. Inferred OS guides the tester toward OS-specific attack vectors, default credential databases, and known exploit chains. Without OS identification, vulnerability assessment is less targeted and may miss platform-specific weaknesses.
remediation_brief: Informational finding. Validate inferred OS with targeted nmap -O scan or authenticated assessment. Use the inferred OS to scope platform-specific vulnerability checks.

title: Discovery: Server Role Identified — Domain Controller
description: Host identified as an Active Directory Domain Controller based on Kerberos (88/tcp), LDAP (389/tcp), and supporting services (Global Catalog, DNS, SMB). Domain Controllers are the central authentication and authorization authority for Windows Active Directory environments.
impact: Domain Controllers hold the keys to the entire Active Directory environment. Compromise of a DC grants access to all domain-joined systems, user credentials (NTDS.dit), Group Policy Objects, and Kerberos ticket-granting services. DCs are prime targets for Kerberoasting, DCSync, Golden Ticket, and Pass-the-Hash attacks. Identifying DCs early directs the tester to the highest-value targets.
remediation_brief: Informational finding. Validate server role and ensure appropriate hardening per role. Apply role-specific security baselines (CIS benchmarks, DISA STIGs) and verify least-privilege network access.

title: Discovery: Server Role Identified — DNS Server
description: Host identified as a DNS server based on port 53 (TCP/UDP) and optionally detected DNS software (BIND, dnsmasq, Unbound, PowerDNS, Microsoft DNS).
impact: DNS servers reveal internal network topology, naming conventions, and service locations through zone transfers (AXFR) and record enumeration. A compromised DNS server enables DNS poisoning, traffic redirection, and man-in-the-middle attacks across the entire network.
remediation_brief: Informational finding. Validate server role and ensure appropriate hardening per role. Apply role-specific security baselines (CIS benchmarks, DISA STIGs) and verify least-privilege network access.

title: Discovery: Server Role Identified — DHCP Server

impact: DHCP servers control IP address assignment and can push configuration to all clients including DNS servers, default gateways, and proxy settings. A rogue or compromised DHCP server enables network-wide man-in-the-middle attacks via malicious gateway or DNS injection.
remediation_brief: Informational finding. Validate server role and ensure appropriate hardening per role. Apply role-specific security baselines (CIS benchmarks, DISA STIGs) and verify least-privilege network access.

title: Discovery: Server Role Identified — Mail Server

impact: Mail servers process and store organizational email containing sensitive communications, credentials, and attachments. They are targets for credential harvesting, phishing relay, open relay abuse, and data exfiltration. Exchange servers in particular may expose OWA and EWS interfaces with known exploitation chains (ProxyShell, ProxyLogon).
remediation_brief: Informational finding. Validate server role and ensure appropriate hardening per role. Apply role-specific security baselines (CIS benchmarks, DISA STIGs) and verify least-privilege network access.

Exposed database ports are high-value targets for credential brute-forcing.

SMB shares are prime targets for credential relay attacks (NTLM relay), sensitive data discovery, and lateral movement. NFS exports may allow unauthorized access when misconfigured.

impact: Print servers process documents that may contain sensitive information. Print protocols (IPP, LPD, JetDirect) historically have weak authentication and known vulnerabilities. CUPS servers may expose administrative interfaces and have been subject to remote code execution vulnerabilities.

impact: Proxy and load balancer infrastructure reveals backend server topology and may expose administrative interfaces. Misconfigured proxies can enable server-side request forgery (SSRF), cache poisoning, and access to internal-only services. Load balancer admin panels may grant control over traffic routing.

description: Host identified as a VPN gateway based on OpenVPN (1194/tcp/udp), IKE (500/udp), NAT-T (4500/udp), L2TP (1701/udp), or PPTP (1723/tcp) ports and optionally detected VPN software.
impact: VPN gateways are the entry point to internal networks from external locations. Compromising a VPN gateway grants authenticated access to the internal network segment. VPN appliances have been subject to critical vulnerabilities (Pulse Secure, Fortinet, Cisco AnyConnect) that enable pre-authentication remote code execution.

Compromising a RADIUS server enables authentication bypass for all connected network access infrastructure, potentially granting access to every network segment protected by 802.1X or VPN authentication.

description: Host identified as a monitoring or observability server based on SNMP (161-162/udp), Prometheus (9090/tcp), Grafana (3000/tcp), Kibana (5601/tcp), or Elasticsearch (9200/tcp) port combinations and optionally detected monitoring software.

Compromising a monitoring server reveals the full infrastructure map and may expose credentials stored in data source configurations. SNMP community strings and monitoring agent credentials are high-value targets.

Compromising a hypervisor grants access to all hosted VMs, their virtual disks, memory contents, and network traffic. impact: Container hosts run containerized workloads and expose orchestration APIs that may grant cluster-wide access. An exposed Docker socket (2375/tcp without TLS) allows arbitrary container creation with host filesystem access. Kubernetes API access enables pod creation, secret extraction, and lateral movement across the cluster.

description: Host identified as a backup server based on Veeam (10000/tcp), Bacula/Bareos (9103/tcp), or monitoring agent (6556/tcp) ports and optionally detected backup software.
impact: Backup servers contain copies of data from across the infrastructure, including databases, file servers, and application data. Compromising a backup server provides access to historical data, potentially including credentials, and may enable restoration of data to attacker-controlled systems. Backup credentials often have broad read access across the environment.

title: Software Detected: {_sw_label}
description: Software product identified on a host without a specific version number. While the product name is known, the absence of version information limits vulnerability assessment.
impact: Identified software presence reveals the technology stack in use. Without version information, targeted CVE matching is not possible, but the product category still aids attack surface mapping.
remediation_brief: Restrict service banner exposure and unnecessary protocol responses to limit software fingerprinting opportunities.

title: Discovery: Environment Tier Inferred — {environment}
description: Server environment tier (e.g. Production, Test, DR, Pre-Production) inferred from hostname naming convention analysis.
impact: Environment classification reveals network segmentation practices and identifies production systems that handle live data, aiding risk prioritization.
remediation_brief: Review hostname naming conventions to ensure they do not inadvertently expose environment classification to unauthenticated users. Consider using opaque hostnames for externally-facing systems.

title: Discovery: Application Identified — {app_name}
description: Enterprise application identified from hostname naming convention. The hostname pattern matches a known product naming scheme.
impact: Application identification from hostnames reveals the technology stack without requiring active probing, aiding targeted vulnerability research and attack surface mapping.
remediation_brief: Use opaque hostnames that do not embed application or product names for internet-facing systems.

title: Discovery: Hardware Model Identified — {model}
description: Server hardware model inferred from hostname naming convention. The hostname contains a pattern matching a known server hardware model number.
impact: Hardware model identification reveals the physical infrastructure platform, which may have known firmware vulnerabilities or BIOS/BMC attack surfaces (e.g., iDRAC, iLO).
remediation_brief: Avoid embedding hardware model identifiers in hostnames. Review BIOS/firmware update status on identified hardware platforms.

title: Discovery: Server Role Inferred — {role}
description: Server role inferred from hostname token analysis. Keywords in the hostname suggest a specific server function (e.g., sql=Database, api=API Server, vpn=VPN Gateway).
impact: Server role identification aids in targeting specific service types and identifying high-value targets such as database servers, domain controllers, or backup systems.
remediation_brief: Use role-neutral hostnames for externally-facing systems. Ensure hostname-implied services are properly hardened for their role.

title: SSH Configuration: Keyboard-Interactive Only (No Public Key)
description: The SSH server accepts only keyboard-interactive authentication with no public key option. Keyboard-interactive may be PAM-based password prompts, TOTP/OTP, Duo push, or other challenge-response mechanisms. Without public key authentication available, the server relies entirely on challenge-response security.
impact: Without public key authentication, the SSH server cannot accept key-based or certificate-based login. If the keyboard-interactive backend is password-based PAM, the server is susceptible to brute-force attacks. Even if the backend is 2FA, the absence of a public key option limits authentication flexibility and violates CIS/STIG hardening requirements.
remediation_brief: Enable public key authentication in /etc/ssh/sshd_config. If keyboard-interactive is used for 2FA, ensure public key is also available as a primary authentication factor. Deploy SSH key pairs for all authorized users.

title: Discovery: Live Host — No Services Exposed
description: Host responded to discovery probes (confirmed alive) but no open TCP or UDP ports were identified. The majority of scanned ports returned RST (closed), indicating the host is genuinely reachable with no exposed services. It may be a network device, a hardened endpoint, or a host with services on non-standard ports outside the scanned range.
impact: A live host with no exposed services still represents an asset on the network that must be inventoried. It may be running services accessible only via UDP or on non-standard ports not covered by the scan range. The host should be included in the asset inventory and evaluated for whether its presence on the network is expected.
remediation_brief: Verify the host is expected on this network segment. If it is an unmanaged or unauthorized device, investigate and either decommission or bring under management. Ensure asset inventory reflects this host.

title: Discovery: Live Host — Filtered (Possible Segmentation)
description: Host responded to discovery probes (confirmed alive) but 90% or more of scanned ports are filtered — probes received no response, indicating a firewall or ACL is actively dropping traffic to this host. When an entire subnet exhibits this behavior while adjacent subnets respond normally, it is strong evidence of network segmentation enforcement.
impact: A host behind a fully-filtered firewall indicates active access control enforcement at the network layer. This is a positive security control when intentional (segmentation between VLANs, DMZ boundaries, production/test isolation). Compare against other scanned subnets to map segmentation boundaries. If segmentation is expected, this confirms the control is operating. If unexpected, it may indicate misconfigured ACLs blocking legitimate traffic or an undocumented security zone.
remediation_brief: No remediation required if segmentation is intentional. Document the segmentation boundary and verify it aligns with the network architecture diagram. If the host should be accessible from the scan source, investigate firewall rules or ACLs that may be blocking traffic.

title: SMB Signing Enforced — Verify Re-Authentication Bypass Patch (KB5124008)
description: SMB signing is enforced on this host, which prevents traditional NTLM relay attacks. However, research published October 2026 (blackfield.ch) demonstrated that enforced signing can be bypassed via SMB session re-authentication: an attacker opens a signed session with their own credentials, then re-authenticates it with a relayed privileged identity. The server retains the original signing key (per MS-SMB2 spec) while granting the new identity's privileges. Microsoft silently patched this with a same-identity check in KB5124008 (September 2026).
impact: If the target has not applied KB5124008, an attacker with low-privilege domain credentials and a network position for authentication coercion (LLMNR poisoning, PetitPotam, PrinterBug) can relay a privileged user's authentication to this host and gain that user's privileges — even though SMB signing is enforced. Domain Controllers are the highest-value target for this attack since DCSync or secretsdump becomes possible.

mitre_attack.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle: LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay

remediation_brief: Install KB5124008 (September 2026 cumulative update) or later on all Windows hosts, prioritizing Domain Controllers. Validate the fix with the NetExec reauth_swap module or patchcheck.py from the reauthx toolkit (blackfield.ch). Continue enforcing SMB signing — the patch adds a same-identity check on re-authentication that closes this bypass.

title: RDP: NTLM Information Disclosure
remediation_brief: Enable NLA to prevent unauthenticated NTLM negotiation. Consider requiring Kerberos-only authentication for RDP. Restrict RDP to management VLANs to limit reconnaissance surface.
description: The RDP service discloses internal network information (Windows domain name, computer name, DNS domain, OS version) via the NTLM authentication handshake before any credentials are provided. This information aids attackers in mapping the internal network topology, identifying domain membership, and fingerprinting the operating system version.
impact: An unauthenticated attacker can enumerate Windows domain structure, computer names, and OS versions from the network, enabling more targeted attacks including credential stuffing against identified domain accounts, exploitation of version-specific vulnerabilities, and lateral movement planning.
_x_remediation: Enable NLA to prevent unauthenticated NTLM negotiation. Consider Kerberos-only auth for RDP.

title: AI/ML Service Exposed — {service}
remediation_brief: Place AI/ML services behind authentication (OAuth2/API keys) and network segmentation. Restrict access to authorized clients only. Monitor inference API usage for anomalous patterns.
description: AI/ML inference or model-serving infrastructure is exposed on the network. Services like Ollama, vLLM, Triton, or Gradio provide direct access to language models, image generators, or vector databases that may process sensitive data or enable prompt injection attacks against business-critical AI pipelines.
impact: An attacker who reaches an exposed AI service can abuse inference endpoints to exfiltrate training data, poison model outputs, run prompt injection attacks, pivot to backend data stores (vector DBs, feature stores), or consume GPU resources for cryptocurrency mining. If the models process PII/PHI, exposure also creates regulatory liability.
_x_remediation: Place AI/ML services behind authentication (OAuth2/API keys) and network segmentation. Restrict access to authorized clients only. Monitor inference API usage for anomalous patterns.

title: AI Service Unauthenticated Access
remediation_brief: Enforce authentication on all AI service endpoints. Deploy API gateway with key management. Enable audit logging for all inference requests.
description: An AI/ML service endpoint responds to unauthenticated API requests (HTTP 200 on /api/tags, /v1/models, or equivalent). No authentication token, API key, or credentials are required to interact with the service.
impact: Unauthenticated access to AI inference APIs allows any network-reachable attacker to query models, extract model metadata, submit adversarial inputs, exfiltrate training data via model inversion, or weaponize the compute for abuse (cryptomining, spam generation). For services handling regulated data (PII/PHI), this constitutes a data breach vector.
_x_remediation: Enforce authentication on all AI service endpoints. Deploy API gateway with key management. Enable audit logging for all inference requests.

title: AI Model Inventory Disclosed
owasp_api: API3:2023 Broken Object Property Level Authorization
remediation_brief: Restrict model listing endpoints to authenticated administrators. Avoid exposing model metadata to unauthenticated users. If public-facing, return only model identifiers without detailed metadata.
description: The AI service API endpoint discloses a list of loaded or available models, including model names, sizes, and metadata. This information reveals the organization's AI capabilities and technology stack.
impact: Disclosed model inventories help attackers select targets for prompt injection, identify high-value models (fine-tuned on proprietary data), and plan model extraction attacks. Knowledge of specific model versions enables targeted adversarial attacks using known model weaknesses.
_x_remediation: Restrict model listing endpoints to authenticated administrators. Avoid exposing model metadata to unauthenticated users. If public-facing, return only model identifiers without detailed metadata.

title: AI Service Version Disclosed
remediation_brief: Suppress version information from API responses and HTTP headers. Configure the AI service to omit version strings from health check and status endpoints.
description: The AI service discloses its software version in HTTP response headers or API endpoint responses. Version information aids attackers in identifying known vulnerabilities.
impact: Version disclosure allows attackers to search CVE databases and exploit repositories for known vulnerabilities affecting the exact running version. Combined with other findings, this accelerates exploitation timelines.
_x_remediation: Suppress version information from API responses and HTTP headers. Configure the AI service to omit version strings from health check and status endpoints.

title: Non-Standard AI Service Port
remediation_brief: Document all AI service deployments including non-standard ports. Ensure vulnerability scanning covers the full port range. Add non-standard AI service ports to monitoring and firewall rules.
description: An AI/ML service was identified running on a non-standard port — a port not typically associated with the detected AI platform. This may indicate a custom deployment or attempt to obscure the service.
impact: AI services on non-standard ports may evade standard vulnerability scanning and security monitoring. Automated security tools often only scan well-known AI ports, leaving these services unassessed during routine audits.
_x_remediation: Document all AI service deployments including non-standard ports. Ensure vulnerability scanning covers the full port range. Add non-standard AI service ports to monitoring and firewall rules.

title: Discovery: API Endpoint Discovered
remediation_brief: Review all discovered endpoints and confirm each is intentional and documented. Remove or disable any endpoints that are no longer in use. Ensure API gateway or WAF rules restrict access to known-good paths. Maintain an up-to-date API inventory.
description: Siphon discovered an API endpoint via directory and path brute-forcing using dirsearch. The endpoint was not necessarily documented in any provided API specification and was identified by receiving a non-404 HTTP response. Discovery of undocumented or unintended endpoints increases the attack surface available to an adversary. This finding is informational and represents an enumeration result rather than a confirmed vulnerability.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening.
_x_remediation: Review all discovered endpoints and confirm each is intentional and documented. Remove or disable any endpoints that are no longer in use. Ensure API gateway or WAF rules restrict access to known-good paths. Maintain an up-to-date API inventory.

title: Discovery: API Endpoint Discovered
remediation_brief: Audit all live endpoints and compare against the official API inventory. Decommission endpoints that are no longer needed. Apply allowlist-based routing at the API gateway layer so only documented paths are reachable. Ensure staging or debug paths are not deployed to production.
description: Siphon discovered an API endpoint via recursive content discovery using Feroxbuster. The endpoint responded with a non-404 status code during automated path enumeration. Feroxbuster performs recursive brute-forcing and can uncover deeply nested or legacy paths not surfaced by shallow scanners. Discovery of additional endpoints widens the attack surface and may expose functionality not intended for public access.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening.
_x_remediation: Audit all live endpoints and compare against the official API inventory. Decommission endpoints that are no longer needed. Apply allowlist-based routing at the API gateway layer so only documented paths are reachable. Ensure staging or debug paths are not deployed to production.

title: Discovery: API Endpoint Discovered
remediation_brief: Compare discovered endpoints against the authoritative API specification and remove any that are undocumented or deprecated. Implement strict path-based ACLs at the API gateway. Disable directory listing and ensure all routes are explicitly registered in the application router.
description: Siphon discovered an API endpoint using FFUF (Fuzz Faster U Fool), a high-speed web fuzzer. The endpoint returned a response code indicating its existence during wordlist-based path fuzzing. FFUF is commonly used to find hidden API routes, versioned paths, and alternative content types. Each discovered endpoint is a potential pivot point for further vulnerability testing.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening. Input validation failures may allow injection attacks, data manipulation, or unauthorized code execution.
_x_remediation: Compare discovered endpoints against the authoritative API specification and remove any that are undocumented or deprecated. Implement strict path-based ACLs at the API gateway. Disable directory listing and ensure all routes are explicitly registered in the application router.

title: Discovery: API Endpoint Discovered
remediation_brief: Review all Kiterunner-discovered endpoints against the official API documentation. Ensure the API gateway enforces an allowlist of permitted routes. Remove undocumented or decommissioned routes from the application. Implement authentication requirements on all non-public endpoints.
description: Siphon discovered an API endpoint using Kiterunner, a tool purpose-built for API route discovery that replays real-world API route signatures. Unlike generic directory brute-forcers, Kiterunner uses curated wordlists derived from thousands of real APIs and supports context-aware request construction. Endpoints found via Kiterunner often represent API-specific paths that generic scanners miss, including internal or administrative routes.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening.
_x_remediation: Review all Kiterunner-discovered endpoints against the official API documentation. Ensure the API gateway enforces an allowlist of permitted routes. Remove undocumented or decommissioned routes from the application. Implement authentication requirements on all non-public endpoints.

title: Discovery: API Framework Identified
remediation_brief: Suppress framework-identifying headers such as X-Powered-By, Server, and custom framework headers. Customize error pages to avoid leaking framework version information. Keep the identified framework patched to the latest stable release. Apply virtual patching at the WAF layer for any known CVEs in the identified version.
description: Siphon successfully fingerprinted the API framework in use (e.g., FastAPI, Django REST Framework, Spring Boot, Express, Laravel) through analysis of HTTP response headers, error page content, URL patterns, and response body signatures. Knowing the exact framework and version enables targeted exploitation of known CVEs and framework-specific vulnerabilities. This information materially aids an attacker in scoping follow-on attacks.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening.
_x_remediation: Suppress framework-identifying headers such as X-Powered-By, Server, and custom framework headers. Customize error pages to avoid leaking framework version information. Keep the identified framework patched to the latest stable release. Apply virtual patching at the WAF layer for any known CVEs in the identified version.

title: Discovery: Undocumented API Endpoint Detected
remediation_brief: Perform a full audit to determine the purpose of the undocumented endpoint. If it is no longer needed, remove it immediately. If it serves a legitimate function, add it to the official API specification and subject it to the standard security review process. Implement CI/CD checks that fail builds when undocumented routes are detected.
description: Siphon detected a live API endpoint that is not present in the provided API specification (OpenAPI/Swagger). Undocumented endpoints often represent legacy functionality, shadow APIs, or development artifacts that were never formally decommissioned. These endpoints are unlikely to have undergone the same security review as documented ones and may lack proper authentication, rate limiting, or input validation. Their existence represents a governance gap in the API lifecycle.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening. Exposed information aids attacker reconnaissance and reveals sensitive system details.
_x_remediation: Perform a full audit to determine the purpose of the undocumented endpoint. If it is no longer needed, remove it immediately. If it serves a legitimate function, add it to the official API specification and subject it to the standard security review process. Implement CI/CD checks that fail builds when undocumented routes are detected.

title: Discovery: Undocumented HTTP Method Accepted
remediation_brief: Configure the application and API gateway to explicitly reject HTTP methods not defined in the API specification for each endpoint. Return 405 Method Not Allowed for any method not in the allowlist. Review the endpoint's handler logic for each accepted method and ensure proper authorization is applied.
description: Siphon discovered that a documented API endpoint accepts an HTTP method that is not listed in the API specification. For example, a GET-only endpoint also accepts PUT or DELETE. This may indicate that the server-side framework auto-handles methods not explicitly coded, or that an older version of the endpoint accepted additional methods. Accepting undocumented methods can lead to unintended data modification or deletion.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
_x_remediation: Configure the application and API gateway to explicitly reject HTTP methods not defined in the API specification for each endpoint. Return 405 Method Not Allowed for any method not in the allowlist. Review the endpoint's handler logic for each accepted method and ensure proper authorization is applied.

title: Discovery: Undocumented API Parameter Accepted
remediation_brief: Implement strict input validation that rejects any parameter not explicitly defined in the API schema. Use allowlist-based parameter validation at the API gateway or middleware layer. Remove or document any legacy parameters still consumed by the backend. Review all undocumented parameters for security implications.
description: Siphon detected that an API endpoint accepts a query or body parameter that is not declared in the API specification. The server processed the parameter without returning an error, suggesting the backend consumes it silently. Undocumented parameters may enable hidden functionality, alter application behavior, or bypass intended business logic. This is often a precursor to mass assignment or parameter pollution attacks.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
_x_remediation: Implement strict input validation that rejects any parameter not explicitly defined in the API schema. Use allowlist-based parameter validation at the API gateway or middleware layer. Remove or document any legacy parameters still consumed by the backend. Review all undocumented parameters for security implications.

title: Discovery: Undocumented Parameter Accepted
remediation_brief: Apply strict schema validation on all incoming request parameters. Reject any parameter not included in the endpoint's schema definition. Audit the codebase for any parameters that are processed but not documented. Use an API design-first approach to ensure the specification is always the source of truth.
description: Siphon detected that an API endpoint silently accepts an extra parameter that produces a changed or differentiated response compared to the baseline. This indicates the application is consuming the parameter on the server side despite it not being part of the documented API contract. Extra parameters accepted silently can indicate a mass assignment risk, hidden feature flags, or undocumented administrative controls.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
_x_remediation: Apply strict schema validation on all incoming request parameters. Reject any parameter not included in the endpoint's schema definition. Audit the codebase for any parameters that are processed but not documented. Use an API design-first approach to ensure the specification is always the source of truth.

title: Discovery: Endpoint Not in Scope File
remediation_brief: Reconcile the scope file with the actual live API surface. Update the scope definition to explicitly include or exclude each discovered endpoint. Ensure API documentation and scope definitions are kept in sync through a formal API inventory management process.
description: Siphon discovered an endpoint that is not listed in the provided scope file. This is an informational flag indicating that testing of this endpoint may be outside the authorized engagement boundary, or that the API inventory is incomplete. Out-of-scope endpoints that are still reachable from the target host represent an inventory management gap and a potential attack vector.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening.
_x_remediation: Reconcile the scope file with the actual live API surface. Update the scope definition to explicitly include or exclude each discovered endpoint. Ensure API documentation and scope definitions are kept in sync through a formal API inventory management process.

title: Discovery: HTTP Method Not in Scope File
remediation_brief: Update the scope file to accurately reflect all accepted HTTP methods per endpoint. Enforce method restrictions at the server level so only documented methods are accepted. Review the authorization logic applied to each accepted method.
description: Siphon detected an HTTP method being accepted by a scoped endpoint that is not listed in the scope file for that endpoint. This may indicate the scope definition is incomplete or that the server accepts additional methods beyond those intended for testing. Methods not in scope that are live may be tested inadvertently or may represent unreviewed attack surface.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
_x_remediation: Update the scope file to accurately reflect all accepted HTTP methods per endpoint. Enforce method restrictions at the server level so only documented methods are accepted. Review the authorization logic applied to each accepted method.

title: Discovery: GraphQL Subscription Endpoint Detected
remediation_brief: Ensure all GraphQL subscription resolvers enforce the same authentication and authorization checks as query and mutation resolvers. Implement rate limiting and connection count limits on the subscription endpoint. Audit subscription data streams to ensure they do not expose data the subscriber is not authorized to receive.
description: Siphon detected a GraphQL subscription endpoint, which enables real-time data push over WebSocket or Server-Sent Events. Subscription endpoints can be leveraged for data exfiltration by subscribing to sensitive data streams, may bypass rate limiting controls applied only to query/mutation paths, and can expose the server to denial-of-service through unlimited subscription connections. Their existence should be noted and each subscription authorization model reviewed.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening. Exposed information aids attacker reconnaissance and reveals sensitive system details.
_x_remediation: Ensure all GraphQL subscription resolvers enforce the same authentication and authorization checks as query and mutation resolvers. Implement rate limiting and connection count limits on the subscription endpoint. Audit subscription data streams to ensure they do not expose data the subscriber is not authorized to receive.

title: JWT: JWT Contains jku Header
remediation_brief: If jku is required, implement strict allowlist validation of the jku URL on the server side. Reject any token whose jku value is not in the approved list. Prefer embedding the public key directly in server configuration rather than fetching it dynamically. Log and alert on any jku value that does not match the expected URL.
description: Siphon detected a JWT token containing a jku (JWK Set URL) header parameter. The jku header allows the token to specify an external URL from which the server should fetch the public key used to verify the token signature. While this finding is informational (the server may pin allowed jku URLs), the presence of this header indicates potential for JWKS spoofing attacks if the server does not validate the jku URL against an allowlist. This finding is escalated to SI-052 (CRITICAL) if the server was found to accept arbitrary jku values.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening.
_x_remediation: If jku is required, implement strict allowlist validation of the jku URL on the server side. Reject any token whose jku value is not in the approved list. Prefer embedding the public key directly in server configuration rather than fetching it dynamically. Log and alert on any jku value that does not match the expected URL.

title: JWT: JWT Missing Issued-At Claim
remediation_brief: Include the iat claim in all issued JWTs, set to the Unix timestamp at the time of issuance. Validate iat on the server side to enforce maximum token age in addition to the exp claim. Use iat together with exp to implement sliding-window session expiry policies.
description: The JWT issued by the API does not include an iat (issued-at) claim. The iat claim records when the token was created and enables server-side enforcement of token age policies. Without iat, the server cannot determine how long a token has been in circulation, making it impossible to enforce maximum token age, detect token replay from older sessions, or implement clock-skew tolerances. This weakens overall token lifecycle management.
impact: An attacker could use this information or weakness for reconnaissance or to facilitate more targeted attacks against the organization.
_x_remediation: Include the iat claim in all issued JWTs, set to the Unix timestamp at the time of issuance. Validate iat on the server side to enforce maximum token age in addition to the exp claim. Use iat together with exp to implement sliding-window session expiry policies.

title: Discovery: File Upload Endpoint Detected
remediation_brief: Enforce strict file type validation using magic bytes rather than extension or MIME type alone. Store uploaded files outside the web root in a sandboxed directory.
