Restrict the set of methods that can be overridden to a minimal allowlist. Log all method override usage and alert on anomalous patterns. At the API gateway, block or audit requests that use method override headers on sensitive endpoints.

title: Unauthenticated Access: Unauthenticated Access to Endpoint
remediation_brief: Apply authentication middleware as a mandatory, default requirement on all API routes. Adopt a secure-by-default posture where every new route requires explicit opt-out from authentication rather than opt-in. Audit all API routes for endpoints that return 2xx responses to requests without valid credentials. Perform automated regression testing that asserts all non-public endpoints return 401 or 403 when called without authentication. Remove any route-specific authentication bypass rules that are not essential for publicly documented anonymous functionality.
description: Siphon confirmed that an API endpoint which is expected to require authentication returns a successful non-error response to an unauthenticated request (one containing no Authorization header, no session cookie, and no API key). The endpoint may return data belonging to a specific user, return aggregate data, or perform operations that should require an authenticated context. Unlike a complete authentication enforcement absence (SI-083), this finding may affect a subset of endpoints or specific HTTP methods where the authentication middleware is missing or bypassed. Unauthenticated access to any endpoint that handles user data or performs state-changing operations represents a direct breach of the application's security model.

title: Authentication: Missing Rate Limit on Sensitive Endpoint
aliases: Missing Rate Limit on Sensitive Endpoint
remediation_brief: Implement strict, dedicated rate limiting on all sensitive API endpoints, independent of any global rate limiting policy. Authentication endpoints should enforce per-IP limits (e.g., 5 attempts per minute) combined with per-account limits (e.g., 10 attempts per 15 minutes) with exponential backoff and account lockout or CAPTCHA challenge after threshold breach. OTP and password reset endpoints should enforce single-use token policies and short validity windows in addition to request rate limits. Return 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header when limits are exceeded. Monitor sensitive endpoint access patterns for burst anomalies.
description: Siphon confirmed that an API endpoint handling a sensitive operation — such as authentication, password reset, OTP validation, account recovery, or payment processing — does not enforce any rate limiting on incoming requests. An attacker can issue unlimited automated requests against these endpoints without encountering any throttling, lockout, or challenge mechanism.

title: Discovery: CORS Wildcard (*) Detected
remediation_brief: Review whether the wildcard CORS policy is intentional and appropriate for each affected endpoint. For public endpoints returning only non-sensitive, non-authenticated data, a wildcard is acceptable. For endpoints returning any data that should be origin-restricted, replace the wildcard with an explicit origin allowlist. Ensure that no endpoint combining Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true exists (this combination is invalid per spec and indicates misconfiguration). Document the CORS policy for each API endpoint as part of the API security specification.
description: Siphon detected that the API responds with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * on one or more endpoints. A wildcard CORS policy permits any origin to read responses from cross-origin requests made without credentials. While browsers enforce that credentialed requests (those sending cookies or Authorization headers) cannot be used with a wildcard origin, non-credentialed responses are still readable by any cross-origin JavaScript. This is informational for truly public API endpoints, but becomes a vulnerability if the endpoint returns semi-sensitive data (API schema details, user-agnostic configuration, analytics), is intended to be restricted by origin, or is accessible using bearer tokens passed in headers (which are treated as credentials and blocked, but may be overlooked in custom implementations).
impact: This finding provides informational context about the environment useful for security assessment and hardening. Security misconfigurations expose unnecessary attack surface or weaken defensive controls.

title: API Misconfiguration: Enumerated Parameter Value Restriction Not Enforced
remediation_brief: Validate every parameter server-side against its declared allowed value set and reject unknown values with HTTP 400; never rely on client-side or specification-only enforcement.
description: An API parameter that declares a fixed set of allowed (enumerated) values accepted a value outside that set instead of rejecting it, indicating that server-side validation of the parameter is missing or relies solely on the client/specification.
impact: Missing enforcement of declared value constraints lets an attacker submit unexpected values that the application's business logic never anticipated, which can drive it into unhandled states, bypass workflow restrictions, or reach code paths intended only for specific enumerated options. On its own the impact is usually low, but it is a reliable building block for more serious logic and access-control abuse.

title: Input Validation: Numeric Parameter Boundary Not Enforced
remediation_brief: Enforce declared minimum/maximum (and length) constraints on numeric parameters server-side and reject out-of-range values.
description: A numeric API parameter that declares minimum/maximum bounds accepted a value far outside the declared range instead of rejecting it, indicating missing server-side range validation.
impact: Unbounded numeric input can cause integer overflow, excessive resource allocation (e.g. huge page sizes or quantities), pricing/quantity manipulation in business flows, or denial of service. The acceptance itself is low severity but frequently underpins resource-exhaustion and business-logic attacks.

title: Input Validation: Parameter Type Confusion Accepted
remediation_brief: Enforce strict type validation on every input: reject values whose JSON type does not match the declared schema type, and use schema validators (e.g. JSON Schema / Pydantic) at the API boundary.
description: A parameter declared as a scalar type (string/number/boolean) accepted a structurally different JSON type (an array or object) without rejection, indicating the API does not enforce the JSON type of its inputs.
impact: Type confusion lets an attacker substitute arrays or objects where scalars are expected, which is a primary vector for NoSQL operator injection (e.g. {"$ne": null}), authentication bypass via type juggling, and application logic errors that can corrupt data or escalate privileges depending on how the value is consumed downstream.

title: Injection: HTTP Parameter Pollution
remediation_brief: Define deterministic handling for duplicate parameters at every layer; reject or canonicalise repeated keys and perform validation only after canonicalisation.
description: The API accepted duplicate occurrences of the same query parameter and the response differed from the single-value baseline, indicating ambiguous or inconsistent handling of repeated parameters across the application stack.
impact: Inconsistent duplicate-parameter handling between front-end proxies/WAFs and the backend lets an attacker smuggle a second value past input filtering or access-control checks (e.g. one component validates the first occurrence while another uses the last), enabling filter/WAF bypass, authorization confusion, and tainted input reaching sensitive sinks.

title: Misconfigured Security Header: Content-Type Confusion — Alternate Body Format Accepted
remediation_brief: Enforce the expected Content-Type for each endpoint and reject requests whose body media type does not match the declared one.
description: An endpoint documented to consume JSON also accepted a request body in an alternate format (form-urlencoded), showing that the server does not enforce the declared request media type.
impact: Accepting multiple body formats creates a parser-differential surface: validation, authentication, or WAF rules that only inspect the expected format can be bypassed by submitting an equivalent request in another format, and form-encoded acceptance can re-enable CSRF against otherwise JSON-only (CSRF-immune) endpoints.

title: Input Validation: Unbounded Resource Consumption via Pagination Parameter
remediation_brief: Enforce a server-side maximum page size / result-set cap that is applied regardless of the client-supplied value, and return a 400 (or clamp) when the requested size exceeds it.
description: A pagination-style parameter (e.g. limit / page_size / count) accepted an extreme value and the API returned a materially larger result set, demonstrating that result-set size is not capped server-side.
impact: Uncapped result sizes let an attacker force the API to assemble and serialise very large responses, exhausting database, memory, CPU and bandwidth resources and degrading or denying service for other users at low attacker cost; it also amplifies data-exfiltration when combined with broken object-level authorization.

title: WebSocket: Insecure WebSocket Transport (Unencrypted ws://)
remediation_brief: Serve all WebSocket endpoints over wss:// (TLS) and redirect/deny ws:// connections.
description: A WebSocket endpoint is served over unencrypted ws:// rather than wss://, so all frames are transmitted in cleartext.
impact: An attacker on the network path can read and tamper with WebSocket messages, including authentication tokens and session data carried on the socket, enabling session hijacking and message injection.

title: WebSocket: WebSocket Handshake Accepts Arbitrary Origin (CSWSH Risk)
remediation_brief: Validate the Origin header against a strict allowlist during the handshake and require a session-bound authentication token rather than relying on ambient cookies.
description: The WebSocket handshake completed with an attacker-controlled Origin header and without credentials, indicating the server does not validate the Origin during the upgrade.
impact: If the socket is authenticated via cookies, a malicious web page can open an authenticated WebSocket to the target on the victim's behalf (Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking), reading and sending messages as the victim and exfiltrating data or performing privileged actions.

title: Unauthenticated Access: Unauthenticated Server-Sent Events (SSE) Stream
remediation_brief: Require authentication and per-subscriber authorization before establishing an event stream.
description: A Server-Sent Events stream (text/event-stream) is accessible without authentication.
impact: SSE streams commonly push user- or tenant-scoped events in real time; unauthenticated access leaks live data (notifications, records, presence) to any anonymous client and can disclose cross-tenant information.

title: Web Misconfiguration: Server-Sent Events Stream Over Cleartext HTTP
remediation_brief: Serve event streams over HTTPS only.
description: A Server-Sent Events stream is served over cleartext http:// rather than https://.
impact: Pushed events traverse the network in cleartext and can be intercepted or modified by a network attacker, exposing real-time data and enabling injection of forged events.

title: gRPC: gRPC Server Reflection Exposed
remediation_brief: Disable gRPC server reflection in production builds; distribute service definitions only to authorized clients.
description: The gRPC server has server reflection enabled and enumerates its full set of services and methods to any client.
impact: Exposed reflection discloses the complete RPC API surface (services, methods, message schemas) to unauthenticated attackers, removing the need to obtain .proto files and accelerating targeted attacks against internal/unintended methods.

title: gRPC: Insecure gRPC Transport (Plaintext / No TLS)
remediation_brief: Require TLS for all gRPC endpoints and reject plaintext connections.
description: The gRPC endpoint accepted a plaintext (non-TLS) connection.
impact: RPC traffic, including credentials and sensitive payloads, is transmitted in cleartext and can be intercepted or tampered with by a network attacker, enabling credential theft and request/response manipulation.

title: Information Disclosure: Application Responses Identify Valid Accounts
description: The login endpoint returns distinguishable responses (status codes, error messages, response bodies, or timing) for valid vs. invalid usernames. This enables an attacker to enumerate valid user accounts by observing differential responses to authentication attempts with different usernames.
impact: An attacker can compile a list of valid user accounts, which can then be used for targeted brute-force attacks, credential stuffing, password spraying, or social engineering. Confirmed usernames dramatically reduce the search space for password attacks.
remediation_brief: Return identical responses (status code, body, headers, timing) for valid and invalid usernames. Use generic error messages like 'Invalid credentials'. Implement rate limiting and account lockout. Use constant-time comparison functions.

title: Enumeration: Timing-Based Username Enumeration
description: The login endpoint shows a measurable timing difference between valid and invalid username submissions. Non-constant-time credential comparison or early-exit logic exposes a timing side-channel that can be exploited for username enumeration.
impact: An attacker can enumerate valid usernames by measuring response latency, even when error messages are generic. Statistical analysis of timing data can reliably distinguish valid from invalid accounts across multiple samples.
remediation_brief: Use constant-time comparison functions for credential checks. Hash all credentials before comparison regardless of user existence. Introduce artificial jitter to normalize response times.

title: Input Validation: Improper Input Validation Results in Server Error
description: An API endpoint returns a 500-series HTTP status code when sent malformed or unexpected input. This indicates the server does not properly validate inputs before processing, allowing unhandled exceptions to propagate to the client. The error response may expose stack traces, internal paths, or framework details.
impact: Server errors caused by invalid input reveal that the application lacks input validation, potentially exposing information about internal architecture. Repeated 500 errors can also indicate denial-of-service attack vectors through malformed requests.
remediation_brief: Validate all inputs before processing. Return 400/422 with a structured error response instead of allowing unhandled exceptions. Implement a global exception handler that logs details server-side and returns generic errors to clients.

title: Information Disclosure: Internal Hostname in API Response
description: API response headers or body contain internal hostnames (e.g., *.local, *.internal, *.corp). Internal hostnames reveal network topology, naming conventions, and infrastructure details that should not be exposed to external consumers.
impact: Leaked internal hostnames enable targeted SSRF attacks, DNS rebinding, and internal service enumeration. Knowing internal naming conventions helps attackers craft more effective social engineering and spear-phishing campaigns.
remediation_brief: Strip internal hostnames from response headers and error messages. Use a reverse proxy that rewrites backend identifiers. Configure application frameworks to suppress internal names in production.

title: JWT: JWT Scope/Claim Manipulation Accepted
description: The server accepted a JWT with modified scope, role, or permission claims without rejecting the tampered token. This indicates the server does not independently validate JWT claims against the authorization database, allowing privilege escalation through token manipulation.
impact: An attacker can escalate privileges by modifying JWT claims (scope, role, permissions) to gain administrative or higher-privilege access. This bypasses authorization controls entirely, granting access to sensitive data and destructive operations.
remediation_brief: Validate all JWT claims server-side against the authorization database. Never trust client-provided scope/role claims. Use signed, opaque tokens or verify claim integrity with asymmetric signatures.

title: Session: Excessive API Session Timeout
description: API bearer tokens remain valid after extended periods of inactivity. The tested token was still accepted by the server after the configured check interval (default: 30 minutes). Excessive session timeouts increase the window for token theft and replay attacks.
impact: Long-lived sessions give attackers more time to exploit stolen credentials. If a token is captured via XSS, MITM, or log file exposure, the attacker has a wider window to access the API before the token naturally expires.
remediation_brief: Set token expiration to 15-30 minutes for sensitive APIs. Use refresh token rotation for longer-lived sessions. Implement idle timeout detection server-side.

title: Session: Session Tokens Remain Valid After Logout
aliases: Cookie Session Not Invalidated on Logout
description: Cookie-based session tokens remain valid after calling the logout endpoint. The session cookie can be replayed against protected resources and continues to grant access, indicating the server does not invalidate the server-side session record on logout.
impact: An attacker who captures a user's session cookie (via XSS, network sniffing, or shared workstation) can continue accessing the application even after the user logs out, as the session token remains valid server-side.

mitre_attack.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Web Session Cookie

remediation_brief: Invalidate server-side session records on logout. Clear session cookies and rotate session IDs. Implement session binding to prevent token reuse after logout.

title: Information Disclosure: Unhandled Application Exception
description: An API response contains stack traces, exception class names, debug output, or SQL error messages. This typically occurs on 500-series responses but can also appear in 200 responses with JSON error payloads. The disclosure reveals internal implementation details.
impact: Exception details expose framework versions, file paths, database schemas, and internal logic that attackers use to craft targeted exploits. SQL error messages specifically reveal database type and schema structure for injection attacks.
remediation_brief: Implement a global exception handler that returns a generic error message to clients. Log full stack traces server-side only. Disable debug mode and detailed error pages in production.

title: JWT: JWT Token Contains Personally Identifiable Information
description: JWT access token payload contains personally identifiable information (PII) such as email, phone number, or address. JWTs are base64-encoded (not encrypted), so any party that intercepts or extracts the token can read PII directly.
impact: An attacker who obtains the JWT (from browser storage, server logs, Referer headers, or MITM) gains access to the user's personal data without needing to call any additional API endpoint. This violates data minimization principles (GDPR Art. 5).
remediation_brief: Remove PII from JWT payloads. Use opaque tokens or encrypted JWTs (JWE) when personal data must travel with the token. Store user details server-side and look them up by subject claim.

title: Information Disclosure: Bearer Token Transmitted in URL Query Parameter
description: Authentication tokens (access_token, bearer, jwt) are transmitted in URL query parameters rather than in headers or cookies.
impact: Tokens in URLs leak via HTTP Referer headers to third-party sites, appear in server access logs, proxy logs, browser history, and any URL-sharing mechanism. An attacker accessing any of these can hijack the user's session.
remediation_brief: Transmit authentication tokens in the Authorization header or as HttpOnly cookies. Never pass tokens in URL query parameters.

title: Information Disclosure: API Key in URL Query Parameter
description: API keys are transmitted in URL query parameters (api_key, apiKey, client_secret, etc.) rather than in headers.
impact: API keys in URLs leak via Referer headers, server access logs, proxy logs, and browser history. An attacker with a leaked API key gains the same API access level as the legitimate client.
remediation_brief: Transmit API keys in a custom header (e.g. X-API-Key) or the Authorization header. Avoid URL query parameters for secrets.

title: Session: Session Token Not Rotated After Authentication
description: The session cookie retains the same value before and after authentication. An attacker who sets a pre-authentication session cookie can hijack the victim's authenticated session.
impact: An attacker can set a known session token in the victim's browser (via XSS, subdomain cookie injection, or URL parameter) before the victim logs in. After login, the session token remains the same, giving the attacker a fully authenticated session.
remediation_brief: Regenerate the session ID on every privilege-level change (login, logout, role escalation). Invalidate the old session immediately.

title: Permissive Security Header: CORS Allows Null Origin
description: The API reflects 'null' as an allowed CORS origin. Sandboxed iframes, data: URIs, and local files send Origin: null, allowing an attacker to craft pages that read cross-origin API responses.
impact: An attacker can create a sandboxed iframe that sends Origin: null, which the server accepts. If credentials are allowed, the attacker can read authenticated API responses, extracting user data and tokens.
remediation_brief: Never whitelist 'null' as an allowed origin. Use an explicit allowlist of trusted origins for CORS.

title: GraphQL: GraphQL Field Name Suggestions Enabled
description: The GraphQL server returns 'Did you mean ...?' suggestions in error responses for misspelled field names, enabling schema reconstruction even when introspection is disabled.
impact: Attackers can use automated tools (Clairvoyance, graphql-cop) to systematically reconstruct the full schema from error-message suggestions, bypassing introspection restrictions.
remediation_brief: Disable field suggestions in production. In Apollo Server: set validationRules to NoSchemaIntrospectionCustomRule and disable suggestions.

title: GraphQL: GraphQL Batching Enabled Without Limit
description: The GraphQL endpoint accepts batched queries (array of operations) in a single request without enforcing a batch size limit.
impact: Attackers can bypass per-request rate limits by batching hundreds of queries (e.g., login mutations for credential stuffing) into a single HTTP request, evading IP-based throttling.
remediation_brief: Disable batching or enforce a maximum batch size (e.g. 5). Count each batched query against the per-user rate limit.

title: Authentication: GraphQL Alias-Based Rate Limit Bypass
description: The GraphQL endpoint resolves multiple aliased copies of the same field in a single request, allowing attackers to multiply resolver executions and bypass per-request rate limits.
impact: An attacker can send a single HTTP request with 100+ aliased resolver calls (e.g., 100 login mutations with different credentials), bypassing IP-based rate limits that count HTTP requests, not GraphQL operations.
remediation_brief: Count each alias as a separate operation for rate-limiting. Implement query complexity scoring that accounts for aliases.

title: Information Disclosure: OAuth Token via Endpoint
description: The OAuth token info/introspection endpoint returns token metadata (scope, audience, user identity) to any bearer of the token without requiring client authentication.
impact: An attacker with a leaked or stolen token can query the token info endpoint to discover the token's scope, audience, and associated user identity, enabling targeted privilege escalation.
remediation_brief: Restrict token info endpoints to authenticated clients only. Require client_id + client_secret for introspection requests per RFC 7662.

title: Sensitive File Exposed: Postman Collection or Environment File Exposed
description: Postman collection or environment files are publicly accessible. Collections expose full API endpoint inventory with example requests; environment files may contain API keys, tokens, and secrets.
impact: An attacker gains a complete API endpoint map with example requests, parameters, and potentially authentication tokens from the Postman environment file, enabling targeted API attacks.
remediation_brief: Remove Postman collection and environment files from public web paths. Never deploy development/testing files to production servers.

title: Authentication: Rate Limit Headers Expose Throttling Configuration
description: API responses include rate-limiting headers (X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset) that reveal exact throttling thresholds.
impact: An attacker can read the rate limit, remaining quota, and reset window to precisely calibrate brute-force attacks to stay just under the limit, making detection harder.
remediation_brief: Evaluate whether rate limit headers are necessary in production. If kept, combine with exponential backoff enforcement and account lockout.

title: Web Misconfiguration: API Version Header Manipulation Yields Different Response
description: The API accepts version negotiation headers (X-API-Version, Accept-Version, Api-Version) and returns different responses for different version values, indicating deprecated or beta versions may be accessible.
impact: An attacker can access deprecated API versions that may have weaker security controls, missing authentication checks, or known vulnerabilities that were fixed in newer versions.
remediation_brief: Restrict API version negotiation. Disable access to deprecated API versions in production. Return 400 for unrecognized version headers.

title: Discovery: Web Endpoint Discovered (Katana)
description: Katana web crawler discovered accessible web paths, JavaScript-referenced endpoints, and linked resources on the target application. Katana performs headless or passive crawling to enumerate the full reachable surface of a web application, including dynamically generated links.
impact: Discovered endpoints expand the known attack surface for further API and web security testing. Hidden or undocumented paths may expose administrative interfaces, debug endpoints, or sensitive functionality not intended for public access.
remediation_brief: Review all discovered endpoints for unintended exposure. Remove or restrict access to administrative, debug, and development endpoints in production. Implement proper access controls on all discovered paths.

title: SSL/TLS Forward Secrecy: Not Supported
description: The API endpoint's TLS configuration does not offer forward secrecy. Cipher suites without ephemeral key exchange (ECDHE/DHE) leave all recorded API traffic vulnerable to retrospective decryption if the server's private key is later compromised.
impact: API communications often carry authentication tokens, session data, and sensitive business payloads. Without forward secrecy, an attacker who captures encrypted API traffic and later obtains the private key can decrypt every recorded session retroactively.
remediation_brief: Configure the API server to use only cipher suites that provide forward secrecy (ECDHE or DHE key exchange). Disable static RSA key exchange. TLSv1.3 mandates forward secrecy and should be preferred.

title: AI/ML API Service Detected: {service_name}
description: Active probing of common AI/ML API paths detected a responding AI service. This includes OpenAI-compatible APIs (/v1/chat/completions), Ollama (/api/generate), Gradio (/queue/join), MLflow (/api/2.0/mlflow/), Triton Inference Server (/v2/models), Streamlit (/_stcore/), and LangFlow (/api/v1/prediction). The service responded with HTTP 200, 401, 403, or 405, confirming the endpoint exists.
impact: AI/ML APIs are vulnerable to prompt injection, training data extraction, model theft, output manipulation, and denial of service via resource-intensive inference requests. APIs responding with 401/403 confirm existence and may be vulnerable to authentication bypass. Unprotected AI APIs allow arbitrary model interaction without rate limiting or input validation.
remediation_brief: Restrict AI/ML API access to authorized clients. Implement authentication, rate limiting, and input validation on all AI endpoints. Deploy prompt injection defenses and content safety guardrails. Conduct specialized AI security testing with pAIn.

title: AI/ML API Endpoints in Specification
aliases: ML Inference Endpoints in API Spec
description: Analysis of the API specification (OpenAPI/Swagger/Postman/HAR) revealed endpoints with AI/ML characteristics: LLM inference paths, embedding generation, model prediction, or body fields matching known AI API schemas (prompt, messages, model, temperature, max_tokens). These spec-documented AI endpoints warrant specialized security testing beyond standard API fuzzing.
impact: Documented AI endpoints may accept arbitrary prompts, return sensitive training data, or expose model internals. Standard API fuzzing typically misses AI-specific vulnerabilities like prompt injection, jailbreaking, and indirect prompt injection via RAG poisoning. The specification reveals the full AI API surface area including request schemas that can be used to craft targeted attacks.
remediation_brief: Implement AI-specific input validation and output filtering on all AI/ML endpoints documented in the specification. Deploy prompt injection defenses, rate limiting, and content safety guardrails. Test with pAIn for LLM-specific vulnerabilities.

title: Authentication Bypass: Hardcoded Public DNS Resolvers Bypass Enterprise Controls
description: Device sends DNS queries directly to public resolvers (8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1, etc.) instead of using the DHCP-supplied resolver, bypassing enterprise DNS filtering, sinkholing, anomaly detection and split-DNS.
impact: Enterprise DNS controls are bypassed for the device's most security-relevant traffic. Security teams cannot detect or block the device contacting unexpected endpoints, cannot apply DNS-based egress restrictions, and cannot audit data-exfiltration patterns. Represents a HIPAA / SOC 2 logging control gap.
owasp_web: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
remediation_brief: Modify device firmware to use only the DHCP-supplied DNS resolver. Implement DoH/DoT. Provide deployment-time toggle for hospital IT to constrain the resolver.

title: Information Disclosure: Cleartext DNS Exposes External Service Topology
description: All DNS queries are sent over cleartext UDP/53. Any on-path observer can enumerate the full set of external services the device depends on.
impact: An attacker who can passively observe device traffic learns the entire backend architecture without active probing — cloud-provider endpoints, push-notification dependencies, captive-portal probe destinations and SaaS services in use.
remediation_brief: Implement DNS-over-HTTPS (RFC 8484) or DNS-over-TLS (RFC 7858) on the device.

title: Information Disclosure: Device Identity Leaked in TLS Client Certificate (mTLS)
description: The device authenticates with a client X.509 certificate (mTLS). The certificate subject is sent in cleartext during the handshake and exposes identifying information (serial, model, vendor PKI topology).
impact: Passive observers can extract the device's identity from the TLS handshake bytes without decrypting any application data. Privacy-relevant in clinical contexts where the presence of a particular medical device indicates the patient population being served.
remediation_brief: Use opaque per-device identifier (UUID) as the Subject CN. Move human-readable serial / model into a custom certificate extension or SubjectAltName otherName.

title: SSL/TLS Ciphers: TLS ClientHello Offers Legacy CBC Cipher Suites
description: The device's TLS ClientHello offers legacy CBC-mode cipher suites alongside modern AEAD ciphers. While AEAD is typically negotiated, the CBC offer preserves a downgrade surface.
impact: CBC suites are vulnerable to historical attacks (BEAST, Lucky13, POODLE-variants) when paired with TLS 1.0/1.1. In TLS 1.2 with correct implementation the practical exploit cost is high but the offer is unnecessary given AEAD alternatives are universally supported by every modern endpoint.
remediation_brief: Remove CBC cipher suites from the device's TLS ClientHello offer list. Keep only AEAD: TLS 1.3 (0x1301/02/03) and TLS 1.2 ECDHE-AEAD (0xc02c/2b/30/2f).

title: Information Disclosure: DHCP Hostname Discloses Asset Identifier
description: The device populates DHCP option 12 (Host Name) with an asset identifier (serial number, device tag) that is broadcast on every DHCP DISCOVER/REQUEST.
impact: Any host on the broadcast domain can passively map the device's MAC and IP to the broadcast asset tag — vendor, model and serial are derivable without sending a single packet. Combined with mDNS reflection this is reflected across L3 boundaries.
remediation_brief: Replace DHCP Host Name with an opaque per-device identifier (UUID or salted hash). The true serial should only travel inside the encrypted device-to-cloud channel.

title: Traffic Analysis: DNS Search-Suffix Appended to Fully-Qualified Hostnames
description: The device's DNS client appends the DHCP-supplied search domain to hostnames that are already fully-qualified. RFC 1535 and RFC 8767 require resolvers not to apply search-suffix processing to FQDNs.
impact: An attacker controlling the search-suffix DNS zone can redirect the device's cloud traffic to attacker-controlled IPs. TLS server certificate validation usually catches the substitution, but the failure mode leaks connection metadata on every retry. If cert pinning is incorrectly implemented, the substitution succeeds.
remediation_brief: Patch device DNS client so hostnames with three or more labels (or trailing dot) bypass search-domain processing. Set 'ndots' threshold to 1.

title: SMB Vulnerability: SMBv1 Traffic Observed (EternalBlue / NotPetya exposure)
description: SMBv1 protocol traffic observed between the device and one or more internal peers. SMBv1 is deprecated since 2014 and is the transport for EternalBlue (MS17-010) / WannaCry / NotPetya.
impact: Active SMBv1 on a clinical network creates a worm propagation path. Disable per FDA Postmarket Cybersecurity Guidance and Joint Commission EHR-protection expectations.
remediation_brief: Disable SMBv1 on every host. Confirm SMB2+ minimum on file servers. Block 445/tcp at segmentation boundary.

title: Network Misconfiguration: LLMNR / NBT-NS Name Resolution in Use (Responder Surface)
description: LLMNR or NetBIOS Name Service broadcast-based name resolution is in use on the segment. These protocols are abused by Responder / Inveigh to poison name resolution and capture NTLMv2 hashes.
impact: An attacker on the same broadcast domain runs `responder -I eth0` and captures hashes from any device that mistypes a hostname or uses a non-FQDN lookup. Hashes are crackable offline or relayed via ntlmrelayx for immediate authentication elsewhere (CVE-2019-1040 mitigations notwithstanding).
remediation_brief: Disable LLMNR (GPO: Turn Off Multicast Name Resolution = Enabled) and NBT-NS (Network adapter → WINS → Disable NetBIOS over TCP/IP). Block UDP/5355 and UDP/137 at every L3 boundary.

title: Network Misconfiguration: SSDP / UPnP Broadcasts Expose Internal Services
description: SSDP/UPnP discovery traffic observed on the segment. SSDP advertises every UPnP-aware device (smart TVs, consumer routers, printers, NAS, IoT) on the local broadcast domain.
impact: SSDP discovery reveals consumer-IoT, printers, smart TVs, NAS and router admin interfaces to anyone on the LAN. In a clinical network this co-mingles consumer devices with medical equipment and facilitates lateral discovery.
remediation_brief: Disable UPnP/SSDP on clinical-network hosts where not required. Block UDP/1900 at every L3 boundary.

title: Information Disclosure: mDNS Activity Exposes Device Identity on Internal Segment
description: Device emits mDNS queries and/or responses on the local segment. mDNS exposes the device's hostname and services to any host on the multicast-reachable segment, and is reflected across L3 by mDNS-reflector-enabled gateways.
impact: Device fingerprinting and asset enumeration without active probing. Reduces the cost of targeting a specific device for theft, social-engineering, or RF replay attack.
remediation_brief: Disable mDNS on the device if not required. Audit network-side mDNS reflector config (Avahi `reflector=yes`, UniFi 'Multicast DNS') and disable cross-VLAN reflection.

title: Information Disclosure: LLDP Topology / Switch Firmware Disclosure
description: LLDP TLVs observed on the segment leak switch identity, model and firmware. Information that downstream attackers can use to select vendor-specific CVEs.
impact: An attacker passively learns the network gear vendor, model and firmware version without sending any probes. Combined with public CVE databases this is a free vulnerability-research head-start.
remediation_brief: Disable LLDP on access ports facing devices (`no lldp transmit` / `no lldp receive`). Keep LLDP only on inter-switch trunks.

title: Traffic Analysis: ARP Anomalies (Duplicate IP-to-MAC Mappings)
description: Duplicate ARP entries observed — one IP advertised by multiple MAC addresses. Possible legitimate HA pair, gratuitous ARP storm, or active ARP-spoofing / MitM.
impact: If the duplicate is a MitM attack, the attacker is intercepting traffic between the device and another host. Even when legitimate (HA failover), the unannounced duplicate breaks deterministic L2 routing and may drop packets.
remediation_brief: Investigate each duplicate. Configure DAI (Dynamic ARP Inspection) on managed switches. Bind static IP↔MAC for critical clinical-device subnets.

title: Insecure Protocol Detected: Cleartext FTP Traffic Observed (credentials in plaintext)
description: FTP control-channel traffic observed in cleartext. FTP USER/PASS commands and file contents are passively captureable by any on-path observer.
impact: Any L2 / SPAN / WiFi-sniffing attacker can capture FTP credentials and uploaded/downloaded file content. In a clinical setting this may include device firmware, calibration data, or PHI.
remediation_brief: Disable FTP. Use SFTP (SSH) or FTPS (FTP over TLS, explicit AUTH TLS). Block 21/tcp at segmentation boundary.

title: Insecure Protocol Detected: Cleartext Telnet Traffic Observed
description: Telnet traffic observed in cleartext. Telnet credentials and keystrokes are sent in plaintext and trivially captured by passive observers.
impact: Full session capture — usernames, passwords and every keystroke are recoverable from a passive sniff. Common on legacy embedded and industrial-control devices.
remediation_brief: Replace Telnet with SSH. Block 23/tcp at every L3 boundary.

title: Insecure Protocol Detected: SNMPv1/v2c Community String in Cleartext
description: SNMP community strings (passwords) observed in plaintext. Communities like 'public' / 'private' / vendor-default values grant MIB-table read access (or write if RW).
impact: SNMP community strings are passwords. An attacker capturing them can read MIB data (interface stats, ARP tables, routing tables) and with a write community can reconfigure the device.
remediation_brief: Migrate to SNMPv3 with authentication (SHA) + encryption (AES). Disable SNMPv1/v2c. Restrict SNMP source IPs at the device.

title: Authentication: HTTP Basic Authentication Observed in Cleartext
description: HTTP Basic Auth headers observed in cleartext. Authorization: Basic <base64> is one base64-decode step away from username:password.
impact: Basic Auth credentials are base64-encoded usernames+passwords. Any passive observer can decode them in one step (`base64 -d`). Often reused across many systems.
remediation_brief: Wrap the affected service in TLS (HTTPS) or replace Basic Auth with token/cookie-based scheme over TLS. Block plain HTTP on authenticated admin endpoints.

title: Traffic Analysis: LDAP Bind Observed Without TLS
description: LDAP bind request observed in cleartext. Without LDAPS or StartTLS, the bind DN and password are exposed.
impact: An attacker capturing the bind can extract the LDAP credentials. Domain-bound accounts are reusable across the AD forest and may unlock additional services (Kerberos, file shares, mail, VPN).
remediation_brief: Enforce LDAPS (TCP/636) or LDAP+StartTLS. Block plain LDAP (389/tcp) at the firewall.

title: Active Directory credentials dumped via DCSync/SAM ({count} accounts)
description: secretsdump.py extracted NTLM password hashes from the target domain controller via DCSync (replicating AD replication protocol) or direct SAM database access. These hashes allow offline cracking or immediate pass-the-hash lateral movement without knowing the plaintext password.
impact: An attacker with these hashes can impersonate any dumped account, including domain administrators, via pass-the-hash attacks. This grants full domain compromise: lateral movement to any domain-joined host, access to all domain resources, persistence via golden/silver ticket forging, and extraction of all sensitive data stored in Active Directory.

mitre_attack.name: OS Credential Dumping: Security Account Manager

remediation_brief: Restrict DCSync-capable permissions (Replicating Directory Changes) to only Domain Controllers. Enable LSA Protection (RunAsPPL). Rotate the krbtgt account password twice to invalidate golden tickets. Implement tiered administration to limit privileged account exposure.

title: Service tickets captured for Kerberoasting ({count} hash(es))
description: GetUserSPNs.py requested TGS service tickets for accounts with Service Principal Names (SPNs). The resulting TGS-REP hashes are encrypted with the service account's NTLM hash and can be cracked offline to recover plaintext passwords without generating authentication failures.
impact: An attacker who cracks these service account passwords gains access to every resource the service account can reach. Service accounts frequently have elevated privileges (database access, admin group membership, delegation rights) and their passwords are rarely rotated, making this a high-value lateral movement path.

mitre_attack.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Kerberoasting

remediation_brief: Use Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSAs) with automatically rotated 240+ character passwords. For accounts that cannot use gMSAs, enforce 30+ character random passwords and rotate them quarterly. Remove unnecessary SPNs from user accounts.

title: AS-REP roastable accounts found ({count} hash(es))
description: GetNPUsers.py identified accounts with the DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH flag set. AS-REP hashes for these accounts were captured without any authentication, and can be cracked offline to recover plaintext passwords.
impact: An attacker can obtain crackable hashes for these accounts without valid credentials — only network access to the DC is needed. Once cracked, the compromised accounts provide authenticated domain access for further enumeration, lateral movement, and privilege escalation.

mitre_attack.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: AS-REP Roasting

remediation_brief: Disable the DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH flag on all accounts. Audit accounts regularly for this flag via PowerShell: Get-ADUser -Filter {DoesNotRequirePreAuth -eq $true}. Enforce strong passwords on any account that must retain this setting.

title: SMB signing not required on {target}
description: The target host does not require SMB message signing. This makes it vulnerable to man-in-the-middle NTLM relay attacks where an attacker intercepts authentication attempts and relays them to this host.
impact: An attacker positioned on the network can relay captured NTLM authentication from any user (including administrators) to this host, gaining authenticated access without knowing credentials. Combined with LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning (captured by tools like Responder), this enables unauthenticated remote code execution on the target.

mitre_attack.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle: LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay

remediation_brief: Enable SMB signing via Group Policy: set 'Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always)' to Enabled. Apply to all domain-joined hosts. For domain controllers, this is the default and should not be changed.

title: Domain users enumerated via LDAP ({count} accounts)
description: GetADUsers.py enumerated domain user accounts via LDAP queries against the domain controller. This provides a complete inventory of Active Directory users, including their attributes, last logon times, and account status.
impact: A domain user list enables targeted attacks: password spraying against known accounts, social engineering using real names and email addresses, and identification of service accounts, dormant accounts, and privileged users for further exploitation.
remediation_brief: Restrict anonymous LDAP access. Implement LDAP signing and channel binding. Review which accounts have broad LDAP read permissions and reduce them to least privilege.

title: Domain users enumerated via SID brute-force ({count} accounts)
description: lookupsid.py brute-forced Security Identifier (SID) values to enumerate domain users and groups. This technique works even when LDAP anonymous access is restricted because it queries the LSA RPC interface.
impact: Provides an alternative user enumeration path when LDAP is locked down. The resulting user list enables password spraying and targeted social engineering. Also reveals group memberships and domain SID, useful for crafting golden/silver tickets.
remediation_brief: Restrict anonymous access to the SAM and LSA via Group Policy: 'Network access: Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares'. Configure RestrictAnonymousSAM registry key.

title: Weak password policy: minimum length {min_length} characters
description: samrdump.py retrieved the domain password policy via the SAM Remote Interface and identified weak settings: insufficient minimum password length (below 14 characters) or missing account lockout threshold (allowing unlimited brute-force attempts).
impact: A weak password policy directly enables password attacks. Without adequate length requirements, accounts are vulnerable to dictionary and brute-force attacks. Without lockout thresholds, an attacker can make unlimited login attempts without triggering account lockout or alerts.
remediation_brief: Set minimum password length to 14+ characters. Configure account lockout threshold to 5-10 attempts. Enable password complexity requirements. Consider implementing Azure AD Password Protection for banned password lists.

title: Kerberos delegation misconfiguration ({type})
description: findDelegation.py identified accounts with Kerberos delegation configured. Unconstrained delegation allows the account to impersonate any user to any service. Constrained delegation limits impersonation to specified services. Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD) can be abused for privilege escalation if write access to the attribute is granted to a compromised account.
impact: Unconstrained delegation: full domain compromise if the delegating account is compromised, since any user's TGT is cached. Constrained delegation: access to the specific target services as any user. RBCD: privilege escalation from any account with write access to msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity.

mitre_attack.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Golden Ticket

remediation_brief: Remove unconstrained delegation from all accounts except Domain Controllers. Use constrained delegation with protocol transition only where necessary. Audit RBCD configurations and restrict write access to the msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity attribute.

title: Service Principal Names enumerated ({count} SPN(s))
description: GetUserSPNs.py (list mode, no ticket request) enumerated all Service Principal Names registered in the domain. This provides an inventory of service accounts that are potential Kerberoasting targets.
impact: The SPN inventory reveals all service accounts and the services they run. Each SPN is a Kerberoasting target — an attacker can request a service ticket for any of them and attempt offline cracking. The list also reveals the infrastructure topology (SQL servers, web servers, exchange, etc.).
remediation_brief: Remove unnecessary SPNs from user accounts. Migrate service accounts to Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSAs). Enforce strong (30+ character) passwords on remaining SPN-bearing accounts.

title: Pass-the-Hash remote execution validated on {target}
description: Remote code execution was validated on the target using captured NTLM hashes via wmiexec.py, psexec.py, or smbexec.py. The tool tried wmiexec first (stealthiest — no service creation, no disk writes), falling back through psexec (creates a service binary) and smbexec (creates a batch file) if needed.
impact: An attacker with captured NTLM hashes can execute arbitrary commands on the target host as the hash owner. If the hash belongs to a local administrator or domain admin, this grants full control of the host: command execution, file access, credential dumping, persistence installation, and lateral movement to other hosts.

mitre_attack.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash

remediation_brief: Disable local administrator hash reuse via 'Deny access to this computer from the network' for the local admin account. Deploy LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution) to randomize local admin passwords. Enable Credential Guard on Windows 10+ endpoints. Implement tiered administration to limit hash exposure.

title: DCOM remote execution validated on {target}
description: dcomexec.py validated remote code execution via Distributed COM (DCOM) on the target host. DCOM execution uses the MMC20.Application or ShellWindows COM objects to spawn processes remotely, often evading detection rules that monitor SMB-based execution.
impact: An attacker can execute arbitrary commands on the target via DCOM, which operates over RPC (port 135 + high ports) rather than SMB. This lateral movement path bypasses SMB-focused detection and does not require SMB signing. Combined with captured credentials or hashes, it provides full remote control of the target.

mitre_attack.name: Remote Services: Distributed Component Object Model
Component Object Model and Distributed COM

remediation_brief: Disable remote DCOM access where not required. Restrict DCOM permissions via dcomcnfg.exe — remove non-admin users from launch and activation permissions. Block RPC high ports between workstations (firewall segmentation). Monitor Event ID 4688 for suspicious process creation via DCOM.

title: TGT obtained for {user}@{domain} from {target}
description: getTGT.py successfully obtained a Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) from the domain controller using captured credentials. The TGT was saved as a ccache file and proves the credentials are valid for Kerberos authentication against the domain.
impact: A valid TGT grants the holder authenticated access to any Kerberos-enabled service in the domain. It enables lateral movement via Kerberos (without revealing the password to remote hosts), service ticket requests for any SPN, and further exploitation of delegation relationships. The TGT is evidence of successful credential compromise.

mitre_attack.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Kerberoasting

remediation_brief: Immediately reset the compromised account's password. Review how the credential was obtained and remediate the root cause. Enable MFA for the affected account. Monitor for anomalous Kerberos ticket requests (Event ID 4768).

title: Service ticket obtained for SPN {spn} from {target}
description: getST.py successfully obtained a Kerberos service ticket (TGS) for a specific Service Principal Name. This proves the captured credentials can access the target service and the ticket can be used for authentication without re-presenting the password.
impact: A valid service ticket allows the holder to authenticate to the target service as the impersonated user. Depending on the SPN, this could grant access to databases (MSSQLSvc), web applications (HTTP), file shares (CIFS), or remote administration (HOST/WSMAN). The ticket can also be cracked offline if the service account has a weak password.

mitre_attack.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Kerberoasting

remediation_brief: Reset the compromised account's password. Rotate the target service account's password (use a gMSA if possible). Review and restrict SPN assignments. Monitor Event ID 4769 for anomalous service ticket requests.

title: Authenticated share access on {target} ({share_count} shares)
description: Authenticated SMB share enumeration via smbclient.py discovered accessible shares on the target host. This goes beyond null-session enumeration (SS3) by using valid domain credentials to enumerate shares that require authentication, including checking read/write access to administrative shares (ADMIN$, C$, IPC$).
impact: Readable non-default shares may expose sensitive data (configuration files, scripts, backup databases). Writable shares enable malware deployment and persistence. Write access to ADMIN$ or C$ proves local administrator privileges and enables remote code execution via service creation or file overwrite attacks.
remediation_brief: Remove unnecessary shares. Restrict ADMIN$ and C$ access to Domain Admins only (disable remote admin share access for non-admin accounts via registry). Apply least-privilege NTFS and share permissions. Audit share permissions regularly with PowerShell: Get-SmbShare | Get-SmbShareAccess.

title: Auto-logon credentials found in registry on {target}
description: reg.py remotely read the HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon registry key and found auto-logon credentials (DefaultUserName + DefaultPassword stored in cleartext). These credentials are stored unencrypted in the registry for automatic login purposes.
impact: Auto-logon credentials are stored in plaintext and readable by any authenticated user with remote registry access. If the auto-logon account has elevated privileges (administrator, service account), compromise of these credentials enables immediate privilege escalation and lateral movement.
remediation_brief: Remove auto-logon credentials from the registry: delete DefaultPassword from HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon. If auto-logon is required, use Autologon.exe from Sysinternals which encrypts the password with LSA secrets. Restrict remote registry access.

title: GPP cpassword found in SYSVOL on {target}
description: Group Policy Preferences XML files in SYSVOL contain encrypted passwords (cpassword attribute). The AES-256 encryption key was published by Microsoft in 2012 (MS14-025), making every cpassword trivially decryptable. The tool extracted and decrypted these credentials from Groups.xml, Services.xml, Scheduledtasks.xml, DataSources.xml, Printers.xml, and Drives.xml files.
impact: GPP passwords are typically set by administrators for local admin accounts, service accounts, or mapped drive credentials. Decrypting them instantly reveals plaintext credentials that may still be active. If the GPP-set password applies to a local administrator account across multiple machines (common pattern), a single GPP password compromise grants admin access to every affected host.
remediation_brief: Delete all GPP XML files containing cpassword from SYSVOL immediately. Install KB2962486 (MS14-025) on all domain controllers to prevent creation of new GPP passwords. Reset all passwords that were stored in GPP. Deploy LAPS for local administrator password management instead.

title: NTLM relay attack {result} against {target}
description: ntlmrelayx.py was used to validate that NTLM relay attacks are exploitable against the target host. The host does not require SMB signing, allowing intercepted NTLM authentication to be relayed and accepted without modification.
impact: An attacker positioned on the network can relay captured NTLM authentication from any user — including domain administrators — to this host. Combined with LLMNR/NBT-NS/WPAD poisoning, this enables unauthenticated remote code execution. A single relay of a privileged account can lead to full domain compromise.

mitre_attack.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle: LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay

remediation_brief: Enable SMB signing on all domain-joined hosts via Group Policy ('Digitally sign communications (always)'). Disable NTLM authentication where possible via 'Network security: Restrict NTLM' policies. Enable EPA (Extended Protection for Authentication) on all web services. Disable LLMNR and NBT-NS via GPO.

title: Valid credentials discovered via password spray ({count} account(s))
description: getTGT.py was used to perform a controlled password spray against domain accounts. One or more accounts accepted a guessed password, proving that weak or commonly-used passwords are in active use in the domain.
impact: Compromised domain credentials provide authenticated access for enumeration, lateral movement, and privilege escalation. If the sprayed account has elevated privileges (helpdesk, service account, admin), the impact escalates to potential domain compromise. Even a standard user account enables internal reconnaissance and Kerberoasting.
remediation_brief: Enforce 14+ character minimum password length via Group Policy. Deploy Azure AD Password Protection or a similar banned-password list to block common passwords. Configure account lockout (5-10 attempts, 30-minute lockout). Implement MFA for all domain accounts. Monitor Event ID 4771 for Kerberos pre-authentication failures.

title: DPAPI domain backup key extracted from {target}
description: dpapi.py backupkeys retrieved the domain DPAPI backup key from the domain controller. This key is used to encrypt DPAPI master keys for all domain users, allowing decryption of any DPAPI-protected secret on any domain-joined machine.
impact: With the DPAPI backup key, an attacker can decrypt any credential protected by Windows Data Protection API on any domain-joined machine: saved browser passwords, RDP credentials, Wi-Fi keys, EFS-encrypted files, certificate private keys, and application secrets. This is a domain-wide secret-recovery capability that persists until the backup key is rotated.

mitre_attack.name: Credentials from Password Stores: Credentials from Web Browsers

remediation_brief: Rotate the DPAPI domain backup key (requires domain functional level 2012 R2+). Restrict access to the ms-Bkrp-BackupKey attribute to Domain Controllers only. Monitor Event ID 4662 for backup key access. Limit the number of Domain Admin accounts. Consider Credential Guard on sensitive hosts.

title: AI Prompt Injection — Task Hijack via {strategy}
aliases: AI Task Abandonment via Prompt Injection
description: The AI pipeline abandoned its primary task entirely when processing a file containing an injected instruction in its metadata, text layer, or audio content. The AI's response contained only the injected canary token, confirming the model followed the adversarial instruction instead of performing its assigned function (transcription, classification, summarisation, etc.).
impact: An attacker can embed instructions in files submitted to the AI pipeline that completely override the model's intended behaviour. This enables arbitrary output manipulation — the AI can be made to produce any attacker-chosen text, leak system prompts, or return fabricated classifications. In production pipelines processing documents, images, or audio, this means an attacker controls what downstream consumers (dashboards, databases, compliance workflows) receive as AI output.
remediation_brief: Strip or sanitise all file metadata before including it in the LLM context. Enforce a fixed system prompt that explicitly forbids instruction overrides from file content. Process file content in a separate, sandboxed context from system instructions. Validate AI output against expected format/schema — flag responses containing unexpected tokens or format deviations.

title: AI Prompt Injection — Prefix Inject via {strategy}
description: The AI pipeline completed its primary task but also followed an injected instruction to prefix its output with an attacker-controlled token. The response contains both the expected task output and the injected canary, indicating the model treated the embedded instruction as authoritative alongside its system prompt.
impact: An attacker can inject arbitrary prefixes or annotations into AI pipeline output without fully disrupting the primary task. This partial injection is exploitable for output tagging attacks (injecting misleading classification labels), cache poisoning (injected prefixes propagate through cached results), and trust boundary violations (downstream systems may parse the prefix as metadata).
remediation_brief: Enforce strict output schema validation — reject responses that do not match the expected format. Implement input sanitisation to strip embedded instructions from file metadata and text layers before LLM ingestion. Use delimiter-based prompt architecture to clearly separate system instructions from user/file content.

title: AI Prompt Injection — Classify Override via {strategy}
description: The AI pipeline returned an attacker-controlled classification label instead of performing genuine content analysis. The injected instruction directed the model to output a specific category, and the model complied — either abandoning its own classification (CRITICAL) or appending the injected label alongside its real output (HIGH).
impact: An attacker can force arbitrary classification labels on submitted content, bypassing the AI's actual analysis. In document processing pipelines, this enables content to be misclassified (e.g. malware marked as benign, non-compliant documents marked as compliant, spam marked as legitimate). This directly undermines any automated decision-making that depends on the AI's classification output.
remediation_brief: Never allow file content to influence the classification decision prompt. Use a two-stage pipeline: extract content in a sandboxed context, then classify the extracted content with a separate prompt that cannot receive user-injected instructions. Validate classifications against a known-good label set.

title: AI Prompt Injection — System Probe via {strategy}
description: The AI pipeline disclosed its system prompt or internal configuration in response to an injected instruction embedded in file metadata or content. The injected payload directed the model to reveal its operating instructions, and the canary token's presence in the response confirms the model attempted to comply.
impact: System prompt leakage reveals the AI pipeline's internal logic, guardrails, classification rules, and potentially sensitive configuration details to an attacker. This information enables targeted follow-up attacks — an attacker who knows the system prompt can craft payloads specifically designed to bypass its guardrails. System prompts may also contain API keys, internal endpoint URLs, or business logic that should remain confidential.
remediation_brief: Never include sensitive credentials or internal URLs in system prompts. Implement output filtering to detect and block responses that contain system prompt fragments. Use instruction hierarchy (system > user > tool) enforcement so file content cannot override system-level instructions. Monitor for anomalous response patterns indicating prompt extraction attempts.

title: AI Prompt Injection — Authority Claim via {strategy}
description: The AI pipeline followed an injected instruction that claimed special authority (e.g. 'AUTHORIZED EVALUATOR', 'ADMIN OVERRIDE', 'SECURITY TEST IN PROGRESS'). The model treated the claimed role as legitimate and executed the embedded instruction, confirming it does not validate the provenance of instructions embedded in file content.
impact: An attacker can invoke claimed authority roles within file content to bypass AI guardrails. The model's failure to distinguish between legitimate system instructions and authority claims embedded in user-submitted content means any attacker can escalate their privilege level within the AI's decision framework by simply asserting a role. This undermines all role-based access controls in the AI pipeline.
remediation_brief: Implement strict instruction hierarchy — the model must never accept authority claims from file content. Use architectural separation: system instructions arrive through a trusted channel (API system role), while file content is clearly demarcated as untrusted user input. Train or fine-tune models to recognise and reject authority claim patterns in user content.

title: AI Prompt Injection — {category} via {strategy} (Partial Injection)
description: The AI pipeline completed its primary task but also followed the injected instruction — the canary token appeared in the response alongside legitimate task output. This indicates the model treated the embedded instruction as a secondary directive, executing it in addition to (rather than instead of) its assigned task.
impact: Partial injection is more dangerous than full hijack in production contexts because it may go undetected — the pipeline still produces plausible-looking output while also executing attacker instructions. This enables data exfiltration (canary confirms the model reads and acts on embedded content), output poisoning (injected content mixed into legitimate results), and supply chain attacks (downstream consumers receive tainted output that appears valid).
remediation_brief: Implement output schema validation that rejects responses deviating from the expected format. Strip all metadata and embedded instructions from file content before LLM ingestion. Deploy anomaly detection on AI output to flag unexpected tokens or patterns.

title: AI Prompt Injection — {category} via {strategy} (Stored Text Injection)
description: The injected payload was not detected in the immediate AI response but was found persisted in stored results at the verify URL. This indicates a stored/persistent prompt injection — the AI pipeline transcribed, classified, or processed the injected content and wrote it to a database, search index, or result store where it is now accessible to other users or downstream systems.
impact: Stored prompt injection is the AI equivalent of stored XSS. The injected payload persists in the application's data layer and may be rendered to other users, fed into downstream LLM calls (second-order injection), indexed by search engines, or used as training data. In Whisper/transcription pipelines, spoken injection payloads are faithfully transcribed and stored as text, creating a persistent attack vector that outlives the original file submission.
remediation_brief: Sanitise AI output before persisting it to any data store. Implement content security policies on stored transcriptions and classifications. Never render stored AI output as HTML without escaping. Monitor stored results for canary-pattern tokens or instruction-like content that should not appear in legitimate transcriptions.

title: AI Injection Resilient — {category} via {strategy}
description: The AI pipeline did not follow the injected instruction. The canary token was absent from both the immediate response and any stored results. The model completed its primary task without executing the embedded adversarial payload.
impact: Informational — no security impact. The pipeline demonstrated resilience against this specific injection vector, category, and delivery strategy combination. This does not guarantee resilience against other payload variants, encoding schemes, or multi-turn attacks.
remediation_brief: No remediation required. Continue monitoring for new injection techniques and re-test periodically as the AI model or pipeline is updated.

title: AI Injection Dry Run — {category} via {strategy}
description: A test file containing an injected adversarial payload was generated but not submitted to a target AI pipeline (--dry-run mode). The file is available in the test_files output directory for manual inspection or subsequent submission.
impact: Informational — no security testing was performed. The generated file can be used for manual testing, integration into CI/CD security pipelines, or submitted to AI endpoints outside of pAIn's automated workflow.
remediation_brief: No remediation required — this is an informational record of test file generation.

title: AI Prompt Injection — Task Hijack via pdf_docinfo_metadata
description: The AI pipeline abandoned its primary task when processing a PDF whose document-info metadata (Author, Subject, Keywords, Creator) contained an injected instruction. PDF metadata is commonly extracted by document processing pipelines and passed to LLMs as context.
impact: PDFs are the most common document format in enterprise AI pipelines. Document-info metadata injection succeeds silently because the injected content is invisible to the human viewer — only the pipeline's metadata extraction step sees it. This enables zero-interaction attacks where a legitimately-appearing PDF hijacks any AI pipeline that processes it.
remediation_brief: Strip all PDF metadata (Author, Subject, Keywords, Creator, Producer) before feeding document content to the LLM. Use a metadata-free text extraction pipeline that discards everything except the visible text layer.

title: AI Prompt Injection — {category} via pdf_hidden_text_layer
description: The AI pipeline processed a PDF containing a hidden text layer (white text on white background) with an injected instruction. The text is invisible to human viewers but extracted by PDF text extraction libraries (pdfplumber, pdfminer, PyMuPDF) and passed to the LLM. The model followed the hidden instruction.
impact: Hidden text layer injection is especially dangerous because the document appears completely legitimate to any human reviewer — the injected content is only visible to the machine pipeline. This enables supply-chain attacks where documents pass human approval processes before being fed to AI systems that then execute the hidden instructions.
remediation_brief: Implement text layer analysis that detects and strips hidden text (zero-contrast text, extremely small font, off-page positioned text) before LLM ingestion. Use render-then-OCR instead of direct text extraction to ensure only visible content reaches the model.

title: AI Prompt Injection — {category} via png_text_chunk_metadata
description: The AI pipeline followed an injected instruction embedded in a PNG image's tEXt/iTXt metadata chunks (Comment, Description, Author, Source fields). Image metadata is commonly extracted by vision pipelines and may be included in the LLM's context alongside OCR or vision analysis results.
impact: Image metadata injection targets vision-AI and document-processing pipelines. Since metadata is not visible in the rendered image, the attack is invisible to human reviewers. Pipelines that extract and include image metadata in LLM prompts are vulnerable to having their analysis influenced or overridden by injected instructions.
remediation_brief: Strip all image metadata (EXIF, tEXt, iTXt, XMP) before passing images to AI vision models. Process only the pixel data for vision analysis. If metadata is needed for non-AI purposes, process it in a separate context that does not feed into the LLM.

title: AI Prompt Injection — {category} via {format}_text_overlay_ocr
description: The AI pipeline followed an injected instruction rendered as visible text in an image. The text was extracted via OCR (optical character recognition) or multimodal vision analysis and passed to the LLM, which treated it as an instruction rather than image content to be described or classified.
impact: OCR/vision-based injection targets any pipeline that extracts text from images — document digitisation, receipt processing, medical imaging, ID verification, etc. Unlike metadata injection, the payload is technically visible, but in a real attack it would be placed in inconspicuous locations (small text, low contrast, marginal annotations) that human reviewers overlook.
remediation_brief: Implement content-type awareness in the LLM prompt — explicitly instruct the model that OCR-extracted text is untrusted content to be described, never instructions to be followed. Use a two-stage pipeline where OCR extraction and LLM analysis run in isolated contexts.

title: AI Prompt Injection — {category} via wav_spoken_audio_content
description: The AI pipeline followed an injected instruction delivered as synthesised speech in a WAV audio file. The speech-to-text (Whisper/ASR) component transcribed the spoken payload, and the downstream LLM treated the transcribed text as an instruction to execute rather than content to process.
impact: Spoken audio injection is the most dangerous delivery vector for transcription pipelines because it exploits the fundamental purpose of the pipeline — faithfully transcribing speech. The injected instruction arrives through the same channel as legitimate audio content, making it impossible to filter at the transport layer. In customer service, medical dictation, legal transcription, and meeting-notes pipelines, spoken injection can alter transcripts, inject false records, or hijack downstream AI processing.
remediation_brief: Implement post-transcription filtering to detect and strip instruction-like patterns from ASR output before passing to downstream LLMs. Use separate processing contexts for transcription and instruction execution. Apply anomaly detection to transcriptions that contain command-like syntax.

title: AI Prompt Injection — {category} via {format}_id3_tags
description: The AI pipeline followed an injected instruction embedded in audio file metadata (ID3 tags: Title, Artist, Album, Comment, Lyrics). Audio metadata is commonly extracted by media processing pipelines and may be included in the LLM's context alongside transcription results.
impact: Audio metadata injection targets music cataloguing, podcast processing, and media management AI pipelines. ID3 tags are standard metadata fields that many processing pipelines extract automatically. The injected payload is invisible during audio playback but present in the file's binary structure, enabling silent injection into any pipeline that reads tag data.
remediation_brief: Strip all audio metadata (ID3, Vorbis comments, MP4 tags) before including audio file context in LLM prompts. Process only the audio waveform data for transcription and discard metadata entirely.

title: AI Prompt Injection — {category} via docx_body_text_extraction
description: The AI pipeline followed an injected instruction placed in the body text of a DOCX (Word) document. The document XML body was extracted by the pipeline's document parser and passed to the LLM, which treated the injected instruction as authoritative.
impact: DOCX is a standard enterprise document format. Body text injection is the most straightforward attack vector — the payload appears as regular document content. In document review, contract analysis, compliance checking, and summarisation pipelines, an attacker can embed instructions that redirect the AI's analysis, alter its conclusions, or force specific outputs.
remediation_brief: Implement instruction boundary separation — ensure the LLM prompt clearly delineates system instructions from document content using robust delimiters. Apply content filtering to detect instruction-like patterns in extracted text before LLM ingestion.

title: AI Prompt Injection — {category} via docx_comment_text_extraction
description: The AI pipeline followed an injected instruction placed in a DOCX document's comment annotations. Document comments are a secondary content channel that some parsers (python-docx, docx2txt) extract alongside body text. The pipeline included comment text in the LLM context, and the model treated the injected instruction as authoritative.
impact: Comment-based injection targets document review and collaboration pipelines. Comments are a semi-hidden content channel — they appear in sidebars during editing but are often stripped or ignored in final renderings, making them a covert injection vector. Pipelines that extract and process all document content (including comments, headers, footers, and annotations) are vulnerable.
remediation_brief: Strip document comments, headers, footers, and annotations before feeding document content to the LLM. Only extract and process the visible body text for AI analysis.

title: AI Prompt Injection — {category} via zip_member_text_injection
description: The AI pipeline followed an injected instruction placed in text files within a ZIP archive (document.txt, data.csv, notes.md). Pipelines that automatically extract and process archive contents are vulnerable when extracted text is passed to the LLM without sanitisation.
impact: ZIP/archive injection targets document processing and data ingestion pipelines that automatically extract and process compressed archives. The injected payload is spread across multiple archive members (TXT, CSV, Markdown), maximising the chance of reaching the LLM through whichever extraction path the pipeline uses. This vector also enables payload delivery through legitimate-looking data files.
remediation_brief: Implement content scanning on all extracted archive members before LLM ingestion. Apply the same instruction-detection filtering to extracted text files as to directly uploaded documents. Limit the types of files that can be extracted and processed from archives.
